M100. A Novel Curriculum and Model to Teach
Occipital Nerve Blocks to Neurology Residents
Rebecca DiBiase, MD, MPH , Katherine Carroll, MD,
Wayne Bauknight, MD, Toni Cao, MD, Neena Cherayil,
MD. McGaw Medical Center of Northwestern University,
Chicago, IL, USA.
Background: Headache disorders are among the top 5 causes
of disability for ages 10-49 worldwide (GBD, 2019). Occipi-
tal nerve blocks (ONB) are an evidence-based, affordable
method for treating many types of headaches, yet over half of
graduating U.S. neurology residents wish they had more
training in this procedure (Jordan, et al., 2016). The use of
simulation-based procedural training is highly effective in
medical education (McGaghie, et al., 2011). A small number
of training programs in dermatology and plastic surgery have
implemented “hands-on” training in nerve blocks and botuli-
num toxin injections (Paoli et al., 2012 & Mitkov, et al.,
2018), yet there is sparse data on similar interventions for
neurology trainees.
Purpose: We will implement a novel simulation-based
curriculum including a unique task trainer of the posterior
cranium to teach neurology residents how to perform ONB.
We hypothesize that Likert comfort scores with this proce-
dure will increase after simulation completion and that ONB
performance in the neurology resident clinic will increase
with converse decline in outside referral for ONB when com-
pared to the 2 years prior to intervention.
Program Description: In September 2022, the neurology
residency program at the McGaw Medical Center of North-
western University will implement a pilot day of required
didactic-only protected time for second-year residents. This
day will include a novel ONB simulation session. Trainees
will spend approximately 1 hour completing the ONB curric-
ulum, which includes an introduction on the indications/
contraindications for the procedure followed by demonstra-
tion and supervised practice on posterior cranium/occiput
model. This task trainer, which will include lifelike cranial
landmarks, has been designed and created by the Northwest-
ern Innovations Lab speci ﬁcally for ONB simulation use.
Upon curriculum completion, trainees will receive a supple-
mentary handout with key information about the procedure
as a reference for future clinical use.
Data Analysis: Trainees will complete pre-curriculum
and post-curriculum Likert-style surveys assessing their
comfort with this procedure. We will calculate differences
in trainees ’ survey scores to evaluate curriculum success.
We will also compare institutional data to determine
whether ONB are performed more frequently after the
simulation has been implemented. Data will include the
number of referrals for headache management indications
from the neurology residency clinic to the anesthesia pain
clinic, as well as billing code frequency for resident ONB
procedures. The simulation session will be implemented in
September 2022, with preliminary results available by early
October.
M101. Bradyphagia as an Enantiopathy to Burning
Mouth Syndrome
Sunjeet Brar, B.Sc
1, Alan Hirsch, M.D. 2. 1Aureus University
School of Medicine, Oranjestad, Aruba, 2Smell and Taste
Treatment and Research Foundation, Chicago, IL, USA.
Introduction: Burning mouth syndrome (BMS), has
responded to tactile stimulation, as from rinsing with magne-
sium hydroxide suspension rinse (Hirsch, 2009) or tongue
protectors (Gurvits, 2013). Kinetic stimulation of the tongue

has also been reported to improve BMS (Schrag, 1999). Pro-
longation of tactile stimulation from chewing food through
bradyphagia to induce relief of BMS has not heretofore been
described.
Case Study: A 64-year-old right-handed male underwent a
dental procedure where his tongue was accidentally lacerated.
Progression over the next four months was this burning-like
sensation spread to involve the entire tongue, lips, gums,
throat, and palate. The burning was 24/7, 5/10 in severity.
With eating or chewing, it would resolve to 0/10. Immedi-
ately after swallowing or chewing his food, the burning
would resolve, and after forty- ﬁve minutes it would slowly
recur. He learned to prolong eating and to chew small
amounts to reduce his pain.
Results: Abnormalities on Neurological Examination:
Motor Examination: Drift testing: Left pronator drift with
left abductor digiti minimi sign. Chemosensory testing:
Olfactory testing: Brief Smell Identi ﬁcation Test:
11 (normosomia). Retronasal Olfaction: Retronasal Smell
Index: 9 (normal). Gustatory testing: Propylthioruacil Disk
Taste Test: 2 (hypogeusia).
Discussion: Possibly the natural sugar in the food may
have been suf ﬁcient to reduce the BMS pain as has been
demonstrated with sweet taste (Hirsch, 2011). Alternatively,
mastication-induced food movement would have acted to
enhance tactile stimuli. Such tactile stimulation from the
effects of masticating and madefying the food may have
reduced pain through inducing discharge of large nerve
ﬁbers, and associated inhibition of small c nerve ﬁbers
(Melzack, 1965). Alternatively, the kinesthetic action may
have induced stimulation of the Golgi tendon organs, as
well as large alpha proprioceptive ﬁbers and thus inhibition
of pain. The act of chewing alone to reduce pain, indepen-
dent of what was being masticated or if anything was being
mandibulated at all, may have been its mechanism of
action. Mastication of food-inducing, retronasal olfaction
with an increase in olfactory nerve discharge (Gruss, 2015)
may have functioned to reduce pain, as odor inhibition of
pain has been demonstrated in other painful conditions
(Hirsch, 2006). Alternatively, the food may have acted as a
distraction, refocusing his attention away from the BMS
pain and onto the sensation of food. A trial of food or food
substitute, for instance, chewing gum, in treatment of burn-
ing mouth syndrome, may be revealing.

M102. Change in Migraine Diagnosis After Preventive
Treatment with Eptinezumab: Post Hoc Analysis of the
PROMISE Studies
Roger Cady, M.D. FAHS
1, Patricia Pozo-Rosich, MD, PhD 2,
David Dodick, MD, FAAN 3, Anders Ettrup, PhD 4, Joe
Hirman, PhD 5, Divya Asher, PA-C, MSHS 6. 1RK Consults,
Ozark, MO, USA, 2Headache Unit and Research Group, Vall
d’Hebron University Hospital and Research Institute &
Universitat Autonoma de Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain, 3Mayo
Clinic, Scottsdale, AZ, USA, 4H. Lundbeck A/S, Copenhagen,
Denmark, 5Paciﬁc Northwest Statistical Consulting, Inc,
Woodinville, WA, USA, 6Lundbeck LLC, Deer ﬁeld, IL, USA.
Objective: To identify proportions of patients shifting from
higher levels of headache frequency to lower levels over
Months 1-6 of treatment in the PROMISE studies.
Background: In the phase 3 randomized, double-blind,
placebo-controlled PROMISE studies, eptinezumab adminis-
tered every 12 weeks signi ﬁcantly reduced migraine fre-
quency, with onset of preventive ef ﬁcacy demonstrated on
Day 1 after dosing.
Methods: Data from patients in the PROMISE studies
who received approved eptinezumab doses (100mg or
300mg) or placebo were included. Headache frequency was
categorized into 4 groups: chronic migraine (CM;
≥15 monthly headache days [MHDs]), high-frequency epi-
sodic migraine (HFEM; 10-14 MHDs), low-frequency epi-
sodic migraine (LFEM; 4-9 MHDs), and very-low-frequency
episodic migraine (VLFEM; ≤3 MHDs). Outcomes included
the percentage of patients within each MHD group and the
percentage of patients improving by ≥1 diagnostic category.
Results: At PROMISE-1 baseline, most patients were clas-
siﬁed as HFEM (100mg, 46.2% [102/221]; 300mg, 48.2%
[107/222]; placebo, 51.4% [114/222]) or LFEM (100mg,
46.6% [103/221]; 300mg, 42.8% [95/222]; placebo, 42.3%
[94/222]). During Month 1, 28.1% (62/221), 33.8%
(75/222), and 20.3% (45/222) of patients in the
eptinezumab 100mg, 300mg, and placebo groups, respec-
tively, were classi ﬁed as VLFEM, increasing to 43.9%
(97/221), 48.6% (108/222), and 37.8% (84/222) at Month
6. In total, 35.7% (100mg, 79/221), 37.4% (300mg,
83/222), and 30.6% (placebo, 68/222) of patients had
6 months with reduction of ≥1 diagnostic category. At
PROMISE-2 baseline, all patients treated with eptinezumab
100mg (356/356) and placebo (366/366) groups experienced
≥15 MHDs, as did 99.4% (348/350) of patients who
received eptinezumab 300mg. During Month 1, the percent-
age of patients classi ﬁed as CM decreased to 41.3%
(147/356), 38.3% (134/350), and 54.4% (199/366) in the
eptinezumab 100mg, 300mg, and placebo groups, respec-
tively, further decreasing to 32.6% (116/356), 28.9%
(101/350), and 39.6% (145/366) at Month 6. In total,
43.0% (100mg, 153/356), 48.3% (300mg, 169/350), and
31.7% (placebo, 116/366) of patients had 6 months with
reduction of ≥1 diagnostic category. In both studies, the
reductions in MHDs were paralleled with the reductions
in MMDs.
Conclusions: Patients treated with eptinezumab reported
more frequent downward shifts in diagnostic frequency
category over the ﬁrst month and throughout 6 months of
treatment than placebo. The sustained (6-month) shifts in
diagnostic frequency category suggest a change in diagnostic
classiﬁcation for the current and active headache diagnosis
would be warranted in 43-48% of eptinezumab-treated
patients with CM.
M103. Functional Abnormalities in Pain Processing in
Migraineurs: A Coordinate-Based Meta-Analysis of
Neuroimaging Studies
Yaman Ahmed, MD

1, Ayah Al-Bzour, MD 1, Ghayda’a Al-
Majali, MD1, Saja Alzghoul, MD 1, Ruaa Ibrahim, MD 1, Anas
Al-Khalili, MD 1, Ammar Hamza, MD 1, Ramaz Al-Mannai,
MD1, Ahmed Yassin, MD, PhD 2, Alexandra Lef ﬂer, MD,
PhD3, Kefah Al-Hayek, MD, PhD 2, Khalid El-Salem, MD,
PhD2, Majdi Al Qawasmeh, MD, PhD 2. 1Faculty of Medicine,
Jordan University of Science and Technology, Irbid, Jordan,
2Department of Neurosciences, Jordan University of Science and
Technology, Irbid, Jordan, 3SRH Klinikum Naumburg,
Naumburg, Germany.
Background: Neuroimaging studies on migraine patients
have shown structural and functional abnormalities associated
with gray matter volume and sensitization of the trigemi-
novascular pathway. Noxious stimuli have been used to
explore pain processing and perception in migraineurs during
functional MRI. Thus, we aim to investigate and meta-
analyze brain regions of activation and deactivation associated
with pain processing in response to noxious stimuli in
migraineurs compared to healthy controls across studies.
Methods: PubMed database was systematically searched
for functional magnetic resonance (fMRI) studies on
migraine patients and healthy controls who underwent pain
stimulation tasks and reported coordinates in MNI or
Talairach stereotactic space. Title and abstract screening was
done for 1080 studies, and 17 studies were eligible after the
full-text screening. The activation likelihood estimation
(ALE) meta-analysis was done using GingerALE from
brainmap.org with threshold settings of P-value < 0.001
uncorrected for multiple comparisons and a minimum cluster
size of 250 mm
3.
Results: Hundred and eleven foci from 30 experiments
comprising 395 Migraine patients and 339 Healthy controls
were included in the ALE meta-analysis. Migraine patients
showed decreased activation in the left brainstem (Substania
Nigra) [Peak Talairach coordinates x,y,z= -9, -26, -13, Clus-
ter size=1087 mm
3] and the anterior lobe of the right cere-
bellum [Peak Talairach coordinates x,y,z= 9, -25, -16, Cluster
size=448 mm3] in comparison to healthy controls. While
migraine patients showed increased activation in the right
brainstem (Subthalamic Nucleus) [Peak Talairach coordinates
x,y,z= 10, -12, -7, Cluster size=168 mm
3] relative to healthy
controls during pain stimulation tasks.
Conclusion: Decreased activation in the brainstem and
cerebellum in migraine patients observed in our study corre-
sponds to a dysfunction in the antinociceptive network in
migraineurs in response to noxious stimuli. This may also be
associated with structural alterations of gray matter volume
and attacks occurrence and severity in migraine patients.

M104. HaNDL: A Migrainous Headache That Should
Not Be Mis-Handled
Sathvik S. Shastry, BS , Cleo Reyes, MD, Erafat Rehim, MD,
Kathryn E. Cheponis, MD. Lehigh Valley Health Network,
Allentown, PA, USA.
Background: Approximately 1-in-6 Americans suffer from
migraine. The diagnosis of migraine can be challenging due
to a spectrum of presentation and requires careful examina-
tion to evaluate for other etiologies. Here we describe a case
of young man with transient headache and neurologic de ﬁcits
with cerebrospinal ﬂuid lymphocytosis (HaNDL), a diagnosis
of exclusion.
Case Presentation: A 32-year-old right-handed man with
a history of migraine presented with transient left-sided weak-
ness and sensory changes, followed by a severe right-sided
headache. He reported having similar headaches before, but
never any accompanied neurologic symptoms. He was admit-
ted for headache management. MRI and MRA of the brain
were unremarkable and he was discharged once symptoms
resolved. Two days later, he presented as a stroke alert with
sudden onset global aphasia. CT Head did not show any
hemorrhage and patient received thrombolytic agent as he
presented within therapy window. MRI brain with and with-
out contrast was unremarkable. EEG showed left-sided focal
slowing without epileptiform discharges or seizures. Cerebro-
spinal ﬂuid (CSF) studies revealed elevated protein 74 mg/dL,
leukocytosis 390/cmm, lymphocyte predominant (84%).
Meningitis and encephalitis panel, as well as autoimmune
encephalitis panel were negative. The patient ’s history of epi-
sodic headache associated with focal neurological de ﬁcits,
alongside CSF ﬁndings of lymphocytic pleocytosis in the
absence of other objective ﬁndings, is highly consistent with
HaNDL syndrome. Laboratory investigations for hemiplegic
migraine (CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A and PRRT2) are
currently pending. His symptoms resolved within 24 hours
and was discharged with scheduled follow-up.
Discussion: HaNDL syndrome is a rare disease that is
likely underreported or misdiagnosed. Often, when patients
present with headache and transient focal neurological de ﬁ-
cits, they are diagnosed with complicated migraines. CSF
studies are rarely pursued in this population. Lymphocytic
pleocytosis is suggestive of HaNDL syndrome rather than
migraine. This argument is further strengthened in patients
with no family history of migraine, separating HaNDL from
autosomal-dominant migraine syndromes. Recognition of
this disease entity is imperative to avoid unnecessary, costly,
and even harmful laboratory/imaging investigation and thera-
pies. HaNDL has a good prognosis, usually monophasic
course, and many patients recover completely.

change in MIDAS from pre- to post-treatment (B = -11.4,

-10.5, 95% CI = -20..6, -0.4). Reductions in headache day-
s/30 days were not signi ﬁcant from pre- to post-treatment
(B = -0.9, 95% CI = -2.5, 0.6) but more than doubled by
6-month follow-up and were signi ﬁcantly different from pre-
treatment (B = -2.2, 95% CI = -2.2, 95% CI = -4.0, -0.3).
Similarly, small reductions in attack pain intensity pre- to
post-treatment (B = -0.4, 95% CI = -0.8, -0.02) increased in
magnitude at follow-up (B = -0.7, 95% CI = -1.2, -0.2).
Conclusions: Eight weeks of MBCT-M maintains reduc-
tions in migraine disability for six months following treat-
ment completion, suggesting this brief treatment can produce
lasting effects. Reductions in attack frequency emerged, and
attack pain intensity increased in magnitude, at the 6-month
follow-up, suggesting that mindfulness practice may confer
greater bene ﬁt over the long- vs. short-term.

Objective: To determine a threshold number of monthly
headache days (MHDs) that clinicians can use as a therapeu-
tic goal for patients with chronic migraine (CM).
Background: Current therapeutic goals for migraine
treatment include ≥50% or ≥75% reduction in monthly
migraine days (ie, responder rates). MHDs may be a more
straightforward assessment tool for treatment of patients
with CM.
Methods: In PROMISE-2 (NCT02974153), a random-
ized, double-blind study evaluating eptinezumab for the pre-
ventive treatment of CM, patients (N=1072) received
eptinezumab 100mg, 300mg, or placebo on Day 0 and Week
12; all arms were pooled for analysis. Available data for
6-item Headache Impact Test (HIT-6) total score, Patient
Global Impression of Change (PGIC), and days of acute
medication use were combined for Weeks 4, 12, 16, and
24 and analyzed by number of MHDs ( ≤4, 5-9, 10-15, >15)
during the 4 weeks preceding the respective assessment.
Patient-months correspond to 4-week study intervals.
Results: Of patient-months with ≤4 MHDs, 67.6%
(561/830) were associated with “little to none ” or “some”
HIT-6 impairment, vs 47.6% (447/940), 29.9% (240/803),
and 13.9% (210/1507) of patient-months with 5-9, 10-15,
and >15 MHDs, respectively. Of patient-months with ≤4
MHDs, 85.8% (1079/1258) were associated with “very
much” or “much” improved PGIC, vs 69.9% (989/1415),
49.6% (607/1224), and 21.5% (480/2229) of patient-
months with 5-9, 10-15, and >15 MHDs, respectively.
Patient-months with ≤4, 5-9, 10-15, and >15 MHDs used
acute medication for ≥10 days on 1.9% (21/1111), 5.0%
(63/1267), 49.6% (670/1351), and 74.1% (1232/1662) of
patient-months, respectively.
Conclusions: In this post hoc analysis, patients improving
to ≤4 MHDs achieved superior outcomes with the least acute
medication use, suggesting that 4 MHDs may be a useful
treatment goal for patients with CM.
M108. Safety and Ef ﬁcacy of Fremanezumab for Migraine
Prevention over 6 Months: Pooled Analysis of the Phase
3 FOCUS and HALO Studies

1, Verena Ramirez Campos, MD 2,

Yoel Kessler, MD 3, Beryl Ojwang, MD 4, Stephanie Nahas,

Introduction: Fremanezumab is a humanized monoclonal
antibody targeting calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)
that is approved for migraine prevention in adults. This
pooled analysis used data from the phase 3 HALO and
FOCUS studies to evaluate the 6-month safety and ef ﬁcacy
of quarterly fremanezumab and monthly fremanezumab.
Methods: In the 3-month HALO episodic migraine
(EM) and chronic migraine (CM) studies and FOCUS
double-blind period (DBP), participants were randomized
1:1:1 to quarterly fremanezumab, monthly fremanezumab, or
placebo. In the HALO long-term study (LTS), participants
who received quarterly or monthly fremanezumab in the

HALO EM/CM studies continued those dosing regimens,
and those who received placebo were randomized 1:1 to
quarterly or monthly fremanezumab for 12 months. Partici-
pants from the FOCUS DBP continued or switched to
monthly fremanezumab during the 3-month open-label
extension period (OLE). The ﬁrst 6 months of data were
pooled for participants rolling over from HALO EM/CM to
HALO LTS and for participants who completed the FOCUS
DBP and entered the OLE. All participants received
fremanezumab during the second 3-month period in this
pooled 6-month analysis; participants initially randomized to
placebo ﬁrst received 3 months of placebo, then 3 months of
fremanezumab (quarterly or monthly).
Results: Overall, this analysis includes 2373 participants.
Ongoing reductions in monthly migraine days (MMD) were
observed over 6 months of treatment, with reductions from
baseline of -5.6 for patients receiving quarterly fremanezumab
and -5.9 for patients receiving monthly fremanezumab at
6 months. The proportion of participants with ≥50% reduc-
tion in MMD from baseline was 49% for patients receiving
quarterly fremanezumab and 50% for patients receiving
monthly fremanezumab at 6 months. Rates of serious adverse
events (AEs) with fremanezumab treatment were low during
the ﬁrst 3-month period (quarterly fremanezumab, 0.5%
[4/796]; monthly fremanezumab, 1.1%[9/787]) and second
3-month period (quarterly fremanezumab, 1.0%[8/788];
monthly fremanezumab, 1.9%[30/1595]), as were rates of
AEs leading to discontinuation ( ﬁrst 3-month period, 0% for
both dosing regimens; second 3-month period, quarterly
fremanezumab, 1.5%[15/788]; monthly fremanezumab,
1.4%[22/1595]). No individual serious AE was reported by
more than 1 patient, with the exception of uterine
leiomyoma (reported by 2 patients in the placebo group dur-
ing the ﬁrst 3-month period).
Conclusions: Over 6 months of treatment, quarterly and
monthly fremanezumab dosing regimens were safe and well-
tolerated in participants with migraine and were associated
with ongoing reductions in MMD.

Introduction: The prevalence, severity, and burden of
migraine differ by geographic region and across different
racial and ethnic groups. Fremanezumab, a humanized
monoclonal antibody that selectively targets calcitonin gene-
related peptide (CGRP), has proven ef ﬁcacy for migraine pre-
vention in adults. These pooled analyses evaluated the safety
and efﬁcacy of fremanezumab in racial and ethnic subgroups.
Methods: Data from 3 clinical trials (HALO episodic
migraine [EM], HALO chronic migraine [CM], and FOCUS
[EM/CM] with inadequate response to 2-4 prior preventive
classes), in which patients were randomized to 12 weeks of
double-blind treatment with quarterly fremanezumab,
monthly fremanezumab, or matched placebo, were pooled
for these analyses. Changes from baseline in monthly
migraine days (MMD), proportion of patients with 50% or
greater reduction in MMD from baseline, and adverse events
(AEs) were assessed based on patients ’ racial/ethnic groups.
Results: This pooled population included 2,842 patients.
Quarterly and monthly fremanezumab provided reductions
in MMD from baseline during 12 weeks vs placebo across
White and Non-white racial/ethnic groups (White, −4.6 and
−4.8 vs −2.4, P<0.0001; Non-white, −4.8 and −4.5 vs
−3.3, P<0.05 [Black/African American, −4.5 and −3.6 vs
−3.9; Asian, −3.3 and −3.6 vs −0.9, P<0.05; Other, −4.6
and −5.7 vs −2.7]). Increases in the proportion of patients
with 50% or greater reduction in MMD versus placebo were
also observed. In the quarterly fremanezumab, monthly
fremanezumab, and placebo groups, respectively, ≥1 AE was
reported by 64%, 62%, and 59% of White patients and
66%, 61%, and 53% of Non-white patients (Black/African
American patients, 60%, 58%, and 54%; Asian patients,
64%, 62%, and 44%; Other, 85%, 68%, and 81%).
Conclusions: Treatment with fremanezumab was safe
and effective, based on reductions in MMD and increases
in ≥50% response rates versus placebo, across White and
Non-white racial/ethnic groups, including the Asian
subgroup.
M110. Short-Term Resolution of Visual Snow Symptoms
with Occipital and Trigeminal Nerve Blocks in a Patient
with Spontaneous Intracranial Hypotension Headache
Preeta Gupta, MD
1, Rachel Sehgal, MD 1, Larry Charleston,
IV, MD, MSc, FAHS 2. 1University of Michigan, Ann Arbor,
MI, USA, 2Michigan State University College of Human
Medicine, East Lansing, MI, USA.
Background: Visual snow syndrome (VSS) is a distinct neu-
rologic condition with the hallmark feature of static tiny dots
over the entire visual ﬁeld. Static black and white dots are
most common. Classic accompanying features in the diagnos-
tic criteria of VSS include palinopsia, enhanced entopic phe-
nomena, photophobia, and nyctalopia.
Case Report: A 34-year-old man with a history of hyper-
tension, concussions, and myofascial pain presented with
headache and visual symptoms of constant black and white
static and occasional blue/green dots consistent with VSS for
one year. He developed the onset of a new chronic daily
headache a year prior to presentation with the onset of his
visual symptoms. Headache symptoms were consistent with
spontaneous intracranial hypotension headache (SIHH).
Position change of standing up also worsened severity of

visual snow symptoms. Amitriptyline, combination caffeine-
acetaminophen-butalbital, losartan, metoprolol, gabapentin,
magnesium supplement, as well as 1 blood patch were inef-
fective for both headache and VSS. He declined additional
blood patches. An abdominal binder was trialed for six
months with mild but limited improvement in headache with
unchanged VSS. He received occipital and trigeminal (supra-
orbital, supratrochlear, auriculotemporal) peripheral nerve
blocks with 1:1 2% lidocaine and 0.5% ropivicaine with
immediate reduction in his reported headache severity and
complete resolution of VSS symptoms. This resolution in
VSS lasted for a period of 3-5 days immediately after each
nerve block treatment with reduction in visual symptoms in
between blocks. He continued to receive a total of ﬁve ses-
sions of occipital and trigeminal nerve block injections over
the course of one year at which point his headaches became
refractory to nerve block injections. Unfortunately, his visual
snow symptoms have persisted since the cessation of periph-
eral nerve blocks.
Discussion: VSS is a distinct benign neurological condi-
tion that is dif ﬁcult to treat. This case highlights the potential
role of peripheral nerve blocks in VSS as a treatment option,
at least in the short term. Although VSS and migraine with
aura are comorbid and there may be some overlap, this case
also demonstrates a possible association of VSS in patients
with SIHH. Conclusion: Our case highlights peripheral nerve
block injections as a possible therapeutic option for symp-
toms of VSS. Our case demonstrates that VSS may be an
associated manifestation of SIHH syndrome. Further research
on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, and treatment of VSS
is warranted.

K-M100. A Narrative Review of Psychological
Interventions for Migraine: Best Practices and Future
Directions
John A. Sturgeon, PhD . University of Michigan, Ann Arbor,
MI, USA.
Migraine is among the most common medical conditions in
the United States and contributes to substantial work loss,
economic burden, and psychosocial disability. Best practices
in migraine management highli ght the importance of a mul-
tidisciplinary approach consisting of both pharmacological
and non-pharmacological interventions. Among non-
pharmacological interventions, psychological interventions
are an important component to address cognitive, behav-
ioral, and affective reactions to migraine, which can com-
pound migraine-related pain, distress, and disability. The
current project provides a narrative overview of current
best-practice psychological interventions for migraine,
including relaxation therapy, biofeedback, and cognitive
behavioral therapy. We will also review a second set of
interventions for which there is a promising but relatively
smaller base of evidence, including mindfulness-based thera-
pies, acceptance and commitment therapy, and approaches
emphasizing behavioral management of triggers
(e.g., Learning to Cope with Triggers; Martin et al., 2014,
Behaviour Research and Therapy ). Finally, we will discuss
future directions in psychological interventions for migraine,
including novel therapeutic approaches, considerations for
brief and telehealth-based treatment, and considerations for
patients with chronic overlapping pain conditions and psy-
chological comorbidities.

and diagnose patients. The ICHD is based on expert opin-

not included in the ICHD-3, largely due to lack of signi ﬁ-

determine if there were underlying symptom clusters.

inclusion/exclusion criteria were purposefully broad to cap-
ture the fullest range of headache characteristics. The cohort
was likely biased more towards more severe headaches lead-
ing them to seek care. The cohort included 6,662 partici-

K-M102. Sex and Hormonal Differences in Optogenetic
Cortical Spreading Depression Induced Trigeminal Pain
Behavior
Andrea M. Harriott, MD PhD , Andreia Morais, PhD, Cenk
Ayata, MD PhD. Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston,
MA, USA.
Introduction: Cortical spreading depression (SD) is the
underlying cause of migraine aura. Migraine is more preva-
lent in females, raising the possibility that sex and gonadal
hormones play major roles in disease mechanism. We
recently demonstrated that minimally invasive optogenetic
SD (opto-SD) elicits robust trigeminal allodynia. The objec-
tive of this study is to test the hypothesis that SD-induced
migraine-like behavior is dependent on sex and gonadal hor-
mones using the opto-SD mouse model.
Methods: Opto-SD was induced in adult Thy1-
ChR2-YFP transgenic mice under brief iso ﬂurane anesthesia
with 470nM 10mW light for 10sec, con ﬁrmed with optical
intrinsic signal difference imaging or laser doppler
ﬂowmetry (LDF). The effect of sex on pain behavior was
examined in single or repeat ed opto-SD, and sham groups.
Vaginal smears were collected for estrus cycle staging. Peri-
orbital mechanical allodynia was assessed with von Frey
monoﬁlaments. Mouse grimace scale, a measure of sponta-
neous discomfort, was examined at room light (75 lux) and
increasing light intensity (range 400 - 8350 lux) to investi-
gate photophobia-like behavior. Data are presented as mean
/C6SEM.
Results: There was a trend towards lower periorbital
mechanical thresholds in females (F=3.703, p=0.0653 for
sex, two-way ANOVA). Regressi on analysis revealed a sig-
niﬁcant effect of SD (p<0.0001), repeated SD (p=0.007),
and sex (p=0.0126) on periorbital allodynia, and a signi ﬁ-
cant interaction between sex and recovery time
(p=0.0223). In a subset of mice, there were no apparent
sex differences in SD threshold [male (n=3) = 7.0 /C64mW,
female (n=6) = 7.2 /C63mW], % reduction in blood ﬂow
(male = 44.2 /C611%, female = 39.9 /C69%), latency
(male = 67.8 /C610s, female = 60.3 /C69s), or SD duration
(male = 257.7 /C638s, female = 229.6 /C625s). Metestrus-
diestrus sham females had higher periorbital thresholds
[MD, single sham (n=5): 0.34 /C60.07g, repeated sham
(n=4): 0.30 /C60.07g] compared with proestrus-estrus
shams [PE, single sham (n=6): 0.16 /C60.03g, repeated
sham (n=8): 0.13 /C60.01g]. SD produced allodynia during
MD [single SD (n=3): 0.080 /C60.02g, repeated SD (n=6):
0.063 /C60.01g] and PE stages [single SD (n=8): 0.058
/C60.01g, repeated SD (n=8): 0.054 /C60.01g]. There was a
trend towards higher grimace scores at room light and
bright light exposure in SD compared with sham groups
that did not differ by estrus stage.
Conclusions: Sex and gonadal hormones likely play a
mechanistic role in SD-induced trigeminal pain suggesting
sex-dependent activation of migraine-relevant neurolimbic
pain.

Heterogeneity of Cognitive Decline Rate in the Normal
Aging-Early Alzheimer ’s Disease Continuum

1, Yiding Zhang, MS 1, Rebecca A. Betensky,
PhD2, Bradley T. Hyman, MD PhD 3, Alberto Serrano-Pozo,

2New York University, New York City, NY, USA,
3Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA.
Objectives: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is increasingly recognized

as a heterogeneous clinico-pathological construct with fre-
quently disparate syndromic presentations, clinical progression
rates, and severity of AD neuropathological changes (ADNC)
and comorbid pathologies. This heterogeneity is a major obsta-
cle for the success of clinical trials pursuing a disease-modifying
effect. Here we tested the hypothesis that the APOE alleles dif-
ferentially impact the rate of cognitive decline independently
of their effects on ADNC and concurrent pathologies at the
earliest stages of the normal aging-AD continuum.
Methods: We analyzed the cognitive trajectories (CDR-
SOB and MMSE) of a national clinico-pathological sample
with either no, mild (i.e., sparse neuritic plaques and Braak
NFT stage I/II), or intermediate (i.e., moderate neuritic
plaques and Braak NFT stage III/IV) ADNC levels at autopsy
via 2-latent classes reverse-time longitudinal modeling.
Results: Carrying the APOEε4 allele was associated with a
faster rate of cognitive decline by both CDR-SOB and
MMSE relative to APOEε3 homozygosis. This association
remained statistically signi ﬁcant after adjusting for ADNC
severity and for comorbid pathologies and the effects of
ADNC on the slope of cognitive decline. Noteworthy, while
the differences between APOEε4 carriers and APOEε3 homo-
zygotes were statistically signi ﬁcant within the two latent clas-
ses, these differed markedly in the slope, with latent class
1 members representing slow decliners (CDR-SOB: 76.7%
of individuals, 0.195 vs. 0.146 points/year in APOEε4
vs. APOEε3/ε3; MMSE: 88.6% of individuals, -0.304 vs.
-0.154 points/year in APOEε4 vs. APOEε3/ε3), whereas
latent class 2 members were fast decliners (CDR-SOB:
23.3% of subjects, 1.536 vs. 1.487 points/year in APOEε4
vs. APOEε3/ε3; MMSE: 11.4% of subjects, -2.539 vs.
-2.388 points/year in APOEε4 vs. APOEε3/ε3). By contrast,
APOEε2 carriers did not signi ﬁcantly differ from APOEε3
homozygotes. Compared to slow decliners, fast decliners were
not only more likely to carry the APOEε4 allele but also
younger at initial visit and death, more impaired at initial
and last visits, and more likely to have intermediate (vs. none
or mild) ADNC levels as well as concurrent Lewy bodies and
hippocampal sclerosis at autopsy.
Conclusions: In a sample selected to represent the normal
aging-early AD continuum, the APOEε4 allele is associated
with a modest but statistically signi ﬁcant acceleration of the
cognitive decline rate even after controlling for its effects on
ADNC and comorbid pathologies. These ﬁndings have
important implications for clinical trial design and
interpretation.

S101. A Cluster of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease in Spain
Marina Martinez Sanchez, Medicine , Maria del Carmen
Perez Vieitez, Medicine, Maria Dolores Mendoza Grimon,
Medicine, Severino Junior Soaeres Almeida, Medicine, Jesus De
La Nuez Gonzalez, Medicine, Alicia Lopez Santana, Medicine,
Francisco Javier Pareja Herrero, Medicine, Pablo Costa Saez,
Medicine. Hospital Universitario de Gran Canaria Dr Negrin,
Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Spain.
Background: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is a neurodegen-
erative disorder caused by an abnormal isoform of a cellular gly-
coprotein known as the prion protein. CJD occurs worldwide
and the estimated annual incidence in many countries, includ-
ing Spain, has been reported to be about one case per million
population. There are three major categories of CJD: sporadic
CJD, hereditary CJD and acquired CJD. On a few occasions,
however, sporadic CJD occurred with higher than expected
rates, but further investigation has failed to recognize any con-
vincing causal link. In Spain no cluster of sporadic CJD has
been notiﬁed previously.
Objective: This study aimed to conduct a retrospective
revision and analysis of the clinical and epidemiological char-
acteristics of patients with CJD in a Spanish cohort, from the
Northern region of Gran Canaria. The secondary objective
was to investigate the geographical distribution of sporadic
CJD using municipality geographical data of North Gran
Canaria with the aim of detecting spatial clusters of disease.
Patients and Methods: Patients included in this study were
Gran Canaria’s residents. The patients were diagnosed as proba-
ble or de ﬁnite CJD in Dr Negrín University Hospital and San
Roque University Hospital between 1997 and 2021. The analy-
sis was performed using Software for the spatial, temporal, and
space-time scan statics (SatScan) assuming that patients arrive as
a Poisson process with constant rate. A P value and a 95% con-
ﬁdence interval were obtained through Monte Carlo tests.
Results: In the period from 1997 to 2021, 12 patients
have been reported with CJD, all sporadic cases. Six patients
were female. The mean age at death was 73 years (range
62-87). In fact, six of the twelve cases were in the period
from 2017 to 2018. The spatial and temporal analyses con-
ﬁrmed a cluster of 4 cases in that year in Las Palmas de Gran
Canaria within a 0.63 km radius from a population of
16220. The detected annual incidence of cases was 22.7 per
100 000. The relative risk was 216.85 (p = 0.014).
Discussion: A temporal-spatial clustering of CJD sporadic
cases was reported in the Canary Islands between 2017 and
2018, without environmental causes having been identi ﬁed.
There is an ongoing epidemiological study of the authors
aiming to detect the risk factors involved. Since 2019 there
has been a signi ﬁcant reduction in the number of noti ﬁca-
tions, and this also warrants further investigation.
S103. Abnormalities in Glycosphingolipid Degradation
Caused by Progranulin De ﬁciency
Nick Boyle, BS , Andrew Arrant, PhD, Trae Dunn, BS,
Eduardo Listik, PhD, Erik Roberson, MD PhD. University of
Alabama at Birmingham, Birmingham, AL, USA.
Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a leading cause of early-
onset dementia with no disease-modifying therapies.
Heterozygous loss of function progranulin ( GRN) mutations,
causing haploinsuf ﬁciency of the progranulin protein, are
causative of FTD and are inherited in an autosomal-
dominant fashion. Progranulin is a secreted and lysosome-

resident protein with several identi ﬁed functions, acting as a
growth factor, an immunomodulator, and a regulator of lyso-
somal function. Complete loss of progranulin results in
lipofuscinosis and aberrant activities of several lysosomal
enzymes indicating a critical role of progranulin in lysosomal
function. Despite the clear link between progranulin de ﬁ-
ciency and lysosomal dysfunction, the role of progranulin in
lysosomal function remains unclear. Recent reports by our
lab and others have implicated abnormalities in
glycosphingolipid (GSL) degradation caused by progranulin
deﬁciency. GSL degradation is a lysosomal process whereby
complex sugars are successively cleaved off of a sphingolipid
backbone, converging on the production of ceramide, a sug-
arless lipid. The ultimate step of this process, the conversion
of glucosylceramide into ceramide, is catalyzed by the enzyme
β-glucocerebrosidase (GCase). Recently, our lab and others
have found a de ﬁciency of β-glucocerebrosidase (GCase) in
both progranulin-de ﬁcient models and patients with FTD
caused by progranulin mutations (FTD- GRN). We have
found that enzymes upstream in the GSL degradation path-
way have elevated activities accompanied by transcriptional
upregulation of the enzymes. GCase, downstream of these
enzymes, appeared to be a unique case, as it had de ﬁcient
activity with no transcriptional up- or downregulation,
suggesting that the elevations upstream may re ﬂect a com-
pensatory mechanism due to overall lysosomal dysfunction.
The association between GSL abnormalities and neurological
abnormalities is increasingly clear; mutations in several of the
enzymes in the GSL pathway are causative for multiple neu-
rodegenerative diseases, and GCase-associated SNPs are a
leading risk factor for Parkinson Disease. Progranulin inter-
acts with several of these enzymes but does not directly mod-
ify their activities, unlike the related protein prosaposin. We
predicted that GCase was not uniquely de ﬁcient as a result of
progranulin de
ﬁciency, and characterized other enzymes
involved in ceramide production. Here, we report de ﬁciency
of other enzymes in this pathway, also without transcriptional
changes. This discovery suggests that progranulin may play a
much broader role in regulating sphingolipid degradation,
and that further investigation is needed to understand the
effects of progranulin-regulated enzymes to determine the
mechanism by which progranulin de ﬁciency causes FTD.
S104. Association of Long-Term Intake of B Vitamins,
Choline, and Betaine with Subjective Cognitive Decline
in a Sample of US Women and Men
Mario H. Flores-Torres, MD , Kjetil Bjornevik, PhD,
Changzheng Yuan, PhD, Walter Wilett, PhD, Deborah
Blacker, PhD, Alberto Ascherio, PhD. Harvard TH Chan
School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA.
Objective:To prospectively examine the association of long-term
intake of (1) B vitamins (folate, B6 and B12) and (2) choline,
phosphatidylcholine and betaine with subjective cognitive decline
(SCD) in two large cohort studies of US women and men.

Background: Folate, vitamin B6 and B12 have been pro-
posed as protective factors for cognitive decline. Existing
studies have been limited by small samples, short follow-up
and the lack of repeated measures to assess long-term intakes.
Similarly, choline supplementation has been associated with
better cognitive performance, particularly during early life.
The role of choline intake on cognitive function during
adulthood has been less explored, as has the intake of related
nutrients such as phosphatidylcholine and betaine.
Methods: We followed 49, 547 women from the Nurses ’
Health Study (NHS, 1984-2006) and 27,954 men from the
Health Professionals Follow-up Study (HPFS, 1986-2002)
who completed a validated semi-quantitative food frequency
questionnaire (FFQ) at baseline and an SCD assessment in
2012/2014 in the NHS and 2008/2012 in the HPFS. Based
on FFQ responses collected every four years during follow-
up, cumulative averages of total intake of B vitamins and
choline-related nutrients were calculated. We ﬁtted logistic
regression models to estimate the odds ratio (OR) and 95%
conﬁdence interval (CI) of SCD according to quintiles of
intake, with the lowest as the reference. Cohort-speci ﬁc esti-
mates were pooled using ﬁxed-effects meta-analysis.
Results: After adjusting for age, education, race, body
mass index, physical activity, smoking, alcohol and total
energy intake, depression and family history of dementia, we
found that total intakes of folate and choline were associated
with lower odds of SCD. The pooled OR comparing partici-
pants in the top to those in the bottom quintile of intake was
0.87 (95% CI 0.80, 0.94; p-trend <0.001) for folate and
0.87 (95% CI 0.80, 0.94; p-trend <0.001) for choline.
Intake from diet was the main contributor to these inverse
associations and dietary intake of vitamin B6 was also
inversely associated with SCD (pooled OR top vs bottom:
0.79; 95% CI 0.74, 0.96; p-trend <0.001). The associations
with intakes from diet remained signi ﬁcant after adjustment
for ﬂavonoids intake and Mediterranean diet adherence.
Conclusions: The results of this large prospective study
provide support for a possible protective effect of dietary
folate, vitamin B6 and choline intake on cognitive decline.

Background: Vacuolar protein sorting ortholog 35 (VPS35) is
a major stabilizing protein in a retromer-mediated pathway that
regulates the transport of transmembrane proteins such as Amy-
loid Precursor Protein (APP), implicated in amyloid-beta plaque
and phospho-tau tangle development, which are pathologic hall-
marks of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Based on the existing litera-
ture involving model systems, it has been hypothesized that the
initiation of pathogenic biological cascades following VPS35
depletion is independent of phospho-tau. Pathogenic biological
cascades that follow VPS35 depletion lead to disturbed synaptic
plasticity and the accumulation of extracellular proteins. Here
we explore neuronal VPS35 ’s relationship to the pathologic
accumulation of transactive response DNA binding protein
43 (TDP43), which has been previously described by many
groups to be associated with decreased cognitive test scores in
community-based cohort studies with brain autopsy end points.
Objectives: To examine relationships between VPS35,
Tau, and TDP43 (total and phospho) in cognitive decline.
Methods: NanoString GeoMx
TM Digital Spatial Pro ﬁling
was used for analyzing the expression of 73 proteins in NeuN
“masked” cells in the hippocampus. Comparisons: Neuronal
VPS35 was compared in Tau+ (Braak stage II) vs Tau- (Braak
stage 0) subjects. Both groups were cognitively intact during
life. Additional comparisons were made between neuronal
VPS35 in Tau+/Braak stage II/phospho-TDP43+/demented vs
Tau+/Braak stage II/phospho-TDP43-/nondemented groups.
Neuronal VPS35, in ﬂammatory proteins (markers of AD pro-
gression), phospho-TDP43, total TDP43, and phosphorylated
Tau (proin ﬂammatory stimuli in AD) were also compared
across the spectrum of Alzheimer ’s disease neuropathologic
change (ADNC): "resistant" to ADNC (not demented), Pri-
mary Age-Related Tauopathy (PART) with tangles alone
(demented), and high ADNC (demented).
Results: In non-demented individuals, increased neuronal
VPS35 is associated with the presence of increased Tau neu-
roﬁbrillary tangles (P=0.002). When comparing TDP43+
vs. TDP43- cases matched for tangles (Braak stage II), neuro-
nal VPS35 was found to be decreased in the TDP43+ group
(p=0.03). ANOVA test results assessing resistant, PART, and
demented pathologic AD groups revealed that cognitively
intact individuals had higher levels of neuronal VPS35 (inde-
pendent of Tau status and A β42/Aβ40 ratio) (P<0.005).
Conclusion: Increased VPS35, even in the presence of
phospho-Tau, increased APP, in ﬂammatory markers, and
classic pathological features of AD, appears to have a protec-
tive effect on cognitive status, which might be directly
impacted by various pathologic alterations in TDP43.

Alzheimer’s Disease Screening

Introduction: There is a critical unmet need to develop bio-
markers for Alzheimer ’s Disease (AD) diagnosis. We have
previously shown that retinal vascular tortuosity correlates
with cognitive dysfunction and may predict AD. Retinal
color fundus photography (CFP) is a cost-effective high-
resolution imaging tool to study retinal vascular changes in
AD and emerges as a noninvasive biomarker for early AD
diagnosis and monitoring. Handcrafted identi ﬁcation of the
retinal vascular features on CFP is laborious, subjective, and
prone to bias. Here, we leverage deep neural networks to
develop an automatic framework to classify AD and extract
AD retinal CFP biomarkers using weakly supervised localiza-
tion and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping.
Methods: Our proposed framework is a two-stage system.
We used non-mydriatic color retinal fundus images from AD
patients from Mayo Clinic and cognitively normal controls
(NC) from the Eyepacs database. In the ﬁrst stage, a U-Net
based network was applied to raw macula-centered and optic-
disc-centered color fundus images to produce vascular seg-
mentation. The obtained binary vessel segmentation was sub-
sequently fed into the encoder of the U-Net for feature
extraction. The extracted features were fed to an average
pooling layer and a fully connected layer with a Softmax acti-
vation to output probabilistic prediction.
Results: The U-Net was pretrained on the Digital Retinal
Images for Vessel Extraction (DRIVE) dataset. We selected
one image with the best segmentation from each subject,
which resulted in 40 training images and 16 testing images.
The problem is formulated as a binary classi ﬁcation task with
positive class (AD) and negative class (NC). Our trained
model achieved an area under ROC curve of 0.938 on the
testing set. The generated heatmap via Grad-CAM at the last
convolutional layer demonstrated that the network mainly
pays attention to the medium or distal retinal vascular bra-
nches in AD cases, whereas large vessel branches close to
optic head are highlighted in NC. Overall, our proposed net-
work identi ﬁes retinal blood vessel branches with tortuosity
change as potential identi ﬁer of AD.
Conclusions: We present a novel retinal imaging-based
deep learning analysis framework for AD screening. Our pre-
liminary results in a small data set demonstrated the feasibil-
ity of our deep learning model and a strong promise to
identify automated retinal imaging biomarkers for AD diag-
nosis. Future research will include larger datasets of AD and
preclinical AD subjects.
S107. Bioequivalence and Safety Comparison of Once-
Weekly Donepezil Transdermal System with Once-Daily
Oral Donepezil: Results of a Phase 1 Trial in Healthy
Volunteers
Pierre N. Tariot, MD
1, Rene Braeckman, PhD 2, Charles Oh,
MD3. 1Banner Alzheimer ’s Institute, Phoenix, AZ, USA,
2KemPharm, Inc, Celebration, FL, USA, 3Corium Inc, Boston,
MA, USA.
Background: Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause
of dementia in older adults. Long duration of the disease and
progressive decline of cognitive function are major contribu-
tors to patient and caregiver burden. Oral donepezil is a
widely used treatment for dementia of the Alzheimer type.
Dose escalation of oral donepezil has been associated with
gastrointestinal distress, leading to treatment discontinuation,
which emphasizes the need for a transdermal system (TDS).
Donepezil TDS (Adlarity
®) was recently approved for the

treatment of mild, moderate, and severe dementia of the
Alzheimer’s type.
Methods: This open-label, randomized, crossover,
3-period trial (NCT04617782) with healthy volunteers (aged
18-55 years) was conducted to assess bioequivalence of once-
weekly 10-mg/d and 5-mg/d donepezil TDS with once-daily
10-mg oral donepezil. All participants received 5-mg/d done-
pezil TDS during the 5-week Period 1, followed by 10-mg/d
TDS or 10-mg/d oral donepezil in the 5-week Period 2;
treatments were switched in Period 3. Bioequivalence was
assessed at steady state in Week 5 of each treatment. Safety
and tolerability were also evaluated.
Results: Of 60 participants enrolled, all received 5-mg/d
TDS, 55 received 10-mg/d TDS, and 56 received oral done-
pezil. At steady state, adjusted geometric mean ratio (%
[90% CI]) of TDS to oral donepezil for maximum plasma
concentration and area under the plasma concentration versus
time curve (0-168 h) were 88.7 (81.7-96.2) and 108.6
(100.5-117.4) for 10-mg/d and 86.1 (79.8-92.9) and 105.3
(97.6-113.6) for 5-mg/d TDS (dose normalized). The 90%
CIs for the geometric mean ratios were generally within the
accepted 80%-125% range for establishing bioequivalence.
Adverse events (AEs) were reported in 80% of participants —
53.3% for the 5-mg/d TDS, 54.5% for the 10-mg/d TDS,
and 57.1% for oral donepezil. Except for abdominal pain
(5.5% vs 1.8%), fewer gastrointestinal AEs were reported
with 10-mg/d TDS than oral donepezil (constipation, 5.5%
vs 17.9%; nausea 1.8% vs 30.4%; diarrhea 3.6% vs 12.5%),
respectively. There were also fewer incidences of dizziness
(3.6% vs 19.6%) and no incidence of somnolence (0 vs
10.7%) reported with TDS. No serious AEs, AEs leading to
treatment discontinuation, or deaths were reported.
Conclusion: Both donepezil TDS strengths were bioequiv-
alent to oral donepezil on a mg/d basis. The safety pro ﬁle of
donepezil TDS supports its use in treating dementia of the
Alzheimer type.

Objective: Determine factors associated with emotional and
behavioral dyscontrol (EBD) after hemorrhagic stroke.
Background: EBD can be distressful to patients and fam-
ily and may complicate hospitalization and rehabilitation.
Design/Methods: We prospectively identiﬁed patients from

cerebral hemorrhage (ICH) or subarachnoid hemorrhage

(SAH) - and EBD assessed via telephone at 3-months and
12-months using the Quality of Life in Neurological Disorders
EBD Inventory. We examined the relationship between EBD
(T-score >50) at 3-months and bleed characteristics, pre-
hospitalization social and neuropsychiatric history, neurologi-
cal/systemic illness severity, and hospital complications. We
then compared EBD at 3-months and 12-months.
Results: 72 patients completed the 3-month call; 15 (21%)
had EBD. At 3-months, EBD was more common in patients
with ICH than SAH (14/46 (30% vs. 1/26 (3.8%), p=0.007))
and was associated with lower admission GCS score (13 (IQR
9-15) vs. 15 (IQR 14-15), p=0.009), and higher APACHE II
score (17 (IQR 10-18) vs. 11 (IQR 8.5-15.5), p=0.038). Mul-
tivariate analysis including bleed type, GCS score, APACHE II
score, and neuropsychiatric history, found ICH had a signi ﬁ-
cant relationship with EBD at 3-months (OR 9.6 (95% CI
1.12-83.33, p=0.039). There was no signi ﬁcant relationship
between EBD at 3-months and ICH laterality/location/vol-
ume, age, sex, race, ethnicity, handedness, education, pre-
admission employment, neuropsychiatric/dementia history,
tobacco-use, premorbid mRS-score, ventilator-days, infection,
or hospital length-of-stay. There were 32 (44%) patients who
completed the 12-month follow-up call. There was no agree-
ment ( κ=0.083) between EBD at 3-months and 12-months;
19 (59%) patients had no EBD, 2 (6%) had EBD at both
timepoints, 9 (28%) only had EBD at 3-months, and 1 (3%)
developed EBD at 12-months.
Conclusions: Compared to patients with SAH, patients
with ICH appear more likely to experience emotional and
behavioral dyscontrol 3-months post-stroke, especially with
higher ICH severity. These ﬁndings help identify patients
who may bene ﬁt from early neuropsychiatric interventions
following hemorrhagic stroke.
S110. Case Series of Manic Symptoms Following
Concussion
Jordyn P. Anklam, BS, MPH
1, Paige Buddenhagen, MS,
LAT2, Kate M. Essad, MD 2. 1University of Wisconsin School of
Medicine and Public Health, Madison, WI, USA, 2Advocate
Aurora Health, Milwaukee, WI, USA.
Purpose: To highlight the similarities and differences among
cases of manic symptoms following concussion
Background: Mood disturbance following concussion is a
well-established but only partially-understood phenomena.
Prior research in this area focuses on depression, though
manic symptoms after concussion occur with greater fre-
quency than in the general population (1).
It is necessary to determine whether concussion directly
leads to manic symptoms, or if manic symptoms lead to risky
behaviors and injury. Furthermore, clinicians must distin-
guish manic symptoms without mood disturbance from true
manic episodes, which must include expansive, euphoric, or
irritable mood.
Methods: Within a specialty concussion clinic, patients
with features of mania following head injury were identi ﬁed.
Verbal consent to share patient experience was obtained. Lit-
erature review on medical databases using search terms
“mania,”“ head injury, ” and “concussion” was performed.
Results: Similarities and differences between patients with
manic symptoms following concussion is seen in Table 1.
Case 1: Manic Episode Provoked by Concussion
A 65-year-old male with recurrent major depressive disor-
der presented following acute concussion in a car accident.
One month later, he reported symptoms of irritable mood,
increased talkativeness, distractibility, and racing thoughts.

Treatment for this included lamotrigine, leading to a decrease
in symptoms.
Case 2: Predisposition to Risky Behaviors
A 25-year-old male with a history of bipolar I disorder and
ADHD presented after head injury during a dirt bike race.
One month post-concussion, he experienced symptoms of
elevated mood, racing thoughts, distractibility, and lack of
need for sleep. He reports he had not been on any medica-
tion for months prior to the injury.
Case 3: Manic Symptoms Following Concussion
A 55-year-old male presented after a car accident with con-
cussion, rapid speech, and psychomotor agitation. Over the
following months, he reported inattentiveness, disinhibition,
“zombie-like” mood, and marked sleep disturbance. He was
advised to optimize his sleep schedule and stress levels. He
reports symptoms tapered and resolved over the following six
months.
Discussion: Understanding the nuances between these
cases allows clinicians to target treatment adequately and
safely. If not fully understood, behavioral disturbances may
be treated with unopposed SSRIs, which is potentially unsafe
for a patient with a true manic episode; meanwhile, ﬁrst-line
treatments for manic episodes can lower the seizure threshold
- concerning for provoking post-traumatic seizures. Greater
speciﬁcity in etiology of manic symptoms following concus-
sion allows for a tailored treatment approach, avoiding escala-
tion of symptoms and reducing recovery time.

Background: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a
complex disease characterized by progressive pulmonary vas-
cular remodeling with resultant abnormal increase in pulmo-
nary artery pressure and right heart dysfunction. Although
PAH originates in the pulmonary vasculature, there is grow-
ing evidence that PAH represents a systemic disease with
neurologic sequelae including cognitive impairment. The
mechanism of cognitive impairment in PAH is uncertain, as
is the association between cognition and aberrant cardiopul-
monary parameters. We investigated the prevalence of cogni-
tive impairment in PAH patients presenting to Yale
Pulmonary Vascular Disease (PVD) Clinic, described the
characteristics of the cognitive impairment syndrome, and

Methods: We enrolled adult patients with PAH from the
Yale PVD clinic between 2/27/2020 and 12/9/2021.Subjects

that has been used to detect cognitive impairment in non-
geriatric populations with systemic disease. Cognitive impair-
ment was de ﬁned as SAGE score <17. Multivariate regression
of cardiopulmonary metrics on SAGE score was performed
using Stata.
Results: 23 subjects participated in the study (52%
female, 91% Caucasian, average age 63 years, average
15 years of education, 70% New York Heart Association
Class II or greater). SAGE scores ranged from 12 - 22, with
6 (26%) meeting criteria for co gnitive impairment. Most of
the cognitively impaired subjects met criteria for mild cog-
nitive impairment (SAGE 15-16). Subjects demonstrated
the most de ﬁcits in memory, executi ve function, and visuo-
spatial domains, with ex ecutive functioning de ﬁcits pre-
dominant.The abnormal cardiopulmonary metric most
closely related to cognitive impairment was reduced gas
exchange (pulmonary vascular capacitance (GX
CAP)), which
explained 29% of the variance in SAGE score, followed by
systemic oxygen desaturation with exercise, which
explained 20% of the variance (controlling for age and level
of education).
Conclusions: Signiﬁcant cognitive impairment is present
in a subset of PAH patients and is associated with reduced
pulmonary vascular compliance and increased systemic oxy-
gen desaturation during sub-maximal CPET. This suggests
that measures of increased pulmonary vascular disease burden
are potential mediators of cognitive impairment in this popu-
lation. The syndrome appears consistent with subcortical cog-
nitive impairment, which suggests a cerebrovascular element
to its pathophysiology. Future research should encompass
larger con ﬁrmatory studies examining the relationship
between cerebrovascular dysfunction and cognitive impair-
ment in PAH.
S112. Creutzfeldt Jacob Disease Misdiagnosis, a
Diagnostic Challenge and Psychological Burden: A Case
Series
Morgan Lehman, BS , Habib Yazgi, BS, Jeniece Regan, BS,
Joseph Nguyen, DO, Chen Zhao, MD, MS, MA. Pennsylvania
State University College of Medicine, Hershey, PA, USA.
Introduction: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sCJD) is
the most common prion disease, yet incidence is only 1-1.5
cases diagnosed per 1 million people. Patients with sCJD
experience rapid cognitive decline and live on average six
months from diagnosis, rendering diagnosis challenging
1.
Adding to diagnostic dif ﬁculties are a diverse clinical presen-
tation, extensive differential diagnosis, and evolving diagnos-
tic criteria, with autopsy specimen histology still the gold
standard diagnostic test 2. Due to the aforementioned
characteristics of sCJD, it is often misdiagnosed, with an
average of 3.8 misdiagnoses per patient 3. Delayed diagnosis
leads to an inability to prepare the patient and family for this
inevitably challenging disease course. We present ﬁve cases of
sCJD from a rural medical center to elucidate the variety of
clinical presentations and frequency of misdiagnosis.
Methods: We performed retrospective chart review

(2019-2021) and present ﬁve cases of highly suspected sCJD
(CDC diagnostic criteria).
Cases: The cases were ﬁve non-Hispanic white patients
ages 62-77. Presenting symptoms were variable, including
imbalance, worsening short-term memory, behavioral
changes, weakness, and worsening vision. The clinical
course proved just as heterogeneous: all cases demonstrated
rapidly progressive dementia and memory impairment, four
patients reported visual symptoms and imbalance, three dis-
played parkinsonism and ataxia, and two had dysarthria.
Additional symptoms included urinary incontinence, patho-
logical laughter, insomnia, paranoid ideas, dizziness, and
stuttering speech. However, no patient exhibited startle
myoclonus or akinetic mutism. CSF analysis revealed posi-
tive 14-3-3, RT-QuIC, and elevated total tau in all cases.
EEG contained periodic sharp wave complexes in one case
and generalized background slowing in two other cases.
MRI was abnormal in all cases. Only one patient was ini-
tially diagnosed with sCJD, and another included
“prionopathy ” on the differential. Initial misdiagnoses
included stroke, meningoencephalitis, cerebellar ataxia, and
Wernicke encephalopathy. Time from initial presentation to
diagnosis averaged 120 days.
Conclusion: Even with improving diagnostic tools and
heightened clinical suspicion for sCJD, the initial diagnosis is
often inaccurate. Consequently, when patients are correctly
diagnosed, it is often two-thirds of the way through their dis-
ease course. Incorrect and delayed diagnosis prevent providers
from preparing the patient and family for the mental, ﬁnan-
cial, and emotional burden associated with sCJD
3. Further
research is essential to better understand the heterogeneous
presentation of sCJD and reduce diagnostic error.

manifestations of the disease particularly in patients described
as having “long haul COVID ”. These include but are not
limited to prolonged respiratory injury, cardiac complica-
tions, and neurologic dysfunction. Multiple studies reported

neurocognitive functions. While these phenomena have been
described previously, there are few studies that have com-

visuospatial, language, processing speed, and executive func-

and included the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of
Neuropsychological Status (RBANS), Boston Naming Test
(BNT), Delis-Kaplan Executive Function System (D-KEFS),
among others. The results of these tests were analyzed to
understand performance across the ﬁve domains.
Results: Patients with concerns of long-haul neurocognitive
deﬁcit after COVID-19 infection had depressed neurocognitive
function across the ﬁve domains tested. Though baseline IQ
assessment classiﬁed the patient population to have a score of
104.58 (62
nd percentile; SD=9.6; Range 88 - 116), the patients
performed below the 50 th percentile across all ﬁve domains.
Overall, the patients performed on average at the 38 th percen-
tile across the various tests indicating globally depressed
neurocognitive function. There were select areas in which
patients performed particularly poorly. These included domains
such as learning and memory where patients performed <35

Progressive Dementia: A Clinical Study

Bu, PhD1, John C. Morris, MD 2, Neill R. Graff-Radford,
MD1. 1Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, FL, USA, 2Washington
University School of Medicine, Saint Louis, MO, USA,
3University of San Francisco, San Francisco, FL, USA.
Objective: To improve the accuracy of antemortem diagno-
ses and determine the causes of rapidly progressive dementia
(RPD) in a prospective clinical cohort.
Background: Overlap in clinical features and test results in
patients with rapidly progressive dementia (RPD) confounds
the etiologic diagnoses of RPD, contributing to diagnostic
delays, missed treatment opportunities, and poor outcomes.
There is a need to improve diagnostic accuracy in patients with
RPD, with particular focus on improving early recognition of
patients with treatment-responsive causes of RPD.

Methods: Patients with RPD were prospectively enrolled
and evaluated in inpatient settings and outpatient sub-
specialty (memory) clinics at Washington University (Saint
Louis, MO; 2016-2019) and Mayo Clinic (Jacksonville, FL;
2020-2021). Etiologic diagnoses were independently assigned
by two dementia specialists integrating clinical features and
the results of widely accessible diagnostic tests. Diagnostic
disagreements were resolved via blinded review by a third
specialist. Clinicopathologic correlation was evaluated using
neuropathological and genetic data when available.
Results: 160 patients with RPD were assessed, with average
age-at-symptom onset 60.0 /C615.9 years; 50% were female.
Diagnostic inter-rater reliability (91% agreement; Cohen ’s
κ=0.88, p<0.001) and clinicopathologic correlation were excel-
lent (100% agreement in 24 patients with neuropathologic or
genetic data). Autoimmune encephalitis was the leading cause
of RPD (39%), followed by Alzheimer disease and related
dementias (29% —i.e., frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body
dementia, vascular cognitive impairment), Creutzfeldt-Jakob
disease (15%), and other causes (15% —e.g., neurosarcoid,
metabolic disruptions, neoplastic disease). Patients with poten-
tially treatable causes (AE and selected “other” causes) were
younger, on average (54.4 /C618.2), than those with neurode-
generative dementing illnesses (67.3 /C69.5) or CJD (67.4 /C67.9;
p<0.001). Patients with potentially treatable causes of RPD
were more likely to present with altered level of consciousness
and seizures (p<0.05). CSF pleocytosis (>5 WBC/microliter)
was more common in AE patients (p<0.05).
Interpretation: Etiologic diagnoses can be reliably
established in RPD patients using available clinical data.
Treatment-responsive causes of RPD are common, particu-
larly in younger patients with altered consciousness, seizures,
and CSF pleocytosis.

tom onset to death due to dementia) were identi ﬁed within

Background: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is an inter-
mediate stage between normal cognition and Alzheimer ’s
Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD). Early detection of
MCI and identi ﬁcation of its modi ﬁable risk factors may
delay progression from MCI to ADRD.
Methods: Our study cohort was extracted from
Geisinger’s EMR and includes 1379 MCI patients and
5516 healthy controls such that the ratio between MCI
and controls is 1 to 4 and the distribution of age at index
date is preserved among MCI and control groups. The
index date for MCI patients was set to the MCI diagnosis

date, while the index date for controls was selected such
that each MCI patient had four distinct controls with
adjusted age. The prediction time was set to 1 and 3 years
before the index date. Medication pro ﬁles were computed
from EMR records collected two years before the predic-
tion time. Medications were grouped into 100 groups
based on the Generic Product Identi ﬁer (GPI) drug hierar-
chical classi ﬁcation system. Thus, each patient was repre-
sented using a pro ﬁle of 100 numbers indicating the
aggregated counts of prescribed medications under each
GPI group. We experimented with machine learning
models trained using the eXtreme Gradient Boosting
(XGB) algorithm and 103 features (100 GPI drug groups
and three patient demographic variables including age at
prediction time, gender, and race). The performance of our
models was assessed using the Area Under ROC Curve
(AUC), estimated using the 10-fold cross-validation
procedure.
Results: Our XGB models can predict 1-year and 3-year
MCI risk with AUC scores of 0.74 and 0.72, respectively.
For both prediction tasks, we found that each of the ﬁve top-
most important medication group is signi ﬁcantly (p-value
< 0.0001) more prevalent in the pro ﬁles of MCI patients.
The topmost important features for predicting 1-year risk for
MCI were: antidepressants (35.1% vs 13.4%), psychothera-
peutic and neurological agents (7.9% vs 0.9%),
antihyperlipidemics (51.2% vs 31.5%), antipsychotics anti-
manic agents (4.8% vs 0.02%), and vitamins (14.4% vs
5.3%). The topmost important features for predicting 3-year
risk for MCI were: antidepressants (31.5% vs 12.5%), anti-
psychotics antimanic agents (3.8% vs 0.02%), anticonvul-
sants (17.1% vs 6.4%), endocrine and metabolic agents
(10.1% vs 5.7%), and non-narcotic analgesics (25.8%
vs 12.9%).
Conclusion: A machine learning model trained using
two-year medication pro ﬁles could be a useful tool for
screening patients who have unrecognized or are at high
risk of MCI.

Pierre N. Tariot, MD

Background: Oral donepezil, a reversible acetylcholinesterase
inhibitor, is the most used treatment for dementia of the
Alzheimer type and has been associated with gastrointestinal
distress, leading to treatment discontinuation. Transdermal
systems (TDSs) can provide an alternative mode of adminis-
tration that bypasses the gastrointestinal tract and offers sev-
eral other bene ﬁts over oral administration. Donepezil TDS
(Adlarity

moderate, and severe dementia of the Alzheimer ’s type.

crossover, phase 1 trial (NCT04617782) enrolling healthy volun-
teers aged 18-55 years. All participants received once-weekly

once-weekly 10-mg/d donepezil TDS or once-daily 10-mg oral
donepezil in the 5-week Period 2; treatments were switched in
Period 3. The primary endpoint was steady-state bioequivalence
of once-weekly donepezil TDS with once-daily oral donepezil.

TDS. The number (%) of TDSs with ≥75% adhesion during
weeks 1-5 at all adhesion assessment timepoints during the
1-week wear period was 245 (83.6%) for 5-mg/d TDS and
232 (85.9%) for 10-mg/d TDS. Probability of a TDS
maintaining ≥75% adhesion throughout the wear period was
estimated as 0.8362 for 5-mg/d TDS and 0.8593 for 10-mg/d

and 10-mg/d TDSs (combined skin irritation score of ≥3

are rates of cognitive impairment and dementia, including

that signi ﬁcantly increases the risk of cognitive impairment
and is reaching pandemic levels is obesity and prediabetes/
diabetes. Common mechanisms that could underly the rela-

STING speci ﬁc protein expression using western blotting.

human microglial cell line by treating microglia for 24 hr

palmitate. Cells were then assessed for cGAS/STING protein

increased weights and impaired glucose tolerance along with

S125. Is Chronic Pain a Risk Factor for Cognitive

Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA.
Background: Chronic pain (CP) has been associated with
cognitive de ﬁcits in cross-sectional studies. However, the lon-
gitudinal association between chronic pain and cognitive
decline at a population level is unclear.

and Embase from inception to April 13, 2022. We included
longitudinal studies that reported a contrast between a cohort
with CP (including headache disorders, musculoskeletal pain,
widespread pain, neuropathic pain, among others) and with-
out painful conditions; an objective binary measure of cogni-
tive outcome; and a follow-up of at least one year. We
excluded studies that included autoimmune in ﬂammatory
conditions associated with pain due to competing risks associ-
ated with cognition. The association was calculated as
unadjusted and adjusted hazard ratios (HR) or odds ratios
(OR) and their respective 95% CI. We performed separated
random-effect meta-analyses using the inverse-variance
method. Between-study heterogeneity was assessed and
explored using subgroup analyses. Finally, we assessed publi-
cation bias, risk of bias, and evidence certainty by applying
the GRADE approach.
Results: We included 28 cohort studies (involving
490 684 patients who reported persistent painful conditions
and 2 345 937 subjects who did not). The mean follow-up
was 9.58 years (2 to 21 years). Most of the studies were
populational-based (90.3%). The most common pain condi-
tions were headache disorders (n=14), mixed conditions
(n=6), and musculoskeletal pain (n=5). The unadjusted
pooled HR (n=12 studies) was 1.37 (95% CI 1.25 to 1.51;
I
2=59%) while the adjusted estimate (n=18 studies) was 1.31
(95% CI 1.22 to 1.41; I 2=78%). Eight studies reported the
association as ORs, the unadjusted and adjusted estimates
were 1.66 (95% CI 1.41 to 1.95; I
2=0%) and 1.22 (95% CI
1.07 to 1.40; I 2=0%), respectively. We did not ﬁnd differ-
ences by setting (institutional vs. community) or pain condi-
tion. A third of the studies had high risk of bias due to
unclear de ﬁnitions of CP. No publication bias was found.
The overall evidence certainty was classi ﬁed as moderate.
Conclusion: In this population-based meta-analysis, CP
was associated with an approximately 30% increased proba-
bility of long-term cognitive decline. However, the conclu-
sion is limited by substantial study heterogeneity and

S126. Metabolic Syndrome Produces Insulin Resistance

As of 2021, 1 in 9 people aged 65 and older in the
United States have dementia. Alzheimer ’s disease (AD) and
AD-related dementia (ADRD) constitute the main cause of
dementia leading to poor memory and cognition. A major
risk factor for AD/ADRD is midlife metabolic syndrome
(MetS). MetS-associated AD/ADRD progresses non-cell
autonomously, implicating roles for supporting glia, especially
oligodendrocytes. Our aim is to elucidate how MetS-
associated oligodendrocyte dysfunction leads to cognitive
impairment and AD/ADRD. Young (5-week old) and old
(12-month old) mice were fed either standard diet (SD, 10%
fat) or high fat diet (HFD, 60% fat) for 13 weeks, followed
by full assessment of metabolic parameters, cognitive func-
tion, and isolated oligodendrocyte single cell RNA-
sequencing (scRNA-seq) and protein expression of
monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs). Both young and old
mice on HFD gained more weight and had higher blood glu-
cose and fat mass compared to the SD controls. Old HFD
mice performed poorly in puzzle box and social recognition
tests, re ﬂecting impaired cognition (short- and long-term
memory). scRNA-seq showed a speci ﬁc oligodendrocyte clus-
ter from HFD mice had altered expression of proteins
involved in cognition ( Bc1, Cntn1, Gria2, Fam171a2, Nrsn1,

C1qtnf4, Ndufa5 ) compared to SD mice. Interestingly, oligo-
dendrocyte MCT1 protein expression was upregulated in
young HFD mice and downregulated in old HFD mice com-
pared to their SD counterparts. Collectively, these results
indicate that midlife MetS impairs oligodendrocyte metabolic

ing MetS-associated AD/ADRD. Funding: NIH

S127. Multimodal Machine Learning to Identify Risk of
Progression in Asymptomatic Alzheimer ’s Disease
Raghav Tandon, M.S.
1, Caroline M. Watson, Ph.D. 2, Nicholas
T. Seyfried, Ph.D. 2, James J. Lah, M.D.,Ph.D. 2, Cassie
S. Mitchell, Ph.D. 1. 1Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta,
GA, USA, 2Emory University, Atlanta, GA, USA.
Introduction: Protein changes and aberrant protein accumu-
lation is a hallmark of Alzheimer ’s Disease (AD). Well-
studied neuropathological hallmarks, like amyloid-beta
plaques and neuro ﬁbrillary tangles (tau), depart from normal
levels well before functional cognitive decline. This is the
asymptomatic AD stage, which precedes typical clinical pre-
sentation of the disease and offers an opportunity for early
intervention. The objective of this study was to ﬁnd differ-
ences between asymptomatic AD subjects and control sub-
jects. Machine learning was used to stratify asymptomatic
cases and identify individuals expected to experience func-
tional cognitive decline sooner.
Methods: The study used data from the Emory Healthy

Brain Study (EHBS) to analyze differences in medical history,
cardiovascular health, neuropsychological evaluations, and cere-
brospinal ﬂuid (CSF) biomarker levels across cognitively healthy
controls and cognitively healthy asymptomatic AD subjects.
Stratiﬁcation of asymptomatic cases was performed using low-
dimensional analysis (a combination of feature selection and t-
distributed stochastic neighbor embeddings or t-SNE). Of the
75 peptides measured from CSF samples, 8 peptides were cho-
sen to discriminate between control and AD cases using recur-
sive feature elimination (RFE). These 8 peptides are further
compressed into 2 features using t-SNE, which are used to
compute the proximity of asymptomatic cases to control and
AD cases using the k-nearest neighbors algorithm.

stratify asymptomatic cases into “AD-like” (likely closer to
transitioning to symptomatic AD) or “control-like” (likely
further from transitioning to symptomatic AD) clusters using
8 key CSF peptides. Classi ﬁcation of strati ﬁed patient risk
was closely correlated with the APOE e4 allele status, which
is a well-known genetic risk factor for AD.
Conclusion: Multi-modal data analysis identi ﬁed some
statistical differences in cardiovascular health and minimal
changes of select neuropsychological scores. Biomarkers were
most important to classifying asymptomatic AD risk for fur-
ther progression. Strati ﬁcation of asymptomatic cases assists
in identifying which subjects are expected to experience cog-
nitive decline sooner and who may best respond to potential
early intervention.

neuropathologic processes characterized by the accumulation
of misfolded proteins, such as tau, amyloid, α-synuclein, and
TDP-43 are observed. This study aimed to determine the fre-
quency of copathologies and assess their impact on the rate
of cognitive decline in patients with DLB.

dementias, little is known about the prevalence across demen-
tia severity and the potential in ﬂuence on the trajectory of
cognitive decline.

Coordinating Center Uniform Data Set to evaluate the
hypotheses that the prevalence of insomnia differs by de ﬁni-

features track with established biomarkers of AD, and that
longitudinal changes in sleep disorders affect cognition and

determine the prevalence of clinician-determined insomnia

the patient ’s ﬁrst visit. We evaluated mean MoCA scores,
hippocampal volumes, and CSF phosphorylated tau:beta
amyloid ratios obtained near the ﬁrst visit using Analysis of

evaluations, we classi ﬁed changes in insomnia and nighttime
behaviors as “none”, “remitted”, “acquired”,o r “steady”
between the ﬁrst and last visits. Similar changes in MoCA
scores and HV were assessed with repeated-measure

ANOVA.

dementia groups respectively. Prevalence of clinican-identi ﬁed

ﬁed to be without insomnia. In con-
