Introduction: Measurement of cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF)
levels of the amyloid-beta peptide (A β) and the microtubule-
associated protein tau (MAPT; Tau) and imaging amyloid
plaques and neuro ﬁbrillary tangles with A β and Tau radio-
tracers are important tools for establishing etiological diagno-
sis of Alzheimer ’s disease (AD) in patients experiencing
cognitive decline. Moreover, changes in these biomarkers
allow detection of AD pathology many years prior to the
onset of clinical symptoms. As we approach the advent of
disease-modifying and preventative treatments for AD, appro-
priate use of these tools will be critical in guiding their use.
Unfortunately, the lack of diversity in research cohorts has
generated information regarding biomarker positivity in over-
whelmingly non-Hispanic white (NHW) populations, and
their application to other racial and ethnic groups may be
inappropriate.
Methods: We conducted an analysis of CSF samples from
symptomatic and cognitively normal (CN) individuals from a
large cohort (N=3006) of research volunteers at Emory Uni-
versity, including 2456 (81.7%) self-identi ﬁed White/
Caucasian and 495 (16.5%) self-identi ﬁed Black/African-
American (AA) participants, to examine potential racial differ-
ences in CSF AD biomarkers. CSF samples were collected
using consistent preanalytical methods and levels of A β
42,t o t a l
Tau (tTau), and phospho181 Tau (pTau) were assayed using
ﬁrst generation Roche Elecsys assays in a single laboratory.
Results: Substantial differences were found in A β
42, tTau,
and pTau between White and AA individuals. Using cutoffs
for biomarker positivity derived from the Alzheimer ’s Disease
Imaging Initiative comprised of predominantly NHW indi-
viduals, signi ﬁcantly lower proportions of AA individuals
were classi ﬁed as AD. Among symptomatic individuals,
37.5% of Black patients (101/269) were diagnosed with AD
compared to 61.3% of White patients (769/1254). Among
CN individuals, overall prevalence of biomarker-positive,
asymptomatic AD increased with age, as expected (4.7%
below age 55, 32.8% over age 75). Application of ADNI cut-
offs classi ﬁed 8.0% of CN AA individuals (18/225) as
asymptomatic AD compared to 13.4% of CN White individ-
uals (159/1187).
Conclusions: Although epidemiological data suggest a
higher prevalence of AD in AA, using cutoffs-derived from
NHW populations showed lower AD prevalence suggesting
that race-derived cutoffs are likely to be required to appropri-
ately identify individuals for current and emerging secondary
prevention therapies for AD.

Pathology Among Phenotypic Variants of Alzheimer ’s

Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.
Alzheimer’s disease neuropathologic change (ADNC) is clini-
cally heterogenous and can present with a classic multidomain
amnestic syndrome or focal non-amnestic syndromes. In this
study we explored the regional distribution and burden of
phosphorylated and C-terminally cleaved tau pathologies across
hippocampal subﬁelds and cortical regions among clinical vari-

ants of Alzheimer ’s disease (AD). Here, autopsy-con ﬁrmed
cases with ADNC were classi ﬁed by clinical criteria into
amnestic AD (aAD, n=40) and non-amnestic AD (naAD,
n=39). We used digital histology to measure the percent area-
occupied of tau pathology in hippocampal sub ﬁelds and three
cortical regions (superior/middle temporal cortex, middle fron-
tal cortex, and angular gyrus) in AT8 (phosphorylated tau, rec-
ognizes pretangles and mature tangles), TauC3 (D
421-
truncated tau, identiﬁes mature tangles and ghost tangles), and
MN423 (E 391-truncated tau, primarily immunostains ghost
tangles) stained sections. Linear mixed-effect models were used
to test regional and group differences while adjusting for
demographics. Both groups showed AT8-reactivity across hip-
pocampal subﬁelds that re ﬂected traditional Braak staging with
higher levels of phosphorylated-tau in subregions implicated as
affected early in Braak staging. The burden of phosphorylated-
tau and TauC3-immunoreactive tau in the hippocampus was
largely similar between the aAD and naAD groups. In con-
trast, the naAD group had lower relative distribution of
MN423-reactive tangles in CA1 ( β=-0.2, SE=0.09, p=0.001)
and CA2 ( β=-0.25, SE=0.09, p=0.005) compared to the aAD.
Although the aAD and naAD groups had similar burden of
phosphorylated-tau pathology in cortical regions, there was
higher burden of TauC3 reactivity in sup/mid temporal cortex
(β=0.16, SE=0.07, p=0.02) and MN423 reactivity in all corti-
cal regions (β=0.4-0.43, SE=0.09, p<0.001) in the naAD com-
pared to aAD. In conclusion, AD clinical variants may have a
signature distribution of overall phosphorylated-tau pathology
within the hippocampus re ﬂecting traditional Braak staging;
however, non-amnestic AD has greater relative mature tangle
pathology in the neocortex compared to patients with clinical
amnestic AD, where the hippocampus had greatest relative
burden of C-terminally cleaved tau reactivity. Thus, varying
neuronal susceptibility to tau-mediated neurodegeneration may
inﬂuence the clinical expression of ADNC.

Background: Heterogeneity in clinical presentation,
abundant mimics, and potential for iatrogenic transmission
emphasize the need for accurate diagnostic tests for prions
associated with prion disease. RT-QuIC is an excellent
test, with high sensitivity and speci ﬁcity for prions,

although false negative results are recognized in clinical

Methods: One-hundred twelve patients with probable or
deﬁnite prion disease were assessed at Mayo Clinic Enterprise
(Rochester, MN; Jacksonville, FL; Scottsdale, AZ) or
Washington University School of Medicine (St. Louis, MO)
from 2013-2021. RT-QuIC testing for prions was performed
in cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) in all patients via the National
Prion Disease Pathology Surveillance Center (Cleveland,
OH). Demographic data, clinical features, and results of
common tests and laboratory studies were abstracted from
electronic medical records and differences between RT-QuIC
positive and negative patients considered using univariate
statistics.
Results: Initial RT-QuIC testing was negative in 12/112
patients (sensitivity 89%), including two patients with
autopsy-conﬁrmed fatal familial insomnia. Median age at
presentation was younger in RT-QuIC negative patients
(56.9 vs 66 years, p<0.01), who were also less likely to
present with ataxia (3/12 vs 61/100, p=0.03). Other demo-
graphic and presenting features were similar in RT-QuIC
positive and negative patients. CSF cell count, protein, and
glucose levels were similar between cohorts, while rates of
14-3-3 positivity (2/12 vs 77/100, p<0.01) and median
CSF total tau levels were lower in RT-QuIC negative
patients (2318 vs 4001 pg/mL, p<0.01). RT-QuIC nega-
tive patients also had a longer median days from symptom
onset to ﬁrst presentation (125 vs 47, p=0.04), and longer
symptomatic disease duration (530 vs 148, p<0.01). Two
RT-QuIC-negative patients underwent repeat testing; both
were positive.
Interpretation: RT-QuIC is a sensitive yet imperfect mea-
sure of prions. These ﬁndings emphasize the need to incorpo-
rate the results of additional testing in the diagnostic
evaluation of patients with suspected prion disease and a neg-
ative RT-QuIC test. Patients with negative RT-QuIC had
lower CSF biomarkers of neuronal damage (total-tau and
14-3-3) and longer symptomatic duration of prion disease
raising the possibility that false negative RT-QuIC testing
may associate with a more indolent course.

to Enhance Hippocampal Cholinergic Tone via
Parabacteroides Bacteria

Cholinergic neurons in the central nervous system play a
critical role in sleep and cognitive functions such as learning
and memory. A reduced level of the neurotransmitter acetyl-
choline in the brain is one of the hallmark changes in
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) patients. Here, we found that our
synthetic saccharide mixture (MRM) fed to 5xFAD AD
mice selectively enriched genus Parabacteroides gut bacteria
that carry the choline-phosphate cytidylyltransferase enzyme,
which is known to catalyze CDP-choline synthesis. Impor-
tantly, we demonstrated that Parabacteroidesdistasonis, in
anaerobic culture, synthesize and excrete the CDP-choline
into culture medium. Indeed, in the 5xFAD AD model,
MRM increased hippocampal acetylcholine levels, which
were accompanied by reductions of elevated REM sleep

theta ( θ) and improved spatial memory, both of which are
known to be regulated by cholinergic function. We propose
that MRM elevates acetylcholine precursor, CDP-choline,
synthesis by Parabacteroides, which in turn increases acetyl-
choline levels in the brain and mitigates EEG θ activity and
cognitive function in an AD mouse model.
S137. The Case for Low-Level BACE1 Inhibition for the
Prevention of Alzheimer ’s Disease
Robert Vassar, PhD . Northwestern University, Chicago,
IL, USA.
Alzheimer disease (AD) is the most common cause of demen-
tia in older individuals (>65 years) and has a long pres-
ymptomatic phase. Preventive therapies for AD are not yet
available, and potential disease- modifying therapies targeting
amyloid-β plaques in symptomatic stages of AD have only
just been approved in the United States. Small- molecule
inhibitors of β-site amyloid precursor protein (APP)-cleaving
enzyme 1 (BACE1; also known as β-secretase 1) reduce the
production of amyloid- β peptide and are among the most
advanced drug candidates for AD. However, to date all phase
II and phase III clinical trials of BACE inhibitors were either
concluded without bene ﬁt or discontinued owing to futility
or the occurrence of adverse effects. Adverse effects included
early, mild cognitive impairment that was associated with all
but one inhibitor; preliminary results suggest that the cogni-
tive effects are non- progressive and reversible. These discon-
tinuations have raised questions regarding the suitability of
BACE1 as a drug target for AD. In this Perspective, we dis-
cuss the status of BACE inhibitors and suggest ways in which
the results of the discontinued trials can inform the develop-
ment of future clinical trials of BACE inhibitors and related
secretase modulators as preventative therapies. We also pro-
pose a series of experiments that should be performed to
inform ‘go-no- go ’ decisions in future trials with BACE
inhibitors and consider the possibility that low levels of
BACE1 inhibition could avoid adverse effects while achieving
efﬁcacy for AD prevention.

Background: We previously demonstrated that Alzheimer’sd i s -
ease (AD) patients older than 70 years tended to have smaller
medial temporal volumes in the presence of relatively less medial
temporal
18F-ﬂortaucipir-PET uptake compared to younger AD
patients. Transactive response DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-
43) is frequently found in the brains of AD patients and is asso-
ciated with old age and medial temporal atrophy. In this study,
we aimed to determine whether TDP-43 could be contributing
to the mismatch between medial temporal volumes and
ﬂortaucipir-PET uptake in older AD patients.
Methods: Seventy-seven participants (median age at death
79 years [range: 51-99]) from the NIH funded Neurodegener-
ative Research Group or Alzheimer ’s Disease Research Center
at Mayo Clinic, who had completed volumetric MRI and
ﬂortaucipir-PET scans close to death and had postmortem AD
neuropathological change and TDP-43 pathology assessments,
were included in the study. Grey matter volumes and
ﬂortaucipir standard uptake value ratios (SUVRs) were calcu-
lated for the hippocampus, amygdala, entorhinal cortex, infe-
rior temporal cortex, and midfrontal cortex. Bivariate-response
linear regression modelling, adjusted for Braak neuro ﬁbrillary
tangle stage, was used to estimate the effect of age and TDP-
43 on gray matter volume and ﬂortaucipir uptake, and deter-
mine whether TDP-43 effect sizes varied according to age.
Results: After accounting for Braak neuro ﬁbrillary tangle
stage, older individuals tended to have signi ﬁcantly lower
ﬂortaucipir uptake across all regions and lower hippocampal vol-
umes. TDP-43-immunoreactivity was associated with reduced
hippocampus and entorhinal cortical (ERC) volumes but was
unrelated to ﬂortaucipir SUVRs. Notably, the TDP-43 pathol-
ogy effect sizes for the hippocampus and ERC were largely con-
sistent across age, i.e., at any age, TDP-43-positive participants
had signiﬁcantly smaller hippocampal (12% decrease) and ERC
(13% decrease) volumes than TDP -43-negative participants,
suggesting that TDP-43 effect sizes were age-independent. How-
ever, at older ages, the mean volumes in the whole cohort and,
more evidently, in those with dementia moved closer towards
the mean of those with TDP-43 pathology, a ﬁnding likely
attributable to the increasing frequency of TDP-43 with age.
Conclusion: TDP-43 appears to be a major contributor to
the mismatch between ﬂortaucipir uptake and medial tempo-
ral lobe volumes in older AD patients, where lower medial
temporal regional volumes are observed in the presence of
less ﬂortaucipir uptake.
K-S100. Network Proteomic Analysis Identi ﬁes Diverse
Pathophysiological Signatures in the Lewy Body
Dementia Brain
Lenora Higginbotham, MD
1, Eric B. Dammer, PhD 1,
Ananth Shantaraman, PhD 1, Duc M. Duong, BS 1, Luming
Yin, MS1, Alice Chen-Plotkin, MD 2, Edward B. Lee, MD
PhD2, James J. Lah, MD PhD 1, Allan I. Levey, MD PhD 1,
Nicholas T. Seyfried, PhD 1. 1Emory University School of
Medicine, Atlanta, GA, USA, 2Perelman School of Medicine at
the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.
Background: Lewy body dementia (LBD), a class of disorders
comprising Parkinson’s disease dementia (PDD) and dementia
with Lewy bodies (DLB), features aggressive cognitive and neu-
ropsychiatric decline without cure or effective mitigating thera-

pies. Effective biomarkers of t he corticolimbic dysfunction
underlying these devastating symptoms promise to advance the
recognition, monitoring, and treatment of LBD. However, LBD
biomarker discovery is currently hindered by a poor understand-
ing of the molecular processes comprising its corticolimbic
degeneration. Here, we used unbiased co-expression network
proteomic analysis to de ﬁne the systems-based pathophysiology
of the LBD frontal cortex and protein signatures meaningfully
correlated to clinicopathological manifestations of disease.
Methods: Using quantitative liquid chromatography
coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), we ana-
lyzed dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) tissues from
25 control, 29 PDD, and 7 DLB cases derived from a well-
characterized autopsy cohort within the University of Penn-
sylvania Alzheimer ’s Disease Research Center. A tandem mass
tag (TMT) labeling approach combined with sample fraction-
ation enhanced proteomic depth and limited missing values.
Weighted Gene Correlation Network Analysis (WGCNA)
was used to identify and characterize disease-associated co-
expression trends within the proteomic data.
Results: WGCNA generated a proteomic network com-
prised of 9,092 proteins divided into 63 groups or “modules”
of co-expression. Though data-driven in structure, these
modules mapped strongly to different cell types, organelles,
and molecular functions. Two-thirds of these modules were
signiﬁcantly altered in diseased cases and strongly correlated
with one or both LBD diagnoses. Glial and endothelial mod-
ules were among those most prominently elevated across both
PDD and DLB cases. Neuronal modules linked to synaptic,
mitochondrial, and other metabolic processes were signi ﬁ-
cantly decreased in both diseases. Several modules demon-
strated divergent expression trends in PDD and DLB. These
divergent modules were not linked to speci ﬁc cell types and
prominently featured proteins tasked with responding to
aberrant cellular processes, including heat shock molecules
involved in the unfolded protein response and proteins
responsible for DNA damage repair.
Conclusion: Unbiased co-expression network analysis of
the LBD frontal cortex proteome revealed a diverse array of
disease-related pathophysiology, encompassing various cell
types and molecular functions. Key overlapping and diver-
gent protein signatures were identi ﬁed across PDD and DLB.
These results highlight the LBD brain network proteome as a
promising source of biomarkers that could meaningfully
advance disease diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment.

M112. A 55-Year Old Female with Periodic Hypothermia
Caused by a Hypothalamic Cavernoma
Sarah Kendroud, DO , Ahmed Abbas, MD, Alireza Showraki,
MD. Southern Illinois University School of Medicine,
Springﬁeld, IL, USA.
Objective: Hypothalamic cavernomas are very rare, and these
lesions are known to cause hypothalamic dysfunction. This
dysfunction can take the form of "progressive confusion,
decreased level of arousal, hypothermia, and eventual resolu-
tion with a return to baseline" [2]. We present a case of a
female with multiple intracranial cavernomas, some of which
involve the hypothalamus, who presented with one of multi-
ple episodes of hypothermia, hypoglycemia, and altered men-
tal status.
Case Report: A 55-year old female with a history of
hypertension, hyperlipidemia, multiple resected intracranial
cavernomas, complex partial seizures, and bradycardia requir-
ing a pacemaker was brought to the hospital after she became
altered. She suddenly did not know where she was, who her

husband was, or which pills she was supposed to be taking.
At baseline, she is usually oriented to person and place but
not time. Her vitals were signi ﬁcant for hypothermia with a
temperature of 32.3 degrees Celsius. The rest of her lab work
was within normal limits. After her core temperature was
raised to normothermia, her mental status improved. She had
a routine EEG performed, which did not show any seizures
or epileptiform discharges. The patient was unable to obtain
a brain MRI due her pacemaker and VNS, but a head CT
showed stable changes secondary to her cavernomas. In the
outpatient setting, the patient had had an extensive,
unremarkable endocrinological workup, including a morning
cortisol level, IGF-1 and 2, TSH, and insulin level. Upon
further chart review, the patient was found to have had mul-
tiple admissions for altered mental status, hypothermia, and
hypoglycemia. It was postulated by the neurology team that
the cavernomas had caused signi ﬁcant damage to her
hypothalamus.
Discussion: Core body temperature is mediated by the
preoptic nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus. When there is
damage to this particular area, periodic hypothermia can
develop. The cognitive impairment and other neurologic
symptoms seen during hypothermia may be due to the
"reduction in cerebral blood ﬂow that occurs once the body
temperature falls below 33 degrees Celsius ” [2].
Conclusion: Medications shown to be effective as prophy-
laxis against further episodes include Clonidine, Clomipra-
mine, and Cyproheptadine. It is important to recognize this
rare disease entity as a consequence of any insult to the hypo-
thalamus, as patients with this syndrome undergo multiple
tests to rule out other more common mimics, such as seizures
and metabolic derangements.

Artery Dissection Presenting with Horner Syndrome after
Diving
Sarah Kendroud, DO , Andrew Thaliath, MD, Jeremy
Kulacz, MD. Southern Illinois University School of Medicine,

Objective: Carotid and vertebral artery dissections may occur
after minor trauma or spontaneously, whether a patient has
underlying arteriopathy or not. We present a case of right
internal carotid artery (ICA) dissection that occurred after
diving, which has been associated with dissection per limited
case reports in the literature.
Case Report: A 44-year-old female with no past medical
history presented to the emergency department (ED) with
right-eye ptosis and nausea which started earlier that day. She
initially woke up with ptosis of her right eyelid, followed by
nausea, throbbing headache and then left arm and leg

heaviness. One week prior, she had gone diving in Mexico.
On exam, she was found to have right eye ptosis and miosis,
and left leg drift. Head CT and MRI were unremarkable.
MRA demonstrated a right mid-to-distal internal carotid
artery (ICA) dissection. Aspirin and Clopidogrel were started
with a plan for dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) for three
months. A repeat MRA of the head and neck was planned at
follow up to look for dissection resolution.
Discussion: The extracranial portions of the cervical
arteries are vulnerable to dissection due to mobility from
the origin at the carotid bulb to its entry at the base of the
skull and contact with bony structures. Diving requires
neck hyperextension upon ascending and descending,
which itself causes signi ﬁcant local arterial wall stress [2].
Treatment consists of antiplatelet therapy for three to six
months, with follow-up imaging to ensure dis-
section resolution prior to discontinuing therapy, which
usually takes place mostly within the ﬁrst two to three
months after dissection [5].
Conclusion: Diving is a particularly rare cause of intracra-
nial dissection. Any combination of neck pain, headache,
Horner’s syndrome, or cranial neuropathy in a young patient
must prompt consideration of intracranial arterial dissection.
Lack of rapid recognition and treatment can lead to throm-
boembolic strokes.

Background: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome
(RCVS) is a clinical and radiologic condition typically charac-
terized by a combination of thunderclap headache and revers-
ible vasoconstriction. Here we present a unique, and to the
author’s knowledge, the ﬁrst case of an adult male with
RCVS secondary to the concurrent use of cannabis and
aripiprazole.
Case Presentation: A 38-year-old patient presented to the
emergency department with 24 hours of intractable headache.
He also reported blurry vision, tinnitus, photosensitivity, and
bilateral lower limb weakness. He had a long-standing history
of the use of cannabis gummies as over-the-counter pain-
killers and aripiprazole for his mood issues. He had not been
on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), nasal
decongestants, or recreational drug use. His admission MRI
showed ill-de ﬁned areas of increased ﬂair signals localized in
the left posterior cerebellum, posterior left mid pons, and
bilateral posterior parietal lobes. CTA showed alternating ste-
nosis of the anterior cerebral arteries suspicious for reversible
vasoconstriction syndrome. The patient responded well to
intra-arterial verapamil. A repeat MRI 3 days later demon-
strated an improved ﬂair signal in the cerebellum and pons;
however, new tiny foci were observed in bilateral centrum
semiovale, indicating worsening reversible vasoconstrictive
syndrome. CTA was repeated following verapamil infusion,
which revealed complete resolution of vasospasm in the
ascending frontal branches and improved ﬂow in the middle
and anterior cerebral arteries. The patient was advised to stop

cannabis and aripiprazole and prescribed long-term oral
verapamil for headache prevention.
Discussion: In a French cohort, the use of vasoactive
drugs accounted for more than half (55%) of patients with

M116. Always Look on the Bright Side: Associations of
Optimism with Functional Outcomes After Stroke
Kelly L. Sloane, MD , Scott E. Kasner, MD, MSCE, Roy
H. Hamilton, MD, MS, Andrea LC Schneider, MD, PhD.
University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.
Background: Optimism has been linked to positive mental
and physical health outcomes, but its role in stroke recovery
and interaction with depression in this context has not been
well studied.
Objective: To assess the association of optimism and
depression with one-year functional recovery in adults with
stroke.
Methods: This study was a secondary analysis of the
Stroke Recovery in Underserved Populations 2005-2006
Study data. Participants were aged ≥50 years with ﬁrst-time
stroke (N=986) and admitted to an in-patient medical reha-
bilitation facility across the United States and assessed within
72 hours of discharge. Optimism/pessimism was assessed by
response to question “Are you optimistic about the future? ”
Depression was de ﬁned by Center for Epidemiologic Studies
Depression scale (CES-D) score >16. Participants were
dichotomized as optimistic vs. pessimistic and with depres-
sion v. without depression based on responses. The Func-
tional Independence Measure (FIM) total, motor and
cognition scores were used to assess stroke outcomes at hospi-
tal discharge, 3-months post-stroke, and 1-year post-stroke.
Linear mixed models with random intercepts and slopes
(adjusted for age, sex, race, education, sum of medical com-
orbidities, sum of stroke symptoms, sum of hospital compli-
cations) were used to evaluate associations of optimism/
depression groups (optimistic/without depression; optimistic/
with depression; pessimistic/without depression; pessimistic/
with depression) with FIM total and sub-score trajectories.
Results: Participants were a mean age of 68 years, 52%
female, and 75% white. Over the ﬁrst-year post-stroke, the
total FIM score increased in all groups. The pessimistic with
depression group increased by 6.8 (95% CI: 1.2, 12.5) fewer
points than the optimistic without depression group. The
optimistic with depression group and the pessimistic without

depression group had similar total FIM score increases as the
optimistic without depression group (both p>0.05). Similarly,
in the FIM motor sub-score, where the pessimistic with
depression group increased by 5.2 (95% CI: 0.6, 9.8) fewer
points than the optimistic without depression group, but the
optimistic with depression group and the pessimistic without
depression group had similar FIM motor sub-score increases
as the optimistic without depression group (both p>0.05).
There were no differences between optimism/depression
groups for the FIM cognition sub-score (all p>0.05).
Conclusions: Pessimism in combination with depression,
but not pessimism or depression alone, was associated with
worse functional outcomes one-year post-stroke. These ﬁndings
suggest the importance of considering optimism and depression
as distinct contributors to functional recovery after stroke.

Background: Atrial ﬁbrillation (AF) is responsible for
30-50% of strokes with large vessel occlusion that are treated
with endovascular thrombectomy (EVT). Underutilization of
anticoagulation (AC) is a common and preventable source of
AF-related stroke. Here, we evaluate AC underutilization in
AF patients with stroke, comparing those that did and did
not require EVT to determine if AC underutilization dispro-
portionately results in large vessel occlusion.
Methods: A single-center retrospective cohort included
consecutive patients with a known history of AF admitted to
the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania with ischemic
stroke between 2016 and 2021. Patients were categorized
based on pre-admission antithrombotic medication use: anti-
platelet, anticoagulation, or nothing. Pre-admission anti-
thrombotic use was compared between patients that
underwent EVT and those that did not. When applicable,
the reason for not being on AC was abstracted from the med-
ical record, and patients were categorized as either good or
bad AC candidates (bad AC candidates suffered a prior life-
threatening hemorrhage). Discharge antithrombotics were
abstracted.
Results: 645 patients with AF were admitted with ische-
mic stroke during the study period, 213 of whom underwent
EVT. Comparing AF patients based on EVT status, those
who required EVT were more likely to not be taking any
antithrombotics prior to admission (33% vs 24%, p=0.01) or
have subtherapeutic INR on admission if they were on warfa-
rin (83% vs 61%; p=0.02). Among the AF-EVT patients,
95 (45%) patients were on pre-admission AC, 46 (22%)
were on pre-admission antiplatelet, and 71 (33%) were on
no antithrombotics. Of those on AC, 20% were taking war-
farin and 78% were taking a direct oral anticoagulant

M118. Association Between Cerebral Small Vessel
Disease, Blood Brain Barrier Disruption, and Outcome
After Stroke
Derrick N. Okine, BA , Kyle Kern, MD, Marie Luby, PhD,
Marco Egle, PhD, Rebecca F. Gottesman, MD, PhD. National
Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, Bethesda,
MD, USA.
Background: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) in
patients with acute ischemic stroke is associated with worse
clinical outcomes. We hypothesized that this association is
mediated by increased blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption
as indicated by the hyperintense acute reperfusion
marker (HARM).
Methods: We assessed whether WMH at presentation was
associated with HARM in the prospectively collected Lesion
Evolution in Stroke and Ischemia on Neuroimaging
(LESION) study, a cohort of 213 acute ischemic stroke
patients with NIHSS>4 or who received tPA and were
imaged with MRI<24 hours from stroke onset. As part of the
study, WMH were evaluated on baseline FLAIR MRI scans
as absent, minor, or moderate-severe; HARM was evaluated
for presence and severity on FLAIR at 2 or 24 hours after
administration of gadolinium. Using binomial and multino-
mial logistic regression, we evaluated the association between
WMH category and HARM, adjusted in sequential models
for demographics, vascular risk factors, and stroke characteris-
tics. Additionally, we used structural equation models to eval-
uate mediation of the association between WMH and
discharge NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) by HARM. We evalu-
ated effect modi ﬁcation by acute intervention (IV tPA or
thrombectomy) or stroke severity (NIHSS score ≥ vs<10).
Results: Patients were on average 70 years old, 54% female;
WMH was absent in 47%, mild in 37%, and moderate-severe
in 16%. HARM was absent in 39%, minor in 33%, severe
focal in 15%, severe diffuse in 13%, and combined severe dif-
fuse and focal in 7%. Moderate-severe WMH was associated
with elevated risk of severe focal and/or severe diffuse HARM
(OR:3.37, 95%CI: 1.45-7.81), with loss of statistical signi ﬁ-
cance with multivariable adjustment. Similarly, moderate-
severe WMH vs no WMH was associated with an elevated
risk for severe diffuse HARM but not for severe focal or minor
HARM (demographic-adjusted OR:5.13, 95%CI: 1.21,
21.76), but was no longer signi ﬁcant after adjustment for
vascular risk factors and stroke characteristics. Neither use of
an acute intervention nor stroke severity impacted the associa-
tion between WMH categories and presence of HARM. In a
mediation analysis, roughly 21% of the association between
WMH and discharge NIHSS was explained by HARM.
Conclusion: Our ﬁndings suggest a possible association
between severe diffuse HARM and WMH, although it ’s pri-

marily driven by demographic and vascular risk factors. Some
of WMH ’s effect on post-stroke outcome may be mediated
through BBB disruption. Further studies are needed to evalu-
ate other contributors to stroke outcome.
M119. Basilar Artery Occlusion Initially Presenting as
Worsening Headache Illustrates the Value of CT
Angiography in the Work Up of Acute Onset Secondary
Headache
Peyton Murin, B.S. , Emad Alghazo, M.D., Balaji Krishnaiah,
M.D.. University of Tennessee Health Science Center, Memphis,
TN, USA.
Basilar artery occlusion (BAO) is a rare but a serious form of
cerebrovascular event, comprising 1% of total strokes and
20% of ischemic strokes. (Kwak & Park, 2020; van der
Hoeven et al., 2013) Despite their rarity, BA occlusion is
amongst the most life-threatening medical conditions, with a
morbidity and mortality rate of nearly 70%. (Schonewille
et al., 2009; Singer et al., 2015; van der Hoeven et al., 2013)
The clinical diagnosis of BA occlusions is dif ﬁcult because
the symptoms are often non-speci ﬁc (headache and vertigo)
and do not lateralize as is typical in most types of ischemic
strokes. Despite this lack of speci ﬁc symptomology, the pri-
mary means of diagnosis of BA occlusion remains clinical,
though imaging ﬁndings can help with diagnosis. CT angio-
gram (CTA) of the head and neck is the imaging of choice
for diagnosis, with the Pc-ASPECTs score indicative of post-
treatment outcome. (Puetz et al., 2008) In this case, we pre-
sent a patient with a distal basilar artery occlusion whose pre-
senting symptom was acute onset severe headache and
mental status change. The patient received the standard non-
contrast CT head (NCCT) which was read as negative. High
clinical suspicion allowed for further review of NCCT reveal-
ing a potential dense basilar sign, and as a direct result CTA
being ordered allowing for the diagnosis of a BA occlusion.

M121. Case Report: Cardioembolic Stroke as a
Presenting Symptom of Peripartum Cardiomyopathy
Caleb Lee, MD , Nikita Jain, MD, Tamra Ranasinghe, MD,
Christine Condon, MD. Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist
Neurology, Winston Salem, NC, USA.
Introduction: Pregnancy associated peripartum left ventricu-
lar (LV) dysfunction is an uncommon but life-threatening
condition that develops in 1-4/1000 live births. While most
women typically present with systemic symptoms of heart
failure; thromboembolic events can rarely be the presenting
symptom. Systemic and pulmonary venous thromboembolic
events are thought to occur at an incidence of 20-40%
among women with peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM),
while cardioembolic strokes occur at a much lower incidence
of 5% among these patients.
Case Presentation: A 34-year-old female with a history of
hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, and a cesarean
section (3 weeks prior) at 37 weeks without complication
presented with confusion and unintelligible speech. Her ini-
tial NIHSS was 7 for severe expressive aphasia. She was
14 hours from last known normal. CT head demonstrated a
loss of grey-white differentiation in the left insular cortex

with no hemorrhage. CT angiography visualized a left M2
thrombus with a 25 mL penumbra in the corresponding ter-
ritory with no appreciable core infarct on perfusion imaging.
Patient underwent a mechanical thrombectomy with mTICI
2C reperfusion. MRI brain demonstrated multiple acute
infarcts in the left MCA territory with an additional punctate
infarct in the right occipital lobe. Transthoracic echocardio-
gram demonstrated LV ejection fraction 30-35%, global LV
hypokinesis with no LV thrombus and no patent foramen
ovale. Cardiac MRI did not visualize an intracardiac throm-
bus. Hypercoagulable panel was within normal limits, urine
toxicology was negative, and telemetry was without arrhyth-
mias. The cardiology service was engaged to discuss the
appropriate antithrombotic therapy, and the patient was
started on aspirin 81 mg. Further she was initiated on car-
vedilol, spironolactone, and losartan and discharged home
with out-patient speech therapy. A 14 day cardiac event
monitor did not capture atrial ﬁbrillation. She was followed
in stroke and cardiology clinics at regular intervals over the
past 6 months and has done well without further thrombo-
embolic events on discharged medication regimen.
Conclusion: Although cardioembolic strokes secondary to
PPCM are exceedingly rare, providers should be aware of this
extremely important life threatening complication. There is a
paucity of data on initiating therapeutic anticoagulation for
secondary stroke prevention in PPCM without an intracar-
diac thrombus. More de ﬁnitive guidance is needed regarding
the use of antithrombotic therapy in this highly vulnerable
patient population with PPCM and embolic strokes.

M125. Convulsive Syncope Caught Red-Handed on
Video Electroencephalography! Neurological
Manifestations of a Cardiac Etiology
Dhwani Oza, MD
1, Ridham Patel, MD 2, Naeem Mahfooz,
MD1. 1University of Toledo, Toledo, OH, USA, 2Trinity
Health - St Mary Mercy, Livonia, MI, USA.
Introduction: Convulsive syncope or complex vasovagal syn-
cope is a variant of syncope that is accompanied by tonic
activity, occurring in about 10% of patients. Pain and phobic
stress during invasive procedures can trigger an increase in
parasympathetic tone, leading to bradycardia and rarely
asystole. Asystole is thought to be secondary to complete
withdrawal of sympathetic activity. The neurological sequelae
caused by cerebral hypoperfusion can manifest as ﬂattening
of electroencephalography waves, often mistaken for epilepsy.
We were fortunate to catch a rare occurrence live in action.
Case Description: A 17-year-old female presented to the
emergency department (ED) due to multiple incidences of
loss of consciousness for 2 weeks, with possible seizure-like-
activity. She experienced two witnessed episodes in the ED,
described as generalized tonic-clonic movements while getting
lumbar puncture and venous cannulation (IV). Patient was
admitted for video electroencephalography (vEEG) given the
presentation with seizure-like activity. Next morning, patient
reported prodromal symptoms including lightheadedness,
diaphoresis and vision loss while getting IV ﬁxed. Within a
few seconds, patient had central cyanosis, eye deviation and
full body twitching. Patient went into cardiac asystole for
15 seconds and vEEG showed brain ﬂat lining 5 seconds into
the asystole and return of neuronal activity after 8 seconds.
Asystole resolved spontaneously and patient was started on
ﬂudrocortisone for vasovagal syncope given acute onset of
cardiac dysfunction with possible future consideration of car-
diac pacemaker if symptoms persist.
Discussion: During syncopal events, electroencephalogra-

phy (EEG) usually demonstrates generalized slowing followed
by high-voltage frontal delta activity. It is theorized that the
ﬂattening of the EEG is based on the severity and duration
of cerebral hypoperfusion that occurs after asystole and it is
the stage where nonepileptic, seizure-like movements are
often described. Cerebral hypoxia can cause loss of cortical
inhibition of normally suppressed brainstem activity; known
as brainstem release phenomena. The loss of inhibition leads
to a brief episode of non-epileptic pathological myoclonus.
Typically, diagnosis can be made from history of cardiac
manifestations, however it can easily be misdiagnosed as epi-
lepsy in the acute settings. The brainstem release phenome-
non has been demonstrated in studies where patients
underwent a head-upright tilt table test with continuous elec-
troencephalographic recording.
Conclusion: This case provides a live demonstration of
the association between asystole and EEG ﬂattening and
exempliﬁes the importance of considering a cardiac etiology
in patients presenting with paroxysmal episodes of seizure-
like-activity.

M129. Dural Venous Sinus Thrombosis in Pediatric Age
Group with Severe Iron De ﬁciency Anemia
Surya Suresh, MBBS
1, Neena Viswanathan, MD 2, Himali

Tampa, FL, USA, 3Pediatric Epilepsy and Neurology Specialists,
University of South Florida, Tampa, FL, USA.
Introduction: Dural Venous Sinus Thrombosis (DVST) is
an uncommon but a critical diagnosis among pediatric age
groups. DVST in neonatal period is well documented but
childhood and adolescent DVST is less recognized in the
medical literature due to the rarity and underdiagnosis. We
present a case of dural venous sinus thrombosis in a 17-year-
old female with severe iron de ﬁciency anemia.
Case Report: A 17 year old right-handed female presented
with vomiting for 1-month, right hemibody weakness for
2 days and new onset tonic seizures involving the right upper
and lower extremities without alteration of awareness. Denies
headache or vision changes. On examination, mentation and
cranial nerves were intact, muscle strength was 4/5 in right
hemibody with 3+ re ﬂexes and sustained clonus in right
ankle. Initial investigations were notable for hemoglobin of
5.3 g/dL(very low), hematocrit of 21.6% (low), Iron satura-
tion of 4.7% (low), total iron-binding capacity of 384 mg/dL
(high), serum ferritin of 5.3mg/L (low) and mean cell volume
of 51 fL (low). EEG indicated left central onset clinical and
subclinical seizures. MRI brain revealed acute left parietal
venous infarct with sagittal venous thrombosis extending into
the right transverse sinus. Digital subtraction angiography
showed complete occlusion of superior sagittal sinus and
bilateral transverse sinus. Emergency mechanical
thrombectomy was performed with recanalization of bilateral
transverse sinus. Anticoagulation with Lovenox 1mg/kg twice
daily followed by coumadin was initiated 24 hours after sur-
gery. Despite extensive DVST, the patient ’s symptoms
improved signi ﬁcantly, and she was discharged without com-
plications. Follow up hematology evaluation did not reveal
any abnormalities in von Willebrand Factor, anti-beta2- gly-
coprotein, anti-cardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, protein C/S
levels, antithrombin III activity, Factor II or V Leiden muta-
tion and prothrombin gene mutation.
Discussion: Iron deﬁciency anemia is a common but over-
looked risk factor for DVST in the adolescent age group. It is
necessary to maintain a high index of suspicion for DVST even
if the patient does not have a history of more recognized etiolo-
gies such as CNS infection or prothrombotic states. It is also
important to be aware of the various presentations of DVST in
children that can range from acute onset neurological decline to
non-speciﬁc symptoms that can gradually progress.
Conclusion: We intend to highlight the importance of
increased clinical suspicion of DVST among patients with
iron deﬁciency anemia due to variable presentation of the cat-
astrophic condition.
M130. Early Stroke Recurrence is Reduced by Prior
Statin Therapy in the Point Trial Population
James R. Brorson, MD , Natalie Bourand, B.A. (expected).
The University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA.

Objective: To discern effects of baseline statin treatment on
early stroke recurrence in the POINT trial.
Background: Beneﬁts of statin therapy in reducing risk of
ischemic stroke over the long-term are well-established, but
the immediate effects of statin therapy on early stroke recur-
rence after an initial ischemic event are less clear.
Design/Methods: In secondary analysis of the data of the
Platelet Oriented Inhibition in New TIA and Minor Ische-
mic Stroke (POINT) trial, we evaluated whether there were
effects of pre-treatment with statins on early stroke recurrence
within 7 days of randomization, differentiated from effects of
ongoing statin treatment on later recurrence events over the
90 day duration of the trial. Cox proportional hazard regres-
sion analysis was used to examine statin effects on recurrence
rates over the ﬁrst 7 days of the trial and over the entire trial
duration, and logistic regression was applied to test whether
statin pre-treatment independently reduced dichotomized risk
of recurrence within 7 days.
Results: In the POINT trial, most recurrences of ischemic
stroke were early, with 175 occurring within 7 days of trial
entry, and only 105 occurring over the remainder of the
90 day trial. 39% of POINT trial participants were on statin
treatment at time of entry, while by the 7 day visit, 79%
were on statin therapy. In Cox proportional hazard analysis
over the 90 day trial period, concurrent statin use reduced
stroke recurrence risk (H.R. 0.74, C.I. 0.56 - 0.98, p = 0.03)
but baseline statin treatment on stroke did not have signi ﬁ-
cant effect. In an analysis that focused only on the initial
7 day period following trial entry, baseline statin had a near-
signiﬁcant protective effect on ischemic stroke occurrence
(HR = 0.74, C.I. 0.54 - 1.01, p = 0.06). Logistic regression
analysis comparing subjects dichotomized between those hav-
ing early ischemic stroke recurrence within 7 days of trial ran-
domization and those not having early recurrence showed
that pre-treatment with statin was independently associated
with decreased risk of early recurrence of ischemic stroke
(OR 0.70, C.I. 0.50 - 0.99, p < 0.05).
Conclusion: In the POINT trial population of patients
with minor ischemic stroke or TIA, baseline statin treatment
was associated with decreased risk of the early (7-day) recur-
rence of ischemic stroke.

M133. Hyperhomocysteinemia and Large-Vessel Stroke in
the Young
John Paul B. Aparece, MD
1, Revanth Pasupuleti, MBBS 2,
Sanjana Prakash, MBBS 3. 1Cebu Institute of Medicine, Cebu
City, Philippines, 2Kakatiya Medical College, Warangal, India,
3JJM Medical College, Davanagere, India.
Homocysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid formed by
the metabolic branching point between the transsulfuration
and remethylation pathways of methionine metabolism. Ele-
vations in plasma homocysteine levels are known to increase
the risk of vascular diseases even in apparently healthy indi-
viduals. In this case report, we present a previously healthy
27-year-old Indian male, who presented with sudden onset
left hemiparesis and slurring of speech. Computed tomogra-
phy and magnetic resonance imaging revealed acute
multifocal infarcts in the middle cerebral artery territory with
mass effect, and segments of right internal carotid artery ste-
nosis. Additional workup revealed markedly elevated serum
homocysteine levels at 166 μmol/L (normal <15 μmol/L)
and the presence of a lupus-like anticoagulant, an autoanti-
body that disrupts and prolongs the clotting process. Genetic
studies showed a homozygous mutation of the MTHFR
(methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase) gene, the most com-
monly implicated loci in hyperhomocysteinemia. Risk factors
for stroke in young adults are complex and inherently
different from classic risk factors seen in adults. The associa-
tion between markedly elevated homocysteine levels in a
homozygous MTHFR mutation carrier and a positive lupus-
like anticoagulant is rarely reported. This case report high-
lights the hypercoagulable state in hyperhomocysteinemia
that eventually lead to a large artery stroke in the young.

Adrian Rodriguez-Hernandez, MD
1, Denis Babici, MD 1,
Maryellen Campbell, BA 1, Octavio Carranza-Renteria, MD 1,

Background: We present a unique case of an adult who
experienced a transient acute hemineglect syndrome second-
ary to severe hypoglycemia.

as a stroke alert. Per EMS, the initial ﬁngerstick glucose level
was undetectable. He was given 200ml of 10% glucose solu-
tion. The neurology stroke service assessed the patient upon
arrival. His ﬁngerstick glucose level was 83. The patient volun-
tarily turned his head to the right to answer questions when
addressed on the left. The speech was non dysarthric and he
was able to recall his age and date appropriately. Gaze assess-
ment revealed he was unable to cross the midline from right to
left. His oculocephalic re ﬂex was intact. Visual ﬁeld testing
revealed left-sided homonymous hemianopia. Sensation was
diminished on his left-sided extremities, although he actively
moved all extremities against gravity. During the National
Institute of Health Stroke Scale, he described only the right
side of the “cookie theft picture ” and was able to recall some
objects from to the right of the “object chart ”.W h e n
prompted to read, he skipped the sentences ’ initial words. The
extinction and neglect assessment revealed left-sided extinction
on double tactile and visual stimulation. Computed tomogra-
phy (CT) of the brain was normal. CT perfusion of the brain
showed a perfusion decrease in the right cortical area without
large vessel occlusion on CT angiography of the neck and
brain. Brain magnetic resonance imaging did not reveal any
areas of restricted diffusion or FLAIR abnormalities. The
patient’s insulin regimen was recently changed by his primary
care physician. The following day the patient was back at his
baseline and able to recall the whole episode.
Discussion: Our patient was well oriented, but the repeated
turning of his head to the right in search of us lead us to be
highly suspicious of hemineglect syndrome. Patients with
neglect lack weakness of their eye or limb muscles yet fail to
direct their gaze or hands to explore contralateral space. Hypo-
glycemia is a prevalent complication of anti-glycemic medica-
tions in patients with diabetes, and acute hypoglycemia may
mimic acute ischemic stroke. Imaging ﬁndings in hypoglyce-
mia typically describe bilateral cortical or subcortical changes
on CT or MRI. Few cases have described hypoglycemia-
induced focal cerebral hypoperfusion. Hypoglycemia should be
included in the differential diagnosis for acute neurological
impairment including hemineglect; may not have an immedi-

M135. Intravenous Immunoglobulin Therapy (IvIg)
Induced Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy
Syndrome (PRES)
Shaweta Khosa, MBBS
1, Gurveer Singh Khosa, M.B.B.S. 2,
Shri Kant Mishra, M.D. 1, Neal Rao, M.D. 1, Robert
Freundlich, M.D. 1. 1Olive View-UCLA Medical Center,
Sylmar, CA, USA, 2Indira Gandhi Medical College and
Hospital, Shimla, India.
Objective: To describe a rare case of intravenous immuno-
globulin therapy (IvIg) induced Posterior reversible encepha-
lopathy syndrome (PRES).
Background: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syn-
drome (PRES) is a rare neuro-clinical syndrome characterized
by reversible subcortical vasogenic brain edema caused by
endothelial dysfunction. Clinical presentations in PRES can
include wide variety of neurological manifestations including
headaches, focal neurological de ﬁcits, seizures, visual distur-
bances and encephalopathy.
Methods: We present a 56-year-old female with past medi-
cal history of immune mediated necrotizing myopathy who was
admitted to the hospital for dysphagia and muscle weakness.
Patient was treated with steroids, mycophenolate mofetil and
IVIg (2gm/kg). Hospital course was complicated by new onset
blurry vision and right sided weakness after IVIG infusion.
Results: Cranial nerve examination was normal except for
inconsistent responses to visual ﬁeld testing. Normal pupillary
reﬂex and spontaneous extraocular eye movements were noted.
Motor examination was signi ﬁcant for new onset 0/5 strength
in right upper and lower extremity. Sensory examination rev-
ealed hemineglect, ﬁnger agnosia, R-L disorientation and
diminished sensations in lower extremities and right. Initial CT
head and CTA head and neck was normal. MRI brain/MRA
head showed multiple areas of diffusion restriction involving
the bilateral cerebral hemispheres. There were also noted multi-
ple smaller punctate areas of diffusion restriction seen involving
the bifrontal lobes, bilateral parietal lobes and septal lobes.
Patient underwent lumbar puncture which showed normal
CSF studies. Echocardiogram was normal with no PFO.
Repeat MRI showed interval development of PRES sup-
erimposed over previously seen bilateral multifocal infarcts
along with new infarcts. MRA showed worsening of alternating
focal dilatations and constrictions in the anterior circulation.
Patient was treated with intravenous magnesium sulfate and
oral nimodipine. Repeat MRA after treatment with CCB and
Magnesium demonstrated signi ﬁcant improvement in appear-
ance of intracranial vasculature with previously seen diffuse
arterial narrowing and irregularity no longer visible. Patient
reported improvement in her symptoms of upper extremity
weakness and vision and currently doing well on follow up.
Conclusion: IvIg can lead to serious adverse effects such as
renal impairment, thrombosis, hemolytic anemia,
transfusion-related acute lung injury, arrhythmia and aseptic
meningitis. However, there are only a very few cases of IvIg
induced PRES reported so far with very little information
about the pathophysiology. Symptoms can appear within
hours of treatment or latency of days. Hence, PRES should
be considered in patient with recent history of IvIg infusion
and new neurological signs especially visual disturbances.
M136. Is It Time to Establish Pregnancy Associated
Stroke Clinics? A Case Report Discussing the Importance
of Monitoring Factor Xa Levels in Pregnant Stroke
Patients
Nikita Jain, MD , Caleb J. Lee, MD, Tamra Ranasinghe,

MD. Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist, Winston Salem,
NC, USA.
Background: Acute strokes are associated with a high rate of
maternal mortality and have an incidence rate of 4-67 per
100000 deliveries. The highest risk of recurrent stroke is seen
in the third trimester and up to 6 weeks postpartum period.
Choice of antithrombotic therapy is made challenging as risk
of recurrence must be weighed against risk of side effects in
mother and fetus. The use of anticoagulation, speci ﬁcally low
molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is recommended in cer-
tain high-risk conditions and can be considered in patients
with a patent foramen ovale (PFO) at risk of venous throm-
bosis. Serum factor Xa levels are used to monitor the ef ﬁcacy
of LMWH dosing with a therapeutic range of 0.7-1.2
u/ml. When regularly monitored, over 50% of patients have
been found to be subtherapeutic.
Case History: A 35-year-old (16-weeks) pregnant woman
presented with acute onset right-sided visual loss. On exam
she had an isolated right homonymous hemianopia. The CT
brain showed a hypodensity in the left occipital lobe. MR
angiogram revealed a left posterior cerebral artery (PCA) P2
segment occlusion and MRI brain conclusively noted an
infarct in the left PCA territory. Her transthoracic echocar-
diogram showed a right-to-left shunt, duplexes and pelvic
MR were negative for deep vein thrombosis. Hypercoagulable
labs were within normal limits. Her Risk of Paradoxical
Embolism score (RoPE) was 9 suggestive of 88% chance that
the stroke is due to a PFO. Given the high RoPE-score in
the setting of a possible pregnancy-induced hypercoagulable
status she was started on weight based LMWH. She con-
tinues to follow in the vascular neurology and obstetrics
clinics where serial factor Xa levels are being monitored. She
was initiated on Aspirin by obstetrics for preeclampsia pro-
phylaxis. Following delivery percutaneous closure of her PFO
will be considered.
Conclusion: There is currently limited evidence available
pertaining to secondary stroke prevention in pregnancy asso-
ciated stroke (PAS) patients. In such patients on anti-
coagulation, it is imperative for providers to monitor factor
Xa levels regularly to ensure the weight adjusted dose remains
therapeutic. Given the signi ﬁcant mortality and morbidity
associated with pregnancy we propose the need for a PAS
clinic to be established in institutes where obstetricians and
vascular neurologists can provide individualized comprehen-
sive health care together.

M139. Left Ventricular Non-Compaction: An Uncommon
Cause of Cardoembolic Stroke
Nelson P. Douglass, MD , Jordan Maury, BA, Juebin Huang,
MD. University of Mississippi Medical Center, Jackson,
MS, USA.
Introduction: Left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC) is a
rare, usually congenital or hereditary cardiomyopathy. The for-
mation of deep trabecular recesses increases the likelihood of a
thrombus entering the systemic vasculature which may cause
cardioembolic stroke. Clinical manifestations of LVNC range
from asymptomatic to severe heart failure, thromboembolic
events, and sudden death. In adults, individuals with LVNC
have a 21 - 38% chance of developing a cardioembolic stroke.
Case Presentation: We present a case of a 29-year-old Afri-
can American female, six weeks postpartum with a history of
cleft palate, right sixth nerve palsy, and recent Covid-19 infec-
tion who developed stroke-like symptoms of left side numbness
and weakness, left side facial droop and slurred speech
upon awakening. On initial examination, the patient dis-
played 4/5 strength and decrea sed sensation to pinprick in
left upper and lower extremities as well as left lower facial
palsy and dysarthria. CT head without contrast revealed a
large infarct in the right middle cerebral artery (MCA) ter-
ritory. A brain MRI con ﬁrmed the right MCA infarct but

did not reveal acute infarct in other vascular territory.
CTA head/neck reported right MCA proximal M2 seg-
ment occlusion. During ad mission, stroke work-up
included a normal EKG. A transthoracic echocardiography
(TTE) with bubble study was obtained which reported no
patent foramen ovale but with severely reduced systolic
function with a LVEF estimat ed 15-20%; questionable
right ventricle apical thromb us was also suspected. Cardi-
ology was consulted for acute systolic heart failure with
plans to initiate goal directed medical therapy. A cardiac
MRI was recommended which revealed left ventricle
increased trabeculations meeting MRI criteria for LVNC,
but no cardiac thrombus was detected. Patient was started
on warfarin with enoxaparin br idging for secondary stroke
prevention.
Discussion: Given our case ’s young age of onset of stroke
and the history of postpartum and recent COVID-19 infec-
tion, cardioembolic stroke due to other more common etiolo-
gies such as hypercoagulable disorders, postpartum
cardiomyopathy or COVID-19 associated cardiomyopathy
were initially suspected based on the initial TTE ﬁndings.
Subsequent cardiac MRI revealed LVNC as an unusual cause
of her cardioembolic stroke. This case illustrates the impor-
tance of thoroughly investigating the potential management-
changing causes of stroke, including congenital structural car-
diac abnormalities, in patients with young age of onset.

for LSE. When LSE concurs with APLS, anticoagulation is
recommended as a secondary thromboprophylaxis for APLS.

sion, coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease, and
bilateral lower extremity DVT on apixaban 5 mg BID pres-
ented with sudden onset dysarthria and right hemiparesis.

M141. Neuroradiological and Electroencephalographic
Changes Following COVID-19 Diagnosis in Patients at
OLSU-S

Junaid Ansari, MD. Louisiana State University Health Sciences
Shreveport, Shreveport, LA, USA.
Objective: To determine the spectrum of neuroradiological
and electroencephalographic changes amongst COVID-19
patients admitted to Ochsner-Louisiana State University
Health Sciences Center, Shreveport (OLSU-S) after SARS-
CoV-2 positive results.
Background: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) cau-
sed by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2
(SARS-CoV-2) is known to manifest with a variety of neuro-
logical complications. A spectrum of neuroradiological and
electroencephalographic changes have been associated with
COVID-19.
Methods: We conducted a retrospective, observational
study of hospitalized adult patients (age > 18 years) admitted
to OLSU-S with laboratory con ﬁrmed SARS-CoV-2. All clin-
ical data was reviewed including clinical features, neuroradio-
logical and electroencephalographic ﬁndings, hospital
management and course from 239 patients hospitalized for
COVID-19 management at OLSU-S between March
15, 2020 to March 15, 2021.
Results: Of the 239 patients evaluated in this study,
85 patients underwent neuroimaging. CT head without contrast
was the most common neuroimaging modality followed by
MRI brain, CT head and neck angiogram and electroencepha-
lography. The most frequent CT ﬁndings were microvascular
changes in 18 of 63 (28.57%) patients followed by atrophy and
atherosclerotic changes. Large vessel occlusion seen on CT
angiogram was present in 15 patients in suspected stroke cases.
The most common MRI brain ﬁndings included microvascular

and small vessel changes seen in 7 of 23 (30.43%) patients
followed by ischemic processes. 12 patients out of the total had
new onset seizure-like activity and underwent EEG. 10 of the
12 patients (83.3%) were found to have abnormal EEG ﬁnd-
ings including non-speciﬁc changes, moderate to severe enceph-
alopathy (41%) and EEGs abnormalities with epileptogenic
potential (41%). Patients with new onset seizures with abnormal
EEG had rapidly declining clinical progression and passed away
within 2 weeks of the hospital visit.
Conclusions: Patients with COVID-19 admitted to
OLSU-S presented with a wide range of neuroradiological and
electroencephalographic changes. Cerebrovascular disease was
the most common COVID-19 associated neuroradiological
diagnosis. Additionally, there is low incidence of abnormal
EEG ﬁndings which correlates with poor outcome. Given the
small number of patients evaluated using EEG in this study,
these ﬁndings are limited and should be further evaluated.

abnormalities and supports previously proposed autosomal
dominant inheritance with variable penetrance. Furthermore,

high surgical morbidity. Existing validated models, including

can predict future LTME. However, to effectively impact clini-
cal care, providers need easy and immediate access to personal-
ized model predictions. We will pilot an automatic email
delivery system of individualized LTME risk predictions and
evidence-based guidelines to the clinical team of patients with
large MCA stroke. In this single-center study, we will collect
preliminary data to gain feedback and determine the effect of
automatic risk prediction on clinical practice. We will explore
which features of our personalized tool are well received and
identify areas for improvement. Patients with large MCA
stroke will be screened by our research staff and clinical data
will be recorded. Clinical practitioners will receive an automati-
cally produced email 24 hours after last seen well (LSW) out-
lining their patient ’s risk of LTME using the validated
EDEMA score. They will also be provided with education on
best practices for management based on updated clinical
guidelines. We will conduct structured surveys and use logistic
regression for ordinal data to test the association of email fea-
tures on the outcome of self-reported risk tool utility. We will

also conduct semi-structured interviews and code material
using grounded theory method to subjectively assess if pro-
viders believe that the intervention had an in ﬂuence on patient
care and future practice. Finally, we will report imaging fre-
quency, time to medical and surgical management, and time
to family discussions in providers who received our risk assess-
ment tool versus providers from a historic group of 30 large
MCA stroke patients (2019-2021) who did not have access to
this risk assessment tool. Our results will help inform future
delivery of tailored quantitative risk assessments for clinical
decision making in both LTME after stroke and for other
acute neurologic conditions.

M148. Poor Glycemic Control is Associated with Worse
Blood-Brain Barrier Disruption in Ischemic Stroke
Patients
Richard Leigh, MD , Andreia V. Faria, MD, PhD. Johns
Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA.
Background: Elevated serum glucose is known to be associ-
ated with worse outcome after ischemic stroke. We previ-
ously identi ﬁed an association between elevated glucose levels
and increased disruption of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) in
patients presenting with acute ischemic stroke. We sought to
conﬁrm this ﬁnding in a separate, larger cohort.
Methods: This was a retrospective analysis of a de-
identiﬁed dataset of stroke patients admitted to a single com-
prehensive stroke center over a 10-year period. Patients were
included if they had MRI performed with diffusion weighted
imaging (DWI) demonstrating a stroke and perfusion
weighted imaging (PWI) that showed a corresponding area of
hypoperfusion. BBB disruption was measured from the PWI
source images, detected as gadolinium leakage into the brain
parenchyma and averaged within the perfusion de ﬁcit. Serum
glucose was measured on presentation, glyco-hemaglobin
(HgA1c) was measured as part of their clinical evaluation,
and a history of diabetes mellitus (DM) was determined
based on chart review. BBB disruption was compared with
clinical and radiologic variables using linear regression.
Results: 238 patients were included in the analysis how-
ever samples sizes varied based on available data. The median
age was 61 and 45% were women. More severe BBB disrup-
tion was associated with larger stroke volume (p<0.001,
n=238), higher NIHSS (p<0.001, n=163), and higher serum
glucose (p=0.044, n=185) but not age (p=0.495, n=238), sex
(p=0.466, n=238) or history of DM (p=0.660, n=238).
Higher HgA1c level showed a trend for worse BBB disrup-
tion (p=0.095, n=186) and was included in the multivariate
analysis. Elevated serum glucose remained associated with
increased BBB disruption (p=0.012, n=155) when control-
ling for stroke volume (p<0.001) and NIHSS (p=0.209).
Higher HgA1c was associated with more severe BBB disrup-
tion (p=0.008, n=158) when controlling for stroke volume
(p<0.001) and NIHSS (p=0.042). Serum glucose and HgA1c
were not independent of each other when added to the same
model.
Conclusions: Poor glycemic control at the time of, and
leading up to, an ischemic stroke is associated with more
severe BBB disruption within the ischemic lesion indepen-
dent of stroke lesion size or clinical severity. BBB disruption

may represent a marker, or potentially a target, for treatments
aimed at diminishing the negative impact of hyperglycemia
on stroke outcomes.

Background: Fabry disease (FD) is the second most com-
mon lysosomal storage disorder. This disorder affects many
systems including the cardiac, renal, and nervous systems.
The pulvinar sign (PS) is a relatively common sign seen in
patients with FD. The PS is a bilateral, symmetrical pulvinar
high signal relative to the signal intensity seen on
unenhanced T1-weighted brain MR imaging.
Methods: We conducted a systematic review with metanal-
ysis to analyze the pool prevalence of the disorder. We used
the Meta-analysis of Observational Studies in Epidemiology(
Moose) Guidelines and Preferred Reporting Items for System-
atic Reviews and Meta-Analyses(PRISMA) Protocol for this
systematic review and Robins 1 to assess the Bias of the study.
To analyze the pool prevalence, we used the “Open Meta-Anal-
ysis” software. We used "Review Manager 5.4" to analyze the
odds ratio between patients with and without the PS and
patients with and without stroke among patients with FD.
Results: We gathered 12 studies from 2003 to 2021 for
the analysis of this study. The pool prevalence of the study
was 0.146 (0.076-0.217) (62/385 cases) with a 95% CI
(0.0945 - 0.415) (P<0.01). The prevalence was much higher
in males (59 cases) than in females (3 cases). There was no
relationship between the pulvinar sign and patients with
stroke among patients with Fabry disease. Odds ratio 1.97
95% CI (0.35-11.21), P = 0.44; Tau2 = 0.77. There seems
to be a correlation with renal failure (RF), but there were
very few studies to conduct a metanalysis with RF.
Conclusions: The prevalence of the PS among all studies
was 23.9%; with a higher prevalence of this sign among
males. We found that FD patients who had strokes did not
have higher odds of presenting with the Pulvinar Sign than
the FD patients who did not suffer a stroke. Patients with
renal failure and FD seem to have a higher tendency to have
the PS, but there were not enough studies to analyze the
association. Overall, we think the pulvinar sign is of poor
prognostic value in patients with Fabry ’s disease.

M150. Racial Differences in Left Atrial Structure

Fibrillation
Emma Gootee, MS
1, Katherine Kovrizhkin, BS 2, Michelle
C. Johansen, MD, PhD 1. 1Johns Hopkins School of Medicine,
Baltimore, MD, USA, 2Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore,
MD, USA.
Background and Aims: Blacks have a higher risk of stroke,
and higher prevalence of vascular risk factors but a lower risk
of atrial ﬁbrillation (AF) for reasons that are unknown. Left
atrial function (LA) is important in stroke pathophysiology.
This study aims to determine the association between left
atrial diameter (LAD) and indexed volume (LAVi) with race
among ischemic stroke patients without AF.
Methods: Ischemic stroke patients without AF admitted
to the Johns Hopkins Hospital (2017-2019) underwent
transthoracic echocardiogram. LAD and LAVi were dichoto-
mized into normal versus abnormal using clinical norms
(abnormal LAD ≥4cm, abnormal LAVi ≥34ml/m
2). Adjusted
quantile regression determined the association between
median LAD and LAVi, each, and race (Black vs Other).
Adjusted multinomial logistic regression determined the asso-
ciation of dichotomized LAD and LAVi, each in separate
models, with race. Covariates were age (years), sex, history of
hypertension, history of diabetes, history of coronary artery
disease, left ventricular ejection fraction (%), and heart rate
(BPM). History of diabetes, hypertension, and coronary
artery disease were de ﬁned as present if it were either
reported by the patient at time of admission, or if they had a
documented prior history of the condition.
Results: Participants (N=145) were on average 60 years
(18-98), 45% female, 60% Black and 35% White. Blacks
were more likely to have diabetes (p=0.002) and hypertension
(p<0.001) compared to other races. There was no difference
between median values of LAD ( β-Coefﬁcient=-0.90, 95%
CI=-0.36, 0.19) or LAVi ( β-Coefﬁcient=3.76, 95% CI=-
3.68, 11.19) between Blacks and other races. Blacks had a
signiﬁcantly lower odds of having an abnormal (larger) LAD
compared to other races when adjusting for age, sex, history
of hypertension, history of diabetes, and history of coronary
artery disease (OR=0.25, 95% CI=0.06, 0.97). This associa-
tion remained signi ﬁcant with a slight attenuation in effect
estimate when adding LVEF and HR into the adjustment
model (OR=0.22, 95% CI=0.05, 0.89). There was a trend
towards larger LAVi among Blacks, although not statistically
signiﬁcant (OR=1.10, 95% CI=0.35-2.48).
Conclusion: In this study, we found that Blacks with
ischemic stroke had lower odds of having an enlarged LAD,
with a trend towards larger LAVi compared to non-Blacks.
We suggest that investigation of the inherent differences in
the structure and function of the LA by race may be bene ﬁ-
cial in de ﬁning its role in stroke risk apart from AF.

Objectives: To evaluate the risk factors and hospitalization
outcomes for cerebrovascular diseases (CVD) in patients with
vasculitis.
Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study using the
Nationwide Inpatient Sample (NIS, 2019). We included 26,855

adults (age 18-65 years) with a co-diagnosis of vasculitis and
divided the sample by the primary diagnosis of CVD (N=670).

evaluate the odds ratio (OR) of association with CVD in patients
with vasculitis by comparing it to the non-CVD cohort.
Results: The majority of the vasculitis patients with CVD
were elders (51-65 years, 46%), females (62%), and Whites
(52%). Yet, we found that the Blacks with vasculitis had a
higher risk of CVD (OR 1.32, P<0.001). There was a signi ﬁ-
cant difference in the geographic distribution of CVD with
vasculitis with the highest prevalence in the South Atlantic
(23%) and Middle Atlantic (16%), and the lowest in the
Mountain (4%) and New England (2%). Vasculitis patients
with comorbid lymphoma (OR 2.46, P<0.001), peripheral
vascular diseases (PVD, OR 1.54, P<0.001), and complicated
hypertension (OR 1.31, P<0.001) were associated with
increasing the likelihood for CVD-related hospitalization.

$169,440 per CVD-related hospitalization in vasculitis
patients. CVD with vasculitis patients had a major loss of
body functioning (80%) leading to adverse disposition
including transfer to the skilled nursing facility/intermediate
care facility (22%) and requiring home health care (13%).

tion in vasculitis patients was 2.5% and the females and
Blacks were at 32% higher risk. Comorbid lymphoma, PVD,

culitis. They have a higher loss of functioning that affects

discharge.

lar exposure to these drugs to those who experienced a poor
recovery.This work represents a ﬁrst look at the effects of
these drug classes on the recovery of language after stroke
and should not be interpreted as resolving all potential for
concern. However, it does offer modest reassurance that they
do not appear to harm recovery of post-stroke language when
given for short periods in this population. Additional pro-
spective analyses with greater speci ﬁcity are needed to fully
appreciate the relationship these drugs may have with
plasticity-dependent recovery of language in the post-stroke
period.

extraction fraction (OEF), respectively. Structural images

of white matter (WM) T1 and FLAIR signal intensity distri-

M162. Topography of Cerebral Autoregulation
Impairment After Ischemic Stroke
Navpreet Reehal, BA , Sarah C. Carter, BA, Christopher
G. Favilla, MD, Stephanie Cummings, BA. University of
Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.
Introduction: Cerebral autoregulation (CA) is impaired in
the context of acute stroke, but the topographic distribution
of CA impairment remains largely unexplored. We previously
demonstrated that CA can be differentiated in the anterior,
middle, and posterior cerebral arteries (ACA, MCA, PCA)
using a transcranial Doppler (TCD) based approach. Here,
we compare CA across cerebrovascular territories after acute
ischemic stroke.
Methods: Patients with ischemic stroke affecting a single
cerebrovascular territory (ACA, MCA, or PCA) were eligible
for enrollment if stroke symptom onset was within 72 hours
of hemodynamic monitoring. Cerebral blood ﬂow velocity
(CBFv) and arterial blood pressure (ABP) were synchronized
and continuously monitored using a TCD and a ﬁnger ple-
thysmograph (Finapres
® NOVA) respectively. 5 minutes of
data were collected from the ACA, MCA, and PCA in both
hemispheres. A transfer function analysis (TFA) quanti ﬁed
the relationship between ABP and CBFv in each vessel. Gain
described the magnitude of CBF regulation, and phase
described the time-course of autoregulation. Mx Index, also
calculated for each vessel, quanti ﬁed the correlation between
BP and CBFv. CA parameters were compared across vascular
territories in a paired fashion.
Results: 50 acute stroke patients completed the study pro-
tocol, 84% with MCA stroke, 10% PCA, and 6% ACA.
Based on Mx Index, CA is hemispherically impaired. In the
territory of the stroke (0.49 +/- 0.13), Mx index is similar to
the unaffected vessels in the same hemisphere (0.47 +/- 0.13;
p=0.48), but Mx index is lower in the contralateral hemi-
sphere (0.42 +/- 0.11; p=0.005). In contrast, TFA derived
parameters suggest impairment may be limited the territory
of the stroke. Gain in the territory of the stroke (1.43 +/-
0.26) is higher than the unaffected ipsilateral territories (1.06
+/- 0.37; p=0.05) and the contralateral hemisphere (1.13 +/-
0.34; p=0.004). TFA-derived phase reveals a similar pattern
of focal impairment. Phase in the territory of the stroke
(28.4

/C14+/- 18.0 /C14) is lower than the contralateral hemisphere
(39.7/C14+/- 23.9 /C14; p=0.02) and point estimate suggests it may
be lower that the ipsilateral territories (36.4 /C14+/- 21.8 /C14;
p=0.10), but this did not achieve statistical signi ﬁcance.
Conclusions: When ischemic stroke affects a single vascu-
lar territory, some parameters indicate hemispheric CA
impairment, while other parameters suggest impairment is
isolated to the territory of the stroke. Each CA parameter
describes a unique element of cerebrovascular function, so
this discrepancy may better inform our understanding of CA
after stroke.

Introduction: Transient global amnesia (TGA) is a disor-
der in which patients present with anterograde and/or ret-
rograde memory loss, char acterized by repetitive
questioning and disorientati on. There is usually no long-
term cognitive disturbance and episodes tend to resolve
within 24 hours. The precise mechanism by which it
occurs is still unknown, although cerebral ischemia may
play a role. While isolated TGA is usually benign, it may
be the presenting symptom of stroke. This abstract dis-
cusses a patient who presented with signs and symptoms
consistent with TGA and was found to have an acute
infarction in her hippocampus.
Case: A 60-year-old female with history of hypothyroidism,
hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented with episodic
amnesia. She was repeating questions and did not know the
location or time of day. There were no other focal motor or
sensory neurologic de ﬁcits on exam. She denied headache.
Blood pressure was initially 192/88, and then lowered with an
antihypertensive medication. According to the patient, her last
clear memory before the event was when she went to bed. She
was told by her boyfriend that was she was asking repetitive
questions. The patient did not remember any of this. She ret-
urned to her mental status baseline <24 hours later. The
patient did note that she was under a large amount of stress in
her life. She only occasionally drank alcohol, smoked four ciga-
rettes a day and denied drug usage. Hemoglobin a1c was 6.1
and LDL was 77. An MRI brain showed an area of restricted
diffusion in the right hippocampus/temporal region, con-
cerning for acute infarction. The remainder of stroke workup
including labs, vessel imaging and transthoracic echocardio-
gram were all unremarkable. She was discharged on aspirin
81 mg along with atorvastatin 40mg. She was also counseled
on tobacco cessation and stress relief.
Discussion: The mechanism for TGA is still unknown,
however three main theories include vascular (focal arterial

M165. Trends in Stroke Mortality by Race/Ethnicity and
Sex in the U.S. 2000-2019
Daniel Oh, MD
1, Bruce Ovbiagele, MD, MSc, MAS, MBA,
FAHA2, Daniela Markovic, MS 3, Amytis Tow ﬁghi, MD,
FAHA1. 1University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA,
USA, 2University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco,
CA, USA, 3University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles,
CA, USA.
Introduction: Stroke mortality has declined over the past
several decades. Yet studies have suggested race, ethnic, and
sex disparities in mortality rates. Additionally, little is known
about race/ethnic and sex-speci ﬁc trends in mortality among
individuals with cerebrovascular disease listed as a multiple
cause-of-death. Identifying temporal trends in
sociodemographic disparities in stroke-related mortality is
critical for planning public health and health services inter-
ventions to eliminate inequities.
Methods: Using the Centers for Disease Control and Pre-
vention Wide-ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic
Research (CDC WONDER) database, mortality rates were
extracted for those with cerebrovascular disease (ICD-10 code
I60-I69) listed as a multiple cause-of-death from 2000-2019.
Mean age-adjusted mortality rates per 100,000 persons for
cerebrovascular disease as the underlying cause-of-death over-
all and between ﬁrst (2000-2004) and last (2015-2019)
5-year intervals were compared by race/ethnicity and sex
using linear regression.
Results: The overall 20-year mean age-adjusted mortality
rate per 100,000 persons was signi ﬁcantly lower in Black (56.5
vs 66.4, p<0.0001), Asian/Paci ﬁc Islander (34.6 vs 38.7,
p=0.032), and Hispanic (32.9 vs 37.9, p=0.0002) women
compared to men. White women had similar rates to White
men (41.5 vs 41.7, p=0.69). Race/ethnic differences by sex
showed that Black individuals had higher rates compared to
White individuals (women 56.5 vs 41.5, p<0.0001; men 66.4
vs 41.7, p<0.0001). Asian/Paci ﬁc Islander women had lower
rates compared to White women. (women 34.6 vs 41.5,
p<0.0001; men 38.7 vs 41.7, p=0.053). Hispanic individuals
had lower rates compared to White individuals (women 32.9
vs 41.5, p<0.0001; men 37.9 vs 41.7, p=0.0007). Temporal
analysis showed that the rates decreased across race/ethnicity or
sex (p=<0.0001); however, rates of decline varied. Speci ﬁcally,
it declined more steeply in Black than White men (-27.3 vs
-17.9, p=0.014) and women (-25.4 vs -17.8, p=0.0046). His-
panic women had a gentler decline compared to White indi-
viduals (-10.1 vs -17.8, p =0.0022).
Conclusions: Women and Black individuals saw the
steepest decline in stroke mortality rates while it was rela-
tively slower among Hispanic women. Racial/ethnical dispar-
ities persist despite the overall reduction in stroke mortality.
Black individuals still have the highest overall mortality rates.
To reduce inequities, it is critical to identify the driving fac-
tors behind these trends.

Following Acute Type A Aortic Dissection Repair: A Case
Report
