Shim, MD, Enrique Leira, MD, MS. University of Iowa, Iowa
City, IA, USA.
Introduction: Perioperative focal and global cerebral compli-
cations are common in acute type A aortic dissection (AAAD).
These complications are mostly attributed to hypoperfusion
from either supra-aortic branches stenosis, hypoxia, circula-
tory collapse, or thromboembolism. Additionally, variations
in circle of Willis (CW) can impact left hemisphere perfusion
during unilateral antegrade cerebral perfusion (ACP); a com-
mon implemented technique for cerebral protection during
AAAD surgery. While different vascular phenomena may
have similar presentations, dysfunctional autoregulation and
reperfusion injury may be positively diagnosed with CT per-
fusion of brain (CTP).

sion phenomenon masking ischemic stroke in the setting of
surgical treatment of AAAD in the presence of an
incomplete CW.
Case: A 57-year-old right-handed man presented to the
emergency department with acute onset transient
lightheadedness and chest pain. CTA of the chest, abdomen
and pelvis revealed moderate volume hemopericardium, and
aortic intramural hematoma involving the brachiocephalic
artery and origins of bilateral common carotid arteries
(CCAs). He underwent an emergent replacement of the
ascending aorta with a graft, as well as aortic arch patch repair
of posterior wall erosion noted intraoperatively between the
origin of brachiocephalic artery and left CCA, while
maintaining ACP through the brachiocephalic artery.
The following day, he acutely developed aphasia, left gaze
deviation, right facial droop and right hemiparesis. His
unenhanced brain CT showed two small left parietal and left
frontal hypodensities. CTA of the head and neck did not
show vessel occlusion or signi ﬁcant stenosis, but his CW was
incomplete and notable for aplastic left posterior communi-
cating artery. A CTP showed increased cerebral blood ﬂow
with corresponding decrease in mean transit time and time-
to-maximum (Tmax) along the whole left MCA vascular ter-
ritory, suggesting unilateral hyperperfusion syndrome. Subse-
quently, measures to control and monitor hyperperfusion
and cerebral edema were initiated included aggressive blood
pressure monitoring and control and the use of hypertonic
saline. Continuous EEG showed left frontal LPDs on the
ﬁrst day. A follow-up brain MRI 2 days later showed large
left MCA, left cerebellar and scattered right hemisphere
border-zone acute infarcts. He was ultimately discharged to
an inpatient rehabilitation facility. Three months later he still
had signiﬁcant aphasia and right sided weakness.
Conclusion: This case illustrates that unilateral hyper-
perfusion syndrome may explain acute focal neurological

M167. Validating Diffuse Correlation Spectroscopy for
Dynamic Cerebral Autoregulation
Christopher G. Favilla, MD
1, Michael T. Mullen, MD 2,
Steven R. Messe, MD 1, Arjun G. Yodh, PhD 1. 1University of
Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA, 2Lewis Katz School of
Medicine at Temple University, Philadelphia, PA, USA.
Introduction: Dynamic cerebral autoregulation (dCA) can
be derived from spontaneous oscillations in cerebral blood
ﬂow (CBF) and arterial blood pressure (ABP) using trans-
cranial Doppler (TCD) without the need for arti ﬁcially
imposing a rapid change in ABP, which is the standard
approach to assess autoregulation. Diffuse correlation spec-
troscopy (DCS) is a promising optical technique for non-
invasive monitoring of CBF. Here we validate DCS as a tool
for quantifying dCA.
Methods: We measured dCA in 40 healthy adults and
30 acute ischemic stroke patients using high-speed (20Hz)
DCS over the lateral frontal lobe and TCD of the middle cere-
bral artery; both were synchronized with non-invasive ABP
(ﬁnometry). A transfer function analysis using a Fourier
decomposition of ABP and CBF quanti ﬁed dCA (performed
separately for DCS CBF or TCD velocity). The transfer func-
tion analysis calculates gain and phase which re ﬂect the magni-
tude of CBF buffering and time course of autoregulation
respectively (higher gain and lower phase re ﬂect poor
autoregulation). The dCA parameters derived using DCS and
TCD were compared by correlation. Interclass correlation
assessed test-retest reliability of DCS derived dCA parameters.
Results: Strong correlation was noted between the DCS and
TCD measured gain in both healthy volunteers (r=0.73,
p<0.001) and acute stroke patients (r=0.76, p=0.003). Strong
test-retest reliability of DCS derived gain was noted in both
healthy volunteers and stroke patients (ICC 0.87 and 0.82,
respectively). DCS-based phase and TCD-based phase were not
signiﬁcantly correlated in healthy volunteers (r=0.12, p=0.50)
but was moderately correlated in stroke patients (r=0.65,
p=0.006). DCS derived phase was reproducible in both healthy
adults and stroke patients (ICC 0.88 and 0.90, respectively).
Conclusions: High frequency DCS is a promising non-
invasive and passive bedside technique with high test-retest
reliability that can be leveraged to quantify dCA from
resting-state hemodynamic data. The discrepancy between
TCD and DCS derived phase, particularly in healthy volun-
teers, requires further investigation.
M168. Wake-Up Stroke Treated with Intravenous
Thrombolysis and Delayed Intervention- A Case Report
Pankhuri Banerjee, MBBS
1, Danny Abdullah, BA 2, Schweta
Rane, M1, Heitor Cabral Frade, M.D. 1, Arun Chhabra,
M.D.1, Zeeshan Memon, M.D. 1, Anand Patel, M.D. 1, Hashem
Shaltoni, M.D. 1. 1UTMB Neurology, Galveston, TX, USA,
2UTMB, Galveston, TX, USA.
Introduction: Current guidelines limit the use of tissue plas-
minogen activator (tPA) in acute ischemic stroke to 4.5 hours
from last seen normal (LSN) due to steep decline in bene ﬁt
and increase in hemorrhagic complication after the time win-
dow. However, there is subset of patients who possibly have
their symptoms onset in the latter hours of sleep that may
beneﬁt from tPA. Additionally, endovascular recanalization
has been used routinely in acute stroke patients presenting
with Large Vessel Occlusion (LVO) within 24 hours of
symptom-onset in the presence of sizable penumbra.

Case Presentation: 62-year-old man with multiple stroke
risk factors who presented with acute onset of right upper
extremity weakness, dysarthria and right facial droop; NIHSS
4. He was LSN 9 hours ago, before falling asleep. Non con-
trast CT head showed hyperdense left Middle Cerebral
Artery (MCA) with Aspect score 9-10; CTA head & neck
showed cervical right Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) high-
grade atherosclerotic stenosis, complete occlusion of the cervi-
cal left ICA with distal reconstitution and tandem M1occlu-
sion of the left MCA. CT perfusion showed a core infarct
volume of 8cc in left MCA territory with mismatch volume
TMax of 78cc. Intravenous tPA was given per standard dose.
Cerebral angiography showed near complete occlusion of left
ICA with minimal ﬂow within its cervical segment and tan-
dem carotid terminus occlusion. However, there were good
collaterals via left Anterior cerebral and posterior cerebral
arteries associated with a stable clinical exam. Risks of acute
neuro-intervention were deemed to outweigh bene ﬁts.
Patient continued to improve clinically on dual antiplatelet
therapy. A week later, repeat CT perfusion showed no core
infarct and TMax of 67cc and cerebral angiography showed
recanalization of the left ICA and MCA, with high critical
stenosis of both cervical ICAs. The right ICA was treated
with a stent to improve perfusion globally. After a month,
CT perfusion showed no abnormality, and the left ICA was
treated then with a stent.
Discussion/Conclusion: As shown in the EXTEND trial,
our case encourages consideration of tPA post the 4.5-hour
window in wake-up strokes in select patients. Additionally,
clinical presentation remains the core in selecting patients for
acute endovascular intervention.

Degradation of Network Function That Resembles the
Networks of Aged Mice

MD/PhD. Washington University School of Medicine, St Louis,
MO, USA.
Normal aging is associated with many cerebral changes
including changes in cognition and sensory processing. Deg-
radation of global cerebral networks likely contributes to
these changes. Ischemic stroke also disrupts cerebral networks
and is associated with similar long-term de ﬁcits. Furthermore,
analysis of age-related methylation changes has shown that
stroke patients are biologically older than their chronologic
age. We hypothesized that focal stroke in young animals
would cause network changes like those seen in aged animals
and would be associated with behavioral changes resembling
the baseline behavior of aged animals. To examine this, we
performed whole-cortex calcium imaging (454nm LED exci-

neuronal activity (power) and connectivity (seed-based func-
tional connectivity and node degree) in young (3 month) and
aged (18 month) Thy1-GCaMP6f mice before and 1,7, and
12 weeks after experimental stroke. Strokes were elicited via
injection of Rose Bengal (200 μL, 10g/L) and exposure of the
somatosensory cortex to a laser (10min, 23mW). Power
spectral analysis of neuronal GCaMP ﬂuorescence was com-
puted via fast Fourier transform. Functional connectivity
maps were generated by correlating the time series within
regions of interest against those of every pixel. Node degree
was calculated by determining the number of pixels each

pixel was correlated to above a threshold (z>0.4). Behavioral
response was assessed by placing the mouse in a cylinder and
scoring exploration (8 min). Young mice demonstrated a pro-
gressive decline in cortical delta (1-4Hz) power at each time-
point post-stroke. Aged mice had lower baseline delta power
which did not change after stroke. At 12 weeks post-stroke
there was no difference in delta power between aged and
young mice. Somatosensory stroke disrupted somatomotor
connectivity in young mice. Aged mice had reduced
somatomotor connectivity at baseline which did not decline
after stroke. Focal stroke in young, but not aged mice caused
an increase in contralateral node degree which peaked at
7 weeks before declining at 12 weeks. We previously showed
that cortical delta power correlates with exploratory behavior.
Stroke in young animals was associated with a progressive
decline in exploratory behavior in young, but not aged ani-
mals. At week 12, there was no difference in exploration
between young and old mice. These data suggest that stroke
in young animals causes progressive degradation of cortical
delta power, connectivity, and exploration resulting in net-
work activity and behavior resembling the baselines of aged
animals.

K-M108. Twenty Year Disparity Trends in United States
Stroke Death Rate by Age, Race/Ethnicity, Geography,
and Socioeconomic Status
Adam de Havenon, MD, MS
1, Lily W. Zhou, MD 2, Kevin
N. Sheth, MD 1. 1Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA,
2Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA.
Background: In 2017 the CDC issued an alert that, after
decades of consistent decline, the stroke death rate levelled
off in 2013, particularly in younger individuals. The origin of
this attenuation is unclear, and the objective of this analysis
is to understand how social determinants of health have
inﬂuenced trends in stroke mortality.
Methods: We performed a post hoc analysis of county-
level stroke death rate per 100,0 00 adults, for ischemic and
hemorrhagic stroke, from 1999-2018 using a Bayesian spa-
tiotemporally smoothed CDC dataset which was strati ﬁed
by age [35-64 (younger) and ≥65 (older)] and then by
county-level social determinants of health. We report stroke
death rate by county and the baseline-adjusted percentage
change in stroke death rate in 2014-18 compared to
2009-13.
Results: We included data from 3,082 counties for younger
individuals and 3,019 counties for older individuals. The
stroke death rate began to increase for younger patients in
2013 (β = -4.8 in 1999-2013 versus 0.1 in 2013-18, p<0.001)
and the slope of the decrease in stroke death rate tapered for
older individuals ( β = -15.6 in 1999-2013 versus -1.9 in
2013-18, p<0.001). In younger individuals, 1,796 (58.3%)
counties had a ≥1% raw increase in stroke death rate in
2014-18 compared to 2009-13, with larger baseline-adjusted
percentage change seen in rural (vs. urban) counties (2.7%
vs. 1.9%, p<0.001), counties with ≥90% (vs. <90%) non-
Hispanic White residents (2.8% vs. 2.1%, p=0.007), high
(vs. low) poverty level (4.0% vs. 1.9%, p<0.001), and high
(vs. low) substance abuse and self-harm (suicide) mortality
(3.0% vs. 1.6%, p<0.001; 3.4% vs 1.3%, p<0.001). In older
individuals, 452 (15.0%) counties had a ≥1% raw increase

stroke death rate, with associations seen for more traditional
social determinants of health including the Social Deprivation
Index, urban location, unemployment rate, and proportion of
Black race and Hispanic ethnicity residents.
Conclusions: The rate of improvement in stroke death
rate is slowing and even reversing in younger individuals and
many US counties. County-level increases in stroke death
rate were associated with distinct social determinants of
health for younger versus older individuals. These ﬁndings
may inform public health strategies that are targeted for dif-
ferent age groups.

Background: Hemiparesis following subcortical stroke has
been classically accepted to be greater in the distal upper
extremity (UE) compared to proximal UE. Subsequently,
many studies have examined and proposed mechanisms that
underlie this phenomenon. However, there is lack of preva-
lence data for this distal predominant weakness in chronic
stroke, and therefore this will be examined in a retrospective
study as follows.
Methods: We retrospectively reviewed outpatient medical
records from stroke, physiotherapy, and physiatry clinics at
University of California, Irvine Medical Center for patients
aged 18-80 with history of chronic stroke, excluding those
with subarachnoid hemorrhage (over a 12-month period).
Subcortical strokes were de ﬁned as those with lesions exclu-
sively in the corona radiata and/or basal ganglia based on
existing radiographic data. A distal predominant weakness
pattern was de ﬁned as lower average muscle strength among
intrinsic/extrinsic hand and wrist muscles compared to that
among the deltoids, triceps, and biceps muscles (Medical
Research Council Rating Scale). Prevalence of distal predomi-
nant weakness was compared between subcortical and non-
subcortical locations using a chi-squared test.
Results: A total of 259 patients with chronic stroke were
identiﬁed on chart review, of which 13 were excluded due to
incomplete data. Of the remaining 246, 102 were subcortical
and 144 were non-subcortical. Among the subcortical stroke
cases, 33 displayed distal predominant weakness (32.4%).
Comparatively, 13 non-subcortical stroke cases exhibited this
pattern (9.0%). This represents a signi ﬁcantly higher preva-
lence of distal predominant weakness pattern in subcortical
stroke cases (p-value < 0.01).

prospective study will more accurately determine prevalence
of distal predominant weakness pattern along with other

LB-M100. Gender-Dependent Outcomes of
Recanalization Treatments of Patients with Acute
Ischemic Stroke at Shamir (Assaf Harofeh) Medical
Center, Israel, 2011-2020
Itzhak Kimiagar, MD
1, Fikri Khiri, MD 1, Ronen Levite,
MD1, Shani Kalmanovich-Avnery, MD 1, Carmel Armon,
MD, MSc, MHS 1,2. 1Shamir (Assaf Harofeh) Medical Center,
Zerifﬁn, Israel, 2Loma Linda University Department of
Neurology, Loma Linda, CA, USA.
Background: Shamir (Assaf Harofeh) Medical Center
(SMC), a teaching hospital af ﬁliated with the Tel Aviv Uni-
versity School of Medicine, provides recanalization treatments
to over 100 patients/year with acute ischemic strokes (AIS).
We analyze our outcomes data periodically in a standardized
manner to monitor the quality of our care, and perform addi-
tional pre-planned analyses to address contemporary ques-
tions. We report outcomes strati ﬁed by patients ’ gender,
disease severity, and treatment delivered between 2011-2020.
Design/Methods: This was a retrospective chart review.
We combined data for all AIS patients presenting between
2011- 2020 who received recanalization treatment to com-
pare outcomes strati ﬁed by gender and disease severity.
Results: 811 patients received recanalization treatment
between 2011-2020: 472 (58.1%) men and 339 (41.8%)
women. These percentages mirror the incidence of AIS in the
SMC and the general Israeli population. Mean age, NIHSS
score and proportion with an NIHSS score > 6 were higher for
women. Cerebrovascular risk factors were more prevalent in
women, particularly atrial ﬁbrillation, except current smoking
that was more prevalent in men. 620 patients (78.1%) were
treated with TPA alone, 89 (11.2%) with TPA and endo-
vascular treatment (EVT), and 85 (10.7%) with EVT alone.
Fifty percent of patients were discharged home, 41% to a reha-
bilitation hospital or nursing home, and 9% did not survive.
Twenty-four patients (3%) sustained symptomatic bleeds. Out-
comes were worse in patients with NIHSS score >6. Treat-
ments and outcomes did not differ by gender The sample was
underpowered for minor, nominal, gender-related differences in
the more severely affected group to attain statistical signiﬁcance.
Conclusions: While treated women presented with more
severe AIS and more risk factors, we did not ﬁnd signi ﬁcant
gender-related differences in workﬂow or outcomes. Meticulous
adherence to risk factor modi ﬁcation remains the best strategy
to reduce stroke incidence, morbidity, and mortality in both
genders.

S140. A Novel Nonsense Mutation in the mTOR Gene as
a Cause of Refractory Epilepsy
Yong Woo Shin, MD , Jangsup Moon, MD, Ph.D., Keun-

Hwa Jung, MD. PhD., Kon Chu, MD. PhD., Sang Kun Lee,
MD. PhD. Seoul National University Hospital, Seoul, Korea,
Republic of.
Introduction: The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR)
is a serine-threonine kinase and is highly associated with epi-
lepsy. We report a case of intractable epilepsy related to a
new mTOR nonsense mutation.
Methods: Case report
Results: A 33-year-old male with a 25-year history of focal
seizures with impaired awareness was referred to a tertiary epi-
lepsy center for surgery evaluation. He had his ﬁrst seizure dur-
ing sleep at the age of eight. Since then, he has been taking
antiepileptic drugs. During his adolescence, the seizure was
controlled with antiepileptics. However, in his late twenties,
the frequency of seizures increased, and the semiology of sei-
zures changed. General and neurologic examinations were
unremarkable except for mental retardation. Brain MRI rev-
ealed subependymal heterotopia in the right frontal per-
iventricular area. Interictal electroencephalography (EEG)
showed frequent spike and wave discharges independently
from the right frontal, right temporal, left temporal, and
bifrontal areas. Ictal EEG revealed ictal rhythm in the left
frontotemporal area followed by generalized rhythmic delta
activity. The patient underwent multigene panel testing for
epilepsy, including 213 genes, and was found to have a novel
mTOR nonsense mutation before the FATC domain.
(NM_004958.3:c.7570C>T, p.Gln2524 * heterogeneous).
Further genetic testing showed that the proband ’s parents did
not have this mutation, con ﬁrming it was a de novo mutation.
Conclusion: Here, we report a novel heterogeneous stop-
gain mutation in mTOR in an intractable epilepsy patient
with mental retardation. This case suggests that the deletion
of the FATC domain can lead to hyperactivation of the path-
way causing epilepsy, considering that the hyperactivation of
the mTOR signaling is associated with epilepsy, and the
FATC domain can regulate the degradation of the protein.
Further functional studies are warranted to elucidate the
pathogenic mechanism of the mutation.

Background: SAFER is a retrospective multicenter compara-
tive effectiveness trial comparing rapid-EEG(r-EEG) to
conventional-EEG (c-EEG).
Methods: Four tertiary care centers reviewed r-EEG and
c-EEG from 2018 to 2022 for a planned enrollment of
500 and 600 respectively (total N=1100) on adult patients
with inpatient EEG ≥1H. Clinical variables are extracted
from medical records. EEGs are reviewed by experts. In this
preliminary analysis, we compare baseline clinical and EEG
variables between conventional-EEG (N=572) and rapid-
EEG (N=187) cohorts.
Results: The most common r-EEG type of use is combined
with c-EEG (81%). When used alone, r-EEG studies have a
mean duration of 15.6 hours, when combined, 1-17hours with
27-42.7 hours of c-EEG. C-EEGs alone last 62 hours on aver-
age. Between the r-EEG and c-EEG cohorts the prevalence of
acute brain injury (r-EEG 84%, c-EEG 78%, p=0.11) was
similar, as was the incidence of seizures, overall (r-EEG 19%
c-EEG 24% p=0.2) and in the ﬁrst 24 hours (r-EEG 12%,
12.8% c-EEG, p= 0.9188). Altered mental status (AMS) was
more common in r-EEG 83% than c-EEG 65% p<0.01. Epi-
lepsy history was more common in r-EEG 34% than c-EEG
23%, p<0.01. The overall incidence of EEG abnormalities
within the ﬁrst hour of EEG was similar between r-EEG and
c-EEG with no signi ﬁcant differences for lateralized periodic
discharges (LPDs), generalized periodic discharges (GPDs) and
sporadic epileptiform discharges (SEDs): LPDs (r-EEG 11%
c-EEG 7% p=0.13), GPDs (r-EEG 7%, c-EEG 8% p=0.9),
SEDs (r-EEG 26%, c-EEG 23% p=0.6).
Conclusion: In these preliminary results from the SAFER
study there were differences in baseline incidence of AMS
and history of epilepsy. The planned analysis will use a
matching procedure to adjust for baseline differences in these
and other covariates. The overall incidence of seizures and
EEG ﬁndings are similar between groups suggesting that r-
EEG has a similar sensitivity to detect these EEG ﬁndings,
but this result will need con ﬁrmation. Additional planned
endpoints include time from admission to ﬁrst seizure detec-
tion, the difference in 24-hour seizure burden, and whether
r-EEG can triage patients into high and low-risk patients and
determine the need for follow-on c-EEG.

Based on Disease Type and Therapy
Fahham Asghar, M.B.B.S , Mary E. Haines, Ph.D, ABPP,
Sidra Saleem, M.B.B.S, Ajaz Sheikh, M.D, Imran Ali, M.D,
Vicki A. Ramsey-Williams, M.D, Ph.D, Mehmood Rashid,
M.D. The University of Toledo, Toledo, OH, USA.
Background: Persons with Epilepsy (PWE) commonly
report signi ﬁcant cognitive issues that impact daily function-
ing and impair quality of life. However, studies investigating
cognitive de ﬁcits speci ﬁc to the type of epilepsy and treat-
ment paradigms such as monotherapy versus polytherapy are
limited.
Objective: This study aimed to gauge the levels of
neurocognitive functioning in PWE using the Repeatable
Battery for Assessment of Neuropsychological Status
(RBANS; Randolph, 1998). RBANS is a brief, individually
administered set of 12 tasks that measures a broad range of

cognitive domains. It yields ﬁve index scores (attention, lan-
guage, visuospatial/construction, and immediate and delayed
memory) and a total score. Normative data provides age-cor-
rection. The index and total scores are based on a mean of
100 with a standard deviation of 15.
Methods: The cross-sectional study recruited 79 PWE
from the Epilepsy Clinic. Exclusion criteria included diagno-
ses of dementia, intellectual disabilities, or progressive brain
lesions affecting memory functioning. Each participant was
administered the RBANS. Patient demographics, details of
disease, and treatment were also obtained.
Results: Study participants (34% men vs 66% women;
mean age /C6SD: 45.5 /C615.4), overall performed more than
one standard deviation below the normative group (Total
RBANS = 82.9 /C616.5). PWE performed signi ﬁcantly lower
across all RBANS domains compared to normative groups.
Mean/C6SD for the ﬁve indices were as follows: Immediate
Memory 86.4 /C617, Visuospatial/Construction 87.8 /C618.5,
Language 90.4 /C615.2, Attention 83.1 /C6
21.1, and Delayed
Memory 85.3 /C620.4. No signi ﬁcant differences in cognitive
abilities were found based on gender alone. A trend was
found for participants with focal epilepsy to have higher
scores on all indices compared to participants with general-
ized epilepsy, and individuals on monotherapy had higher
scores compared to individuals on polytherapy with statisti-
cally signi ﬁcant differences found for language (95.2 /C613.1 vs
87.5/C615.8) (p=0.02) and attention (89.9 /C620.2 vs
79/C620.7) (p=0.02).
Conclusions: In our study, PWE exhibit a higher degree
of cognitive impairment compared to the general population.
Lowest RBANS scores were related to attention, immediate
and delayed memory. Further, a trend for reduced cognition
in those with generalized epilepsy versus focal was also seen.
Statistically signi ﬁcant lower scores on language and attention
were found for those on polytherapy versus monotherapy.
Continued research correlating cognition with disease type
and treatment is vital for a better understanding of cognitive
strengths and weaknesses in PWE.

Background: A recent multicenter prospective study examined
the use of a point-of-care EEG (pocEEG; Ceribell Inc.) in the
evaluation and management of suspected non-convulsive sei-
zures in critically ill patients. We present a detailed, patient-
level examination of seizures detected either on initial pocEEG
or subsequent conventional EEG within 24 hours to
investigate whether seizures were missed on pocEEG due to
the exclusion of midline/parasagittal coverage.
Methods: We identi ﬁed the subset of 19 patients with sei-
zures detected either on pocEEG only (n=6), conventional
EEG only (n=4), or both pocEEG and conventional EEG
(n=9). We examined the electrographic characteristics of ictal

and interictal ﬁndings on both devices, including focality
with regard to detection in lateral or midline/parasagittal
chains, and patient clinical histories to identify contributors
towards discordant seizure detection. Given the limited
nature of the study, analysis was limited to descriptive statis-
tics and qualitative summary.
Results: Seizures detected on both EEG systems had simi-
lar electrographic appearance and location. Notably, ﬁve of
these patients had focal seizures, none of which were
restricted exclusively to the midline/parasagittal regions, that
were captured on both EEG systems. Seizures detected only
on conventional EEG (within 24 hours following pocEEG)
were visible in the temporal chains, and external clinical fac-
tors (empiric treatment with anti-seizure medications,
weaning sedation) explained the delayed presentation of sei-
zures. Patients with seizures detected only by pocEEG were
treated with anti-seizure medications, and subsequent con-
ventional EEG detected interictal highly epileptiform pat-

pocEEG was longer for patients with seizures detected only
on pocEEG (median 3.9 hours [IQR 3.6-8.7]) compared to
patients with seizures detected only on conventional EEG
(median 2.4 hours [IQR 1.9-5.5]).

electrographic data obtained from initial point-of-care EEG
and subsequent conventional EEG monitoring are largely
concordant. Delayed seizure detection on conventional EEG
could be related to anti-seizure medication treatment rather
than reduction in electrode coverage sparing the midline/
parasagittal regions. Future, larger studies could further
investigate the value of pocEEG ﬁndings for forecasting and
predicting seizures in long-term EEG recordings.

24 hours of rrEEG. Rapid-EEG helped identify patients with
ongoing subclinical seizures or highly epileptiform patterns.

be treated with ASMs after rrEEG. By contrast, ruling out

more informed management of patients suspected to have
non-convulsive seizures.

Rationale: In China, more than 9 million people have epi-
lepsy with 6.5 million active cases, which is increasing yearly
with 45,000 new cases. More than 50% of patients with epi-
lepsy need multiple anti-seizure medications (ASMs). Per-
ampanel is approved for partial onset seizures (POS) in
patients aged ≥4 years in China. This study aims to con ﬁrm
the effectiveness and safety of perampanel as an early adjunc-
tive therapy in Chinese patients aged ≥12 years with POS
(ChiCTR#: ChiCTR2000039510).

spective study. It was planned to enroll 170 Chinese patients
aged ≥12 years with POS with/witho ut secondarily generalized
seizures (SGS) and who have failed ASM monotherapy. Patients
underwent a titration period of 8 weeks during which per-
ampanel dose was gradually titrated up to 8 mg/day, followed
by a maintenance period of 24 weeks. The primary endpoint
was the patient ’s 50% responder rate (patients with ≥50% sei-
zure frequency reduction), and the secondary endpoint included
seizure-freedom rate and safety. This interim analysis included
data up to 8 weeks of maintenance treatment.

19 patients with SGTCS) were included in the interim analysis

set, of which 80 patients completed the 8-week titration period.

46 patients (including 14 patients with SGTCS) were included
in the analysis of maintenance period. For POS, 50%
responder rate and seizure-freedom rate were 61.25% (49/80)
and 21.25% (17/80) during titration period, and 71.74%
(33/46) and 41.3% (19/46) during maintenance period, respec-
tively. For SGTCS, 50% responder rate and seizure-freedom
rate were 89.47% (17/19) and 73.68% (14/19) during titration
period, 100% (14/14) and 78.57% (11/14) during mainte-
nance period, respectively. Treatment-emergent adverse events
(TEAEs) occurred in 65 (69.2%) patients, of which
11 (11.7%) patients dropped out. Most common TEAEs were
dizziness (n=37), headache (n=9), and somnolence (n=9).

that early adjunctive therapy with perampanel can be an
effective treatment and is safe in patients over 12 years old
with poorly controlled POS.

S151. Generalized Tonic-Clonic Seizure During
Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy: A Case Report
Sarah Kendroud, DO , Ahmed Abbas, MD, Paul Guerin,
DO, Syed Shah, MD. Southern Illinois University School of
Medicine, Spring ﬁeld, IL, USA.
Introduction: CNS O2 toxicity during hyperbaric oxygen
treatment (HBO2) can present with a wide array of neuro-
logic symptoms[1]. We present a rare case of generalized
tonic-clonic seizure provoked by HBO2.
Case Report: An 87-year-old male with history of prostate
adenocarcinoma (stage T3aN0) status-post radiation pres-
ented after a 1-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure while
receiving HBO2 therapy for rectal bleeding secondary to soft
tissue radionecrosis. He had urinary incontinence and was
amnestic to the event. The seizure happened 65 minutes into
the treatment at a depth/pressure of 2 atmosphere absolute
(ATA). This was his third treatment and he tolerated the ﬁrst
two treatments of 120 minute duration with no neurologic
side effects. His neurologic exam and EEG were normal.
Brain MRI didn ’t show a de ﬁnite seizure focus. Etiology of
seizure was thought to be CNS O2 toxicity and he was
started on Levetiracetam 500mg orally twice daily. He
resumed HBO2 therapy 10 days later and tolerated the next
3 sessions well but the 4th one had to be terminated after
about 60 minutes due to generalized twitching with perse-
vered awareness that was also attributed to CNS O2 toxicity
after which he decided to stop HBO2 treatment.
Discussion: CNS oxygen toxicity is a complication of
HBO2 due to increased reactive oxygen speci ﬁes (ROS) for-
mation which disrupts the balance between excitatory and
inhibitory neurotransmitters in the brain. CNS O2 toxicity
present with visual symptoms, ear symptoms, nausea, dizzi-
ness and irritability but on rare occasions can present with
seizures at a rate of 0.023%[2]. Most patients don ’t experi-
ence these symptoms due to the presence of a latency period
which is different between patients and in the same patient
on different days[3] . The risk for developing seizures tends
to increase with increased chamber pressure, inspired oxygen
pressure, CO2 retention and cold. Prevention mainly focus
on risk factors modi ﬁcation, if possible. Antiepileptic medica-
tions, antiadrenergic medications and ketogenic diet showed
promise in animal studies[3] .
Conclusion: CNS O2 toxicity can signi ﬁcantly affect the
tolerability of HBO2 therapy. Further research is needed to
better identify patients with short latency periods and ways
to mitigate these side effects.
S152. Inter-Ictally Negative Drug Resistant Epilepsies:
Localization and Characteristics
Ifrah Zawar, MD

Punia, MD MS 2. 1University of Virginia, Charlottesville, VA,

Objectives: To localize anatomic origins and describe charac-
teristics of drug resistant focal epilepsies that demonstrate no
inter-ictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) on scalp EEG
[referred here as interictally negative (IIN)].
Background: Even though IIN epilepsies represent
roughly 8 - 17% of focal epilepsies, literature on these epilep-
sies is scant and they have not been well-described.

Methods: Adults (> 18 years of age) evaluated in the epi-
lepsy monitoring unit (EMU) from 01/01/2015 to
12/31/2019 were screened.
Inclusion Criteria: 1) Patients monitored for 48 hours or
longer 2) With inter-ictally negative EEGs 3) At least one
clinical seizures recorded on EEG 4) Patients who underwent
epilepsy surgery 5) Patient with Engel 1 outcome after 1 or
more than 1 year of follow up of epilepsy surgery.
Exclusion Criteria: 1) Patients with prior EMU admis-
sions or routine electroencephalogram showing IEDs 2)
Patients meeting the inclusion criteria but with a follow up
period of less than 1 year after epilepsy surgery.
Results: Of 249 patients with IIN epilepsies, 31 patients
[mean age 33.2+11.6 years; 16 (51.6%) females] with Engel
I outcome at > 1 year after surgery were included. Eighteen
(58.1%) patients had lesional MRIs (17 unilateral and 1 bilat-
eral). Twenty-one (67.7%) underwent magnetoencephalogra-
phy of whom 17 (81.0%) were IIN and 4 (19%) had IEDs.
Fourteen (45.1%) patients underwent intracranial evaluation.
Twenty-eight (90.3%) underwent resective surgeries and
3 had laser ablations. Nineteen (61.3) had surgery on the
right side. Two-thirds (64.5%) of epilepsies localized to
either mesial (n=9; 29.7%) or neocortical (n=2) temporal
(n=11, 35.5%) and opercular (n=9, 29.0%) regions. The
remaining epilepsies localized to the cingulate/mesial frontal
(n=4, 12.9%), orbitofrontal (n=3, 9.7%), middle frontal
gyrus (n=2) and mesial occipital (n=2) regions. Pathology
showed malformation of cortical development among
17 (60.7%) patient, including 2 with associated hippocampal
sclerosis. Other pathologies were hippocampal sclerosis
(n=3), gliosis (n=4), glial tumor (n=1), cavernoma (n=1),
infarct (n=1) and reactive astrocytes (n=1).
Conclusion: Majority of IIN focal epilepsies localize to
mesial temporal or opercular regions. Some may localize to
other deeper regions including mesial frontal, cingulate,
orbitofrontal and mesial occipital regions. These regions
should be considered as primary epileptogenic zone candi-
dates during epilepsy surgery evaluation of these epilepsies.

Introduction: Perampanel is a once-daily oral anti-seizure
medication (ASM) for focal-onset seizures (FOS) and
generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS). Study 311
(NCT02849626) was a multicenter, open-label, single-arm
study of once-daily perampanel oral suspension in pediatric
patients (aged 4 to <12 years) with inadequately controlled
FOS (with/without focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures) or
GTCS. As psychiatric adverse events and suicidality have
been associated with ASMs, this post hoc analysis assessed
long-term (>1 year) incidence of psychiatric treatment-
emergent adverse events (TEAEs) and suicidal ideation/
behavior in Study 311.

Pretreatment, ≤11-week Titration [ ≤16 mg/day, based on
concomitant enzyme-inducing ASMs, clinical response, and
tolerability], and ≤12-week Maintenance), Extension A
(≤29 weeks), and Extension B (for patients in Japan or coun-
tries without an Extended Access Program). TEAEs, includ-
ing psychiatric TEAEs, were assessed throughout. Suicidal
ideation/behavior were monitored, and clinically signi ﬁcant
observations were recorded as TEAEs. Suicidality was also
assessed via the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-
SSRS) in patients aged ≥6 years at consent/assent (Core
Study/Extension A).

136 patients entered Extension A, of whom 43 further con-
tinued in Extension B (Japan, n=41; France, n=2); one
patient did not receive treatment in Extension B. At baseline,
64/180 (35.6%) patients in the Core Study ( /C6Extension A),
and 11/42 (26.2%) patients in Extension B had a history of
psychiatric disorders (Safety Analysis Set). Across the Core
Study + Extension A, 71/180 (39.4%) patients experienced
psychiatric TEAEs, most commonly irritability (n=24
[13.3%]). In Extension B, 5/42 (11.9%) patients experienced
psychiatric TEAEs, most commonly insomnia (n=2 [4.8%]).

no reported lifetime history of suicidality had a positive score
on the C-SSRS during perampanel treatment; one patient
reported two non-serious TEAEs of suicidal ideation. In
Extension B, one patient reported self-injury; no other
TEAEs related to suicidal ideation/behavior were reported.

does not appear to increase the frequency of psychiatric
TEAEs. Together with the low incidence of suicidality, the
data suggest that adjunctive perampanel is generally safe and
well tolerated in terms of mental health in pediatric patients
with epilepsy. Similar to other ASMs, patients receiving per-
ampanel should be monitored for psychiatric TEAEs.

S155. Pilomotor Seizures Arising from the Ipsilateral
Frontal Lobe Con ﬁrmed by Stereoelectroencephalography
Cody L. Nathan, MD , Assia Meziane-Tani, MD, Dina
Ghandour, MD, Micheal Macken, MD, Yara Mikhaeil-Demo,
MD, Stephan Schuele, MD, MPH, Elizabeth E. Gerard,
MD. Northwestern Memorial Hospital, Chicago, IL, USA.
Introduction: Pilomotor seizures are a subset of autonomic
seizures characterized by unilateral or bilateral piloerection
(goosebumps)
1. The majority of cases are associated with sei-

zure onset from the ipsilateral temporal lobe, though there are
rare cases arising from extra-temporal regions 1,2. We present a
case of pilomotor seizures arising from a malformation of corti-
cal development within the ipsilateral frontal lobe. Semiology
was recognized by real-time bedside exam and localization con-
ﬁrmed by stereoelectroencephalography (sEEG).
Case Report: A 25-year-old man with left frontal
schizencephaly and polymicrogyria was admitted to the Epi-
lepsy Monitoring Unit (EMU) for surgical evaluation of
medically refractory epilepsy. He described typical seizures as
clusters of recurrent cold/tightness in his left face, arm, then
leg followed by a "ripple" down the left side of his body.
Symptoms occur intermittently for hours and may progress
to seizures with impairment of awareness. In the EMU, a
neurology resident observed that the “ripple” sensation cor-
responded to piloerection migrating from the left arm to left
leg in a Jacksonian march-like pattern. This con ﬁrmed that
the patient ’s habitual symptoms represent autonomic sei-
zures. Seizures occurred approximately every 30-120 seconds
for 6 hours without impaired awareness ultimately culminat-
ing in an automotor seizure. Brief episodes of piloerection
had no consistent correlate on scalp EEG. However, sEEG
evaluation demonstrated that even the briefest “ripples” cor-
responded to an ictal pattern arising from the frontal
polymicrogyria.
Discussion: Pilomotor seizures can result from a variety of
neurologic insults including brain tumors, limbic encephali-
tis, developmental malformations, traumatic brain injury, and
hippocampal atrophy
1,2. The exact network for pilomotor
seizures has not been identi ﬁed. The temporal lobe is the
most frequently reported area of seizure onset though other
regions implicated in the seizure network include the limbic
system, insula, and medial prefrontal cortex
1,2. Seo et al.
reported the ﬁrst case of a non-lesional patient with
pilomotor seizures arising from the ipsilateral frontal lobe
with subdural electrodes
2. Our case is unique in that it is the
ﬁrst to capture pilomotor seizures on sEEG arising from an
area of polymicrogyria in the ipsilateral frontal lobe.
Conclusion: We present a case of ictal piloerection arising
from an area of polymicrogyria within the ipsilateral frontal
lobe con ﬁrmed by sEEG evaluation. The case highlights the
importance of a detailed clinical exam during non-speci ﬁc
symptoms to characterize and classify a patient ’s semiology.

DW, 2003, Seizure

Background: Nonconvulsive seizures (NCS) are increasingly
recognized as a cause of persiste nt encephalopathy in the emer-
gency department (ED). NCS is primarily diagnosed using
EEG, which is often delayed or unavailable in many academic
and community hospitals, especially in the ED. The resultant
uncertainty in clinically diagnosing NCS is signiﬁcant and leads
to delayed/inappropriate treatment with antiseizure medications
(ASMs), unnecessary intubation, and increased morbidity. A
point-of-care device, such as Ceribell ’sP o i n t - o f - C a r eE E G
(pocEEG), could ﬁll this critical gap in the ED, as it has in
inpatient and intensive care unit (ICU) settings. In this study,
we describe our institutional experience with pocEEG and its
impact in the management of ED patients with suspected NCS.
Methods: We retrospectively identi ﬁed 319 patients who
underwent at least one episode of pocEEG monitoring at Provi-
dence Mission Medical Center (1/1/2020-12/31/2020);
157 patients were monitored in the ED. We reviewed each
patient’s medical record and extracted pocEEG ﬁndings (cate-
gorized as seizure, highly epileptiform patterns [HEP], and
slow/normal activity; excluding repeat studies for the same
patient) and ASM treatment information (prehospital, pre-
pocEEG, post-pocEEG) to determine whether pocEEG led to
appropriate ASM escalation or avoidance of inappropriate ASM
escalation. Chi-square tests with Bonferroni correction for mul-
tiple comparisons were used to assess statistical signiﬁcance.
Results: Of 157 ED patients (mean age 57.7 /C622.4 years,
49% female), pocEEG revealed seizures in 22 (14%), HEP
in 33 (21%), and slow/normal activity in 102 (65%). The
majority of studies (53%) were performed after-hours (5p-
8a), and most patients were admitted (54% to ICU, 41% to
ﬂoor). Only 5 patients (3%) were treated with ASMs prior to
ED arrival, but 93 (59%) were treated in the ED prior to
pocEEG monitoring and 80 (51%) were treated after
pocEEG monitoring. By reviewing each patient ’s ED course
and the relationship between pocEEG monitoring and ASM
treatment, we found a signi ﬁcant association between
pocEEG ﬁndings and changes in management (p<0.001).
Patients with seizures were signi ﬁcantly more likely to be
treated than patients with slow/normal activity (59%
vs. 25%, p=0.002) and patients with slow/normal activity
were signiﬁcantly more likely to not have treatment escalation
(28% vs. 0% for seizure/HEP patterns, p<0.001).
Conclusion: By guiding bedside diagnosis, point-of-care
EEG can empower ED physicians and consulting neurolo-
gists to evaluate and manage patients with suspected NCS
and can positively and substantially impact the care of
patients with neurological emergencies.

Epilepsy
Ioannis Karakis, MD, PhD, MSc
1, Nada Boualam, PhD
Student2, Lidia M.V.R. Moura, MD, PhD, MPH 3, David
Howard, PhD 2. 1Department of Neurology, Emory University

Boston, MA, USA.
Rationale: Seizures and/or epilepsy exert a negative impact
on the quality of life (QOL), functionality, and social partici-
pation of their bearers. Yet, there is scarcity of large,
population-based, controlled studies to characterize that

impact. The objective of this study was to characterize the
effect of seizures and/or epilepsy on patients ’ QOL and func-
tionality and compare it with other chronic medical
conditions.
Methods: This was a cross-sectional study using nationally
representative, pooled data from the Medical Expenditure
Panel Survey (MEPS) household component ﬁles for 2010 to
2018. Data were collected from a population-based sample of
MEPS respondents with records associated with a medical
event (e.g., outpatient visit; hospital inpatient) for seizure, epi-
lepsy, or both, and matched cases to control for age and sex.
Outcomes were weighted to be representative of the civilian,
non-institutionalized population. We estimated the QOL and
functionality (educational attainment, school/household/work
limitations, employment status, and missed workdays) of per-
sons with epilepsy, seizures, and both conditions, but our main
outcome focused on persons with epilepsy (PWE) as compared
to that of matched controls and select chronic conditions
(migraine, depression, and diabetes).
Results: We identi ﬁed 1,078 epilepsy cases, 2,344 seizure
cases, and 3,422 cases of either condition. PWE exhibited
worse QOL and poorer functionality in all domains and were
more likely to have ≥2 work loss days in the past year com-
pared to controls. Compared to cases with other selected
chronic conditions, PWE reported worse physical health sta-
tus and were surpassed in impairment of their mental health
status only by patients with depression. The impact of sei-
zures and/or epilepsy on QOL and functionality was univer-
sal, irrespective of patient age, gender, education, race, and
income.
Conclusions: The impact of seizures and/or epilepsy in
QOL and functionality is substantial and warrants interven-
tions to ameliorate it.

Objective: Systematic review to explain the Prognosis of the
Extreme Delta Brush Pattern in Anti-N-Methyl-D-Aspartate
(NMDA) Receptor Encephalitis.
Background: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
(ANMDARE) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by
neurological and psychiatric features. The disease presents ini-
tially with a viral prodrome, followed by psychiatric manifesta-
tions. In the next phase, movement disorders or/and seizures
occur. Finally, the last phase is characterized by decreased level
of consciousness. Central hypoventilation and autonomic dys-
function can also occur. In recent years, a unique electroen-
cephalogram (EEG) pattern, known as extreme delta brush
(EDB), has been associated with ANMDARE. Although the
association of the EDB with ANMDARE is known by the
medical community, data regarding its prognosis is still lac-
king. Hence, we decided to conduct a systematic review on
this topic to consolidate the knowledge and establish the
importance of the EDB as a prognostic factor.
Methods: To conduct this systematic review, we used only
studies conducted in humans, written in English, and published
in the last 20 years. We used PubMed as a database and
searched the following search terms: "NMDA encephalitis"
AND "Epilepsy" OR NMDA encephalitis AND "seizures" OR
"NMDA encephalitis" AND "extreme delta brush". The proto-
col used for this systematic review was the Meta-analyses of
Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) protocol.
ROBINS-1 tool was used to analyze the bias of the studies.
Results: Eight studies were collected from our search strat-
egy which included 249 cases of ANMDARE. Our data
pulling revealed that seizures were present in 178/249
(71.48%) patients. Status Epilepticus was reported in 29/96
(30.20%), and the EDB was seen in 30.89% (55/178)
patients with seizures. The prevalence of EDB ranged between
5.9% and 33% among the studies. The wide range in the
results could be related to the timing of the EEG recording.
Because the sample size was small, the statistical power was
decreased. However, we had a low overall risk of bias.
Conclusion:EDB was associated overall with increased length
of hospital stay, increased ICU admission, and incidence of status
epilepticus. Some studies concluded worse short-term outcomes
in patients with EDB but the other studies displayed a lack of
such evidence. Theseﬁndings suggest that the EDB pattern may
be a marker of more severe disease and worse short-term out-
comes, while long-term outcomes are not affected.

Disability in patients with epilepsy (PWE) is multifactorial,
modulated by variations in seizure frequency/recency, anti-
convulsant side effects and the burden of comorbid psychiat-

explore how objective, continuous and in situ assessments of
rest and activity rhythms (RARs) correlate with epilepsy-
speciﬁc variables and psychometric scales of emotional
wellbeing and somatic symptoms. Our IRB-approved study

enrolled during ambulatory clinic visits. We excluded preg-
nant patients, those with co-existing motor impairments
(e.g., hemiparesis), and intellectual disability or
neurocognitive de ﬁcits that would preclude independent con-
sent. Subjects were instructed to (i) wear an FDA-approved
device (Actigraph 2) on their non-dominant wrist for at least
7 days, (ii) maintain seizure logs, and (iii) complete standard-
ized questionnaires: the Adverse Event Pro ﬁle [AEP], Quick
Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology - Self Report
[QIDS-SR], Epworth Sleepiness Scale [ESS], and Patient
Health Questionnaires for Somatic [PHQ15], Anxiety
[GAD7] and Depressive [PHQ9]. We applied an extended
sigmoidal cosinor analysis (Krafty et al., 2019) to objectively
quantify RAR morphology, and compared these PWE values

to age- and gender-matched controls from a publicly available
repository of actograms from a large multi-center epidemio-
logic effort (The Study of Latinos, Redline et al., 2014).

active times. Within PWE, RAR parameters were most
closely linked to subjective measures of anxiety: patients with
high GAD7 scores (>5, n = 25, 64% female) displayed a sig-
niﬁcantly lower pseudo-F statistic (indicating a poorer ﬁt)
and lower RAR amplitudes than those with low GAD7 scores
(≤5, n = 33, 50% female). Both groups were similar in
median #ASMs used (2), mean age (41.6 Vs 44.2) and rates
of drug-refractory epilepsy (66 vs 56%, p>0.5). High GAD7
patients were more likely to take lamotrigine, zonisamide and
clobazam, and were less likely to be prescribed lacosamide or
oxcarbazepine, while levetiracetam use was similar. Our
results shed light on the potentially modi ﬁable determinants
of interictal mental health in patients with focal epilepsy.
Can we improve subjective measures of anxiety and depres-
sion by modifying their landscape of ASM use? Can we
achieve similar therapeutic effects by instituting behavioral
modiﬁcations that reshape a subject ’s RAR? In ongoing stud-
ies, we are characterizing RAR structure in PWE with
broader comorbidities, including intellectual disability, lim-

K-S103. Eye Tracking to Measure Episodic Memory in
Temporal Lobe Epilepsy Patients
Simon Henin, PhD, Helen Borges, MS, Anli A. Liu, MD MA .
NYU Grossman School of Medicine, New York, NY, USA.
Background: Memory impairment af ﬂicts patients with
diverse neurobiological disorders, including epilepsy (4 mil
US) and depression (15 mil US). Recent visual comparison
tasks have used eye-tracking to identify patients with mild
cognitive impairment (MCI), by measuring novelty prefer-
ence between old and new objects (Crutcher et al, 2009).
However, these measures may be insensitive to subtler mem-
ory dysfunction, have not been tested for lateralized hippo-
campal dysfunction, and have not been directly linked to
hippocampal events in humans.
Methods: Patients aged 18 to 60 years with unilateral tem-
poral lobe epilepsy (TLE) and healthy controls (HCs) were
eligible. A visual memory task testing for direct (AB, AC)
and indirect (BC) associations was given. During encoding,
pairs of common objects were presented serially. During
recall, the anchor object (A) was presented and subjects were
asked to select the correctly paired object (target), for direct
(AB) and indirect (BC) associations. Accuracy of responses
was averaged by group and compared with a t-test. Eye-
tracking behavior between anchor, target, and lure was
recorded with TOBII SDK and ProFusion devices, then ana-
lyzed using the ClusterFix algorithm, which detects ﬁxations
and saccades by k-means clustering (Konig and Buffalo
2014) . Duration of ﬁxations and number of saccades was
derived for each subject, compared by group using Wilcoxon
Rank Sum.
Results: Seven patients with left TLE (LTLE) and 6 HCs
were included. LTLEs and HCs were matched by age (mean,
SD: 27.9 /C68.0y vs. 24.8 /C66.0, p=0..466), handedness (RH:
7 LTLE, 6 HC), sex (4 vs. 3 F, p=0.797), educational level
(p=0.940), and MOCA scores (27.4 /C61.9y vs. 28.3 /C61.9,
p=0.406). LTLE patients and HCs had similar performance
scores for direct (87.3% /C64.6% vs. 90.6% /C62%) and indi-
rect associations (55.9% /C62% vs 59.6% /C66%). On direct
testing, LTLE patients and HCs looked longer at the target
object during correct vs. incorrect trials (Z=2.94, p=0.003
vs. Z=4.3, p<0.001,). During correct trials, TLE patients
looked at the target object for a longer duration compared to
HCs (Z=6.21, p<0.001).
Conclusions: TLE patients demonstrate longer total gaze
duration across saccades compared to HCs, even when overt
memory performance is similar. Eye-tracking behavior can be
a sensitive measure of visual associative memory function.

Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE) is the most common
focal epilepsy subtype and is treatment-refractory in roughly
one-third of the patients. Most MTLE patients do not have a
known cause for their seizures and the contribution of genet-
ics to this condition is largely unknown. Recently, post-
zygotic mutations (somatic variants) in mTOR pathway genes
have emerged as a major cause of lesional focal epilepsies such
as focal cortical dysplasia. We now also know that variants in
non-mTOR genes can cause focal epilepsies without always
producing a visible lesion. To investigate the contribution of
somatic mutations to MTLE, we performed deep whole-
exome sequencing (>500X) in106 MTLE patients undergoing
anterior mesial temporal lobectomy for medication-refractory
epilepsy, and 34 neurotypical controls. The hippocampal tis-
sue was analyzed in all the subjects and blood and/or temporal
neocortex were analyzed when available. Overall, we detected
a lower burden of somatic variants in MTLE compared to the
neurotypical controls, which may be attributed to the pro-
found neuronal loss seen in MTS. Despite that, we detected
likely causal somatic variants —all activating the Ras/Raf/
MAPK signaling pathway —in 9 MTLE patients and none in
the control cohort. In 5 patients, MTS was the only ﬁnding
after careful review of clinical imaging and histopathology. In
every case, the mutant allele was less abundant or absent in
the temporal neocortex, further supporting the potential
causal role of these variants in hippocampal epileptogenesis.
To localize the cells harboring pathogenic variants in situ, we
performed immunohistochemical studies that demonstrated
increased phosphorylation of Erk1/2 (a downstream effector
of the Ras/Raf/MAPK pathway) predominantly in hippocam-
pal subregions showing the greatest degree of sclerosis. Inter-
estingly, glial cells —and not neurons —accounted for most
phospho-Erk1/2 staining, though this may also re ﬂect neuro-
nal loss. In summary, our ﬁndings suggest a role for Ras/Raf/
MAPK activation in epileptogenesis in a subset of MTLE
patients, even in the absence of associated dysplastic or neo-
plastic lesions. Since many targeted therapies for Ras/Raf/
MAPK activation already are in various stages of clinical test-
ing for cancer, these agents could be leveraged for the treat-
ment of medication-refractory MTLE.

Rationale: Overactivation of the mammalian target of
rapamycin (mTOR) pathway causes “mTORopathies” that are
characterized by cortical malformations and epilepsy.One such
disease, polyhydramnios, megalencephaly, and symptomatic
epilepsy (PMSE) syndrome is characterized by facial dys-
morphism, macrocephaly, severe epilepsy, signi ﬁcant cognitive
impairment, and focal cortical dysplasia. PMSE is caused by
homozygous variants in the STRADA gene, an upstream regu-
lator of the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1). We aim to eluci-
date how mTOR overactivation in the developing nervous
system results in structural brain abnormalities and epilepsy, to
uncover therapeutic targets for PMSE as well as other
mTORopathies. Methods: Fibroblasts from 2 subjects with
PMSE and 2 controls were reprogrammed into induced plurip-
otent stem cells (iPSCs). iPSCs were differentiated into cortical
organoids, three-dimensional neural cultures that resemble
structural aspects of the developing human brain. Size and
morphology of live organoids were measured over time, and
processed for histology at time intervals up to 16 weeks
in vitro. Longitudinal multielectrode array recordings were per-
formed. Results: During the second week of differentiation,
PMSE organoids were 35% larger in size (p<0.0001), displayed
a 2.8-fold increase in budding of neuroepithelial tissue com-
pared to controls (p<0.0001), and had a delay in neurogenesis.
Addition of the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin attenuated the
neuroepithelial budding in day 8 PMSE organoids (0.3-fold,
p<0.0001), although this effect was diminished at day 10 and
day 12. At 12 weeks, PMSE organoids had increased expres-
sion of HOPX+ outer radial glia as well as GFAP+ glia. After
16 weeks, PMSE organoids displayed balloon-like cells
(an abnormal cell type found in focal cortical dysplasia Type
IIb) and that expressed nestin, GFAP, and neuronal markers.
Multielectrode array recordings from organoids demonstrated
network bursts and seizure-like events. Conclusions: At early
timepoints, PMSE organoids are larger with increased neur-
oepithelial budding, consistent with the phenotype of mega-
lencephaly. mTOR hyperactivity results in preservation of a
neural stem cell fate and a shift toward an increase in outer
radial glia, neural progenitors that contribute to the expanded
human cortex, and this could also result in megalencephaly.
The ﬁnding of balloon cells in this model recapitulates one of
the principal pathological ﬁndings seen in focal cortical dyspla-
sia. Because balloon cells are a rare feature in animal models,
our organoid model may better recapitulate some aspects of
mTORopathies. Further characterization of multielectrode
recordings may provide an in vitro model of epilepsy.

Intracranial recordings in patients with drug-resistant epi-
lepsy provide a novel approach to studying hippocampal
neurophysiology in vivo. This includes how oscillations and
other transient phenomena pro pagate within this structure.

ing waves moving up and down the hippocampal structure
using novel thin- ﬁlm micro-grid arrays conformed over this
structure ’s ventricular surface. Here, we extend our exami-
nation to the spatiotemporal p roperties of transient bursts
of activity including both normal and abnormal (epilepti-
form) phenomena. Six participants undergoing temporal
lobe surgery ( ﬁve with medically-refractory seizures and one
with a circumscribed lateral temporal lobe glioma) under-
went limited excision of the antero-lateral temporal lobe for
clinical purposes (four under anesthesia and R-sided, two
awake and L-sided). A 32-ch annel micro-grid array (4 x
8 layout, 2mm spacing, 1.22mm diameter platinum/iridium
contacts) was carefully placed and conformed onto the lat-
eral hippocampal surface over the CA1 region. Activity was
recorded at 24 kHz from all 32 contacts for approximately
8-22 minutes for each participa nt. Using two-dimensional
regression modeling, we found that traveling low-frequency
(1-15 Hz) oscillations occurred in transient bouts, with
medians ranging from approx imately 1.2 to 3.0 seconds.
Maximum bout durations ranged from 3.4 to 9.3 seconds,
and these values were not corre lated with oscillation fre-
quency (p=0.141, Spearman ’s rho). Interictal epileptiform
discharges (IEDs) were observed in ﬁve participants (rang-
ing approx. 2 to 28 spikes per minute). Normal physiologi-
cal hippocampal ripples were also observed, with a trend
toward occurring less frequently in participants with more
IEDs, though we were underpowered to assess this further.

traveled) along the hippocampal long axis, coursing in simi-
lar paths as low frequency oscillations. In summary, low-
frequency traveling oscillations occur in short (seconds-
long) bouts, translating to several or dozens of continuous
cycles ﬂowing toward either the septal or temporal hippo-
campal pole. The two-dimensional spatial perspective also
suggested that physiological ripples also travel along the
hippocampal axis, perhaps facilitating dynamic exchanges
between this structure and other diverse cortical structures
interconnected along its axis. T hough further investigation
is required, these intricate p roperties appear vulnerable to
epileptiform discharges, potentially representing a new spa-
tiotemporal mechanism by which the nociferous in ﬂuences
of pathophysiological circuitry in epilepsy disrupt
cognition.

LB-S102. Factors Associated with Refusal of Epilepsy
Surgery in Refractory Epilepsy Patients
Maryam Syed, MD , Deepti Zutshi, MD. Wayne State
University School of Medicine, Detroit, MI, USA.
Background: Epilepsy surgery is proven to be highly bene ﬁ-
cial for refractory epilepsy patients. However, patients ’ hesi-
tancy toward alternative surgical treatments for epilepsy
results in delays between initial referrals and surgical treat-
ment. Objective: To understand the demographic factors
associated with different opinions towards epilepsy surgery.
Methods: We surveyed adult epilepsy patients between
June 2020 to October 2021 at the Detroit Medical Center
using the NeuroMeasures ™ application which collected
demographic information, seizure frequency/type, and vali-
dated scales for depression, anxiety, and quality of life
(NDDI-E, GAD-7 and QOLIE-10-P). Descriptive analysis
was performed to describe patients who met criteria for
refractory epilepsy (failure of seizure control with ≥ 2 anti-
seizure medications) who did not pursue surgical options.
Results: Of 525 surveys completed, 179 met criteria for
refractory epilepsy. Twenty-seven (15.1%) patients had
already had epilepsy surgery or a neuromodulation device
implant. Sixty-eight reported discussing epilepsy surgery with
their doctors but did not wish to proceed.
Results: Of these patients, 47.1% were male and most
patients were between the ages of 18-44 years (63.2%)
followed by 45-64 years (27.9%). By race, Blacks made up
the 63.2% of the patients followed by 20.6% White and
8.8% Latinx. Focal onset with spread to bilateral tonic-clonic
(45.6%) and focal without spread (29.4%) were the most
commonly self-reported seizure type. “I am scared about hav-
ing brain surgery ” was the most selected opinion about epi-
lepsy surgery (42.6%), “I don ’t trust surgery to cure my
seizures” (14.7%) and “my friends and family are against me

having surgery ” (10.3%). Seventeen (25%) selected “Ia m
planning epilepsy surgery with my doctor ” and were mostly
to be younger patients (ages 18-44) (76.5%). Black patients
were most likely to choose “I don ’t trust surgery to cure my
epilepsy” (100%) and “I am scared about having brain sur-
gery” (69%) as their main reason for surgery refusal. Older
patients (ages > 64 years) chose “I am scared about having
epilepsy surgery ” as the main reason for surgery refusal.
Severe anxiety on the GAD-7 scale was associated with “My
friends and family are against me having surgery ”. Impaired
QoL (QOLIE-10-P score of > 25) and depression (NDDI-E
score of > 15) were reported in 58.8% and 25% of patients
overall, respectively.
Conclusion: Multiple different concerns are associated
with patients with refractory epilepsy who do not pursue sur-
gical treatment. Understanding these concerns for each
demographic group can help physicians with better counsel-

levels of entropy (i.e., more microstructural disorganization)

duration immediately before) normalized by inter-ictal

S164. Assessment of the Perceived Bene ﬁt and Barriers of
a Virtual Neuroscience Course for Practitioners in Low-
and Middle-Income Countries
George T. Kannarkat, MD, PhD
1, Sanika Chirwa, MD,
PhD2, Deanna Saylor, MD, MHS 1. 1Johns Hopkins Hospital,
Baltimore, MD, USA, 2Department of Internal Medicine,
Meharry Medical College School of Medicine, Nashville,
TN, USA.
Background: Healthcare worker shortages, particularly in
neuroscience, are common in low- and middle-income coun-
tries (LMICs). This shortage not only impacts delivery of
high-quality care but also limits neuroscience-speci ﬁc training
opportunities for practitioners that care for individuals with
neurologic illness. Virtual neuroscience education, which
could serve to increase access to neuroscience training in
LMICs, has not been widely assessed or implemented as a
potential solution. Despite challenges related to technology
and access, virtual medical education in other ﬁelds of medi-
cine has demonstrated ef ﬁcacy and perceived bene ﬁt.
Objective: To evaluate bene ﬁts and challenges associated
with a virtual neuroscience course targeting African
healthcare workers.
Methods: Using pre- and post-course surveys, we assessed
the perceived utility of a free month-long virtual synchronous
course on basic science and clinical aspects of neuroscience
administered via a Zoom platform targeting practitioners in
LMICs. Descriptive statistics from surveys are presented.
Results: While over 400 individuals registered for the
course, attendance for any individual lecture ranged from
50 to 150 individuals, 154 completed pre-course surveys and
44 completed post-course surveys. Nearly all survey respon-
dents (n=146, 95%) practiced medicine in African countries.
Only one-third reported any prior formal neurology training,
although 131 (90%) reported managing patients with neuro-
logic issues as part of their regular duties. Of survey respon-
dents who attended the course (n = 44), over 70% rated the
course as “excellent” with signi ﬁcantly improved self-reported
comfort in the neuroscience topics covered in the course.

The main reported barriers to course participation were con-
ﬂict with regular work, education obligations, and technologi-
cal access. Suggestions from survey respondents to improve
course accessibility included recordings for asynchronous
learning, improved internet connectivity, an alternate lecture
timing, and an increased number of lectures. Limitations
include that <40% of individuals who registered for the
course actually attended any individual lecture, and we did
not record attendance so the total proportion of registered
participants who attended at least one lecture could not be
calculated. Only 11 individuals who registered but could not
attend any lectures completed a survey to identify relevant
barriers.
Conclusions: Overall, our data indicate that virtual neuro-
science education is feasible and well-received in LMICs but
could be improved with asynchronous formats and other
interventions to enable better course access.

Background: Blood -cerebrospinal ﬂuid (B-CSF) barrier dis-
ruption in tuberculous meningitis (TBM) may be mediated
by in ﬂammatory cytokines and may determine clinico-
radiological severity and outcome.

tionship with in ﬂammatory cytokines (TNF- α, IL-1 β, and
IL-6), clinical severity, MRI changes, and outcome.
Methods: Fifty-ﬁve TBM patients with a median age of
26 years were included. Their clinical, CSF, and MRI ﬁndings
were noted. Severity of meningitis was graded into stages I to
III. Cranial MRI was done and presence of exudates, granu-
loma, hydrocephalus, and infarctions was noted. B-CSF perme-
ability was assessed by a ratio of CSF albumin to serum
albumin (Q
alb). The concentration of TNF- α,I L - 1β,a n dI L - 6
in CSF was measured by cytokine bead array. Q alb and CSF
cytokines were also measured in 15 controls. The outcome was
deﬁned at 6 months using modi ﬁed Rankin Scale (mRS).
Results: The Q
alb in the patients was more than mean
+2.5 SD of controls. Q alb in TBM correlated with TNF- α
(r=0.36; p=0.01), CSF cells (r=0.29; p=0.02) and exudate on
MRI (0.18 /C60.009 Vs 0.13 /C60.008; p=0.04). Q
alb, however,
did not correlate with demographic variables, stage, and MRI
evidences of tuberculoma, infraction, and hydrocephalus. At
6 months, 11 died, 10 had poor and 34 had good recovery,
which was not associated with outcome.

S166. Development and Implementation of an Observed
Structured Teaching Experience as Part of a Resident as
Teacher Curriculum
Adam Daniels, BS , Isabella Dana, BS, Nicholas Sullivan, BS,
Nicole Ackerman, BS, Yanal Shaheen, MD, Jaehan Park, MD,
Lisa Merlin, MD, Elka Jacobson-Dickman, MD, Nuri Jacoby,
MD. SUNY Downstate Health Sciences University, Brooklyn,
NY, USA.
Introduction: Resident physicians are tasked not only with
providing quality medical care for their patients, but also
serving as teachers and role models for medical students.
Residents often receive no formal training in teaching and
providing effective feedback. An observed structured teach-
ing experience (OSTE) is a method used to observe and
assess the performance of a speci ﬁc educational skill. As part
of a resident-as-teacher curri culum, a formative 3 station
OSTE was developed focused on giving effective feedback,
teaching utilizing the one-minute preceptor, and recogniz-
ing an impaired colleague. Pre-and post-intervention surveys
assessed residents ’ conﬁdence and interest in these three
topics.
Methods: Twenty-one PGY-2 to PGY-4 neurology resi-
dents from SUNY Downstate Health Sciences University
participated in the OSTE, with residents split into two four-
hour sessions one week apart. Each station was 10 minutes
followed by a 5 minute debrief. Medical students volunteered
as standardized learners. The week prior to the ﬁrst OSTE
session residents received a lecture on feedback and teaching
methods and two days prior they were emailed information
on the one-minute preceptor. Twenty-one residents com-
pleted the pre-intervention survey and ﬁfteen residents com-
pleted the post-intervention survey one week after their
OSTE session. Statistical analysis utilized a paired T-test
assessing pre-and post mean scores on a ﬁve point Likert scale
from “1 = strongly agree ” to 5 = “strongly disagree ”.
Results: Following the intervention, con ﬁdence in the fol-
lowing domains increased: ability to give constructive feed-
back (2.29 vs 1.69, p=0.004), ability to provide speci ﬁc,
nonjudgmental feedback (2.19 vs 1.75, p=0.045), overall
teaching ability (2.24 vs 1.94, p=0.041), ability to utilize the
one-minute preceptor (2.76 vs 1.81, p<0.001), ability to rec-
ognize the symptoms and signs of an impaired colleague
(2.14 vs 1.75, p=0.048), and ability to take appropriate steps
if encountering an impaired colleague (2.48 vs 1.94,
p=0.014). While attitudes indicated residents felt these topics
were important, there was no signi ﬁcant difference between
the pre-and post-intervention surveys. Residents overwhelm-
ingly felt that the OSTE ’s were useful and should be contin-
ued on a yearly basis.
Conclusion: OSTE’s improved resident con ﬁdence in giv-
ing effective feedback, teaching utilizing the one-minute pre-
ceptor, and recognizing an impaired colleague. These results
highlight the potential for utilization of OSTE ’s as an educa-
tional tool as part of a resident as teacher curriculum.
S167. Diversity of Neurologic Disorders at a Free
Neurology Community Health Clinic
Juan Deliz, MD, Dan Tong Jia, MD , Hrayr Attarian, MD,
Yvonne Curran, MD, Neena R. Cherayil, MD, Katherine
Carroll, MD. Northwestern University, Chicago, IL, USA.
Introduction: Uninsured patients have less access to outpatient

care compared to insured patients. Free community health
clinics have come far in addressing these inequalities, but often
lack specialty neurologic care. The few free neurology commu-
nity clinics are supported by volunteer providers, including
neurology residents and attendings. Understanding the breadth
of neurologic disorders and diversity of these patients can pro-
vide perspective on the educational value and sustainability of
the volunteers. We aim to characterize our neurology patient
population at Community Health Clinic, a free clinic that
serves the uninsured patient population in Chicago.
Methods: A volunteer group of eight resident and four
attending physicians partnered with the Community Health
Clinic to evaluate their patients with neurologic complaints
on one half day per month. Each clinic half day has 4-6
patient slots, staffed by one resident and one attending. New
patients are referred to our neurology subspeciality clinic by
other Community Health Clinic providers and return
patients follow up at our suggested intervals. Diagnostic
imaging and tests are carried out through agreements with
the county hospital and partner facilities. Medications are
prescribed and given to patients free of charge through the
subsidized clinic formulary. Patient assessments were docu-
mented in the clinic electronic health record. Variables of
interest, including sociodemographic variables, categories of
chief complaint, diagnostic tests and prescriptions, are col-
lected for the descriptive statistics below.
Results: Over the course of ten months since inception,
44 new or return neurology clinic appointments were sched-
uled, 39 of which were seen (88.6% show rate). Those which
were not seen were either due to canceled appointments or the
patient no-shows. Most patients’
primary spoken language was
Spanish (62%), followed by Polish (18%). The most common
chief complaint was headache (54%), followed by seizures
(13%), double vision (10%) a nd parasthesias (8%). Most ﬁelds
of neurology were represented in terms of diagnoses made,
including headache neurology, neuromuscular, epilepsy, move-
ment disorders, and sleep neurology. Most new therapeutics ini-
tiated were targeted at headache management (both abortive
and maintenance agents), followed by antiseizure (levetiracetam)
and myasthenic (pyridostigmine, prednisone) medications.
Conclusion: The range of neurologic disorders is well rep-
resented in the Free Neurology Community Health Clinic.
The diverse patient population offers the opportunity for cli-
nicians in training to and give back to their community. Fur-
ther investigation into resident feedback can provide insight
on the clinic ’s impact on resident education and wellness.

(MS) globally has increased from 2.3 million in 2013 to 2.8
million in 2020. However, MS and other demyelinating dis-
eases are reported to be very rare in sub-Saharan Africa.
Objective: We aimed to describe demographic and clinical
characteristics of the ﬁrst cohort of patients with MS and
neuromyelitis optica (NMO) from Zambia and one of the
ﬁrst such cohorts from the sub-Saharan African region.
Methods: Adults diagnosed with either MS, NMO,
NMO spectrum disorder (NMOSD), or clinically isolated
syndrome (CIS) at the neurology outpatient clinic at the
University Teaching Hospital in Lusaka, Zambia, the only
neurology clinic in the country, were eligible to participate.
Participants were enrolled from October 2019 through
February 2022 with signi ﬁcant interruptions due to Covid-
19. An MS-trained nurse administered structured question-
naires regarding sociodemographic characteristics, and each
participant also underwent a comprehensive neurological his-
tory and examination by a neurologist. Finally, plasma
25-hydroxyvitamin D levels were obtained. For analysis, the
cohort was dichotimized into a MS/CIS disease group and
NMO/NMOSD disease group. Descriptive statistics of the
cohort are presented and compared between both groups.
Results: Amongst the 34 participants, mean age was 36 +
9 years, 65% (n=22) were female, 90% were Black-African,
10% were of Southeast Asian decent, 50% had MS/CIS, and
50% had NMO/NMOSD. The average age was 34 +
11 years in the MS/CIS group and 37 + 7 years in the
NMO/NMOSD group (p=0.28). Females constituted 65%
(n=11) of both disease groups. Median time to diagnosis was
242 days (interquartile range IQR: 91-974) and did not dif-
fer signi ﬁcantly between the groups. The majority (82%) of
the NMO/NMOSD group presented with bilateral optic
neuritis. Among the MS/CIS group, median EDSS was
4 (IQR: 2.25-4.25), median Disease Steps were 2 (IQR:
1-2), and 59% (n=10) had an abnormal gait at enrollment.

ng/mL in the overall cohort but did not differ by disease
group or supplementation status.

with demyelinating diseases, MS and NMO were equally
prevalent. Furthermore, delays in diagnosis resulted in high
levels of disability in both groups. This demonstrates the
need for more research and funding towards demyelinating
diseases in sub-Saharan Africa.

Continent: A Systematic Review

MHS1. 1Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine,
Baltimore, MD, USA, 2Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston,

Center, Baltimore, MD, USA, 5Thomas Jefferson University
Hospital, Philadelphia, PA, USA, 6University of Iowa Carver
College of Medicine, Iowa City, IA, USA, 7University of

Background: The global prevalence of multiple sclerosis

(MS) has increase substantially from previous years, with a
current estimate of approximately 2.8 million people. How-
ever, MS remains considered a rare neurological disorder
among African populations, despite the fact that original MS-
related research based in African countries is extremely lim-
ited or non-existent. Objective: To summarize the contem-
porary state of MS-related research across the African
continent and to identify knowledge gaps from the current
research landscape.
Methods: Boolean searches on the PubMed, SCOPUS
and Embase databases were conducted for articles published
from 1990 to February 2022. Two reviewers evaluated the
title and abstract of each identi ﬁed record for inclusion based
on pre-de ﬁned eligibility criteria. Discrepancies between
reviewers were resolved by discussion until consensus was
reached. Full-text review and, where applicable, data extrac-
tion were conducted by a single reviewer for all articles which
passed the initial title and abstract screening process.
Results: After removal of duplicates, 2491 records were ini-
tially identiﬁed and underwent screening, of which 332 records
were selected for full-text review and 251 were ultimately
deemed eligible for inclusion. The majority of included studies
were from the Northern African region ( n=204; 81%), particu-
larly from Egypt ( n=166; 66%), and had a case-control study
design (n=145; 58%). Yet, there were no original studies from
36 African countries, whereas Egypt, Tunisia and South Africa
accounted for
>90% of included studies. Over 50% ( n=150)
of selected studies were published from 2016-2022, highlight-
ing the substantial increase in research output in recent years.
Studies investigating the utility of diagnostic tools such as
blood/serum biomarkers and neuroimaging technology were
most common (n=105; 42%), followed by studies investigating
MS risk factors ( n=41; 16%).
Conclusion: The MS research landscape across the African
continent has grown substantially over the past few decades
and especially in the past seven years. Yet, the majority of the
output comes from only a few countries with virtually no
data from the majority of African countries. In particular,
longitudinal cohort studies and randomized controlled trials
are lacking. As such, notable gaps and barriers in our knowl-
edge of the burden of MS in Africa remain, and further
efforts to promote clinical and epidemiological MS research
in sub-Saharan Africa are needed to improve our understand-
ing of the burden of MS amongst African patients.
