Background: Hereditary transthyretin-mediated (hATTR)
amyloidosis, also known as ATTRv amyloidosis, is a rare,
rapidly progressive, and fatal disease. Diagnosis is cumber-
some and often delayed, and monitoring treatment response
can be challenging. Neuro ﬁlament light chain (NfL) is a
potential biomarker of disease progression and treatment
response in patients with hATTR amyloidosis with poly-
neuropathy. NfL levels were analyzed in patients with
hATTR amyloidosis with polyneuropathy from the Phase
3 APOLLO and HELIOS-A studies to further assess the
potential utility of NfL in this disease.
Methods: NfL plasma levels were measured using the
Quanterix
® SimoaTM platform in healthy controls and in a
subset of patients with hATTR amyloidosis with poly-
neuropathy who participated in the APOLLO or HELIOS-A
studies, gave consent, and had suf ﬁcient volume of samples.
Timepoints analyzed from APOLLO were baseline, 21 days,
4 months, and 18 months in placebo and patisiran groups,
while samples from HELIOS-A were analyzed at baseline,
43 days, 4 months, 9 months, and 18 months in vutrisiran
and patisiran groups.

higher in APOLLO than in HELIOS-A (69.4 pg/mL and
58.2 pg/mL, respectively) and did not differ signi ﬁcantly

APOLLO placebo arm, NfL levels increased signi ﬁcantly rela-

NfL levels decreased signi ﬁcantly at 4 months and 18 months
relative to baseline (-20.0 pg/mL and -23.2 pg/mL respec-
tively; p<0.001 for both). Similarly, in HELIOS-A, NfL
levels in both patisiran and vutrisiran groups signi ﬁcantly
decreased relative to baseline at 4 months (-9.7 pg/mL and
-11.0 pg/mL, respectively; p<0.05 for both), and these
decreases in NfL levels were maintained at 18 months post-

levels observed in untreated patients, making it potentially
useful for monitoring disease progression and treatment
response over time in patients with hATTR amyloidosis with
polyneuropathy.
S171. Pathways to Diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis in Zambia
Mashina Chomba, MMED
1, Maria Dominique Mortel,
MD2, Deanna Saylor, MD, MHS 2. 1University of Zambia,
Lusaka, Zambia, 2John Hopkins University School of Medicine,
Baltimore, MD, USA.
Background: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is signi ﬁcantly under-

diagnosed in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Patients ’ journeys to
MS diagnoses in this region remain unknown.
Objective: Describe pathways to diagnosis of adults with
MS in Zambia.
Methods: We conducted a qualitative study of adults with
MS enrolled in the Zambia Multiple Sclerosis Study
(ZAMSS) between October 2019 and February 2022. MS
diagnoses were made or con ﬁrmed by neurologists at the
University Teaching Hospital (UTH) in Lusaka; the only
neurology service in Zambia. In-depth interviews using a
standard interview guide were conducted by phone and in
person. All interviews were recorded and transcribed verba-
tim. Transcripts were reviewed and data extracted to establish
time between onset of ﬁrst MS symptom(s) and MS diagno-
sis, and details of healthcare encounters during this process.
Results: Among 16 participants with MS from ZAMSS,
13 (81%) completed the interview. Participants ’ mean age was
34/C611 years, and 9 (70%) were female. Median time between
ﬁrst MS symptom(s) and MS diagnosis was 14 months (IQR
6-36 months) with the shortest time being three months and
the longest 168 months. Prior to MS diagnosis, the average
number of clinical encounters with healthcare facilities was 4
+3 with up to 8 encounters for one participant. These encoun-
ters were with general practitioners, orthopedic surgeons, neu-
rosurgeons, internists, ophthalmologists and neurologists; and
occurred at local health facilities including government clinics
(n=16, 47%), private hospitals (n=14, 41%), and UTH (n=4,
12%). Eight participants (62%) reported that at least one
MRI of the brain and/or spine which did not lead to the cor-
rect diagnosis was performed during the encounters. Self-
referral was common, with two participants being diagnosed
with MS by chance encounters with a neurologist from UTH.
Five participants (38%) additionally sought medical care at
hospitals outside Zambia in India, USA and South Africa;
three received their initial MS diagnosis at these hospitals.
Two participants reported consulting spiritual/traditional
healers with one utilizing herbal medications. All participants
received at least one misdiagnosis of MS symptoms. These
included stroke (n=4), type 2 diabetes, orthopedic disease, ane-
mia, brain mass, and drug abuse (each n=1).
Conclusions: Duration between MS symptom onset and
MS diagnosis in Zambian adults is long, and multiple clinical
encounters and misdiagnoses occur before diagnosis. Future
interventions are required to improve recognition of MS in
Zambia; particularly educational interventions to improve
MS knowledge among a variety of healthcare workers.

Background: Lumbar punctures (LPs) are standard of care in
evaluation of CNS infections, but, in Zambia, they are often
not completed even when clinically indicated. Most prior
studies focus on patient/proxy willingness to undergo LP, but
the role of other non-patient-related factors in LP non-
performance has not been systematically investigated.
Objective: To investigate patient-, provider, and health
systems-related factors associated with lumbar puncture non-
performance at two urban and two rural hospitals in Zambia.
Methods: Focus group discussions (FGDs) were con-
ducted in-person among adult caregivers of hospitalized adult
and pediatric inpatients at the two rural hospitals. In-depth
interviews (IDIs) were conducted with nurses, clinicians
(e.g. doctors, clinical of ﬁcers, medical licentiates), pharmacy
and laboratory workers at all hospitals via telephone. FGDs
and IDIs were audio recorded, translated, and transcribed.
Data were then categorized by themes using an inductive
coding approach to identify patient-, provider, and health
systems-related barriers to LP performance.
Results: Multiple barriers to LP performance were identi-
ﬁed at the patient, provider an health systems levels. Nine
patient-related barriers were identi ﬁed, including (1) lack of
LP knowledge; (2) belief that LPs cause death; (3) perception
that LPs are only performed when all other investigations
have been exhausted; (4) mistrust of doctors; (5) delays in
granting consent; (6) concerns about blame; (7) peer pressure
to withdraw or withhold consent; (8) concerns about posi-
tioning during the LP; and (9) association of LP performance
with highly stigmatized conditions (e.g. HIV and epilepsy).
Six clinician-related barriers were identi ﬁed, including
(1) competence in LP performance; (2) time constraints;
(3) inadequate patient counseling; (4) concerns about the
severity of a patient ’s illness; (5) delayed requests for LP; and
(6) concerns about harming the clinician-patient relationship
and about blame. Finally, four health systems-related factors
associated with LP non-performance were identi ﬁed, includ-
ing (1) supply shortages; (2) laboratory factors; (3) pharmacy
factors; and (4) cost barriers.
Conclusions: Multiple patient-, clinician, and health
systems-related factors are associated with LP non-performance
in Zambia. As such, any efforts to improve LP uptake in this
setting will need to include multifactorial interventions focused
not just on improving patient/proxy willingness to consent but
also on improving clinician competence, willingness and
understanding of LPs as well as health systems factors both
upstream (availability of consumable supplies and neuroimag-
ing) and downstream (availability and reliability of laboratory
assays and antimicrobials) of LP performance.
S173. Reducing Cost and Improving Access to MRI:
Correcting Image Distortions from Nonlinear B
1-
Gradients in Frequency-Modulated Rabi-Encoded Echoes

Paul Wang, PhD , Taylor Froelich, BSc, Efraín Torres, BSc,
Lance DelaBarre, PhD, Parker Jenkins, MS, Jerahmie Radder,
MS, Michael Mullen, PhD, Michael Garwood, PhD. University
of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA.
Objective: To correct magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
distortions arising from B
1-gradient nonlinearity in frequency
modulated Rabi encoded echoes (FREE) with the aim of
reducing cost and improving portability/accessibility of MRI
by eliminating the need for pulsed ﬁeld (B
0) gradient coils in
MRI scanners.
Background: MRI permits high-resolution imaging of soft
tissue with unsurpassed contrast making it an indispensable
tool in neurology. One of the major drawbacks is high cost
and lack of portability. In particular, B
0 gradient coils - the
hardware used for spatial encoding in most clinical MRI
scanners - are expensive and bulky. Recently, we published a
new way to perform MRI called FREE that eliminates the
need for conventional linear B
0 gradient coils in one spatial
dimension by encoding with the B 1 gradient from a simple
surface coil. This method can be expanded so that B 1 gradi-
ents alone can encode two- or three-dimensional images,
which would make clinical MRI scanners cheaper to pur-
chase, operate, and maintain. The work herein expands upon
the theoretical description of FREE and mathematically dem-
onstrates the symmetry between this B
1-gradient spatial
encoding method and conventional B 0-gradient encoding.
The theoretical framework is then utilized in a practical man-
ner to develop an algorithm that corrects image distortions
arising from nonlinear B
1 gradients in FREE.
Methods: A previously described B 0-gradient distortion
correction algorithm was adapted to correct B 1-gradient dis-
tortions in FREE. The algorithm was validated with MR
imaging of the human occipital lobe and a grid phantom.
Effectiveness was quantitatively assessed by calculation of the
normalized difference (z-score) before and after correction.
Results: The distortion-correction algorithm substantially
reduced image distortions arising from the spatial dimension
that was encoded solely by the nonlinear B
1 gradient of a cir-
cular surface coil in phantom and in vivo images of the human
occipital lobe acquired with FREE. Normalized difference (z-
score) improved from .763 to .567 after correction.
Conclusions: Distortions in FREE images acquired with
nonlinear B
1 gradients can be corrected with the algorithm
presented herein, removing one of the practical barriers to
use of FREE in the clinical setting. FREE is a new and prom-
ising way to perform MRI that can potentially eliminate the
need for B
0 gradient coils in MRI scanners, which would lead
to signi ﬁcant reductions in cost as well as improvements in
portability/accessibility of MRI.

Background: Stroke incidence is increasing in countries of
sub-Saharan Africa, but questions regarding sex-speci ﬁc dif-
ferences in stroke features, risk factors, and mortality are
largely understudied in the region. We investigated sex-
speciﬁc differences in clinical characteristics and outcomes
among adults with stroke in Zambia.
Methods: We used standardized data collection instru-
ments to retrospectively collect information for 324 adults
consecutively hospitalized for stroke on the neurology inpa-
tient service at the University Teaching Hospital in Lusaka,
Zambia between October 2018 - March 2019. Stroke sub-
types were classi ﬁed as ischemic or hemorrhagic based on CT
imaging ﬁndings and as unknown stroke for clinically
suspected strokes without neuroimaging. Stroke characteris-
tics were then compared by biological sex.
Results: Females constituted 62% (n=200) of the cohort
and had lower rates of hemorrhagic stroke than males (22% vs
37%, p=0.001), a trend toward older age (61+19 vs 57-
+16 years, p=0.06), and higher rates of hypertension (84% vs
74%, p=0.04), diabetes (19% vs 13%, p=0.04), heart disease
(38% vs. 27%, p=0.04) and prior history of stroke (26%
vs. 14%, p=0.01). Males had signi ﬁcantly higher rates of alco-
hol (33% vs. 4%, p<0.001) and tobacco use (19% vs. 2%,
p<0.001). Both sexes faced similar delays between stroke onset
and obtaining specialized neurological care, but females were
less likely to have neuroimaging completed during their hospi-
talization (82% vs 94%, p=0.002). In-hospital mortality was
similar by sex. However, among those who survived their inpa-
tient hospitalization, 90-day post-discharge mortality was
higher among females (82% vs 58%, p=0.002) independent of
age and stroke subtype (OR 2.48, 95% CI 1.1-5.58, p=0.03).
Discussion: Females in this Zambian stroke cohort had a
higher prevalence of stroke risk factors such as hypertension
and diabetes, but were less likely to have neuroimaging com-
pleted. While in-hospital mortality did not differ by sex,
post-discharge mortality was markedly higher among females
even after adjusting for age and stroke subtype. We identi ﬁed
several differences in stroke epidemiology between male and
female adults with stroke in Zambia, including sex disparities
in access to stroke care and post-discharge outcomes. Our
data highlight the need for future studies of social and socio-
economic factors that may in ﬂuence stroke-related outcomes.

Stroke in Zambia
Aparna Nutakki, BA

MMED2, Mashina Chomba, BSc.HB, MBChB, MMED 2,
Stanley Zimba, MBChB, MMED, STP 2, Deanna Saylor, MD,
MHS3. 1Rush Medical College, Chicago, IL, USA, 2University
Teaching Hospital - Adult Hospital, Lusaka, Zambia, 3Johns

Background: Stroke epidemiology among young adults
remains under-studied in sub-Saharan African countries,
including Zambia. We compared stroke risk factors, post-stroke
complications, and mortality between young (<50 years) and
older (>50 years) adults with stroke in Zambia.
Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of
consecutive adults admitted with stroke to the neurology

inpatient service at University Teaching Hospital in Lusaka,
Zambia between October 2018 - April 2019. We collected
data including demographics, clinical, laboratory and imaging
results, in-hospital complications and ﬁnal hospital outcomes.
Post-discharge outcomes were ascertained by telephone. Vari-
ables were compared between participants <50 years (young
adults) and participants >50 years (older adults) in the overall
cohort and among those with ischemic and hemorrhagic
stroke.
Results: In the overall cohort (n=323), younger adults
(n=106, 33%) had a higher rate of HIV (39% vs. 12%,
p<0.001) while older adults (n=217) had higher rates of
hypertension (88% vs 63%, p<0.001), diabetes (21%
vs. 5%, p<0.001), and atrial ﬁbrillation (12% vs 3%,
p=0.004). Similarly, among participants with ischemic stroke
(n=188), older adults constituted the majority (n=141, 75%)
and had higher rates of hypertension (87% vs. 40%,
p<0.001) and heart disease (46% vs. 26%, p=0.01) while
younger adults had higher rates of HIV (52% vs. 12%,
p<0.001) and alcohol use (40% vs. 18%, p=0.002). Among
individuals with hemorrhagic stroke, younger participants
constituted the majority (n=48, 53%). No signi ﬁcant differ-
ences were observed in demographic or clinical characteristics
between age groups. Older adults in all groups had signi ﬁ-
cantly higher rates of in-hospital aspiration pneumonia. In-
hospital mortality did not differ by age in any group. Older
adults with ischemic stroke had higher 3-month post-
discharge mortality (43% vs. 17%, p=0.001).
Discussion: Young adults constituted one-third of this
Zambian stroke cohort and the majority of participants with
hemorrhagic stroke. No differences in demographics, clinical
characteristics or outcomes were seen by age group among
those with hemorrhagic stroke. However, young adults with
ischemic stroke were less likely to have traditional stroke risk
factors like hypertension and heart disease, but more than
half had HIV infection. While in-hospital mortality was simi-
lar, older adults with ischemic stroke died at signi ﬁcantly
higher rates in the ﬁrst 90-days after discharge. These data
demonstrate the need for targeted primary prevention strate-
gies by age group, especially among people with HIV, and
directed interventions to improve post-discharge mortality
amongst older adults with ischemic stroke.
S176. Text Topic Modeling Application for Expedited
Neurology Meta-Analysis
Victor Lim, B.S. , Pranav Murthy, B.S., Davi Nakajima An,
B.S., Cassie S. Mitchell, Ph.D.. Georgia Institute of Technology,
Atlanta, GA, USA.
Introduction: Clinical meta-analysis, called PICO
(Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome), is
critical for examining cross-cohort neurological trends for
drug repurposing, adverse event analysis, risk identi ﬁcation
and more. Typically, human curators manually identify rele-
vant articles and extract data for statistical analysis.

Identifying the most relevant articles among millions within a
standard PubMed or similar biomedical database search is
extremely time consuming. Furthermore, standard biomedi-
cal database queries are often insensitive or inef ﬁcient in
identifying candidate articles for inclusion. This study con-
structs an automated topic modeling pipeline application to
identify and rank the most relevant articles for PICO data
extraction and analysis.
Methods: The Python-based application is a topic model
that utilizes a latent dirichlet allocation (LDA) algorithm and
probability distribution to assign percentage ranks to text-
mined topics. The model identi ﬁes keywords, or topics,
within the abstracts and calculates term frequency (TF) and
term frequency inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) for
the corpus. Using LDA, the application calculates the percent
relevance of each journal article with respect to the array of
all extracted topics (analogous to an extended set of key-
words). A set of 30,000 PubMed abstracts was used to train
and test the algorithm ’s ability to classify journal articles rele-
vant to two neurological disease PICO test cases.
Results: A sensitivity analysis assessed the number of
topics that should be included for optimal PICO article rank-
ing by the LDA-based application. That is, how many of the
extracted topics should be included by the algorithm to rank
the relevance of the article for a user-de ﬁned PICO analysis?
Results based on Alzheimer ’s Disease and Parkinson ’s Disease
test cases illustrated that approximately 100 term-frequency
topics are needed to capture greater than 80% of true positive
articles (i.e. articles identi ﬁed as relevant for data extraction
that match what a human curator would select). The topic
modeling application signi ﬁcantly decreased false positives
and false negatives compared to standard PubMed or bio-
medical database ﬁlters. Additionally, it decreased human
curator time to identify relevant PICO articles by several
orders of magnitude.
Conclusion: The developed topic modeling pipeline sig-
niﬁcantly enhances ef ﬁciency and ef ﬁcacy of identifying arti-
cles for PICO inclusion. Future work will bootstrap towards
full automation of PICO.

Background: Clinical care guidelines encourage people with
NF1, a rare neurogenetic disorder, to attend specialized
neuroﬁbromatosis clinics, but the majority of U.S. NF1
patients do not do so. We sought to assess the bene ﬁts of
and barriers to attending specialized NF clinics in the U.S.
Methods: An electronic survey was sent to U.S.-based NF1
patients and caregivers (n=6908) enrolled in the Children ’s
Tumor Foundation Neuro ﬁbromatosis Registry in May 2021.
Survey topics included demographics, self-reported attendance

at specialized NF clinics, rating of potential barriers to clinic
attendance, and self-reported receipt of guideline-concordant
clinical care. We used inverse propensity score reweighting of
survey responses to estimate the rate of NF clinic attendance,
barriers to NF clinic attendance, and receipt of guideline-
concordant care among the entire NF1 registry population and
used weighted logistic regression to look for demographic dis-
parities in these measures. Guideline-concordant care was
assessed as the number of recommended NF1-related evalua-
tions completed in the last year, strati ﬁed by age group
(e.g. blood pressure measurement, skin exam, scoliosis screen-
ing, family planning discussions, etc.)
Results: Responses were received from 322 patients/
caregivers (160 adults and 162 children, 58% female, 78%
white). An estimated 50.1% of Neuro ﬁbromatosis Registry
participants with NF1 attended a specialized neuro ﬁbromato-
sis clinic in the past 3 years. Older patients, those living in
rural areas, those with Medicaid or who were uninsured, and
those with a household income of <$25,000 were signi ﬁ-
cantly less likely to attend a specialized clinic (p<0.05 for all).
Major barriers to attending a specialized clinic were not
knowing they existed (22.0%), not wanting to travel/clinics
too far away (21.1%), and lack of insurance coverage
(19.5%); very few people endorsed not seeing the value in
attending a specialized clinic (2.4%). Patients who attended a
specialized clinic in the Children ’s Tumor Foundation Neu-
roﬁbromatosis Clinic Network received more guideline-
concordant NF1-related evaluations in the past year than
those attending non-specialized providers (percent receiving
all recommended evaluations, 10.1% vs. 3.7% for adults,
p=0.0002 and 26.7% vs 16.7% for children, p=0.026).
Conclusions: Attending specialized neuro ﬁbromatosis
clinics leads to more guideline-concordant NF1 care, but dis-
parities in accessing these clinics persist based on age, rurality,
insurance coverage, and income. Promoting patient awareness
of specialized clinics, utilizing telemedicine and hub-and-
spoke models of care, and insurance reform may improve
equitable provision of NF1 care in the U.S.

Education Program with the Chicago South Asian
Community During the COVID Era

IL, USA.
Introduction: There is a well-established relationship
between cardiovascular disease (CVD) and cognitive decline.
Recognizing the CVD risk factors has encouraged the use of
lifestyle modi ﬁcation interventions, which have been very
successful. This project aims to implement and assess the fea-

sibility and acceptance of a cognitive health and wellness edu-
cation program in a community- based setting, focusing on
South Asians, a community with known high rates of CVD.
Methods: This study was delivered during the COVID-19
pandemic and as such all delivery was by Zoom. Participants
ages 55 and older took part in a virtual six-week educational
and dance program based on research that supports a multi-
modal approach to lifestyle intervention. The weekly meetings
included topics such as physical exercise, nutritional counseling
as well as cognitive and social stimulation. The discussions
encouraged participants to self-manage their health and
addressed barriers faced by the South Asian audience. Delivery
of the programming including the dance instruction were by
team members who were of South Asian descent. At the start
and end of the program, participants ﬁlled surveys about diet,
the impact of COVID-19 on behavior as well as awareness of
risk factors for CVD, dementia and stroke.
Results: Five participants were included in this pilot study.
Between 3-5 participants attended each session. At the comple-
tion of the program, participants had improved feelings of using
the knowledge they learned to make lifestyle differences in the
way of eating and physical activity level. Two participants
agreed to further screening for a national non-pharmacological
lifestyle clinical trial known as the U.S. POINTER.
Conclusion: Preliminary data from this small pilot suggests
that community members gained a greater understanding of
CVD risk factors, stroke and risk for cognitive impairment
and dementia. Despite the high prevalence of such illnesses
amongst South Asians, current research has not examined the
feasibility of a combined educational and physical activity pro-
gram like ours. By offering culturally sensitive programs in
widely accessible formats, increased representation of this
group may be included in nationally based studies.

delays in presentation to the hospital and targeted stroke
reduction to prevent recurrent strokes.

S183. Low Neighborhood Socioeconomic Status is
Associated with Increased 30-Day Mortality and
Readmission Rates for Patients with Common
Neurological Disorders
Jay B. Lusk, BSc
1, Molly N. Hoffman, MPH 2, Amy G. Clark,
PhD2, Bradley G. Hammill, DrPH 2. 1Duke University School
of Medicine, Durham, NC, USA, 2Duke University
Department of Population Health Science, Durham, NC, USA.
Objective: To determine the association between neighbor-
hood socioeconomic status (SES) and 30-day mortality and
readmission for patients hospitalized with common neurolog-
ical conditions after adjusting for demographics, individual
socioeconomic status, and comorbidity burden.
Design, Setting, and Participants: Retrospective cohort
study of a 100% nationwide sample of Medicare bene ﬁciaries
between 2017-2019. Five groups of disorders were included
based on reason for admission indicated by diagnosis related
group (DRG): Multiple Sclerosis and Cerebellar Ataxia
[DRG 058-060]; Stroke, which included acute ischemic
stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, transient ischemia, and non-
speciﬁc cerebrovascular disorders [DRGs 061-072]; Degener-
ative Nervous System disorders [056-057]; Epilepsy
[100-101]; and Coma, including both nontraumatic and
traumatic coma [DRG 080-087].
Exposures: Neighborhood-level SES measured by the Area
Deprivation Index (ADI), divided into high (ADI 1-15),
middle (ADI 16-85), and low (ADI 86-100) neighborhood-
level SES. Covariates included in multivariable analyses
included age, sex, Medicare-Medicaid dual eligibility, and
comorbidity burden measured using the Elixhauser mortality
and readmission indices.
Primary Outcomes: 30-day mortality and readmission
rates
Results: A total of 937,277 patients were included in the
mortality analysis, and 1,203,085 patients were included in
the readmission analysis. After multivariable adjustment,
patients from the lowest SES neighborhoods had higher rates
of 30-day mortality compared with patients from the highest
SES neighborhoods for all admission groups except the mul-
tiple sclerosis and cerebellar ataxia group. Estimated effect
sizes ranged from an odds ratio (OR) of 1.12 (95% con ﬁ-
dence interval (CI) 1.09-1.16) for the stroke admission group
to 1.34 (1.25-1.44) for the coma group. After adjustment,
only patients with stroke (OR 1.05 [1.02-1.08]) and neuro-
degenerative diseases (OR 1.07 [1.02-1.13]) from the lowest
SES neighborhoods had higher rates of 30-day readmission
compared to patients from the highest SES neighborhoods.
Conclusion: Neighborhood socioeconomic status was
strongly associated with mortality for patients admitted for
stroke, neurodegenerative diseases, epilepsy, and coma, and
was strongly associated with readmission for patients admitted
for stroke and neurodegenerative diseases. The magnitude of
this effect was substantial: for example, patients with stroke
from low SES neighborhoods were 16% more likely to die
within 30 days compared to patients from high SES
neighborhoods after adjustment. The magnitude of this effect
is particularly shocking when compared to transformative
interventions in neurology: for example, the relative risk reduc-
tion of 90-day mortality from ischemic stroke associated with
receipt of mechanical thrombectomy is estimated at 17%.
S184. Race/Ethnicity Disparities Among Migraine
Clinical Trials Between 1995-2021: An Assessment of

Race/Ethnicity Reporting and Prevalence of Participants
Across Race/Ethnicity Categories
Maya Pandit, MPH , Ebtisam Zeynu, MS. New York Medical
College, New York, NY, USA.
There are known disparities in racial and ethnic representation
of participants in US clinical trials of new drugs and biologics.
These disparities are more evident in certainﬁelds, including car-
diovascular and oncology trials. In this study, we perform a
meta-analysis of clinical trials in neurology, speci ﬁcally on
migraine drugs or biologics, with the objective of assessing the
prevalence of migraine clinical tr ials that include race/ethnicity
data and the prevalence of participants in the trials based on
race/ethnicity. This meta-analysis consisted of publicly available
migraine clinical trials of pharmacologic agents using
ClinicalTrials.gov and included demographic data on race/
ethnicity and sex categories. 2 independent reviewers extracted
study level data for a random effects analysis. Microsoft Excel
was used for data collection and analysis. The primary outcome
is the prevalence of studies that did not incorporate race/
ethnicity data. The secondary outcomes are the prevalence of
each demographic subgroup (White, Black, Combined Other)
among all migraine clinical trialswith demographic information.
A total of 1171 studies were identi ﬁed through a search of ran-
domized clinical trials using ClinicalTrials.gov with search term
Migraine including years 1995 to 2021.After including only
completed interventional studies with results, 246 total trials
were chosen for further analysis. 35 trials were excluded because
they were non-pharmacologic interventions. Out of 211 studies,
92 (46.3%) were excluded because they did not report demo-
graphic data. 119 pharmacologic clinical trials with demographic
data were analyzed. 84.03% of trial participants were female and
15.98% were male. 76.18% of trial participants were white,
9.95% were black and 13.21% were a “combined other” cate-
gory (Asian, American Indian, N ative Hawaiian, Other, and
Unknown/Not reported). Analyses are underway to assess study
sponsors, region, and start date by race/ethnicity categories. Our
preliminary results display a large proportion of migraine clinical
trials on ClinicalTrials.gov between 1995 to 2021 did not report
racial data. Furthermore, the majority of clinical trial participants
were white (76.18%). These results display disparities in clinical
trial participation which raise questions regarding access to clini-
cal trials and warrant further investigation of barriers to equitable
clinical trial recruitment and participation.

Background: Huntington’s Disease (HD) has been believed
to be more prevalent in White Caucasian communities. Even
in the ENROLL-HD data, the largest HD dataset, 93% of
participants identify as White-Non-Hispanic. Given social
and structural determinants of health, including systemic rac-
ism, and bias in healthcare, minoritized communities may
not be well represented in ENROLL-HD and other research
studies. We present sociodemographic data of our
Huntington’s Disease Society of America (HDSA) Center of
Excellence (COE) at UCLA, including patient neighborhood
area of deprivation index (ADI) scores, a marker of neighbor-
hood disadvantage.
Methods: We performed a chart review of patients seen
with a diagnosis of HD at UCLA ’s HDSCA COE
between January 2013 and December 2021. Our electronic
health record system (EHR) was queried for ICD-10 diag-
nosis of Huntington ’s Disease and we collected
sociodemographic data including patients ’ sex, race, ethnic-
ity, neighborhood income, and area of deprivation index
(ADI) scores at a state level. We used descriptive statistics
to present our data.
Results: Since 2013 our center has seen 388 patients
with HD, with 57.47% being women. During this time,
16% of patients identi ﬁed as Hispanic or Latino, 5% as
Black or African American, 2.6% as Asian, and 11% as
Other. Only 57% identi ﬁed as White or Caucasian. Close
to 8% of our patients spoke languages other than English,
including Spanish, Armenian, Farsi, Vietnamese, and Chi-
nese. We had neighborhood income and ADI data for
330 patients. Of those, 4.55% lived in a neighborhood
with an average income below the poverty line for the
state of California (< $35,000 per year), and 13.33%
lived in neighborhoods with households earning less than
$50,000 per year. Over 20% of our patients lived in a
neighborhood with a state ADI decile score of 7 or
higher, indicative of a high level of neighborhood
disadvantage.

and ethnically diverse HD patient population in a single cen-
ter in the United States. Our results suggest that individual
HD centers in the US may care for diverse patient
populations which may not be adequately captured in exis-
tent datasets such as ENROLL-HD. We also provide data on
HD patients ’ neighborhood characteristics, including house-
hold incomes and neighborhood disadvantage. Additional
studies are warranted to better understand social and struc-
tural determinants in HD, and tailor policy interventions to
patients’ needs.

Pilot Study

Hospital, Boston, MA, USA.
Objective: The addition of advance practice providers (APPs)
to neurologic practice is one proposed method of ameliorat-
ing the growing shortage of neurologists. APP degree
programs offer limited experience in clinical Neurology, so
on-the-job neurologic education is critical for ensuring an
APP’s success in neurologic practice. Data to inform optimal
educational methods and the appropriate pace of graduated
clinical responsibility are lacking. By assessing APPs through-
out their ﬁrst year of neurologic practice, we aimed to
describe the typical acquisition of neurologic knowledge and
skills and progression of scope of practice.
Methods: Participants were APPs in their ﬁrst year of neu-

rology practice in hospitals of two academic medical centers.
We developed a survey instrument to evaluate their self-
efﬁcacy and scope of practice. The survey was administered
at 0-, 1-, 3-, 6-, and 12-months post-hire.
Results: 11 APPs participated, completing the survey
19 times. No participants had completed a Neurology resi-
dency program or had prior experience working as a Neurol-
ogy APP. Outpatient providers stopped shadowing and
started conducting independent visits at 3 months. After
3 months, providers expressed universal con ﬁdence in neuro-
logic history and exam skills. By 12 months, providers
reported increasing con ﬁdence in ordering appropriate diag-
nostic testing, generating a differential, and prescribing
appropriate therapies, but had not yet universally achieved
self-efﬁcacy. For outpatient providers, total visits increased
linearly until 6 months (r= 0.59, p= 0.07) then plateaued.
Independent visits began as early as 3 months and continued
to increase linearly through 12 months (r= 0.57, p= 0.05).
Inpatient providers increased the number of patients they
cross covered linearly until 6 months (r= 0.76, p= 0.02)
followed by a plateau. Among disorders, con ﬁdence in man-
aging neuroophthalmological problems was lowest early in
training, but improved throughout the study period.
Interpretation:APPs in this study became con ﬁdent in his-
tory and exam skills in the ﬁrst 3 months after starting a ﬁrst job
in Neurology. Skills related to disease diagnosis and management
were continuing to develop 12 months after start date. Self-
reported total clinical volume plateaued at around 6 months for
our cohort, but independence continued to increase throughout
the ﬁrst year of practice. A multi-center effort is needed to deter-
mine whether this timeline could be expected of a general popu-
lation of APPs practicing Neurology and could inform creation
of onboarding programs for APPs in Neurology.

Huntington’s Disease Care in North America: Analysis

Adys Mendizabal, MD, MS , Susan Perlman, MD, Yvette

Bordelon, MD/PhD. University of California Los Angeles, Los
Angeles, CA, USA.
Introduction: Huntington’s Disease (HD) is a rare neu-
rogenetic condition felt to have a higher prevalence in White
Non-Hispanic patients. Although the exact disease prevalence
in minoritized communities is unknown, there are well-
documented racial and ethnic disparities in access to care for
common neurological conditions. This study aimed to evalu-
ate delays in HD diagnosis and level of disability at the time
of enrollment in ENROLL HD.
Methods: We used multivariate linear regression models
to evaluate differences in the time from the age of symptom
onset to the age of HD diagnosis. Models included biological
variables such as age, sex, CAG repeat length, and type of
symptom at disease onset. Sociodemographic variables
included education, employment status, and geographic loca-
tion. To evaluate the level of disability, we analyzed racial
and ethnic differences in the total functional capacity score
(TFC) during the baseline visit. Multivariate linear regression
models included age, sex, CAG repeat length, level of educa-
tion, and geographic location.
Results: Of 4717 patients in the North America region
with genetically con ﬁrmed Huntington ’s Disease, only 10%
identiﬁed as an ethnicity other than white. 3.35% identi ﬁed
as Latino, 2.29% as Black, 1.12% as Native American, and
0.68% (n=32) as Asian. The average time to HD diagnosis
was 3.78 years, and the average TFC score was 10.22, consis-
tent with Early Manifest HD Stage II. The relationship
between race and ethnicity and delays in diagnosis is mostly
mediated by the type of symptom, with a 2.43-year delay in
diagnosis noted for patients with psychiatric symptoms
(p<0.001). Black patients experienced delays in diagnosis,
with most diagnosed with HD after 4.94 years of symptom
onset compared to White Non-Hispanic patients (p=0.018).
Black and Asian patients had a higher disability at the time
of enrollment, with TFC scores of 9.22 (p<0.001) and 9.39
(p=0.067), respectively.
Conclusion: Despite a limited sample size, Black patients
with HD experience delays in HD diagnosis and enter
ENROLL-HD with higher disability than other racial/ethnic
groups. Not seeing differences in other racial/ethnic groups
may be due to patient selection bias in ENROLL-HD and
the small sample size. Additional HD studies are needed to
understand the causes for delays in access to HD care and
develop appropriate interventions to reduce disparities in
access to HD care.

M169. A Case Series of Children with Choreo-Athetoid

MD, Gulam Qutubuddin Khan, MD. University of Kentucky,
Lexington, KY, USA.
Background: Anti-N-Methyl-D-Aspartate (NMDA) Recep-
tor antibody is the second most common immune mediated
encephalitis, after acute disseminated encephalomyelitis in
pediatric population. In 70% of patients, the clinical course
is preceded by a non-speci ﬁc prodrome of fever, headache,
nausea, or upper respiratory symptoms. Common clinical
presentation includes prominent psychiatric symptoms, cog-
nitive impairment, seizures, autonomic instability, and move-
ment disorders (MD). MDs are seen in 90% of cases and
three principal MDs are chorea, stereotypies, and dystonia.
The hypothesized pathophysiology is that immune response
initiated by a tumor, or a non-speci ﬁc infectious etiology
resulting in production of antibodies that cross the com-
promised blood brain barrier where they interact with
NR1/NR2 subunits of NMDA receptor resulting in
encephalitis.
Design/Methods: Children admitted to Pediatric neurol-
ogy service at University of Kentucky with initial presenta-
tion consistent with abnormal movements and subsequently
diagnosed with Anti-NMDA-receptor antibody encephalitis
were discussed. A detailed workup including history, perti-
nent labs, EEG, imaging were obtained.
Results: Between 2016 and 2021, we had three pediatric
cases that presented with abnormal choreo-athetoid move-
ments as the initial symptom and were subsequently diag-
nosed with Anti-NMDA-receptor antibody encephalitis.
Two of the three cases were infants (2.5 months and
7.5 months) and one of them was a 5-year-old child. Two of
the three children presented with generalized choreoathetoid
movements and one of them presented with left sided chorei-
form movements. One of the cases had a preceding infection
with Herpes simplex virus encephalitis, while the other case
had a Respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis complicated by
Neisseria meningitides pneumonia. EEG captured move-
ments in all three cases with no epileptiform correlate. Two
of the three cases had elevated serum Anti- NMDA antibody
titers and one of them had only CSF antibody positivity.
Treatment options included high dose IV methyl predniso-
lone with good response, followed by Rituximab infusions in
resistant cases.
Conclusions: Clinicians should have high suspicion for
Anti-NMDA-receptor antibody encephalitis in children pre-
senting with abnormal movements and a preceding history of
an infectious prodrome. NMDAR antibody-testing is more
sensitive in CSF than serum. Aggressive testing in both serum
and CSF is warranted when EEG is not consistent with sei-
zures, because Anti-NMDA-receptor antibody encephalitis is
a treatable neurological condition with high morbidity and
mortality if left untreated.

result in non-negligible inclusion of cases with PD diagnosis
uncertainty, or other parkinsonian disorders (e.g., atypical
neurodegenerative conditions, secondary parkinsonism, essen-

accuracy of case reporting will improve the usefulness of PD

from other parkinsonian disorders, while revealing informa-

medical history, medications, diagnosis codes, encounter fre-

learning models for unbiased identi ﬁcation of EHR criteria

one parkinsonism ICD code, where the majority of non-PD

deployed in EHR systems to report PD more accurately.

RBD (REM without atonia (PD+RWA)).
Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we conducted
power spectral analysis on polysomnographic electroencepha-
logram data. The sample consisted of 55 individuals with
PD: 10 PD-DEB-RWA and 45 PD+RBD (8 without DEB
but with RWA (PD+RWA); 13 with DEB but without
RWA (PD+DEB); and 24 with both DEB and RWA (PD
+DEB+RWA)). Relative spindle power (rSP; 11-15Hz) and
relative slow oscillations power (rSO; 0,5-1,5Hz) were calcu-
lated as SP and SO power, respectively, divided by total
power (0,5-30Hz) and averaged across sleep stages N2-N3.
To limit variability, we only used the ﬁrst sleep cycle. Frontal
and central SPA and SOA were calculated as the absolute
value of the differences between mean relative values for left
and right; higher values translate to greater asymmetry.
Mann-Whitney test was used to compare SPA and SOA
between PD-DEB-RWA and combined PD+RBD groups.
Kruskal-Wallis test was used to compare all 4 groups.

(SD 52,22min). We found no signi ﬁcant differences in central
SPA or SOA between PD-DEB-RWA vs. PD+RBD. For fron-
tal SPA we found that PD-DEB-RWA had greater asymmetry
(p=0,03) compared to PD+RBD and a trend for a difference
between PD-DEB-RWA, PD+DEB+RWA, PD +RWA and
PD+DEB was observed (p=0,05), where PD-DEB-RWA had
the most asymmetry, compared to other 3 groups. For frontal

and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index in Assessing Sleep in
Parkinson’s Disease
Corina Catiul, MD

MS1, Raima Memon, MD1, Jennifer Pilkington, .1,K i m b e r l y
H. Wood, PhD2, Amy W. Amara, MD PhD1. 1UAB, Birmingham,
AL, USA,2Samford University, Birmingham, AL, USA.
Objective: Compare polysomnography (PSG)-derived sleep

parameters to estimated sleep measures derived from
actigraphy and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) in a
cross-sectional, observational study to determine which mea-
sure is superior in assessing sleep in Parkinson ’s disease (PD).
Background: Sleep quality is known to play an essential role
in the cognitive health of the general population. Sleep disorders
are among the most prevalent and disabling non-motor symp-
toms of PD. PSG is the gold standard for sleep evaluation, but is
sometimes unavailable or impractical. Several measures for
assessing sleep parameters exist. In this study, we compare the
gold standard PSG to 1) actigraphy combined with sleep diary
and 2) PSQI to better characterize their use in a PD population.
Methods: 62 persons with PD underwent a one-time
laboratory-based PSG and wore an actigraph on the wrist for
two weeks (accompanied by a sleep diary) in the home envi-
ronment. Subjective sleep was evaluated with the PSQI ques-
tionnaire, which measures perceived sleep quality over a
1-month period. Outcomes derived from each measure
included sleep ef ﬁciency (SE), total sleep time (TST), sleep
onset latency (SOL), and wake after sleep onset (WASO).
Descriptive statistics were used to characterize the demo-
graphic data and disease characteristics and Pearson ’s correla-
tion coef ﬁcient to compare relationships between each
measured outcome: 1) PSG and actigraphy, 2) PSG and
PSQI, and 3) actigraphy and PSQI.
Results: Our sample was 65.5 /C67.2 years of age (mean /C6
SD), 65% male, and 92% Caucasian, with 16 (14-18) years
of education (median (IQR)). Disease characteristics included
duration of disease: 5.0 (2.0 - 9.0) years, levodopa equivalent
dose: 600.0 (317.5 - 843.75) mg, and MDS-UPDRS total
score 53.7 /C619.1. There were signi ﬁcant correlations
between actigraphy and PSG for all sleep parameters (all
p<0.01). However, only SE signi ﬁcantly correlated between
actigraphy and PSQI ( p=0.029), and no signi ﬁcant correla-
tions were observed between PSQI and PSG.
Conclusion: Actigraphy was found to be a reliable method
of assessing sleep in this sample of mild-moderate
PD. Although it lacks the sleep staging information that PSG
offers, actigraphy measures sleep in the home environment and
is a more affordable method. In addition, PSQI can be a valu-
able and rapid method to assess subjective sleep quality and
could inform need for further sleep investigation, being the
quickest and easiest method among the ones investigated here.

Introduction: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is a neurode-
generative condition characterized by subcortical atrophy,
where subcortical volume has been proposed as a biomarker of
disease progression. Contemporary segmentation algorithms
may not accurately identify subcortical structures in MSA due
to unclear anatomic boundaries in these structures and ele-
vated iron concentration, especially in the putamen and
globus pallidus (GP). Here, we assessed the accuracy of three
different segmentation techniques in a cohort of early MSA
patients and compared basal ganglia volumes to age matched
healthy control (HC) and Parkinson ’s disease (PD) cohorts.
Methods: We enrolled 21 early MSA patients
(age=64.4/C69.3) (motor symptoms for less than 3 years),
17 with PD (age=63.2 /C66.1), and 18 HC (age=65.6 /C66.8).
All underwent 3T brain MRI. Early MSA patients had mild
to moderate clinical severity, based on neurologic assessment.
A neuroradiologist manually delineated putamen, caudate,
and GP structures using T
1-weighted scans over 8 patients.
Then, segmentation was computed over the entire dataset
using FSL FIRST, joint label fusion (JLF), and AssemblyNet
(an ensemble deep-learning technique). Segmentation accu-
racy was estimated using Sørensen-Dice coef ﬁcient (DSC) on
the subset composed of manually delineated early MSA
patients. Group difference was evaluated on the whole cohort
using generalized linear model (group, age, and total intracra-
nial volume as co-variates).
Results: Compared to FSL FIRST, segmentation using
JLF and AssemblyNet were more accurate for delineation of
putamen (DSC difference=4.6 and 4.4; p-value=0.01 and
0.002) and globus pallidus (DSC difference=3.8 and 4.8 per-
cent; p-value=0.01 and 0.007). No differences were evident
for delineation of the caudate nucleus. Using AssemblyNet,
lower subcortical volumes were observed in MSA patients
versus HC for the putamen (volume difference=-1.05 cm
3,
p-value=0.028) and GP (volume difference=-0.27cm 3, p-val-
ue= 0.004), and MSA versus PD in the GP (volume differ-
ence=-0.29cm3, p-value=0.034) and in the putamen (volume
difference=-0.53cm3, p-value=0.22).
Conclusions: Ensemble deep-learning segmentation out-
performs classical methods. This improvement was observed
in subcortical structures with notable MSA pathology. In early
MSA, signiﬁcant reductions in putamen and GP volume were
observed compared to HC, and in GP volume compared to
PD. This work will allow for a more accurate de ﬁnition of
subcortical structures, an essential step for quantifying changes
in MSA, such as tissue atrophy and iron deposition.
M176. Development of a Quantitative Pull-Test in Early
Parkinson’s Disease
Tuhin Virmani, MD, PhD , Mousumi Patra, PhD, Aliyah
Glover, BS, Lakshmi Pillai, MS. University of Arkansas for
Medical Sciences, Little Rock, AR, USA.
Objective: To develop a test that quanti ﬁably measures the
backward stepping response on the pull-test in early
Parkinson’s disease (PD).
Background: Postural instability can occur in latter stages
of PD. The clinical pull-test on the Uni ﬁed Parkinson ’s dis-
ease rating scale (UPDRS) documents postural instability as
2 or higher on a 0-4 scale. This ordinal scale does not ade-
quately track progression in early-PD or predict development
of postural instability. Additionally, not all people step back-
wards when pulled, making it dif ﬁcult to stratify people with

a normal response (score 0).
Methods: Participants were asked to either step backwards
as needed (classic pull-test), or step backwards with each
shoulder pull (modi ﬁed pull-test) at four pull strengths. Four
spatiotemporal parameters (reaction-time, step-back-time,
step-back-distance, step-back-velocity) were quanti ﬁed in
35 controls and 79 PD participants using an instrumented
gait-mat and compared to standard PD measures using linear
regression and Kendall ’s tau b correlation coef ﬁcients (with
Benjamini-Hochberg corrections). Repeated measures analysis
of variance (ANOVA) was used to determine group differ-
ences. In a subset of participants Bland-Altman plots were
used to determine reproducibility of these measures.
Results: Participants were well matched for age (con-
trols: 66.3 /C67.2, PD 68.3 /C68.1 years old). On the classic
pull-test, 36% controls and 30% PD participants did not
step backwards on the hardest p ull. Step-back-distance in
PD participants on the hardest pull was predicted by motor
UPDRS scores (F(1,78)=19.092, R2=0.199, p<0.001) and
they were inversely correlated (Kendall ’s=-0.291; p=0.009).
Step-back-distance was also p redicted by freezing of gait
questionnaire (FOG-Q) scores (F(1,78)=14.521,
R2=0.159, p<0.001) with inverse correlation (Kendall ’s=-
0.260; p=0.018). Step-back-velocity was predicted by
motor UPDRS scores (F(1,78)=11.280, R2=0.128,
p=0.001) and FOG-Q scores (F(1,78)=6.287, R2=0.075,
p=0.014), and inversely correlated with motor UPDRS
scores (Kendall ’s=-0.224; p=0.038). Repeated measures
ANOVA over the four pull strengths, with age and sex as
covariates, showed signi ﬁcant group differences (PD vs con-
trol) for step-back-distance (F(1, 110)=4.431, p=0.038).
Repeat assessments in 16 parti cipants, on average 0.7 years
apart, showed good agreement on step-back-distance at all
pull strengths using Bland-Altman plots.
Conclusions: Our quanti ﬁable modi ﬁed pull-test most
closely reproduces the clinical pull-test using equipment that
is becoming more readily available in the clinical setting and
does not require additional training outside of the UPDRS.
The backward stepping response in PD participants was
quantiﬁable, reproducible, and related to disease severity.
Our method could thereby help to quantify disease progres-
sion on the pull-test in early PD without postural instability.

Background and Objective: Mutations in leucine-rich repeat
kinase 2 (LRRK2) are one of the most common causes of
familial Parkinson ’s disease (PD). Lewy bodies are late-stage
aggregates of αSYN ( αSYN) and are considered pathological
hallmarks in PD. Although clinical presentations of PD
patients with LRRK2 mutations are indistinguishable from
sporadic PD, some of the LRRK2-PD patients lack Lewy
bodies. Recently, the toxicity of αSYN oligomers, which are
early aggregates of αSYN, has attracted attention; however,
the distribution of αSYN oligomers in LRRK2-PD remains
unknown. We hypothesized that the accumulation of αSYN
oligomers is involved in the pathogenesis of LRRK2-PD and
aimed to elucidate the distribution of αSYN oligomers in
LRRK2-PD brains.
Methods: We examined for accumulation of synuclein
oligomers in brain samples from four LRRK2-PD patients
with G2019S mutation and ﬁve LRRK2-PD patients with
I2020T mutation. Among LRRK2-PD brains, two with
G2019S mutation and three with I2020T mutation had no
Lewy bodies. We also used ﬁve brain samples with no clinical
history of Parkinsonism or no Lewy pathologies in the neuro-
pathological examination as control samples. We visualized
αSYN oligomers by a homotypic proximity ligation assay and
examined the distribution of αSYN oligomers in the
brainstem, basal ganglia, limbic, and neocortex. We evaluated
the αSYN oligomer burden in each brain region.
Results: All LRRK2-PD patients, including those without
Lewy bodies, showed an accumulation of αSYN oligomers in
all regions. Control brains showed no αSYN-PLA signals
except for slight signals in the locus coeruleus and parietal
cortex in one brain and in the caudate nucleus and occipital
cortex in another brain. The αSYN oligomer burden in the
neocortex, brainstem, and hippocampus was signi ﬁcantly
higher in LRRK2-PD patients with G2019S mutation than
in those with I2020T mutation. When we compare the
αSYN oligomer burden within LRRK2-PD patients, in the
entorhinal cortex, the burden was higher in LRRK2-PD
patients without Lewy bodies than that in LRRK2-PD
patients with Lewy bodies.
Conclusions: We observed a widespread accumulation of
αSYN oligomers in LRRK2-PD patient brains regardless of
the presence of Lewy bodies, suggesting αSYN oligomers
may contribute to the pathogenesis of LRRK2-PD.
M178. Eleven-Year Medication Use and Costs from the
Deep Brain Stimulation in Early-Stage Parkinson ’s
Disease Pilot Clinical Trial

Kelly A. Harper, BPS, Thomas L. Davis, MD, Peter E. Konrad,
MD, David Charles, MD, Mallory L. Hacker, PhD, MSCI.
Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN, USA.
Background: Subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation
(STN-DBS) is widely recognized to reduce the need for
Parkinson’s disease (PD) medications and their associated
costs in mid- and advanced-staged PD [1]. Prior analysis of
the only clinical trial to evaluate DBS in early-stage PD
patients suggest that STN-DBS applied early in the disease
course may also provide long-term medication cost reduction
compared to standard care [2]. Patients from the early DBS
pilot clinical trial were evaluated at a long-term follow-up
visit eleven years after randomization to collect data regarding
their PD medication regimens.
Objective: To report the 11-year medication use and costs

from the DBS in early-stage Parkinson ’s disease pilot clinical
trial.
Methods: Thirty patients with early-stage PD were ran-
domized 1:1 in the trial to receive optimal drug therapy
(ODT) alone or bilateral STN-DBS plus ODT. This analysis
includes the mean annual costs and levodopa equivalent daily
doses (LEDD) at the 11-year study visit for subjects who
completed this long-term observational follow-up study
(n = 12: early ODT, n = 8: early DBS+ODT n = 4). Medica-
tion strengths, doses, and frequencies were collected from
subjects at each visit. PD medication costs were calculated
using prices from the Drug Topics Red Book.
Results: Three out of eight early ODT subjects received
bilateral STN-DBS as standard of care by the 11-year study
visit. On average, early DBS+ODT subjects were taking
339mg less LEDD than early ODT subjects at the 11-year
study visit (early DBS+ODT = 565 /C6262mg; early
ODT = 904 /C6431mg). Annual PD medication costs was
$12,217/C6$6,683 for early ODT subjects and
$12,757/C611,180 for the early DBS+ODT subjects.
Conclusion: Although more than one-third of early ODT
subjects were receiving STN-DBS, early DBS+ODT subjects
continued to have lower LEDD 11 years after randomization.
A larger cohort is needed to understand the long-term impact
of early DBS on PD medication costs. The FDA has
approved the conduct of a prospective, randomized, double-
blind clinical trial evaluating DBS in patients with very early-
stage PD.

M180. Functional Characterization of Genetically
Deﬁned Subtypes of Nigrostriatal Dopamine Neurons
During Movement and Rewards

A. Dombeck, PhD. Northwestern University, Evanston,
IL, USA.
Recent single cell studies have identiﬁed several molecularly dis-
tinct subtypes of midbrain dopamine neurons (Poulin et al.
2016), with different cell body locations, projection patterns,
and vulnerability in Parkinson ’s Disease models. But whether
this genetic division relates to the function of the neurons
remains unanswered. Here, we characterized the activity of sev-
eral of these subtypes in the mouse during dopamine related
behaviors, such as locomotion, reward consumption, and
response to aversive stimuli. We used intersectional genetic strat-
egies to label the individual dopaminergic subtypes with the cal-
cium indicator GCaMP6f, and recorded changes in ﬂuorescence
using one-photon ﬁber photometry. We found that, beyond the
previously identi ﬁed morphological differences, nigrostriatal
dopamine subtypes have distinct functional signaling patterns.
For example, locomotion related calcium transients correlated
mostly with accelerations in some subtypes, but mostly with
decelerations in others. These results could explain previous
incongruences in dopamine signaling patterns found during
recordings of unde ﬁned dopamine neuron subtypes during
movements (Howe et al. 2016, Dodson et al. 2016, Da Silva
et al. 2016 Coddington et al. 2018), and have implications for
the research and treatment of dopamine related disorders.

Improvement: Patient Experience of Receiving Deep
Brain Stimulation Early versus Later in Parkinson ’s
Disease

Background: Patients receiving deep brain stimulation
(DBS) in mid-to-late-stage Parkinson ’s disease (PD) often
describe dramatic improvements in symptoms and quality of
life. Such “life changing ” and “miraculous” post-surgical
descriptions [1, 2] are expected given the state of PD when
DBS is currently applied. The DBS in early-stage PD pilot
clinical trial randomized very early-stage PD patients to
receive subthalamic nucleus (STN) DBS plus optimal drug
therapy (early DBS+ODT) versus optimal drug therapy (early
ODT). Trial participants were interviewed 11 years after ran-
domization to understand their experience living with PD.
Objective: To report the patient experience of receiving
DBS in early-stage PD compared to receiving DBS in mid-
to-late PD, per current standard of care.
Methods: Patients approached for enrollment in an
11-year follow-up of the pilot trial (IRB#180766) were also
offered participation in this interview study (IRB#191728).
Semi-structured interviews were audio-recorded and tran-
scribed. Transcripts were coded and analyzed using an itera-
tive inductive-deductive approach.
Results: Seven PD patients with DBS were interviewed
(n=4 early DBS+ODT; n=3 early ODT + standard-of-care
DBS). Patients randomized to early ODT in the trial but
who later received standard-of-care DBS articulated signi ﬁ-
cant improvement in symptoms following DBS implementa-
tion. In contrast, early DBS patients did not describe
immediate, impactful improvement to speci ﬁc symptoms,
aside from one patient whose tremor was eliminated. Early
DBS patients instead spoke of the stability of their lives
despite living with PD, commenting how they were not
greatly affected by PD for many years after DBS or were even
“unaware” daily that they had PD. Unlike standard-of-care
DBS patients, early DBS patients were often unable to iden-
tify speci ﬁc ways that DBS helped them, instead noticing
that DBS seemed to prevent symptoms that they knew devel-
oped in others with PD.
Conclusion: This study suggests that the experience of
early DBS differs substantially from that of standard-of-care
DBS due to the difference in Parkinson ’s disease severity at
the time when the treatment is applied, with early DBS being
described as maintaining, rather than drastically altering,
quality of life. More investigation is needed to understand
the patient experience after receiving early DBS, and the
FDA has approved a randomized, double-blind, pivotal clini-
cal trial evaluating DBS in early-stage PD (IDEG050016).

® Huntington’s Disease App: Usability
Assessment and Design Implications
Ellen Wagner, MS , Emma Waddell, BA, E. Ray Dorsey, MD,
MBA, Jamie L. Adams, MD. University of Rochester, Rochester,
NY, USA.
Objective: To assess issues in app usability to inform interface
reﬁnements for optimal user engagement in clinical research.
Background: Advancements in digital health technologies
are transforming clinical trials. As the complexity of these tools

evolves, however, the need to involve users early on in the
design process becomes essential to limit usability challenges.
In 2019 we conducted a usability assessment of GEORGE
®,
an Android app for Huntington ’s disease (HD), which lever-
ages the smartphone screen, sensors, and microphone to cap-
ture tapping speed, chorea, balance, gait, and voice.
Methods: This mixed-method usability assessment was
completed during and following a 1-month observational pilot
study aimed at evaluating the feasibility of using the GEO-
RGE
® app to quantify motor symptoms of HD and assess
their daily variability in the home environment. Participants
in the pilot study voluntarily took part in the usability assess-
ment. Of 23 total study participants, 11 completed in-person
interviews, 21 were observed completing tasks in-clinic or via
video recording, and 23 provided feedback via a survey. A
coding process allowed for the categorization of common
themes. This approach afforded a nuanced understanding of
the design issues impacting app use and engagement.
Results: While the pilot study demonstrated the feasibility
and ef ﬁcacy of the GEORGE
® app, the usability assessment
identiﬁed four categories of issues: (1) variability in partici-
pant capacity for mobile-speci ﬁc gestures, (2) cognitive bur-
den associated with app use, (3) mismatch between visual
design elements and intended user action, (4) confusion with
wording, presentation, and placement of content. These ﬁnd-
ings informed the following recommendations: facilitate mul-
timodal data entry, rewrite task instructions in more
accessible language, provide alternative modes of instruction
such as voice, images, and video options to complement writ-
ten instructions, and enlarge touchable areas.
Conclusion:This usability assessment underscores the impor-
tance of integrating participant “voice” in the design process of
apps for use by individuals with HD, especially given the variable
and complex combination of motor, cognitive, and psychological
symptoms experienced. While the ﬁndings and recommenda-
tions are GEORGE
® speciﬁc, they have applicability to the
design of digital health technologies for other neurodegenerative
disorders. A user-centered design approach ensures that distinct
sets of accessibility challenges are addressed to create tools that
are usable and engaging - as well as useful from a research and/or
clinical perspective. In addition, positive user engagement helps
to ensure the validity and integrity of study data generated.

Background: Hepatolenticular Degeneration, or Wilson ’s
disease, is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabo-
lism in which the ATP7B gene is mutated. This mutation
leads to the impaired function of an intracellular copper
transporter, resulting in the buildup of copper primarily in
the liver, brain, and cornea. There can be a myriad of presen-
tations including damage to the liver, neurologic distur-
bances, psychiatric changes, and copper rings in the descemet
membrane of the cornea, or Kayser-Fleischer rings. Below is
a case of Wilson ’s initially presenting with neurologic distur-
bances during an acute postoperative period.
Case Presentation: A 27-year-old male without medical his-
tory presented to the hospital with appendicitis warranting
emergent appendectomy, during which the liver was visualized
as abnormal, and a biopsy was taken. In the immediate postop-
erative period he began drooling, developed dysphagia, dysar-
thria, and gait ataxia. Liver biopsy revealed quiescent cirrhosis
without increased copper stores. Laboratory testing revealed uri-
nary copper of 138mcg/dL, elevated PT, elevated INR. PTT,
AST, ALT, and Alkaline Phosphatase were within normal
limits. Physical exam was pertinent for masked facies, risus
sardonicus, and mild dystonia. H e later developed personality
changes including lowered inhibitions and his expressions
shifted from introversion to extroversion. After genetic testing
conﬁrmed Wilson’s disease, he began copper chelator and zinc
therapy. In addition, he also started physical and occupational
therapy, which improved his dysphagia and dysarthria.
Conclusions: This case demonstrates Wilson ’s disease with
neurologic symptom onset in a postoperative state and an
incidental ﬁnding of liver cirrhosis, prompting further investi-
gation. The variability in presentation of Wilson ’s disease as
well as the rare nature of this illness should put it higher on a
differential list. Despite the incidental biopsy results, labora-
tory tests of liver function were normal in this case, indicat-
ing that this rare disease could have gone unnoticed if not for
the emergent appendectomy that allowed visualization of a
cirrhotic liver. The use of copper chelators and zinc in con-
junction with physical and occupational therapy improved
dysarthria and dysphagia, demonstrating the value of early
diagnosis and multimodal intervention.

Background: The Parkinson Disease Patient Reports of
Problems (PD-PROP) comprises open-ended questions that
ask PD patients to report in their own words the problems

that bother them and how these problems affect functioning.
Respondents may report up to ﬁve problems that they priori-
tize from most to least bothersome. We have developed a
‘human-in-the-loop’ method for curating PD-PROP data
into classiﬁable symptoms.
Methods: The sample is comprised of participants in Fox
Insight, an online longitudinal research study that collects self-
reported health related infor mation (https://foxinsight.
michaeljfox.org/). The PD-PROP has been included since 2017.
As of 2020, >25,000 participants who af ﬁrmed a PD diagnosis
had completed the PD-PROP by keyboard entry. Nine curators,
the majority clinicians and incl uding three experience experts
(PD patients) developed conceptual boundaries for symptoms
across multiple domains. Based on collective and independent
reviews, the curators classiﬁed verbatim reports analyzed by natu-
ral language processing into symptoms and provided key phrases
for each symptom. . Concordance of machine classi ﬁcation,
compared with expert classiﬁcations, was evaluated in a separate
sample. De-identiﬁed symptom classi ﬁcations are available to
researchers on the Fox Insight Data Exploration Network
https://foxden.michaeljfox.org/insight/explore/insight.jsp.
Results: Boundaries for 65 symptoms in domains of
tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability, gait, other
motor, sleep, fatigue, cognition, psychological, pain, auto-
nomic dysfunction, ﬂuctuations and dyskinesias were
established. Final agreement between the machine and expert
curators for each symptom ranged between 96 and 100%.
The dataset included baseline reports of 25,202 PD patients
with median three years since diagnosis and median age 67.
Problems reported were most commonly in the domains of
“other motor ” (dystonia, posture, dexterity, speech) (54%),
tremor (45%), and psychological (affect/motivation/thought-
perception/other psychiatric) (43%). The least commonly
reported domains were ﬂuctuations (5%), and dyskinesias
(5%). During the curation process, additional problems were
identiﬁed including fear of the future, medication side effects,
restlessness, loss of sense of taste/smell, reduced self esteem/
embarrassment, tingling, and drooling.
Conclusions: Verbatim reports using natural language
processing and human-in-the loop curation can be used to
analyze problems reported by PD patients in their own words
and applied to observational studies and clinical trials.

M187. Inﬂammatory Changes in Subjects with De Novo
Parkinson’s Disease
Talene A. Yacoubian, MD, PhD, Adam Gerstenecker, PhD,
Yu-Hua Fang, PhD, Amy Amara, MD, PhD, Natividad
Stover, MD, Lauren Ruffrage, MS, Christopher Collette, BS,
Richard Kennedy, PhD, Yue Zhang, PhD, Hongwei Qin, PhD,
Etty Benveniste, PhD, Jonathan McConathy, MD, PhD,
David G. Standaert, MD, PhD, FANA . University of
Alabama at Birmingham, Birmingham, AL, USA.
Objective: To examine whether in ﬂammation is present in
subjects newly diagnosed with Parkinson ’s disease (PD).
Background: Evidence for the role of in ﬂammation in PD
has been growing. Brain in ﬂammation has been observed in
postmortem PD brains. Cross-sectional studies from living
persons with PD show increased cytokines and chemokines
and changes in circulating immune cells. PET studies and
genetic studies also support the role of in ﬂammation in
PD. Several key gaps remain as to the impact of in ﬂamma-
tion in the degenerative process, including the extent of
immune activation in persons with PD early in the disease
and whether increased pro-in ﬂammatory signals predict more
rapid clinical decline.
Methods: In the present study, we enrolled subjects with
de novo PD (n=58) and age-matched healthy controls
(n=62). Inclusion criteria for PD subjects included a diagno-
sis for PD by UK Brain Bank criteria within 2 years and no

prior treatment with PD medications. Subjects underwent
clinical assessments, including demographics, medication his-
tory, neurological examination, Movement Disorder Society-
United Parkinson ’s Disease rating scale (MDS-UPDRS),
among other scales. Subjects underwent comprehensive
neurocognitive assessment that met requirements as a Level
II diagnostic MCI assessment as recommended by the MDS
task force. Blood was obtained for ﬂow cytometry and cyto-
kine/chemokine analyses. Subjects underwent dynamic brain
PET/MR imaging with the TSPO ligand [F-18]DPA-714
imaging and lumbar puncture if eligible and consented.
Results: Baseline demographics and medical history were
comparable between groups. PD subjects showed signi ﬁcant
differences in University of Pennsylvania Smell Identi ﬁcation
Test, Schwab and England Activities of Daily Living, Scales
for Outcomes in PD autonomic dysfunction, and MDS-
UPDRS scores. Cognitive testing demonstrated signi ﬁcant
differences in cognitive composite, executive function, and
visuospatial ability at baseline. Brain PET showed increased
DPA-714 signal in PD subjects compared to healthy con-
trols. Analyses of cytokines, chemokines, and other in ﬂam-
matory markers are currently in process.
Conclusions: Our data show signi ﬁcant cognitive differ-
ences in controls compared to de novo PD subjects. We also
observed evidence for increased central in ﬂammation in these
subjects, based on DPA-714 imaging. Longitudinal follow-up
is in process to determine whether the presence of in ﬂamma-
tion is predictive of cognitive decline in this cohort.

M189. Literature-Based Discovery to Assess Parkinson ’s
Disease Adjuvants to Levodopa

B.S., Minzhi Wang, B.S., Cassie S. Mitchell, Ph.D.. Georgia
Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA.
Introduction: The objective of this study was to ﬁnd thera-
peutic drugs that may be repurposed for the treatment of
Parkinson’s disease (PD). L-Dihydroxyphenylalanine or levo-
dopa (L-Dopa) is a precursor of dopamine that is widely used
in the symptomatic treatment of Parkinson ’s disease. How-
ever, with long-time use, the ef ﬁcacy of L-Dopa decreases,
leading to ﬂuctuations of dopamine in the brain. The goal of
this study was to use literature-based discovery to identify
drugs or substances that could improve Parkinsonian symp-
toms or serve as adjuvant therapies.
Methods: SemNet 2.0, a literature-based discovery soft-
ware that uses machine learning, was utilized to explore pos-
sible alternatives or adjuvants of levodopa (L-dopa) by
querying the National Library of Medicine ’s SemMedDB.
The query found source nodes in a knowledge graph that
relate to L-dopa. Drugs or substances were ranked using
HeteSim score. A HeteSim score is feature measuring the
relevance of a given metapath, or speci ﬁed relationship,
between a source node and user-speci ﬁed target.
Results: The simulation resulted in a list of 1890 source
nodes ranked by their HeteSim scores. Examples of selected
source nodes with highly ranked relationships with levodopa
included piroxicam, le ﬂunomide, and loratadine. Most of the

highly ranked drugs or substances that showed potential in
ameliorating Parkinsonian symptoms and/or aiding in the
preservation of levodopa ’se f
ﬁcacy were either anti-
inﬂammatory agents or antihistamines. Ranked candidates
were compared using statistical analysis and supporting evi-
dence was examined using human-in-the-loop validation.
Conclusion: Cross-domain literature connections between
levodopa and other drugs consistently point to substances
with anti-in ﬂammatory or antihistamine properties. Further
exploration of repurposed drugs with SemNet 2.0 or link
prediction could expedite identi ﬁcation of etiological drug
targets or ideal adjuvant therapeutic candidates.

Network Dynamics and Contact Site Misregulation in
Neurodegenerative Diseases

G. Molakal, None, Jasmine Cisneros, BS, Eric D. Leisten, BS,
Yvette C. Wong, PhD . Northwestern University Feinberg
School of Medicine, Chicago, IL, USA.
Both mitochondria and lysosomes are key organelles for regu-
lating neuronal function and homeostasis, and have been
implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple neurodegenerative
diseases. We recently identi ﬁed their direct interaction with
one another at mitochondria-lysosome membrane contact
sites, allowing for their bidirectional crosstalk. However, the
role of mitochondria-lysosome contact sites and their contri-
butions to neurological disorders are still not well under-
stood. We used super-resolution live structured illumination
microscopy, and high spatial and temporal resolution imaging
to investigate mitochondrial/lysosomal network dynamics and
function in different genetic models of neurodegenerative dis-
eases, including the peripheral neuropathy Charcot-Marie-
Tooth Type 2 Disease. Our studies demonstrate that the for-
mation and tethering of mitochondria-lysosome contacts are
directly misregulated in multiple neurodegenerative diseases,
contributing to further defects in mitochondrial and lyso-
somal network dynamics. These studies highlight a major
role for mitochondria-lysosome contact sites and the precise
regulation of their dynamics in the etiology of multiple neu-
rological disorders and neuropathies.

with Multiple System Atrophy

Phillip A. Low, M.D., Wolfgang Singer, M.D., Elizabeth
A. Coon, M.D.. Mayo Clinic, Rochester, MN, USA.
Objectives: To describe outcomes of patients with multiple
system atrophy (MSA) who had previously undergone deep
brain stimulation (DBS) surgery.
Background: MSA patients with predominant parkinson-
ism may initially be diagnosed with Parkinson ’s disease
(PD) and undergo DBS. Previous case reports have suggested
unfavorable effects of DBS in these patients; however, their
outcomes are unclear.
Methods: We retrospectively reviewed medical records of all
patients with a diagnosis of probable or possible MSA evaluated
at Mayo Clinic sites from 1998 to 2021. Patients with DBS
were selected, and the timeline of disease course was analyzed.
Results: Of 847 patients diagnosed with probable or possi-
ble MSA, 12 patients had DBS. Eleven patients were female,
and 1 patient had the surgery at our institution. The mean age
of symptom onset was 51.25 ( /C68.14) years. The indications

for surgery are listed: motor ﬂuctuations (2 patients), inade-
quate response to levodopa (3 patients), medical-refractory
tremor (2 patients), and levodopa intolerance (1 patient), with
4 patients had more than one of the aforementioned indica-
tions. The diagnosis was PD in 9 patients and parkinsonism
or atypical parkinsonism in 3 patients at the time of surgery.
Excluding those three patients, the mean duration from the
time of PD diagnosis to DBS surgery was 5.22 ( /C63.59) years.
In all patients, the surgery was associated with partial/
signiﬁcant improvement for a short period (days to months).
After this initial symptom improvement, 8 patients reported
recurrence/worsening of previous symptoms. New motor and
autonomic symptoms were reported in 6 and 5 patients,
respectively. Also, 2 patients developed new cognitive symp-
toms such as hallucinations. Four patients reported relatively
stable improvement in tremor or levodopa-induced dyskinesia
with DBS. DBS was eventually turned off in 4 patients. In ret-
rospect, all patients had at least one red ﬂag sign or symptom
suggesting atypical parkinsonism (including autonomic dys-
function, early falls, dysphagia, dysarthria, dysphonia, dystonia,
or poor levodopa responsiveness) prior to surgery. All patients
developed symptoms of autonomic failure during their disease
course; 7 patients reported autonomic dysfunction prior to sur-
gery. Composite autonomic severity score could be calculated
in 6 patients with a mean score of 6.16 ( /C62.13), indicating a
moderate autonomic failure.

supporting poor outcomes in patients with MSA undergoing
DBS surgery. Autonomic dysfunction in a patient with par-
kinsonism should be considered a red ﬂag which deserves fur-
ther evaluation prior to DBS surgery.

patients with ALS.
Methods: Study MT-1186-A01 is a global, multicenter,

185 patients. Oral edaravone was generally safe and well toler-

of ALS symptoms (6.5%), dysphagia (3.2%), dyspnea (2.7%),

Background: Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP) is a com-
plex neurodegenerative disease, with unique clinical and path-
ological entities. Although PSP can have varied phenotypic
presentations, it is classically recognized by frequent falls, ver-
tical ophthalmoparesis and bradykinesia or rigidity. The
deﬁnitive diagnosis of PSP is based on pathological studies
showing misfolded tau proteins, however, clinical presenta-
tion along with imaging ﬁndings are used for diagnosis. Pho-
tosensitive and photophobia have been seen in PSP but have
never been described in the literature as a presenting symp-
tom. We describe a case with photosensitivity as the pre-
senting feature in a patient with PSP.
Case Presentation: We present a case of a 71 female with
history of hypothyroidism who presented with 6 month his-
tory of photosensitivity requiring her to wear dark sunglasses
both indoors and outdoors, followed by a 4 month history of
frequent falls, progressive slowness in her movements and
slurred speech. On exam, she had restricted vertical gaze,
slurred speech and bradykinesia was evident. MRI of the
brain showed midbrain atrophy with sparing of the pons
resulting in the classic hummingbird sign as well as superior

Discussion: Although PSP can have many different clini-

usually frequent falls. Photosensitivity has been described as
an associated ﬁnding in PSP but never as a presenting fea-
