M199. Monitoring and Preventing Neuroleptic Use in
Parkinsonian Population in an Inpatient Setup - Quality
Control Measure
Richa Tripathi, MD , Ryder Dalton, Undergraduate student,
Deanna Carter, NA, Joy Shea, PharmD, Jami Pincavitch,
MD. West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA.
Introduction: Exposure to neuroleptics including antipsy-
chotics and antiemetics, is a major cause for worsened motor
and cognitive outcomes in patients with Parkinsonism.
Elderly parkinsonian patients admitted to a hospital are prone
to delirium and psychosis that results in inadvertent use of
such medications. We attempted to introduce Best Practice
Alert (BPA) for use in patients with Parkinsonism to warn
providers of possible risks associated with neuroleptic use
while providing alternatives.
Methods: Patients admitted with diagnosis of Parkinsonism
at tertiary care center, were monitored from February 2021 to
April 2022. BPA was triggered when a neuroleptic medication
was used in this population. The alert would warn about the
need to use alternative medications such as quetiapine, cloza-
pine or pimavanserin for psychosis and ondansetron or
trimethobenzamide for nausea treatment. Providers could
choose to follow the suggestion, cancel the suggestion or over-
ride the suggestion after providing a reason.
Results: There were 231 events associated with use of anti-
psychotic. Alert was overriden125/231 (54.1%) times, of
which 33/125 (26.4%) times it was due to continuation of
home medication and 22/125 times (17.6%) it was per psy-
chiatry recommendations. 39/231 times (16.8%) preferred
medication order was placed. Further, 19/231 (8.2%) times
the offending agent was removed and 48/231 (20.7%) BPA
was cancelled and provider did not proceed with any medica-
tion. The success rate of this alert is effective 45.7% of the
time in keeping the patient from getting the sub-optimal
therapy and/or ordered the right medication. For antiemetics,
32/136 (23.5%) of the time BPA was followed and rec-
ommended order was placed. Alert was overridden 29/136
(21.3%) times due to failed therapy from recommended
medication. Offending agent was removed 47/136 (34.5%).
BPA was canceled 28/136 (20.5%) times. The success rate of
this alert was effective 78.5% of the time from either keeping
the patient from getting the sub-optimal medication and/or
ordered the right medication.
Conclusion: The incorporation of BPA alert within the
hospital system caused a good shift of practice amongst pro-
viders. This approach may help primary care providers bridge
the care gap and provide appropriate care resulting in better
quality of life for this patient population in the absence of
neurology service.

M200. Properties and Function of a Closed Loop
Pallidocortical Circuit
Emily A. Ferenczi, BM BCh, PhD , Wengang Wang, PhD,
Anushka Biswas, BS, Madeline A. Albanese, BS, Trent Pottala,
BS, Bernardo L. Sabatini, MD PhD. Harvard Medical School,
Boston, MA, USA.
Background: The globus pallidus externa (GPe) is a hub
nucleus of the basal ganglia and a target for deep brain stimu-
lation. Previous work has shown that the GPe contains out-
put neurons that project directly to cortex (Saunders et al.,
2015, Chen et al., 2015, Abecassis et al., 2020, Cui et al.,
2021). It remains unknown how these pallidocortical neu-
rons are embedded within canonical basal ganglia circuits,
how they contribute to behavior and how they are disrupted
in disorders of the basal ganglia. In this study we de ﬁned the
anatomical, molecular, and circuit properties of pal-
lidocortical neurons and probed the role of these circuits in
modulating behavior.
Methods: We performed retrograde tracing using rabies
virus or cholera toxin b injected into cortex to map the loca-
tion and cortical projection patterns of neurons in GPe. We
next performed triple channel in situ mRNA hybridization
(RNAscope, Wang et al., 2012) to de ﬁne the molecular
expression pro ﬁles of pallidocortical neurons. We then per-
formed in vitro electrophysiology in combination with
optogenetic stimulation of cortical inputs to GPe to deter-
mine whether a closed loop pallidocortical circuit exists.
Finally, we explored the contribution of pallidocortical cir-
cuits to reward-based learning using a head- ﬁxed operant
reward conditioning task, together with optogenetic manipu-
lation of genetically-de ﬁned GPe neurons.
Results: 1) Pallidocortical neurons projected to a range of
motor, sensory and association cortical areas, including the
insular and prefrontal cortices. Pallidocortical neurons
encircled the GPe, with insular cortex neurons located pre-
dominantly at the anterolateral borders of GPe whereas
motor and prefrontal cortex neurons were located at the post-
eromedial borders of GPe. 2) Pallidocortical neurons
maintained distinct parallel pathways to motor and non-
motor regions of cortex. 3) Pallidocortical neurons segregated
into two main molecular groups - ChAT-NKx2.1 expressing,
or VGAT-Npr3 expressing neurons. 4) Pallidocortical neu-
rons received monosynaptic, glutamatergic input directly
from the cortical regions that they projected to. 5)
Optogenetic manipulation of genetically targeted GPe neu-
rons was associated with a disrupted behavioral phenotype in
a head-ﬁxed operant reward-conditioning task.
Conclusion: Pallidocortical neurons maintain parallel path-
ways to diverse motor and non-motor cortical regions and
receive closed loop input back from those same cortical
regions. We hypothesize that these pathways serve to segregate

Syndrome without Presynaptic Dopaminergic De ﬁciency

Background & Aims: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a neurode-
generative disorder with a heterogeneous clinical course. PD
patients with predominantly tremor dominant presentation
commonly show slower clinical progression with less motor
and non-motor de ﬁcits than PD patients with predominantly
postural instability and gait dif ﬁculty (PIGD) presentation.
We aimed to study if quantitative striatal [
123I] io ﬂupane
uptakes differ in patients who presented with tremor syn-
drome versus PIGD syndrome but without presynaptic dopa-
minergic de ﬁciency.
Methods: We identi ﬁed 135 patients presenting with
tremor or PIGD syndromes but with normal presynaptic
dopaminergic function, which was determined by visual
inspection of [
123I] io ﬂupane SPECT imaging. Quantitative
[123I] io ﬂupane uptakes as measured by striatal binding ratios
(SBR) were computed by DaTQUANT software. We com-
pared SBRs of the left and right striatum and its sub-regions
(caudate, anterior putamen and posterior putamen) between
patients who presented with tremor syndrome versus PIGD
syndrome.
Results: Among these 135 patients with normal [
123I]
ioﬂupane SPECT scans, distribution of age, and gender were
statistically comparable between patients with PIGD syn-
drome (N=43, mean age 69.21 /C610.09, 39.53% female) and
patients with tremor syndrome (N=92, mean age
66.78/C68.10, 40.22% female). Patients presenting with
PIGD syndrome had signi ﬁcant lower quantitative [
123I]
ioﬂupane uptakes as measured by SBRs in right striatum
(1.59/C60.50 vs. 1.81 /C60.53, P=0.020) and left striatum
(1.55/C60.49 vs. 1.81 /C60.55, P=0.006), compared with
patients presenting with tremor syndrome. Similar signi ﬁcant
differences were also detected in most sub-regions, including
left caudate (1.86 /C60.57 vs. 2.10 /C60.63, P=0.030), right ante-
rior putamen (1.58 /C60.51 vs. 1.80 /C60.54, P=0.046), left ante-
rior putamen (1.54 /C60.50 vs. 1.83 /C60.55, P=0.003), right

left posterior putamen (0.95 /C60.45 vs. 1.15 /C60.43, P=0.016).
Conclusions: In this preliminary analysis of patients with
normal [ 123I] io ﬂupane SPECT scans, we observed statisti-
cally lower quantitative [ 123I] io ﬂupane uptakes in patients

ﬁndings may suggest ongoing subtle dopaminergic neuronal

123I]
ioﬂupane SPECT was reported as normal and close follow-up
to repeat neurological exam and/or [ 123I] io ﬂupane imaging

further examine the clinical and pathological heterogeneity of
patients with normal [ 123I] ioﬂupane SPECT studies.
M202. Reverse Translating Dystonia Assessment
Following Neonatal Brain Injury Across Species: From

medically refractory disorder. In young people, the most
common cause of dystonia is cerebral palsy (CP) due to neo-
natal brain injury (NBI) including hypoxic-ischemic encepha-
lopathy (HIE) and premature birth. Treatment development
requires: 1) Standardizing clinical dystonia assessment; 2)
Translating clinical dystonia assessment to animal models; 3)
Developing clinically-relevant animal models of NBI.
Methods: To derive an objective dystonia identi ﬁcation
method from clinical subjective diagnosis, we ﬁrst determined
how experts pragmatically assess dystonia severity in gait videos
of people with spastic CP following NBI. After determining
the movement features they cite when diagnosing dystonia,
we leveraged learning-based pose estimation techniques to
determine kinematic variables that correlated with these fea-
tures and expert severity scores. We then assessed these
same clinically-derived dystonia analogues across two
clinically-relevant NBI models we developed in mice: 1)
HIE: severe abrupt global hypoxia at postnatal day 10 (P10,
human term-equivalent gestation) with systemic in ﬂamma-
tion induced with lipopolysaccharide injection at P9. 2)
Premature birth at embryonic day 18.1-18.3 (human
22 weeks gestation) precipitated by mifepristone injection
to the dam. Dystonia analogues were longitudinally assessed
in mice during treadmill gait and tail suspension, the canon-
ical dystonia provoking task in mice.

commonly cited by experts when assessing gait dystonia in peo-
ple with CP (Chi square, p<0.01, n=116). Corresponding kine-
matic variables (inter-knee distance variance and foot adduction
amplitude) correlated with qualitative expert assessments of dys-
tonia severity (multiple linear regression, p<0.01). Compared to
sham littermates, mice after HIE exhibited increased hindlimb
a n df o r e l i m ba d d u c t i o na m p l i tude during tail suspension and
treadmill gait (t-tests, p<0.05, n=43) while mice born prema-
turely only exhibited signiﬁcantly increased hindlimb adduction
amplitude (t-tests, p<0.05, n=17) compared to term-born mice.
Hindlimb abnormalities emerged in mice after HIE starting at
P35 whereas mice born premature displayed these abnormalities
as early as P21, thus recapitulating a delay in dystonia onset that
may vary across etiologies and is observed clinically.
Conclusions: We have demonstrated: 1) Salient features
of dystonia following NBI in people; 2) Kinematic markers
of dystonia that track with dystonia severity in people; 3)
Presence of comparable kinematic markers of dystonia in our
novel clinically-relevant mouse models of NBI. This reverse
translational approach is critical for studying dystonia patho-
physiology which provides our best hope of developing effec-
tive treatments for dystonia following NBI.

Introduction: Bosutinib, a dual Abelson/Src inhibitor, was
investigated in individuals with Dementia with Lewy Bod-
ies (DLB).
Methods: A single site, randomized, double-blind, placebo-
controlled study of the effects of oral bosutinib, 100 mg once
daily for 12 weeks on safety, pharmacokinetics and biomarkers.
Results: Twenty-six participants were randomized and
included male and female (12:1) in the bosutinib arm and all
male (13) in the placebo arm. The average age 72.9 /C68.1
(year/C6SD). There were no serious adverse events and no
dropouts. Bosutinib was measured in the CSF and inhibited
Abelson. Bosutinib reduced CSF alpha-synuclein and dopa-
mine catabolism and improved activities of daily living.
Discussion: Bosutinib is safe and well-tolerated, and pene-
trates the blood brain barrier to inhibit Abelson, reduce CSF
alpha-synuclein, and improve activities of daily living,
suggesting a lowest effective dose (100mg) in DLB. These
results will guide adequately powered DLB treatment studies

M204. Selective Ablation of Sox6-Expressing Dopamine
Neurons Causes Parkinsonism in Mice
Zachary Gaertner, B.S. , Seraﬁn Gatica, B.S., Rajeshwar
Awatramani, PhD. Northwestern University, Chicago,
IL, USA.
Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the second most common neuro-
degenerative disorder, causing devastating disabilities in both
motor and non-motor domains. The motor symptoms of PD
are believed to be due to the loss of midbrain dopamine
(DA) neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta.
Molecularly-deﬁned DA neurons located ventrally within this
nucleus are particularly vulnerable to degeneration, and can
be isolated by their post-mitotic expression of the transcrip-
tion factor Sox6, however it is unclear if the loss of these spe-
ciﬁc neurons is responsible for driving Parkinsonism, or
simply a generic de ﬁcit of DA signaling. Here, we selectively
ablated Sox6-expressing DA neurons while leaving the rest of
the midbrain DA system intact. We found that this selective
ablation results in signi ﬁcant PD-like motor de ﬁcits in multi-
ple behavioral tasks, despite the many substantia nigra dopa-
mine neurons surviving. These results suggest that this
population may be vital in driving the motor de ﬁcits of PD.

involved in reward circuitry are also affected in PD patients

with ICD (Biundo et al, Mov Disord, 2015). The overarch-
ing aim of this study was to utilize high-dimensional brain
mapping procedures to characterize surface-based shape fea-
tures of reward circuitry, namely the hippocampus, amygdala,
nucleus accumbens and thalamus, in PD with ICD (Palacios
et al, Cortex, 2013) and examine whether perseverative
behavior relates to surface alterations in this population. It
was hypothesized that patients with ICD would have abnor-
mal surface morphometry in reward circuit structures com-
pared to patients without ICD. Additionally, it was
hypothesized that shape deformation in reward structures
would relate to poorer perseverative behavior in PD patients.
Methods: Nineteen patients with diagnosis of PD were
selected. 10 PD patients reported ICD (PD-ICD) symptoms
and 9 PD patients did not report ICD (PD-nonICD) symp-
toms. T1-weighted 1mm
3 MPRAGE MR images were used
for shape analysis procedures using large-deformation dif-
feomorphic metric mapping (Csernansky et al, Neuroimage,
2004). General linear models were used to compare shape
deformation patterns of the hippocampus, amygdala, nucleus
accumbens and thalamus between PD-ICD and PD-non-
ICD. Relationships between perseverative responses on the
Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) and brain shape of all
structures was accomplished using Pearson correlations in a
subset of patients (N=14).
Results: No signi ﬁcant differences in surface shape
emerged between the PD-ICD and PD-nonICD groups.

subiculum (r = -0.47, p<0.05) and tail (r = -0.49, p<0.05) of

deep-brain reward circuitry between patients with and with-
out ICD, likely as a function of small sample sizes. However,
relationships between hippocampal shape and WCST persev-
eration were observed. These ﬁndings suggest that structural
changes to the hippocampus may affect impaired impulse
control in PD.

M207. Stiff Person Syndrome in a Patient with Atypical
Carcinoid Tumor of the Lung Secondary to
Antiamphiphysin Antibodies: A Case Report and
Literature Review
Khawla Abusamra, MD , Mangayarkarasi Thandampallayam,
MD, Padmaja Sudhakar, MD, Douglas Lukins,
MD. University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA.
Introduction: Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS) is a rare neurologi-
cal disorder characterized by skeletal muscle stiffness and rigid-
ity, affecting the truncal musculature. Mechanism is unclear;
however, an autoimmune etiology is likely- as most cases are
associated with auto-antibodies against glutamic acid decarbox-
ylase. Paraneoplastic SPS is mostly linked to anti-amphiphysin
auto-antibodies and has been linked to malignancy of the
breast, colon, lung, thymus, and lymphoma. We present a rare
case of SPS in association with atypical lung carcinoid.
Case Report: 48-year-old man with metastatic atypical lung
carcinoid presented with progressive bilateral lower extremity
stiffness, and painful spasms. Examination showed bilateral
lower extremity weakness, increased tone and hyperre ﬂexia in
the upper and lower extremities. MRI of the brain showed
extensive white matter T2 hyperintensity without abnormal dif-
fusion restriction or contrast enhancement. MRI of the Cervi-
cal, Thoracic and Lumbar spine showed T2 hyperintensity in
the dorsal column of the spinal cord. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF)
analysis showed 72 nucleated cells and protein
109 mg/dl. Paraneoplastic panel was positive for anti-
Amphiphysin antibodies 1:30,720 dilution in serum and 1:
256 dilutions in CSF. He was diagnosed with paraneoplastic
SPS and received 5 sessions of plasma exchange (PLEX) with
signiﬁcant improvement of symptoms. However, few months
later he had worsening of his symptoms thus he received 4 ses-
sions of PLEX. Unfortunately, his hospital course was compli-
cated by acute hypoxic respiratory failure, diffuse rigidity and
fever (103.5 F), cardiac arrest and he subsequently passed away.

Discussion: Due to the rarity of paraneoplastic SPS,
established diagnostic criteria is lacking. Suggested major diag-
nostic criteria include progressive rigidity and muscle spasms
affecting the axial and limb muscle, and EMG ﬁnding of con-
tinuous motor unit activity of agonists and antagonist muscles.
Minor criteria include antibodies in the serum and response to
benzodiazepines. Our patient had had symptoms suggestive of
SPS in the setting of high titers of Anti-amphiphysin anti-
bodies and metastatic atypical carcinoid and It is believed that
his symptoms were caused by paraneoplastic SPS. To the best
of authors knowledge, Anti-amphiphysin antibody associated
paraneoplastic SPS in metastatic atypical lung carcinoid has
not been previously reported in the literature
Conclusion: This case highlights the importance of keeping
a high degree of suspicion for SPS in patients presents with typ-
ical symptoms in the setting of rare and atypical malignancy.

Introduction: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) typically pre-
sents with parkinsonism, ataxia and/or autonomic dysfunc-
tion. Occasional clinically atypical (ca-MSA) cases lack the
characteristic signs and symptoms and may masquerade as
progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). We aimed to investigate
whether different neuroimaging modalities could facilitate the
clinical differentiation between ca-MSA and PSP, and
whether histopathologic characteristics could explain the
atypical presentation of ca-MSA.
Methods: We identi ﬁed 3 neuropathologically-de ﬁned ca-
MSA patients with a premortem clinical diagnosis of PSP,
who had completed various brain imaging, including a 3T
brain structural MRI and a subset of PET imaging using
11C-Pittsburgh compound B (PiB) for β-amyloid deposition,
18F-ﬂortaucipir for tau protein deposition, and 18F-
ﬂuorodeoxyglucose (FDG) for glucose metabolism. We com-
pared clinical features, brainstem planimetric measurements,
and radiotracer standardized uptake value ratios in ca-MSA
to 10 autopsy-con ﬁrmed PSP patients. We also compared
histologic counts of neuronal loss, iron deposition and α
-synuclein-immunoreactive glial cytoplasmic inclusion burden
to 10 autopsy-con ﬁrmed typical MSA-P (parkinsonian vari-
ant) cases.
Results: Ca-MSA patients had better performance on the
PSP Saccadic Impairment Scale ( p=0.003) and more frequently
demonstrated good response to levodopa ( p=0.061) than PSP
patients. In terms of MRI planimetric measures, ca-MSA

patients showed higher midbrain-to-pons ratio and lower Mag-
netic Resonance Parkinsonism Index than PSP (each,
p=0.036). With FDG-PET, ca-MSA patients exhibited lower
glucose metabolism in the putamen and globus pallidus versus
PSP (each, p=0.017) and controls (each, p=0.007). These same
regions showed higher ﬂortaucipir uptake in ca-MSA than PSP
(p=0.007 for putamen, p=0.049 for pallidum) and controls
(each, p=0.012). Conversely, lower ﬂortaucipir retention was
observed in the subthalamic nucleus versus PSP ( p=0.007).
Finally, the ratio between putaminal and subthalamic nucleus
uptake was signi ﬁcantly higher in ca-MSA compared to PSP
(p=0.007) and controls (p=0.012), clearly separating ca-MSA
patients from the other groups. No histopathological differ-
ences were observed compared to typical MSA-P.
Conclusion: MSA clinical features may overlap with PSP.
Less severe saccadic impairment and relatively good response
to levodopa can help distinguish ca-MSA from PSP.

diagnostic dilemma. The advantages of brain MRI in terms
of availability, cost, and non-invasiveness make it a suitable
biomarker in clinical settings. In research settings, the use of
FDG-PET and ﬂortaucipir-PET can further potentiate diag-
nostic accuracy.

Multiple Parkinson Disease Pathologies

Parkinson’s disease (PD) may start in the gut and spread to
the brain. It is well-established that the overall composition
of the gut microbiome is altered in PD, but little is known
about the nature of the dysbiosis and the key players. To
characterize the dysbiosis at species resolution, we enrolled
490 PD and 234 age and geographically matched neurologi-
cally healthy individuals, collected stool and metadata, and
conducted deep shotgun sequencing of fecal DNA, using
uniform methods from start to ﬁnish, strict thresholds for
quality control (BBMap and bioBakery), and required statisti-
cal signi ﬁcance by two methods (ANCOM-BC and
MaAsLin2) to declare disease association. Metagenome-wide
association study identi ﬁed 33% of species tested as having
signiﬁcantly altered abundances in PD, similarly, 15% of
gene families and 32% of metabolic pathways were affected,
depicting a far more complex and widespread dysbiosis than
previously known. We replicated previously nominated PD-
associated taxa and resolved them to species. In addition, we
detected anomalies at species-level which were missed at
genus and higher taxonomic levels. We show proof of princi-
pal for heterogeneity, where species within a genus have dif-
ferent associations with disease. Network analysis (SparCC)
revealed interconnected polymicrobial clusters, and insight to
co-occurrence as well as competition among PD-associated
species. Functional inference of species, genes, and pathways
implicate PD microbiome in enrichment of immunogenic
components (LPS, BLP, LTA), loss of anti-in ﬂammatory

molecules (dopamine, GABA, glutamate, serotonin), loss of
neuroprotective molecules (trehalose, nicotinamide),
increased amyloidogenic triggers of alpha-synuclein pathology

(curli), and increased toxic metabolites (Trimethylamine).

of concrete testable hypotheses to discern the role of the gut
microbiome in PD.

K-M109. Home Aerobic versus Balance Training in
Cerebellar Ataxias
Scott Barbuto, MD PhD , Sheng-Han Kuo, MD, Lauren
Winterbottom, OTR, Yaakov Stern, PhD, Joel Stein,
MD. Columbia University Medical Center, New York,
NY, USA.
Spinocerebellar ataxias are a group of disorders that result
from cerebellar degeneration and cause balance and coordina-
tion loss. The diseases are devastatingly debilitating with
many individuals requiring wheelchairs for mobility within
ten years from initial diagnoses.
1 With no disease modifying
medications currently available, most guidelines recommend
individuals with cerebellar ataxia to perform balance training
to maintain functional abilities.
2,3 Although con ﬂicting
results have been reported, most studies indicate that balance
training can help improve symptoms of ataxia if the training
is adequately challenging.
4-10
The bene ﬁts of aerobic training for cerebellar ataxia have
been less well-studied. After promising results in animals, the
ﬁrst study examining aerobic training in humans with cere-
bellar degeneration showed minimal bene ﬁts.
11 However,
participants were not provided a structured exercise program,
and the training was limited to three, ﬁfteen-minute sessions
per week for one month. Hypothesizing that a larger dose of
training could be bene ﬁcial, our research group conducted a
pilot study having individuals with cerebellar degeneration
perform one month of rigorous aerobic training, de ﬁned as
thirty-minutes sessions, ﬁve times per week at 65-80% of
their maximum heart rate. Our results indicated that individ-
uals with cerebellar ataxias were able to safely perform rigor-
ous aerobic exercise and that a phase II study comparing
balance and aerobic training was feasible.
12,13
After completion of the pilot study, we conducted a single
center, assessor-blinded, randomized controlled phase II trial.
Individuals with cerebellar ataxia were assigned (1:1) to either
home aerobic or balance training for 6-months. The primary
outcome was improvement in ataxia severity as measured by
the Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA).

Secondary outcomes included safety, training adherence, and
balance improvements. Nineteen subjects were randomized
to aerobic training and 17 subjects to balance training. There
were no differences between groups at baseline. Thirty-one
participants completed the trial, and there were no training-
related serious adverse events. Compliance to training was
over 70%. There was a mean improvement in ataxia severity
of 1.9 SARA points (SD 1.62) in the aerobic group com-
pared to an improvement of 0.6 points (SD 1.34) in the bal-
ance group. Although two other measures of balance were
equivocal between groups, one measure of balance showed
greater improvement with balance training compared to aero-
bic training.
14
Overall, this 6-month trial comparing home aerobic versus
balance training in individuals with cerebellar ataxia had
excellent retention and adherence to training. There was a
signiﬁcant improvement in ataxia severity with aerobic train-
ing compared to balance training, and a phase III trial will be
conducted.

K-M111. Nicotine-Mediated Rescue of Alpha-Synuclein
Toxicity Requires Synaptic Vesicle Glycoprotein 2C
Sabrina Clemens, BA
1, Abby Olsen, MD PhD 2. 1Brigham
and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA, 2University of
Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA.
Background: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is characterized by
α-synuclein aggregation and loss of dopamine (DA) neurons
in the substantia nigra. Risk of PD arises due to a combina-
tion of genetic and environmental factors, which may inter-
act, termed gene-environment (GxE) interactions. An inverse
association between smoking and risk of PD is well-
established, and a previous genome-wide GxE interaction
study identiﬁed genetic variation in the synaptic-vesicle glyco-
protein 2C ( SV2C) locus as an important mediator of the
degree to which smoking is inversely associated with PD.
Objective: We sought to determine the mechanism of the
smoking-SV2C interaction in a Drosophila model of PD.
Methods: Flies expressing human α-synuclein in all neu-
rons develop the hallmarks of PD, including motor dysfunc-
tion, loss of DA neurons, and formation of α-synuclein
inclusions. We assessed the effects of increasing doses of nico-
tine on these parameters of neurodegeneration, in the pres-
ence or absence of SV2C knockdown.
Results: α-synuclein-expressing ﬂies treated with nicotine
had improvement in locomotion, DA neuron counts, and in
α-synuclein aggregation. However, in α-synuclein-expressing
ﬂies in which Drosophila homologs of SV2C are knocked
down, nicotine failed to rescue neurodegeneration.
Conclusions: This work con ﬁrms a GxE interaction
between nicotine and SV2C,d eﬁnes a role for this interaction
in α-synuclein proteostasis, and suggests that future clinical
trials on nicotine should consider genetic variation in SV2C.
Further, this provides proof of concept that our model can
be used for mechanistic study of GxE, paving the way for
investigation of additional GxE interactions or identi ﬁcation
of novel GxE.

difﬁculties in clinical rating scale assessment. We performed
sensor-based motion analysis in XDP to quantitatively char-

trial endpoint.

ized examination. Disease severity was assessed with the Uni-

trained model correctly classi ﬁed 78.3% (60%-94%) of sam-
ples across the considered tasks. The projections/ML-gait
analysis data revealed that gait spatio-temporal parameters

LB-M102. Pro ﬁling Tau Pathology in Essential Tremor
Nil Saez Calveras, MD
1, Joshua Beaver, BS 1, Phyllis Faust,
MD, PhD2, Marc Diamond, MD 1, Elan Louis, MD, MS 1.
1University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX,
USA, 2Columbia University, New York City, NY, USA.
Background: Patients with essential tremor (ET) have a higher
prevalence of mild cognitive impairment and dementia when
compared to the general population. Thepostmortem neuropath-
ological exam of these patients has also revealed the presence of
Tau aggregates with a unique isoform pro ﬁle. In this project,
we aimed to con ﬁrm whether the brains of ET patients con-
tained pathologic tau capable of forming self-propagating aggre-
gates. We also sought to characterize the structure of tau in
these assemblies to determine whether it resembled that of other
tauopathies or, otherwise, represented a unique conformation.
Methods: We evaluated post-mortem brain samples from
ET patients across the spectrum of cognitive status who were
also found to have tau aggregates in their neuropathological
exam. Their brain homogenates were incubated with biosen-
sor cells expressing the Tau repeat domain (RD) conjugated
to ﬂuorophores. These cells generate a FRET signal if tau
aggregation occurs, which can be quanti ﬁed by ﬂow cyto-
metry as the seeding activity of the assay. To further de ﬁne
the structure of Tau in ET we performed immunoprecipita-
tion (IP) assays with antibodies that bind sequential epitopes
in the Tau repeat domain. The different binding af ﬁnity pat-
tern of these antibodies for Tau ﬁbrils in different tauopathies
can help distinguish between them.
Results: The seeding activity of the assays in ET, as
assessed by the percentage of FRET positivity, correlated with
the presence of cognitive impairment and the degree of tau
pathology in the neuropathological exam. We performed two
sets of IP assays with antibodies binding sequential amino
acid epitopes in Tau (MD and TRD family). The results rev-
ealed that the binding af ﬁnity pro ﬁle of these antibodies in
ET resembled the pattern seen in Alzheimer ’s disease and
Progressive Supranuclear Palsy but was different from the
pattern in other tauopathies such as Corticobasal Degenera-
tion or Argyrophilic Grain Disease.
Conclusions: This study provided preliminary evidence
that the brains of ET patients contain pathologic tau capable
of forming aggregates similarly to what is observed in other
tauopathies. The use of IP assays also provided initial insight
into the conformational structure of tau in these aggregates.

We are currently developing more precise tools that can help
us better de ﬁne pathologic tau in these patients and deter-
mine whether they harbor a unique conformational structure.

MS. University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston,
Houston, TX, USA.
Introduction: Nitrous oxide, colloquially known as laughing
gas, is an inhaled anesthetic that is recreationally abused at
increasing rates because it is relatively easy to access

B12 is integral in myelin synthesis and is inactivated by nitrous
oxide
1. Chronic nitrous oxide use can cause a vitamin B12
deﬁciency which can lead to subacute combined degeneration
(SCD) and macrocytic anemia. We report a patient who was
brought to the emergency department (ED) by EMS for possi-
ble acute stroke and was found to have clinical and imaging
features consistent with SCD. Later during a clinic visit, the
patient endorsed recreational use of nitrous oxide.
Case Presentation: A man in his early 30s with a history of
alcohol use was brought to the ED for facial droop, slurred
speech, and confusion. He reported paresthesia of his bilateral
upper and lower limbs and gait imbalance. On exam he was
noted to have diffuse hyperre ﬂexia, bilateral ankle clonus, loss
of vibration in feet, and a positive Romberg ’s sign. Brain com-
puted tomography (CT), brain magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI), and head and neck CT angiogram (CTA) were
unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed mild macrocytic ane-
mia and a vitamin B12 level of 385 pg/mL. MRI of the spine
showed subtle T2 hyperintense signal abnormality in the dor-
sal cervical spinal cord. His symptoms improved with intensive
B12, folate, and thiamine supplementation. During a clinic
follow up, he endorsed use of nitrous oxide use and he was
counseled. He regained most of the vibratory sensation in his
feet and no longer has a positive Romberg ’s sign. Furthermore,
he has regained much of his upper extremity sensation. How-
ever, a repeat spinal cord MRI showed persistent T2
hyperintense signal throughout the majority of the spinal cord.
Discussion: When taking the history for patients with
suspected SCD, it is extremely important to ask about
nitrous oxide use and to counsel them to prevent progression
from continued use. Alcohol use is an additional risk factor
and can cause further depletion of vitamin B12 stores.
Patients with SCD can experience substantial improvement
in clinical symptoms with intensive vitamin B12, folate, and
thiamine repletion.

S190. A Case of Overlapping Clinical Syndromes in a
Patient with Anti-NMDAR, GFAP, and NMO Antibody
Positive Disease
Rebecca Massey, B.A. , Shruti Agnihotri, M.D., Vanessa Sui,
M.D.. University of Alabama at Birmingham, Birmingham,
AL, USA.
Objective: To describe a unique case of overlapping clinical
syndromes due to anti-NMDAR, GFAP, and NMO anti-
body positive autoimmune CNS disease.
Background: Anti-NMDA receptor (anti-NMDAR)
encephalitis is associated with a characteristic clinical syn-
drome of prominent psychiatric symptoms, disordered sleep,
cognitive changes, dyskinesias, and seizures. Neuromyelitis
optica spectrum disorders (NMOSD) represent a full spec-
trum of CNS demyelinating disorders, typically affecting the
optic nerves and spinal cord. NMOSD is associated with
antibodies against aquaporin-4 (AQP4). The presence of
autoantibodies against glial ﬁbrillary acidic protein (GFAP),
while less well-de ﬁned, has been associated with relapsing
autoimmune meningoencephalitis.
Case Summary: A 20-year-old woman presented with
1-week history of binocular vertical diplopia and reduced
hearing in the left ear. Past medical history was notable for a
9-month history of sudden onset depression, executive dys-
function, personality changes, and a “psychotic episode ”
requiring hospitalization 7 months ago. She was noted to
have left CN IV palsy, nystagmus on horizontal gaze, and
diffuse hyperre ﬂexia. MRI brain with and without contrast
showed several areas of patchy bilateral periventricular, per-
iaqueductal, and basal ganglia FLAIR hyperintensities with
patchy enhancement. MRI cervical spine was normal. CSF
analysis was notable for WBC count of 8/mm
3, protein of
54mg/dl, glucose of 54mg/dl, and >5 unique oligoclonal
bands. She was treated with high dose steroids and PLEX for
suspected autoimmune in ﬂammatory CNS disease, with trace
symptomatic improvement. Subsequently, CSF studies rev-
ealed positive antibodies against NMDAR, AQP-4, and
GFAP. Upon follow up in clinic, patient showed gradual
improvement in vision and mood with near resolution of dip-
lopia, and eventual improvement to baseline while being on
B-cell depletion therapy.
Discussion: While rare, overlapping neuronal antibody
syndromes is an important consideration in patients with vex-
ing clinical presentations and/or imaging that is not classic
for one individual syndrome. Thorough history, physical
exam, and imaging can provide clues that allow for empiric
treatment of suspected mixed autoimmune CNS syndromes,
even while key studies are pending. Overlapping neuronal
antibody syndromes are more likely to be due to autoimmu-
nity than paraneoplastic processes and may provide clues to
the mechanisms of these antibodies. The case also highlights
both the challenges in and importance of prompt diagnosis
and treatment of these syndromes.
S191. A Case Report on Anti- MAG Peripheral
Neuropathy
Thandampallayam Ajjeya, MD , Saniya Pervin, MD, Zabeen
Mahuwala, MD. University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY, USA.
Introduction: Monoclonal gammopathies are 10 times more
frequent in patients with polyneuropathy than age-matched
controls, and 10% of adults with acquired polyneuropathy
have a monoclonal gammopathy. Polyneuropathy with immu-
noglobulin M (IgM) monoclonal gammopathy is the most
common paraproteinemic neuropathy, comprising a clinico-
pathologically and immunologically distinct entity. ⁣ It is also
of importance to detect paraproteinemic polyneuropathies as

they comprise a potentially treatable group of autoimmune
neuropathies, as proposed to 35 years ago.
Case Report: 69-year-old right-handed male with Wal-
denstorm macroglobunemia and anti -MAG neuropathy pres-
ented with worsening symptoms. ⁣ Patient was diagnosed
with anti -MAG neuropathy approximately 10 years ago in the
setting of IgM monoclonal proteins. His main symptoms were
in his feet and hands with decreased dexterity and numbness.
He was treated with IVIG initially with minimal response,
and symptoms ultimately stabilized on Rituximab requir-
ing infusions every two mo nths. These symptoms had
worsened in the last two years. Examination showed ﬁrst
dorsal interossei wasting wit h 4/5 strength on toe exten-
sion and plantar ﬂexion. Vibration sense was absent in
bilateral toes and sensation decreased to pinprick up to
mid-leg and in both hands. Patient had a wide-based gait
with absent re ﬂexes. Work up revealed anti MAG antibody
of 66,000 and anti-sulfatide antibody was positive. Nerve
conduction studies showed demyelinating length depen-
dent polyneuropathy. Due to progression of weakness in
UE and loss of balance, EMG NCS was repeated and the
median sensory was absent and motor study was worse in
amplitude indicative of worsening correlating with clinical
features. Plan was made to change rituximab to ibrutinib.
Discussion: In approximately 75% of patients, the mono-
clonal IgM immunoreacts with myelin-associated glycopro-
tein (MAG) and sulfoglucuronyl glycosphingolipid (SGPG),
or other peripheral nerve glycolipids serve as antigens. These
antibodies are considered pathogenic because IgM and com-
plement are deposited on the myelin sheath, splitting the
myelin lamellae. Patients with IgM-MGUS typically manifest
symptoms associated with dysfunction or loss of large myelin-
ated ﬁbers. Patients most often present with slowly progres-
sive distal paresthesias, prominent in the feet, and impaired
balance.
Conclusion: Anti-MAG antibodies are pathogenic, and
rituximab, a chimeric anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, is
currently the standard treatment. However, rituximab pro-
vides bene ﬁt in less than 50% of patients, and repeated cycles
are often necessary with progressive loss of bene ﬁt. Long-term
beneﬁts may be obtained probably by suppressing IgM anti-
MAG antibodies or inducing immunoregulatory T cells.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) and neuromyelitis optica (NMO) are
chronic autoimmune conditions that are dif ﬁcult but impor-
tant to distinguish, since early diagnosis is critical. We pre-
sent an individual who was aquaporin-4 (AQP4) antibody-
negative with area postrema syndrome nonresponsive to mul-
tiple rounds of treatment, questioning: NMO or MS?
Case Report: A previously healthy 47-year-old man pres-
ented with acute intractable diplopia, vertigo, hearing loss
and vomiting. Initial MRI studies showed hyperintensities
without enhancement in the lateral pons, periventricular area
with some perpendicular lesions to the lateral ventricles.
There were also two short-segment peripheral lesions in the
cervical spine. Autoimmune laboratory studies were negative
for mimicking conditions. Imaging/clinical presentation ini-
tially led to a MS diagnosis, with treatment of ﬁve days of
intravenous methylprednisolone (IVMP). NMO/AQP4 cell-

clonal bands in the CSF not seen in serum. He was treated
with ﬁve volumes of plasma exchange (PLEX) followed by
1000 mg of rituximab. Over the next three months, he was
readmitted to the hospital with refractory symptoms. Follow-
up MRIs showed new lesions at the left cerebellopontine
angle extending into the posterolateral left medulla along
with additional known plaques in the supra and infratentorial
cerebral regions keeping with known history. There was also
bilateral optic nerve enhancement. He received additional
IVMP every 48 hours alternating with seven volumes of
PLEX. After his ﬁnal discharge, he declined further rituximab
treatment, switching to natalizumab. Symptoms gradually
improved although not to his previous neurological baseline.

(meeting McDonald ’s criteria) characterized by area postrema
syndrome (APS). Factors con ﬁrming an MS diagnosis
included CSF oligoclonal bands, a negative NMO/AQP4

weren’t longitudinally extensive, and typical periventricular,
juxtacortical and infratentorial brain lesions. This was further
supported by bilateral optic nerve enhancement closer to the
retina than to the optic chiasm. In this case, the clinical
course, consistent therapeutic response to natalizumab, and
analysis of the labs/imaging led to a correct MS diagnosis, in
spite of an area postrema syndrome which is more consistent
with NMOSD.

Case Presentation: A 55-year-old right-handed Caucasian
woman with history of idiopathic polyneuropathy was admit-
ted for status epilepticus, had 3 breakthrough seizures within
an hour. She did not have any preceding symptoms. Neuro-
logical exam was signi ﬁcant for poor delayed recall, diffuse
hyperreﬂexia except at ankles, diminished sensation in lower
limbs to pinprick, cold temperature and vibration in length-
dependent fashion. MRI brain ﬁndings raised possibility of
limbic encephalitis. CSF studies were unremarkable. There
was signi ﬁcant improvement with high dose steroids. Auto-
immune encephalopathy panel was negative in serum and
CSF. A SPECT scan favored diagnosis of AE, and she was
started on rituximab for presumed autoimmune encephalitis
after extensive discussion in a case conference with our col-
leagues. After 2 months, patient developed new onset weak-
ness on left side and a repeat MRI brain showed progression
of lesions. Patient was admitted to hospital and a brain
biopsy was done, which was consistent with primary CNS
lymphoma. Methotrexate was added to rituximab, and she
responded well.

cal nuclear scan ﬁndings suggestive of autoimmune encepha-
litis. This can respond well to IV steroids and rituximab
similar to autoimmune encephalitis, which can lead to del-
ayed diagnosis. Clinicians should be careful and should fol-
low the patient closely if biopsy is not performed to con ﬁrm
the diagnosis.

S197. A Refractory Case of Tolosa Hunt Syndrome
Requiring Multiple In ﬂiximab Infusions

Ore-Ofeoluwatomi O. Adesina, MD, Michelle S. Chen, BSA.

Houston, TX, USA.
Background: Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (THS) is a rare disor-
der presenting with unilateral headache and painful
ophthalmoplegia secondary to involvement of cranial nerve
3, 4, 5 and 6, and ocular sympathetic paralysis. Most patient
respond to steroid therapy with good control of symptoms,
however there are occasional cases of THS that do not
respond adequately to steroids or some long-term immuno-
suppressive therapies. We report a patient with THS who
failed trials of azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil but
responded well to in ﬂiximab. There is no reported case in the
literature describing use of multiple in ﬂiximab infusions
in THS.
Case Presentation: A 31-year-old man with remote his-
tory of Crohn ’s disease presented to a neuro-ophthalmology
clinic with 3 week history of right frontal headache and
binocular diplopia. On examination he was found to have
right side ptosis and lateral rectus palsy. Magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) of brain and orbit showed an enhancing
lesion involving petrous apex bilaterally and the dura around
left cerebellar tentorium. Initial cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF)
studies were unremarkable but repeat testing showed lym-
phocytic pleocytosis with negative infectious work
up. Testing for rheumatological and other autoimmune cau-
ses including sarcoid, and IgG4 related disease was

unremarkable. CT chest showed patchy and nodular ground
glass opacities in both lungs. A transbronchial lung biopsy
was unremarkable. He responded well to steroids, and was
started on azathioprine that he couldn ’t tolerate. He was lost
to follow-up for two years and then he was readmitted with
similar symptoms. Repeat imaging showed enhancement of
petrous apex bilaterally with additional involvement of right
side of the clivus, Dorello canal, cavernous sinus and 5th cra-
nial nerve at Meckel ’s cave. Biopsy of right petrous apex
lesion showed dense ﬁbroconnective tissue. There were no
granulomas. Mycophenolate mofetil was started for long term
immunosuppression, without any symptomatic improvement.
After 2 months, this was switched to In ﬂiximab and patient
had complete resolution of symptoms within a month.
Repeat MRI six months later showed signi ﬁcant improve-
ment of the above skull base abnormalities.
Conclusion: The dramatic and persisting improvement in
the patient ’s symptoms with in ﬂiximab highlights the impor-
tance of considering this as a treatment option for THS.

S199. A Woman with Monophasic Presentation of
Marburg Variant of Tumefactive MS Who Remains
Relapse Free on Ocrevus
Jessi Cai, BS , Rohan Samant, MD, Rajesh Gupta,
MD. University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston,
Houston, TX, USA.
Introduction: Marburg variant of tumefactive multiple scle-
rosis is considered a very rare life threatening condition with
very high mortality. Tumefactive MS is a rare form of multi-
ple sclerosis typically characterized on MRI by large (>2 cm)
tumor-like lesions in the CNS (Abdoli, Mult Scler Relat Dis-
ord., 2015). There is no de ﬁnite DMT studied for this spe-
ciﬁc form of MS.
Case Presentation: We describe the case of a 40 year old
previously healthy Hispanic woman who presented with
insomnia, headache, and poor appetite. Within one month,
her family members noticed that she developed dif ﬁculty
with language and memory, to the point that she could not
read, write, or remember her birth date. She had gait instabil-
ity and would veer to the left. She was initially evaluated in
Mexico and diagnosed with a brain tumor that required
biopsy. Two months later, when she came to United States
for second opinion, she was noted have global aphasia with
difﬁculty naming, repetition, and following simple com-
mands. Brain MRI showed a dominant left frontoparietal
lesion with associated enhancement and mass effect, a smaller
focus of active in ﬂammation in the right temporal lobe, and
enhancement of the left optic nerve. CSF showed 5 oligo-
clonal bands. Her speech dif ﬁculty and gait instability
improved signi ﬁcantly after 5 days of IV corticosteroid ther-
apy. Six months later, she developed focal seizure with
impaired awareness. Repeat MRI brain showed a new non
enhancing lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere and a
diagnosis of MS was established. She was started on ocrevus
and has remained relapse free since then over the last 5 years.

similarities in presentation to brain tumors. Uncertainty in
diagnosis may result in patient referral for potentially unnec-
essary biopsies. Ocrevus seem to work well for this
form of MS.

routinely at ARUP Laboratories and a live cell-based
ﬂuorescence-activated cell sorting assay performed at Mayo

between the two tests in over 300 paired samples sent to

S202. An Atypical Presentation of Progressive Multifocal
Leukoencephalopathy with Newly Diagnosed HIV
Infection: A Case Report
Abhishek Dutta, B.S.
1, Kishan V. Patel, DO 1, Marcela
K. Roger, MD 2. 1Rowan University School of Osteopathic
Medicine, Stratford, NJ, USA, 2Jefferson Health NJ, Stratford,
NJ, USA.
Background: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
(PML) is a rare demyelinating infectious disease of the CNS
that typically presents in immunosuppressed patients with
history of AIDS, hematologic malignancies or immunosup-
pressant drug treatment. Caused by reactivation of latent
John Cunningham (JC) polyomavirus, it results in subacute
neurological damage that causes cognitive dysfunction, vision
loss, speech disturbances, facial drooping, focal weakness, and
problems with gait, coordination or sensory loss. We report a
case that highlights the importance of differentiating PML
from acute/chronic ischemic stroke.
Case Description: A 48-year-old male with history of left
MCA stroke and protein S de ﬁciency presented with worsen-
ing aphasia and new right sided weakness ten weeks after his
stroke. Results of a brain MRI performed four weeks prior for
worsening aphasia and blurry vision were interpreted as old left
MCA infarction. A new MRI revealed left temporoparietal and
subinsular encephalomalacia, likely a subacute extension of his
stroke. Hospital course was remarkable for bicytopenia leuko-
cytosis and thrombocytopenia. Workup for hepatitis B, crypto-
coccus, syphilis and TB was negative. ANA, ANCA and ESR
were unremarkable. HIV1 and CMV antibody test was posi-
tive, with initial CD4 count of 25. Reinterpretation of new
MRI indicated progressively worsening left frontal and parietal
lesion, suggesting a demyelinating process. The patient was
positive for 281,844 JCV DNA copies/mL and PML was
suspected. Two weeks ’ rehab yielded appropriate functional
gains. Six weeks later, the patient reported worsening myalgias.
Repeat MRI brain revealed interval increase in con ﬂuent white
matter signal abnormality in left cerebral hemisphere, with
increased mass effect resulting in new 3- 4 mm left-to-right
midline shift. Findings were compatible with progression of
PML. Patient was discharged to homecare on continued highly
active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) therapy.
Discussion: PML can be diagnosed in a brain MRI by
hypodensity on T1 with hyperintensity on T2-FLAIR. Dis-
tinction is made between acute ischemic stroke and demye-
linating disease with the T2 gradient recalled echo weighted
imaging, a highly sensitive method for detecting thrombi.
Earlier HAART treatment of patients with HIV-related PML

can increase the 1-year survival rate to 50%, versus 10% in
those not treated with HAART.
Conclusions: Failure to test for HIV in patients with
suspected chronic ischemic stroke can lead to increased mor-
bidity, decreased HAART ef ﬁcacy and poorer patient out-
comes. Clinicians should strongly consider PML in
immunocompromised patients with frequent, progressive
neurological symptoms.

S204. Anti-IgLON5 Disease Unmasked by Asymptomatic
COVID Infection
Xiaoyang Li, M.D. , Timothy Landis, M.D., Monica M. Diaz,
M.D., M.S.. University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill,
Chapel Hill, NC, USA.
Objective: To report a case of anti-IgLON5 disease
unmasked by asymptomatic COVID-19 infection.
Background: Anti-IgLON5 disease is a clinically heteroge-
neous disease that shares features of both neurodegeneration
and neuroin ﬂammation. The onset can be insidious, posing
diagnostic challenges and oftentimes resulting in treatment
delay.
Method: Case report.
Results: A 64-year-old male presented with a 7-month his-
tory of progressive parasomnia, cognitive decline and parkin-
sonism which precipitously worsened over the course of
1 month after asymptomatic COVID-19 infection, resulting
in dysphagia, visual hallucinations, 100-lb weight loss over
10 months, and dependence on all activities of daily living.
The exam was notable for a Montreal Cognitive Assessment
(MOCA) score of 19/30 with mild to moderate impairment
of memory, attention, and executive function, proximal bilat-
eral lower extremity weakness, fasciculations and atrophy,
diminished re ﬂexes with downgoing toes and a waddling gait.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed chronic
small vessel ischemia and atrophy. Electromyography and
nerve conduction study did not show evidence of motor neu-
ron disease. Sleep study suggested mild sleep apnea and rapid
eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder. The ﬂuctuat-
ing cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep
behavior disorder and parkinsonism may be consistent with
Lewy body dementia. However, the rapid progression after
COVID-19 infection and signi ﬁcant weight loss raised con-
cerns for a secondary immune-mediated or paraneoplastic
process. Serum autoimmune encephalopathy panel was posi-
tive for high titer (1:3840) anti-IgLON5 antibody. Com-
puted tomography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis showed
no evidence of malignancy. He was treated with intravenous
methylprednisolone 1000 mg daily for 5 days followed by
7 sessions of serial therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE). He
was maintained on a slow prednisone taper and weekly TPE
prior to starting rituximab. Cognition markedly improved
and visual hallucinations were completely resolved. However,
he continued to have signi ﬁcant bulbar weakness requiring
tracheostomy and percutaneous gastrostomy tube placement.
Positive pressure ventilatory support was required during
sleep due to apnea. Patient unfortunately passed away one
month after discharge due to aspiration pneumonia.
Conclusion: This case highlights the importance of recog-
nizing anti-IgLON5 disease as a potentially reversible cause
of neurodegenerative syndrome in patients with atypical fea-
tures. Timely treatment and appropriate management of
disease-associated complications may improve clinical out-
comes. It is also worth noting that symptoms precipitously
worsened following COVID-19 infection, which led to the

ﬁnal diagnosis. We suspect that a COVID-19-mediated
immune activation response exacerbated the underlying auto-
immune encephalitis process, unmasking his symptoms.

S207. Case Report: Challenges and Triumphs in a Case of
Chronic Lymphocytic In ﬂammation with Pontine
Perivascular Enhancement Responsive to Steroids
Dan Tong Jia, MD , Sarah Brooker, MD, PHD, Mireille
Bitar, MD, Elena Grebenciucova, MD. Northwestern
University, Chicago, IL, USA.
Objective: To delineate a case of CLIPPERS with atypical
imaging ﬁndings that posed diagnostic challenges and
exhibited remarkable clinical improvement with therapy.
Background: CLIPPERS syndrome is a recently described
inﬂammatory central nervous system disease that predomi-
nantly affects the brainstem. Given the rare incidence of
CLIPPERS, its neuroimaging, treatment and prognosis are
not well understood.
Results: We present a case of a 67-year-old otherwise
healthy African American woman who ﬁrst sought medical
attention for dizziness and odd behavior. She was found to
have contrast-enhancing brain lesions, but deferred biopsy
and was discharged with one month of empiric corticoste-
roids. She re-presents 3 weeks after completing her corticoste-
roids with acute double vision. Her subsequent exam showed
impairment in semantic memory, dysarthria, restricted lateral
gaze bilaterally, horizontal nystagmus, right facial droop, and
left sided extremity hyperre ﬂexia. Magnetic resonance imag-
ing showed supratentorial lesions measuring up to 10mm in
the right frontal lobe, innumerable punctate contrast-
enhancing lesions within midbrain, pons and cerebellar hemi-
spheres and intramedullary spinal lesions. Serologic workup
was notable for lymphopenia. CSF pro ﬁle was bland with
normal CSF glucose and ACE levels. Body CT was negative
for malignancy. PET scan revealed a hypermetabolic axillary
lymph node, but biopsied to be reactive to the COVID-19
vaccine. Brain biopsy revealed predominantly CD4+ T lym-
phohistocytic in ﬁltrates in the perivascular space and paren-
chyma suggestive of CLIPPERS. Patient was started on
prednisone 1mg/kg per day with interval imaging demon-
strating improvement in size and number of CNS lesions.
The prednisone was slowly tapered by 10mg per month to
10mg per day, while mycophenolate mofetil was started from
500mg and increased to 1500mg twice per day. Repeat scans
showed near resolution of all contrast-enhancing lesions and,
four months later, she has returned to her high functioning
job and remained fully independent.
Conclusion: This was a successful case of a diagnosis and
treatment of CLIPPERS. We demonstrated ef ﬁcacious disease
maintenance with low-dose corticosteroids and mycophenolate
mofetil. Recognition of this rare in ﬂammatory disorder is cru-
cial to reverse signi ﬁcant neurology morbidity.

Background: Autoimmune encephalitis (AIE) refers to a
group of rare, severe, antibody-mediated neurological diseases
characterized by prominent neuropsychiatric symptoms, the
most common subtypes being anti-N-methyl-D-aspartic acid-
receptor (NMDAR)-antibody and leucine-rich-glioma-
inactivated-1 (LGI1)-antibody AIE. Currently, no approved
therapies for AIE exist. Evidence suggests T cells, B cells, and
interleukin-6 (IL-6) play key roles in AIE pathogenesis.
Satralizumab, a monoclonal, recycling antibody targeting the
IL-6 receptor, was engineered to provide sustained suppres-
sion of IL-6 signalling.
Objective: CIELO is a randomized, double-blind (DB),
placebo-controlled basket study evaluating the ef ﬁcacy, safety,
pharmacokinetics (PK) and pharmacodynamics (PD) of
satralizumab in participants with NMDAR or LGI1 AIE.
Study Design: CIELO will enroll approximately 102 partic-
ipants aged ≥12 years with NMDAR AIE and 50 participants
aged ≥18 years with LGI1 AIE from 12 countries. Participants,
who must have an onset of AIE symptoms ≤9m o n t h sb e f o r e
randomization, will be classi ﬁed into “new onset ” or “incom-
plete responder ” groups de ﬁned by time since initial acute
ﬁrst-line therapy and whether they received prior immunother-
apy treatment. CIELO comprises a 52-week DB primary treat-
ment period (Part 1). Participants will be randomized in a 1:1
ratio to receive either satralizumab or placebo, administered
subcutaneously at Weeks 0, 2, 4, and every 4 weeks thereafter
as monotherapy or in addition to background immunosup-
pressants; corticosteroids must be tapered from Week 4. Fol-
lowing Part 1, participants can enter an optional extension
period (Part 2) and continue randomized DB study treatment,
receive open-label satralizumab, or discontinue study treatment
and continue follow-up assessments.
Endpoints: The primary endpoint in both cohorts is the
proportion of participants with a modi ﬁed Rankin scale
(mRS) score improvement ≥1 from baseline without use of
rescue therapy at Week 24. Key secondary endpoints are
time to mRS improvement ≥1 from baseline without use of
rescue therapy, time to rescue therapy, time to seizure

S209. Comparing Autoimmunity in Patients with MS and
Epilepsy versus MS Patients without Epilepsy
Samiksha Srivastava, MD , Fen Bao, Masters degree, Lazar
Adam, Bachelor degree, Emily Pelc, Bachelor degree, Amanda
Reyes, MD, Zena Azo, Bachelor degree, Carla Santiago-
Martinez, Masters degree, Jacob Rube, MD, Mona Elayed, MD,
Evanthia Bernitsas, MD. Wayne State University, Detroit,
MI, USA.
Objective: This study is to investigate the frequency of auto-
immune diseases in Multiple Sclerosis (MSE) patients with
epilepsy and compare it with MS patients without epilepsy.
Background: In MS active brain in ﬂammation and exces-
sive production of proin ﬂammatory cytokines along with
neurodegeneration may contribute to seizures. The risk of
having epilepsy is much higher for MS patients compared to
the general population, estimated at 2% - 5%. Autoimmune
diseases tend to cluster in MS patients at a rate of 4.5%. We
aim to determine if patients with MS and epilepsy have a
higher number of autoimmune diseases compared with MS
patients, given the higher degree of autoimmunity.
Methodology: This is a retrospective analysis of 49 patients
with MS and epilepsy and 42 patients with MS. Data were
abstracted from electronic medical records by one reviewer
and veri ﬁed by a second reviewer. A descriptive and Chi-
square analysis was performed using SPSS v26.
Results: In the MSE group we identi ﬁed 49 MS patients
(35 female, 14 male). This group was compared with a mat-
ched MS group (42 patients; 31 females, 11 male). The
mean number of autoimmune diseases in the MSE was
1.53/C60.5 versus 1 /C60.1 in the MS group (p<0.001). The
mean age of the MS diagnosis was 36 years old (yo) in the
MSE group versus 44 yo in the MS group (p=<.001), and
the mean age of autoimmune disease diagnosis was 20 yo in
the MSE group, 49 yo in the MS group (p=<.001). The aver-
age duration of autoimmune disease was 15 years in the
MSE group and 4 years in the MS group which is statistically
signiﬁcant (p=<.001).
Conclusions: Our ﬁndings suggest that autoimmune dis-
eases were present earlier and at a higher number in the MSE
group in comparison to the MS group. The duration of auto-
immune disease was also signi ﬁcantly higher in the MSE
group than in the MS group. Our ﬁndings point out a higher
degree of autoimmunity in the MSE group that might affect
the MS course. Further research with a larger cohort is
needed.
S212. Effectiveness of Rituximab and Oral
Immunosuppressive Therapies in Neuromyelitis Optica
Spectrum Disorder
Widad Abou Chaar, MD, Laura Dresser, MD, Adil Javed,
MD, PhD. University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA.
Background and Purpose: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum
disorder (NMOSD) is an autoimmune, in ﬂammatory disor-
der associated with high disability if treatment is delayed.
Despite the availability of recently approved disease modify-

ing therapies (DMTs) for NMOSD, their access and afford-
ability is still limited and challenging globally. Purpose here
was to compare the real-world effectiveness of traditionally
used DMTs for NMOSD.
Methods: A single-center retrospective study was conducted
at the University of Chicago Medical Center. Inclusion
criteria: (1) diagnosis according to the 2015 International
Panel for NMO Diagnostic Criteria, (2) positive anti- AQP4
titers, (3) initiation of immunosuppressant therapy within
5 years of disease onset, (4) ﬁrst-line treatment with
Rituximab, Mycophenolate (MMF) or Azathioprine (AZA).
Both ELISA and cell-based tests were included. Patients with
negative anti-AQP4 titers were excluded. Kaplan-Meier sur-
vival analysis was used to estimate proportion of relapse-free
patients following initiation of ﬁrst line immunosuppressive
therapy. A Cox proportional hazards regression model was
used to assess the association of risk of relapsing with ﬁrst-line
immunosuppressive treatments without and with adjustment
for pre-speciﬁed factors (age at disease onset, duration of dis-
ease, gender, race, location of relapse).
Results: 7 of 29 patients (24%) receiving Rituximab expe-
rienced a relapse within the ﬁrst 3 years of treatment
vs. 13 of 23 (57%) patients receiving either AZA or MMF.
Within the ﬁrst 6 months of treatment, 2 (6.9%) patients
treated with Rituximab experienced a relapse vs. 7 (30.4%)
patients treated with either MMF or AZA. In the 29 patients
treated with Rituximab, the 1-year and 3-year proportion of
relapse-free patients was 88.8% and 70.9%. For the
23 patients treated with either AZA or MMF, the 1-year and
3-year proportion of relapse-free patients was 69.5% and
38.7%. In the univariate analysis, the risk of relapse was sig-
niﬁcantly lower in patients treated with Rituximab compared
to those treated either AZA or MMF (hazard ratio [HR] of
2.48 [0.99 - 6.21]; p = 0.046).
Conclusions: In this real-world, urban cohort of seroposi-
tive NMOSD patients, with a predominance of individuals
of African descent, Rituximab was more effective in
preventing relapses within 3 years of therapy initiation com-
pared to AZA and MMF. Rituximab is a highly ef ﬁcacious
immunosuppressant for seropositive NMOSD, with a 1-year
and 3-year proportion of relapse-free patients of 88.8% and
70.9%, respectively.

Objective: To evaluate differences in concentrations of
serum-based biomarkers obtained from a self-reported,
screened healthy control (HC) population when compared to
age and gender matched treatment naïve multiple sclerosis
(MS) patients.
Background: Protein markers of neuronal and glial injury
are key for understanding development of disability in relapsing
remitting MS (RRMS). The levels of these proteins in healthy
individuals remain unclear and HC are often a sample of con-
venience. We developed an electronic based screening tool to
identify a representative sample of HC between 13 and 85 at
community and wellness events. Neuro ﬁlament light (NfL),
glial ﬁbrillary acidic protein (GFAP), ubiquitin carboxyl-
terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1), and total tau (Tau) levels in
treatment naïve RRMS and HC participants were compared to
determine the utility of the screening tool in identifying healthy
controls. Additionally, data was compared on two SR-X
machines to further conﬁrm reproducibility of the data.
Design/Methods: Treatment naïve, age and sex matched
RRMS and HC participant serum samples were collected to
compare NfL, GFAP, UCH-L1, and Tau protein levels. Dif-
ferences in levels of each protein between the RRMS and
HC groups were analyzed. Each sample was run in duplicate
on two different SR-X systems to assess for reliability between
Quanterix systems. Concentrations were log transformed and
analyzed with mixed model regression. Partial Pearson and
Spearman correlations, adjusted for MS or HC group, were
performed between the two SR-X machines.
Results: Nineteen HC and treatment naïve RRMS partici-
pants were analyzed. Preliminary results for these MS (mean
age 32.8 years, 79% Female, 10.5% Black, 10.5% Hispanic,
5.3% Asian) and HC (mean age 31.9 years, 10.5% Hispanic,
5.3% Black, 5.3% Asian, 5.3% American Indian/Alaskan
Native) demonstrates signi ﬁcantly higher geometric means
for NfL (10.3 pg/mL) and GFAP (78.9 pg/mL) levels in
RRMS participants than HC (4.6 pg/mL, 50.5 pg/mL, p
< 0.05). UCH-L1 and Tau levels were not signi ﬁcantly dif-
ferent. Both Spearman and Pearson correlation estimates
between SR-X machines for all four biomarkers were at 0.91
or above (p < 0.05).
Conclusions: As expected, preliminary results show that
NfL and GFAP levels are signi ﬁcantly higher in RRMS
patients versus HC. A positive correlation was seen between
the machines for each of the protein types, con ﬁrming
machine reproducibility. Utility of the screening tool in iden-
tifying HC is promising.

Objective: To explore genetic association between anti-
NMDA-receptor encephalitis (anti-NMDARE) and human
leukocyte antigen (HLA), killer cell immunoglobulin-like
receptors (KIR) and other potential genome wide
associations.
Background: Prior studies have shown no or minimal
HLA-association, while a small Genome-wide association

study (GWAS) of 178 German patients implicated a locus on
chromosome 15, harboring only the LRRK1 gene, and a
locus on chromosome 11 centered on the ACP2 and
NR1H3 genes in a larger region of high linkage disequilib-
rium (LD).
Design/Methods: We conducted GWAS in 511 cases and
2,827 PCA-matched controls and allelic KIR and HLA
sequencing in 449 cases and 1,577 ethnically matched
controls.
Results: GWAS signi ﬁcant loci include ACP2/NR1H3
and DMXL2 genes. The ACP2/NR1H3 locus is on chromo-
some 11 and in high LD with LRP4 and MADD
(rs11039155; p=10
-13; OR=2.1). The lead variant is a strong
expression quantitative trait (eQTL) for all of these genes
(p< 10-10) across various tissues. The second locus is in the
vicinity of DMXL2 on chromosome 15 (lead variant
rs76144151; p=1.1x10
-8; OR=1.58) and regulates expression
of DMXL2 in various tissues. Of note, LRRK1 is not
signiﬁcant.
Strikingly, there is a weak, but signi ﬁcant signal in the
HLA class II sequencing sample after controlling for popula-
tion strati ﬁcation, suggesting predisposing effects of
DQA1*01:01~DQB1*05:01 (OR=2, p=1.10
-5) and
DRB4*01:01, plus protective effects of DQB1 *02:02,
DPB1*01:03 and DRB1 *01:03. Using KIR sequencing, we
found signi ﬁcant independent associations with
KIR2DL5B*00201 (OR=2.17; p=2.310 -6) and
KIR2DL4*00103 (OR=1.95, p=4x10 -4). KIR2DL5B *00201
is epigenetically silenced, but is frequently associated with
KIR2DS3*00103, which has no known ligand.
Conclusion: This study is the, so far, largest genetic study
on anti-NMDARE. Our results suggest involvement of
innate immunity, HLA and KIR in this disease. Follow-up
on the functional roles of these loci and validation in a larger
cohort is needed.

S217. Mental Health Disorders in the MS Population

Objective: To examine the demographic prevalence of men-
tal health disorders, including anxiety, depression, schizo-
phrenia, and bipolar disorder in Multiple sclerosis
(MS) populations.
Background: In MS active brain in ﬂammation and exces-
sive production of proin ﬂammatory cytokines and neu-
rodegeneration may contribute to anxiety, depression, and
psychosis. Mental health disorders can negatively affect the
quality of life and result in job loss, increased divorce rate,
and family con ﬂict. Therefore, professional counseling, sup-
port groups, and treatment can be helpful in managing men-
tal health disorders.
Methodology: This is a retrospective analysis of
146 patients diagnosed with MS that aims to identify those
with mental comorbidities. Data were abstracted from elec-
tronic medical records by one reviewer and veri ﬁed by a sec-
ond reviewer. A descriptive and Chi-square analysis was
performed using SPSS v26.
Results: We identify ﬁfty patients (34.2%) who were diag-
nosed with mental health disorders. Among them, 37 were
women, 13 were men, 27 were whites, and 23 were non-
whites. Thirty (60%) patients had anxiety, 18 (36%) had
depression, 1(2%) had schizophrenia and 1 (2%) had bipolar
disorder. The average age for diagnosing anxiety was 47-years
old, 54-year-old with depression, 26-year-old with schizo-
phrenia, and 45-year-old with bipolar disorder.
Conclusions: Our ﬁndings suggest a high prevalence of
mental health comorbidities in MS patients with anxiety
being the most common followed by depression. Interest-
ingly, psychotic disorders are more frequent in MS patients
than in the general population. Periodic screening may be of
beneﬁt. Future studies with larger samples are warranted.

using serial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and optical

Methods: Our cohort consisted of 48 people with
MS. NEVs were immunocaptured by targeting neuronal
marker L1 cell adhesion molecule (L1-CAM) from plasma
and mitochondrial complex IV and V activity levels were
measured using commercial assays. Subjects underwent OCT
every 6 months and brain MRI annually. The associations
between baseline mitochondrial complex IV and V activities
and brain substructure and retinal thickness changes were
estimated utilizing linear mixed-effects models.
Results: Participants were predominantly female (79%),
had a mean age of 44.7 years, median disease duration of
12.5 years and median EDSS of 1.75. We found that higher
baseline mitochondrial complex IV activity levels were associ-
ated with faster whole brain volume (WBV) ( β = -0.15
%/year; p = 0.001), cortical gray matter (GM) ( β = -0.18
%/year; p = 0.018), subcortical GM ( β = -0.30 %/year;
p = 0.003), as well as peripapillary retinal nerve ﬁber layer
(pRNFL) ( β = -0.17 μm/year; p = 0.034) and ganglion and
inner plexiform layer (GCIPL) ( β = -0.10 μm/year;
p = 0.001) atrophies, while higher baseline mitochondrial
complex V activity levels were associated with slower WBV
(β = 0.15 %/year; p = 0.004), cortical GM ( β = 0.16 %/year;
p = 0.046), subcortical GM ( β = 0.32 %/year; p = 0.001),
and GCIPL ( β = 0.07 μm/year; p = 0.018) atrophies.
Conclusions: Our results suggest that NEVs in the
periphery may provide a means to assess neuronal mitochon-
drial health and serve as a potential biomarker of disease pro-
gression. Additional larger longitudinal studies will be
required to validate these ﬁndings.
S219. Neuroin ﬂammation in the Post-Partum Period: An
Unusual Presentation of Myelin Oligodendrocyte
Antibody Disease
Valeria Suarez, Masters

Bowling, MD 2, Madihah Hepburn, MD 2. 1Case Western,
Cleveland, OH, USA, 2Summa Health, Akron, OH, USA.
Introduction: The state of pregnancy represents a unique
time of immunological quiescence through suppression of the
host pro-in ﬂammatory responses during the months of gesta-
tion to promote tolerance of fetal antigens and facilitate
embryonic implantation and development. Many women
with autoimmune conditions report improved disease control
during this time. After parturition there is a rapid reversal of

this immune suppression leading to ﬂares of known autoim-
mune conditions, reactivation of latent infection or new man-
ifestations of autoimmune disease(1). New neurological
symptoms in the post-partum period should prompt evalua-
tion and inclusion of autoimmunity as part of the differential
diagnosis.
Case Description: An adolescent patient developed fever
and altered mentation one day following spontaneous vagi-
nal delivery of a full-term infant after an uncomplicated
pregnancy. She had frontal headaches, followed by staring
spells, speech arrest and confusion. Rapidly developed gen-
eralized seizures requiring intubation for airway protection
and treatment of convulsive status epilepticus with
levetiracetam and midazolam infusion. Lumbar puncture
with CSF pleocytosis (WBC 48cells/ul, protein 85.1 mg/dl,
glucose 51mg/dl). Treated empirically for meningitis despite
negative CSF cultures and PCR panel. Seizures resolved and
sedation weaned but patient with low-grade fever, pro-
longed encephalopathy, ophthalmoparesis and ﬂaccid quad-
riplegia. MRI-Brain showed new non-enhancing T2/FLAIR
hyperintense lesions diffusely throughout the pons, medulla,
bilateral hippocampi and thalami along with smaller T2
hyperintense lesions within bilateral frontal and parietal
lobes and periventricular to lateral ventricles. MRI-cervical-
spine with extensive T2-hyperintensity within entire cervical
cord. Serum MOG-antibody positive (1:640) and CSF mye-
lin basic protein >100mg/dl. New diagnosis of myelin oligo-
dendrocyte associated disease(MOGAD) in the post-partum
period treated with IV-solumedrol and plasmapheresis with
dramatic reversal of encephalopathy and return of motor
strength.
Conclusion: MOGAD is a rare demyelinating condition
that may be dif ﬁcult to diagnose since the initial presentation
of with fever, seizures, meningeal symptoms, and CSF
pleocytosis may be misleading to clinicians by masquerading
as infectious meningitis. In our case the lack of improvement
of encephalopathy, persistence of fever despite completion of
antibiotic course led us to further diagnostic testing for
immunological causes. The brain lesions in MOGAD can be
non-speciﬁc but ~25% are not associated with gadolinium
enhancement. The post-partum period is a time of relative
pro-inﬂammation therefore new diagnoses of neuro-
inﬂammatory etiologies should be considered in new onset
neurological symptoms during this time.

Background: The Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (anti-
NMDAR) encephalitis is an entity that encompasses a neuro-
inﬂammatory process that is clinically expressed by various
neurological and psychiatric symptoms, which represent a
diagnosis challenge. When the presence of psychotic symp-
toms misleads to the administration of antipsychotics, a sub-
set of patients could develop neuroleptic intolerance (NI) as a
side effect. NI is hypothesized to be caused by dopaminergic
overactivity, that in the most severe cases includes potentially
lethal dysautonomia (Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome or
NMS). Since this complication is preventable by an accurate
recognition of the encephalitis, we aimed to synthesize the
epidemiological and clinical characteristics of NI in the con-
text of anti-NMDAR as guidance for better clinical
recognition.
Methods: We systematically searched three databases,
including clinical cases, case series, and observational stud-
ies reporting patients with bo th diagnoses. For summariz-
ing the results, we conducte d a narrative synthesis,
including one original case reported by the authors. We
assessed the quality of the included studies with the tool
developed by Murad et al., 2018. Potentially risk factors
such as diagnosis delay, malignancy absence, initial psychi-
atric hospitalization, and type of antipsychotic, were
explored for the presence of certain outcomes such as sta-
tus at discharge and ICU/mechanical ventilation
requirements.
Results: Twenty-two records representing 40 patients
(28 females; mean age, 24.6) with a suggestive presentation of
NI were included. The overall quality of the evidence was low.
Seventy percent of the patients were admitted to a psychiatric
ward, and 37.5% displayed purely psychiatric symptoms. The
mean time to diagnosis of anti-NMDAR encephalitis was
26.7 days. NI triggered the suspicion of anti-NMDAR
encephalitis in six patients. No association was found between
clinical characteristics or antipsychotic type and ICU and/or
mechanical ventilation requirements.
