encephalitis includes both neurological and psychiatric syn-
dromes, the latter could cause the administration of antipsy-
chotic treatment with the potential consequent side effect of
NI. NI generates a signi ﬁcant diagnosis delay. Only a small
proportion of the patients that develop NI presented with
pure psychiatric symptoms; therefore, to prevent this compli-
cation, emergency physicians, neurologists, and psychiatrists
must systematically search for associated subtle neurological
manifestations in young patients with new-onset psychiatric
symptoms and considered anti-NMDAR encephalitis as a dif-
ferential diagnosis.
S221. Neurologic Complications Following mRNA
Vaccinations
Andrea Arevalo, M.D. , Elizabeth Brinkley, M.D., Vidit
Majmundar, MBBS, Rhodemarie Maron, D.O., Mohamed
Kazamel, M.D., William Meador, M.D., Shruti Agnihotri,

M.D.. University of Alabama at Birmingham, Birmingham,
AL, USA.
Objective: To discuss neuro-immunologic complications of
mRNA vaccinations.
Background: Neuro-immunologic complications are a
known risk of various types of vaccines, but little is known
about complications after mRNA vaccines.
Methods: We present a series of four patients from a sin-
gle institution who developed severe neurologic complications
after mRNA COVID-19 vaccinations.
Results: Case One : A 31-year-old female developed arm
paresthesias, leg weakness and urinary retention one week fol-
lowing her ﬁrst dose. MRI demonstrated T2 hyperintensity
at T5 and T8-T9 with enhancement. She received ﬁve days
methylprednisolone and IVIG. She remains wheelchair
bound with urinary retention. Case Two : A 31-year-old male
developed paresthesias in legs and urinary retention four
weeks following his second dose. A year prior, he contracted
COVID-19 and had transient leg paresthesias. MRI demon-
strated T2 hyperintensity from lower medulla to the conus.
He received ﬁve days of intravenous methylprednisolone
followed by oral prednisone. He remains symptomatic requir-
ing gabapentin, baclofen and tamsulosin. Case Three :A
75-year-old female with hypertension, diabetes mellitus and
Crohn’s disease developed leg weakness, complicated by
respiratory failure, three days after her ﬁrst dose. Guillian-
Barre Syndrome was diagnosed based on nerve conduction
studies. She received PLEX followed by IVIG. She can now
ambulate with a walker. Case Four : A 59-year-old healthy
female developed urinary retention, saddle anesthesia and leg
weakness four weeks following her second dose. MRI spine
demonstrated patchy T2 hyperintensities throughout the
pons, C- and T-spine. She continues to have gait imbalance
and urinary incontinence. Other causes of transverse myelitis
including neuromyelitis optica and myelin oligodendrocyte
associated disease were ruled out in Case 1, 2 and 4. CSF
analysis in all were compatible with neuro-in ﬂammation.
Conclusion: These cases raise concern that mRNA vacci-
nations may be associated with neurologic complications due
to heightened immune reactivity. Further studies are needed
to understand the risk associated with mRNA vaccinations.

member due to worsening cognitive impairment and altered
mental status. Her chest x-ray was notable for a dense con-
solidation/mass in the right upper and lower lobe. The ﬁnd-

were further highlighted on a chest computed tomography
(CT). An endobronchial biopsy was performed with pathol-
ogy con ﬁrming a small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma. Her
head CT revealed no intracranial pathology, brain magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) con ﬁrmed no acute infarct, and
no intracranial mass. A lumbar puncture was performed
which did not suggest active infection or antibody mediated
autoimmune process. At that ti me systemic antibiotics and
antivirals were cessated. A twent y-four-hour video electroen-
cephalogram (VEEG) was only notable for mild to moder-
ate diffuse background slowing and negative for any
epileptiform activity. Chemot herapy was started in the hope

the initiation of chemotherapy, the patient ’s mental status
gradually improved, and a full course was completed
outpatient.

Objective: To better characterize the genetic association
between human leukocyte antigen (HLA) and anti-IgLON5
disease and to explore auto-antigen binding to associated
HLA molecules and their functional involvement in
pathophysiology.
Background: Anti-IgLON5 disease is a rare, but likely
underdiagnosed type of autoantibody encephalitis with a het-
erogeneous clinical phenotype, including sleep, movement
and brainstem dysfunction. Its pathophysiology remains elu-
sive, although dominant association with HLA-

DRB1*10:01-DQB1*05:01 strongly supports an autoim-
mune basis.
Design/Methods: A multicentric cohort of 62 patients
and 433 controls matched by principal component analysis
was included. Genome-wide association analysis was per-
formed with 4-digit resolution HLA imputation and selected
8-digit resolution validation typing. A generalized logistic
model was used to determine the association with individual
alleles and haplotype counts to establish haplotype associa-
tions. Furthermore, we computationally predicted binding of
IgLON5-derived peptides to risk-associated HLA-molecules.
Results: Our results indicate a rank wise effect of HLA-
DQA1*01:05~DQB1*05:01 (heterozygotes: OR 46.6), HLA-
DQA1*01:01~DQB1*05:01 (homozygotes: OR 26.9; hetero-
zygotes: OR 2.5) and HLA-DQA1 *01:04-~DQB1* 05:03
(homozygotes: OR 30.9; heterozygotes: OR 5.6), in order of
descending relative risk predisposition. Differences between
encoded heterodimers are minimal (a few amino acids outside
the main HLA sequence binding region), suggesting a com-
mon function. Computational binding predictions support
similar, high binding af ﬁnity for IgLON5
275-283 in a post-
translationally modiﬁed (N-deglycosylated) form by all three of
these HLA-DQ molecules and other common binders. In con-
trast, association analysis suggests that effects of HLA-DR are
likely explained by linkage disequilibrium.

on anti-IgLON5 disease. Our results strongly suggest HLA-
DQ over HLA-DR association, with higher reactivity against
post-translationally modi ﬁed versus physiological peptides, in
line with reduced T cell priming against these epitopes. Fur-
ther studies should address the functional implications of
these HLA associations.

nitric oxide synthase coupling (NOS). When in ﬂammation

impact in ﬂammatory levels, little is known about its in ﬂu-

(healthy, n=20) and MS group (stable relapsing remitting MS
[RRMS], n=20) were enrolled. Stable MS participants were
deﬁned as currently on Natalizumab, a high ef ﬁcacy DMT

ages < 18 and > 40, body mass index (BMI) < 18.5 and
> 29.9, any physical disability affecting mobility, com-
orbidities other than MS, excessive use of alcohol and ciga-
rette smoking. An additional exclusion for the MS group was
any history of fumaric acid esters usage. Blood was collected
through venipunctures and processed immediately to preserve

BH4 stability. Preanalytical methods validation was per-

with age (34 /C65) and BMI (25 /C62.3) and were similar to
control group characteristics. Plasma BH4 peak area was sig-
niﬁcantly reduced in MS group (p<0.01, Cohen ’s d > 0.8).

plasma using a reference compound, BH4 concentration was
(7.7 /C62) versus (6 /C62) ng/mL in control and MS groups,
respectively, suggesting reduced plasma BH4 in MS group
(p<0.01, Cohen’s d > 0.8).

started. Within one week of the ﬁrst dose, her strength and
extraocular movements improved. Furthermore, her platelet
counts improved. She received 2 doses of Efgartigimod. Unfortu-
nately, the patient developed septic shock, cardiac arrested, and
expired.
Conclusions: Our patient did not tolerate IVIG and plas-
mapheresis, the currently recommended treatments for
Pembrolizumab-induced myasthenia gravis-like syndrome.
Initiation of Efgartigimod therapy led to early improvement
of her drug-induced myasthenia gravis and platelet count fol-
lowing the development of severe thrombocytopenia, a recog-
nized side effect of PLEX. Further research into the use of
Efgartigimod in similar patients is necessary, but we propose
an alternative treatment.

K-S109. Ocrelizumab Impacts IgA Coating and
Differential Abundances of Immunomodulatory Gut
Bacteria in Multiple Sclerosis Patients
Guneet Janda, BS, Inessa E. Cohen, BS, Isabella Cruz, n/a,
Erin E. Longbrake, MD, PhD . Yale University, New Haven,
CT, USA.
Objectives: To characterize taxonomic and functional shifts
in the gut microbiota of multiple sclerosis (MS) patients
induced by B-cell depletion.
Background: The mechanisms by which B-cell deple-
tion ameliorates MS have not been fully delineated. Gut
bacteria and their metabolites are important regulators of
t h es y s t e m i ci m m u n er e s p o n s e ,a n de a r l yw o r kd e m o n -
strated dysbiosis in MS. Dysregulation of immunomodula-
tory bacteria may contribute to MS pathobiology. We
hypothesized that ocrelizumab, a B-cell depleting mono-
clonal antibody used to treat MS, would normalize the
phenotype of gut bacteria, promoting an anti-in ﬂammatory
immune milieu.
Methods: We enrolled untreated 58 MS patients at the
onset of their disease and obtained longitudinal samples at
1 (n-21) and 6 months (n=26) after initiating ocrelizumab.
We recruited 43 age/sex matched healthy controls as compar-
ison. Paired blood/stool were collected. Gut microbiota were
characterized using high-throughput long amplicon sequenc-
ing of the 16S-ITS-23S rRNA operon. We additionally char-
acterized the proportions and taxonomies of immunoglobulin
A (IgA) coated bacteria. Immunologically active (IgA-coated)
bacteria and those not eliciting an immune response (IgA-
uncoated) were sequenced and analyzed separately. Sequenc-
ing data were denoised with DADA2 and analysis was per-
formed using QIIME2. Differential abundance was
ascertained using linear determinant analysis effect size
(LEfSe).
Results: Alpha and beta diversity were not signi ﬁcantly
different between MS and controls. Using LEfSe, we
observed increased abundance of Monoglobus and
Erysipelotrichaceae genera in patients with MS compared to
controls, while several genera including Pseudoclostridium,
Christensenella, and Ruminococcus were of decreased abun-
dance in MS. When IgA-coated bacteria were considered sep-
arately, we ﬁrst observed that patients with MS exhibited
decreased IgA coating of their intestinal bacteria compared to
healthy individuals. This phenomenon resolved with increas-
ing time after B-cell depletion. Among untreated patients,
Facalibacterium prausnitzii and Akkermansia muciniphilia had
a higher IgA coating index compared to controls.
Conclusions: Untreated MS patients exhibit a dys-
regulated immune response to gut microbes. Moreover,
RRMS patients exhibit a phenotypically distinct gut micro-
biome compared to healthy individuals. These differences
diminished over time with B-cell depletion.

despite clinical progression. Additionally, interpretation of
elevated plasma NfL without evidence of disease progression
remains unclear. Glial ﬁbrillary acidic protein (GFAP), an

may add clinical prognostic value.

M238. Acute Brain Injury Due to Asymmetric Cerebral
Desaturation is Time Dependent in Veno-Arterial
Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Monitored by
Near Infrared Spectroscopy
David Zhao, BA , Benjamin Shou, BS, Giorgio Caturegli, BS,
Glenn Whitman, MD, Bo Soo Kim, MD, Sung-Min Cho, DO,
MHS. Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore,
MD, USA.
Introduction: Cerebral near-infrared spectroscopy (cNIRS)
offers real-time bedside neuromonitoring of cerebral regional
oxygen saturation (rSO
2) and may detect acute brain injury
(ABI). Since veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygena-
tion (VA-ECMO) patients are at risk for global or asymmet-
ric hypoxic cerebral perfusion, we sought to determine the
association between rSO
2 trends and ABI.
Methods: Consecutive VA-ECMO patients on cNIRS
monitoring were enrolled in a prospective, observational
study from December 2018 to October 2020. ABI was
deﬁned as intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic stroke, hypoxic
ischemic brain injury (HIBI), or brain death during ECMO.
rSO
2 values were collected from left and right frontal cerebral
oximetry sensors every hour beginning at ECMO cannula-
tion. Cerebral desaturation was de ﬁned as left or right
rSO
2<40% for >2, >4, >6, >8, or >10 consecutive hours. Per-
fusion asymmetry was determined by: a) averaging left versus
right rSO 2 difference over the entire ECMO run dichoto-
mized into 5 groups of rSO 2 differences >2%, >4%, >6%,
>8%, or >10%; and b) consecutive hours of rSO 2 asymmetry
using the same dichotomization groupings. Multivariable
logistic regression and Fisher ’s exact test were used to deter-
mine the association of these rSO
2 trends with ABI, with
pre-speciﬁed covariates of monitoring period and cannulation
method.
Results: Sixty-nine VA-ECMO patients (mean age
56 years, 65% male) underwent cNIRS monitoring (median
duration=8 hours, IQR=6-332). Eighteen (26%) experienced
ABI. When the average perfusion asymmetry was >8% (n=8
[12%]) there was signi ﬁcantly increased odds of ABI
(aOR= 9.4; 95% CI= 4.1-381.4; p<0.001). Average perfu-
sion asymmetry >8% was also associated with ischemic stroke
(OR=6.6; 95% CI=1.4-31.9; p=0.026) and HIBI (OR 19.3;
95% CI=3.2-118.0; p=0.002) on univariate analysis.
However, subgroup analysis showed this association between
ABI and average perfusion difference >8% to hold true only
for peripheral cannulation (p=0.002) but not for central can-
nulation (p =0.08). Importantly, concurrent cerebral
desaturation and asymmetrical perfusion of >10% for >10
consecutive hours was also signi ﬁcantly associated with ABI
(aOR=5.2; 95% CI=1.2-22.2). Regardless of duration, cere-
bral desaturation was not associated with ABI (aOR=3.0;
95% CI=0.8-10.5).
Conclusions: Symmetric cerebral desaturation alone was
not associated with ABI. However, desaturation with asym-
metry >10% for >10 hours, was signi ﬁcantly associated with
ABI in VA-ECMO patients. Over the duration of an ECMO

run, average perfusion asymmetry >8% on VA-ECMO with
peripheral cannulation had increased odds of ABI while cen-
tral cannulation did not.
M239. An Unexpected Finding of a Life Threatening
Progressive Epidural Hematoma ( PEDH) on Repeat
Imaging: PEDH, an Under-Recognized Entity
Rajesh K. Gupta, MD, MS , Jessi Cai, BS, Christopher
M. Orlando, MD. McGovern Medical School, UT Health,
Houston, TX, USA.
Background: A progressive epidural hematoma (PEDH) is
deﬁned as a new hematoma, or a 25% or more increase in
the size of hematoma after initial head imaging (1, 2). The
incidence of PEDH varies from 5 % to 13% (1, 2, 3). We
report a patient who presented to the emergency department
(ED) after a fall from a new-onset seizure and had no major
abnormalities on the CT head, however, an MRI of the brain
within few hours for seizure work up showed a large life
threatening epidural hematoma.
Case Description: A woman in her 30s with no signi ﬁ-
cant past medical history experienced a generalized tonic
clinic seizure and fell on the concrete ground . On arrival to
ED, she reported an intractable right temporal headache and
also endorsed feeling unwell with a mild headache for the
preceding one week. The patient ’s physical exam was non-
focal except for being in moderate distress from headache. A
CT head without contrast showed a small fracture but no evi-
dence of any major intracranial hemorrhage. A decision was
made to admit her to neurology service for a new-onset sei-
zure workup. The patient continued to have persistent head-
ache and requested stronger pain medications. Within a few
hours, the patient had an MRI brain that showed a large life-
threatening right temporal epidural hematoma requiring
emergent craniotomy. Patient reported improvement in head-
ache after the procedure and didn ’t have any other neurologi-
cal clinical features.
Conclusion: A delayed or progressive epidural hematoma
(PEDI) is an under-recognized entity and a repeat head imag-
ing should be considered if an initial CT head is done after a
short interval from head trauma.

Objective: To investigate associations of any prior head
injury and number of prior head injuries with mild behav-
ioral impairment domain symptoms.
Methods: Prospective study of 2,534 community-dwelling
older adults in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities
(ARIC) Study selected for a detailed neurocognitive exam
based on age and cognitive status. Prior head injury was
deﬁned using a combination of self-report and ICD-9/10
code data from hospitalizations and emergency department
visits. Mild behavioral impairment domains were de ﬁned
using data from the informant-reported 12-item Neuropsy-
chiatric Inventory Questionnaire (NPI-Q) and an established
algorithm which maps neuropsychiatric symptoms to the
6 mild behavioral impairment domains of decreased motiva-
tion, affective dysregulation, impulse dyscontrol, social inap-
propriateness, and abnormal perception or thought content.
Logistic regression models adjusted for age, sex, race/center,
education, alcohol consumption, smoking, military veteran
status, APOE ε4 genotype, and cognitive status were used to
estimate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% con ﬁdence intervals
(95% CIs) for the associations of head injury with mild
behavioral impairment domain symptoms. Sampling weights
were used to account for study design.
Results: Mean age of participants was 76 years, 59% were
women, 22% were black, 32% sustained a prior head injury
(25% with 1 prior injury and 7% with 2+ prior injuries).
Among participants with a prior head injury, the median
time from ﬁrst head injury to NPI-Q administration was
32 years. The age-adjusted prevalence of symptoms in any
one or more mild behavioral impairment domains was higher
among individuals with versus without prior head injury
(31.3% versus 26.0%, p=0.027). In fully adjusted models, a
history of 2+ head injuries, but not 1 prior head injury, was
associated with increased odds of impairment in the affective
dysregulation and impulse dyscontrol domains, compared to
no history of head injury (OR: 1.83, 95% CI: 1.13, 2.98 for
the affective dysregulation domain and OR: 1.74, 95% CI:
1.08, 2.78 for the impulse dyscontrol domain). Prior head
injury was not associated with symptoms in the mild behav-
ioral impairment domains of decreased motivation, social
inappropriateness, and abnormal perception or thought con-
tent (all p>0.05).

Conclusions: In this community-based population of
older adults, remote prior head injury was associated with
symptoms in mild behavioral impairment domains, speci ﬁ-
cally in the affective dysregulation and impulse dyscontrol
domains. Future work will focus on the intersection of head
injury and mild behavioral impairment symptomology in the
context of cognitive impairment.

Patient Who Had Concomitantly Received the COVID

Vasculitis is a rare autoimmune condition characterized by
inﬂammation damaging the vessel endothelium. We present
a patient with intraparenchymal hemorrhage (IPH) as the
primary symptom, with progression to multiple acute infarc-

an elevated IgA level.

medical history presented with three days of headache and
recent receipt of the P ﬁzer covid vaccine. Her exam was nota-
ble for waxing and waning mentation. There was no rash,
history of arthritis, renal or gastrointestinal symptoms. A CT
head showed acute IPH in the medial left temporal lobe. An
initial MRI/MRA brain noted cerebral and pontine micro-
hemorrhages along with chronic lacunar infarcts bilaterally. A
repeat brain MRI four days later showed interval develop-
ment of innumerable bilateral acute strokes. Pertinent labs
included LDL 114, hemoglobin a1c 13.7 and IgA 694 (nor-
mal range 60-400). ESR was elevated to 117 and C-reactive
protein was elevated to 4.7. Lupus anticoagulant, homocyste-
ine, rheumatoid factor, ANA, C, P-Anca, Ro/La, dsDNA,
beta-2-glycoprotein, cardiolipin, RPR, west nile, HIV, hepa-
titis, C4 and free lambda light chain levels were all normal. A
lumbar puncture showed an elevated protein of 74 but was

showed diffuse focal narrowing within the right and left
intracranial internal carotid arteries, middle cerebral and ante-

were compatible with vasculitis, so the patient was started on
steroids (80mg daily) for 6 weeks, which was to be followed
by a taper. Mentation drastically improved on steroids. Her
ESR and C-reactive protein also trended down.

tial presenting symptom of vasculitis, although it is still

Background: Sex based differences in recovery and treatment
response after traumatic brain injury (TBI) are known but
remain poorly understood. This could limit translation of ther-
apies and clinical care. Glibenclamide (GLI) is being evaluated
in a phase-3 trial of stroke and phase-2 trial of contusional-
TBI. We previously demonstrated that constitutive-knockout
of the channel regulatory subunit (SUR1/ Abcc8) blocked by
GLI showed histological bene ﬁt only in males post-TBI. Sex-
based effects of GLI are unknown.
Methods: Adult C57BL/6J mice(n=24 male, 24 female)
were randomized into four groups (n=6/group); Naïve,
Untreated TBI, TBI+Vehicle, TBI+GLI. Severe TBI was
induced with controlled cortical impact (CCI):
velocity= 5.0m/s, depth=1.2mm, dwell time 50ms, 3mm
pneumatic impactor). GLI (10ug/mouse, IP) was adminis-
tered immediately post-CCI, plus a 7day maintenance infu-
sion (Alzet 1007D, 0.5ul/h, SQ). Neurocognitive, motor and
anxiety-like behaviors were analyzed between D7-D21 post-
TBI by Morris water maze (MWM), novel object recognition
(NOR), rotarod and elevated plus maze (EPM) respectively.
Results: TBI impaired cognitive function as indicated by
MWM and NOR in both sexes, with universal bene ﬁtf r o m
GLI. GLI restored post-TBI MWM spatial memory de ﬁcits
towards control levels in males (p
GLY_vs_TBI =0.001) and females
(pGLY_vs_TBI=0.005). Similar beneﬁt across sex was observed for
NOR. Rotarod impairment was only noted in females and nor-
malized with treatment (p
GLI-vs-TBI_Female=0.001). Conversely,
EPM anxiety levels were markedly higher post-TBI in males
and improved by treatment (p
GLI-vs-TBI_Male=0.008); this was
not signiﬁcant in females (p=0.68).
Conclusion: Unlike Abcc8 genetic knockout, GLI inhibi-
tion bene ﬁtted multiple measures of functional outcome in
both sexes. Treatment bene ﬁts on cognition were similar
between the two sexes, although some sex-based differences
in injury and GLI effect were noted. However, motor func-
tion de ﬁcit with improvement was exclusive to female mice
in this study, and the impact on anxiety reduction was

greater in male mice. Further study is needed to evaluate his-
tological bene ﬁt of GLI, as well as identify effects mediated
by SUR1 and other targets/ mechanisms.
M244. Proin ﬂammatory Cytokines within the
Cerebrospinal Fluid of Patients with Intraventricular
Hemorrhage are Associated with Outcomes

Background: An in ﬂammatory cascade is activated within
the brain and cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) following intraven-
tricular hemorrhage (IVH). In animal models, activation of
NF-κB/TLR4-dependent signaling pathways within the ven-
tricular system results in CSF hypersecretion leading to post-
hemorrhagic hydrocephalus and poor outcomes. Activation
of this pathway within the CSF compartment in humans
with IVH is not well de ﬁned and few studies compare
inﬂammatory pro ﬁles between plasma and CSF samples. We
sought to investigate the in ﬂammatory pro ﬁle of the CSF
and plasma of patients with IVH.

the concentration of a panel of 10 cytokines in CSF and
plasma samples prospectively collected from patients with
IVH complicating intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) or sub-
arachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), who had external ventricular
drains placed as part of their clinical care. Cytokine concen-
trations were compared between plasma and CSF samples for
patients from whom both were collected. The relationship
between CSF cytokine concentrations and outcomes, includ-
ing functional outcome at 3 months, was investigated.
Results: There were 35 patients (20 ICH and 15 SAH) in
the cohort who contributed CSF samples at day 1 and/or day
3. Mortality at 3 months was 52%. C-C motif chemokine
ligand 2 (CCL2) and interleukin (IL)-6 were present at the
highest concentrations of the cytokines measured, and their
concentrations were more than 20-fold higher within CSF
samples compared to plasma samples from the same patients
(mean [CCL2] 4296pg/mL vs 198pg/mL; mean [IL-6]
2154pg/mL vs 117pg/mL). There were no differences in
CCL2 or IL-6 concentrations within the CSF of patients
with IVH complicating ICH compared to SAH. Lower con-
centrations of CCL2 within the CSF at day 1 trended in
association with death at 3 months.
Conclusion: CSF samples collected within the ﬁrst few
days after hemorrhagic stroke have signi ﬁcantly higher con-
centrations of the proin ﬂammatory cytokines CCL2 and IL-6
compared to plasma samples. There appear to be distinct
relationships between neurologic outcome and production of
certain proin ﬂammatory cytokines, which will be further elu-
cidated through prospective collection of serial CSF samples
from patients with hemorrhagic stroke.

M245. Repeated Mild Traumatic Brain Injury is an
Exogenous Trigger for Neurodegeneration in Transgenic
Mice Expressing Human C9orf72 Hexanucleotide Repeat
Expansions

1, James Bouley, B.A. 1, Idil Tuncali,
M.S.2, Mariana Pereira, PhD 3, Samer Jaber, DVM 1, Robert
H. Brown, MD 1, Nils Henninger, MD 1. 1Umass Chan
Medical School, Worcester, MA, USA, 2University of
Massachusetts, Amherst, MA, USA, 3Umass Chan Medical
School, Amherst, MA, USA.
Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and
frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are fatal neurodegenerative
diseases without effective treatment. The most common
cause of dominantly inherited ALS and FTD is a
hexanucleotide repeat expansion (HRE) in the C9orf72 gene
(c9ALS/FTD). Epidemiological data suggest that traumatic
brain injury (TBI) is a risk factor for ALS and FTD; how-
ever, it remains to be established whether TBI can trigger
events that accelerate pathology and clinical disease in HRE
carriers. We sought to determine whether repetitive TBI
(rTBI) promotes pathology in a bacterial arti ﬁcial chromo-
some transgenic C9orf72 (C9BAC) mouse model of c9ALS/
FTD without an overt motor phenotype or neu-
rodegeneration (Peters et al. Neuron. 2015).
Methods: Littermate C9BAC
+/+ (n=21), C9BAC +/-
(n=20), and non-transgenic (Ntg, n=21) mice of both sexes
were subjected to mild rTBI (once daily for 5 consecutive
days) versus sham injury at age 8-10 weeks. Serial behavioral
assessments were conducted using a battery of tests for motor
and cognitive function, social communication and interac-
tion, and ultrasonic vocalizations (USV) followed by histolog-
ical assessment (NeuN, Tuj1, SMI312, IBA-1, GFAP, TDP-
43, AT8) at 1 year after rTBI. Statistical comparisons were
conducted using one way ANOVA, Kaplan-Meier analysis,
Fisher exact test, and linear mixed models.
Results: Sex distribution was similar across genotypes
(P>0.05) and there was no difference in the 12-month survival
between experimental groups (Log rank P=0.423). After TBI,
behavioral performance was similar between Ntg, C9BAC
+/-,
and C9BAC +/+ mice on Rotarod, novel object recognition,
neurological severity score (P>0.05, each). After TBI,
C9BAC
+/- and C9BAC+/+ mice had signi ﬁcantly reduced grip
strength ( P<0.001) and fewer USVs ( P=0.019), and
C9BAC+/+ mice displayed increased self-grooming, rearing,
and defecating when compared to Ntg TBI ( P<0.05, each).
TBI was associated with signi ﬁcant cortical neuroaxonal loss in
both C9BAC +/- and C9BAC +/+ mice when compared to all
other groups as indicated by loss of NeuN, TuJ1, and
SMI312 staining ( P<0.001, each). While there was no signi ﬁ-
cant between-group difference in GFAP staining ( P=0.124),
C9BAC
+/- and C9BAC+/+ mice showed signiﬁcant microgliosis
as compared to all other groups ( P<0.001). Finally, we
observed widespread TDP-43 mislocalization in C9BAC +/-
and C9BAC+/+ TBI mice. No AT8 (hyperphosphorylated tau)
stained cells were found in any of the groups.
Conclusions: Our data indicates that repetitive mild TBI
serves as exogenous trigger for neurodegeneration and behav-
ioral deﬁcits in at risk HRE carriers.

Predictor of Outcomes
Rebecca Stafford, BA 1, Ivy So Yeon Kim, MPH 1, Ben Brush,
MD2, Asim Mian, MD 1, David Greer, MD, MA 1, Stelios
Smirnakis, MD,PhD 3, Steven Feske, MD 1, Charlene Ong,
MD, MPHS1. 1Boston University Medical Center, Boston, MA,

USA, 2Mass General Brigham, Boston, MA, USA, 3Brigham
and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA.
Background and Purpose: Assessment of ischemia at base-
line using the Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score
(ASPECTS) is a useful tool to inform management, and this
score has been shown to be associated with clinical outcome.
Recent work has demonstrated that both follow-up
ASPECTS done within 18-48 hours of presentation and spe-
ciﬁc ASPECTS locations at baseline may better predict clini-
cal outcomes. We sought to determine whether the
ASPECTS region progression after large MCA stroke is asso-
ciated with relevant radiographic and clinical outcomes.
Methods: Baseline and 24-hour ASPECTS were retrospec-
tively scored in patients with large MCA strokes (involve-
ment of more than 1/3 MCA territory). ASPECTS were
calculated from non-contrast CTs using 5-mm slice thickness
and 40/40 windowing for stroke. We used logistic and linear
regressions to test the association between the initial and
follow-up ASPECTS regions and primary outcomes includ-
ing midline shift (MLS) ≥ 5 mm, hemicraniectomy, and
modiﬁed Rankin Scale (mRS) at discharge.
Results: We scored 50 baseline images and 43 follow up
images from 50 patients (median (IQR) age 64 (56, 81);
19 (38%) females; median (IQR) baseline ASPECTS of 7 (6, 9)).
Twenty-one (42%) developed at least 5 mm of MLS, 7 (14%)
had hemicraniectomy, and median (IQR) mRS at discharge was
5 (4, 6). We found that neither total ASPECTS nor speci ﬁc
regions at baseline were associated with outcomes. Higher total
ASPECTS at follow up was associated with decreased odds of
hemicraniectomy (OR=0.35; 95% CI, 0.11-0.73; p=0.03) and
decreased odds of MLS ≥ 5 mm (OR=0.43; 95% CI, 0.17-0.79;
p=0.02) while lower total ASPECTS at follow up was associated
with greater mRS at discharge (OR=2.40; 95% CI, 1.72-2.82;
p<0.01). Increased deep region score (caudate, internal capsule,
and lentiform nucleus) from baseline to follow up was strongly
associated with the development of MLS ≥ 5 mm (OR=10.09;
95% CI, 2.14-96.30; p=0.01) and with greater mRS at discharge
(OR=2.97; 95% CI, 1.39-3.68; p=0.04).
Conclusion: We found that new involvement of deep
regions from baseline to follow-up was associated with MLS
≥ 5 mm and greater mRS at discharge for patients with large
MCA strokes. ASPECTS at baseline was not associated with
intermediate or functional outcomes at discharge. The evolution
of ASPECT scoring in the ﬁrst several days after stroke may
contribute additional information to predict clinical outcome.

(PVA-ECMO)

BS, Christian Bermudez, MD. Perelman School of Medicine at
the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.

PVA-ECMO is a form of life support that has revolutionized
care for patients in cardiac failure. It can provide support
until cardiac recovery or serve as a bridge to transplant. With
its increasing use, we have come to recognize neurologic
complications. Herein, we discuss two cases of spinal cord
ischemia that developed while patients were on PVA-ECMO.
Patient 1 is an 18-year-old woman with a multi-week course
of presumed respiratory symptoms that progressed to cardio-
genic shock, ultimately found to be representative of heart
failure due to non-compaction cardiomyopathy. She devel-
oped cardiogenic shock and was placed on PVA-ECMO as a
bridge to transplant. While awaiting transplantation, she
developed sensory loss (predominately vibratory and position
sense) with a T-12 level one week after beginning PVA-
ECMO. On serial neurologic exams, she only had mild
weakness in her left leg. She was diagnosed with spinal cord
ischemia and treated with increased systemic blood pressure
augmentation and adjustment of her arterial catheter. Despite
these interventions, four days later, she suddenly progressed
to complete lower extremity paraplegia. Her paraplegia did
not improve even with strategies to increase spinal cord per-
fusion, including blood pressure augmentation, spinal ﬂuid
drainage via insertion of a lumbar drain and pRBC transfu-
sions. She underwent successful cardiac transplant 15 days
after initiation of VA ECMO, but remained paraplegic. MRI
conﬁrmed spinal infarction from the mid-thoracic spine to
the caudal roots. Patient 2 is 48-year-old man with a history
of multiple congenital cardiac repairs admitted for successful
redo aortic root/arch repair. He required emergent PVA-
ECMO in the setting of post-operative cardiac arrest. He was
stable from a cardiac and neurologic standpoint 7 days fol-
lowing VA ECMO initiation and was being prepared for
elective decannulation when he suddenly became paraplegic.
He was emergently decannulated from PVA-ECMO and spi-
nal cord perfusion strategies were started: blood pressure aug-
mentation, transfusion, and spinal ﬂuid drainage. He had a
gradual improvement in lower extremity strength over the
following week with only moderate residual paraparesis.
These cases represent a devastating neurologic complication
of PVA-ECMO. The etiology is likely multifactorial: cannula
position and occlusion leading to reduced ﬂow to the iliac
and clonal arteries, systemic hypotension, elevated central
venous pressure, induced anemia, PVA-ECMO ﬂow dynam-
ics, and patient and artery dimensions. The second case dem-
onstrates the potential to reverse ongoing ischemia by
employing ECMO revision strategies and maneuvers to
improve spinal perfusion.
M249. The Impact of Concomitant Traumatic Brain
Injury on the Epidemiology of Spinal Cord Injury, Access
to Treatment Services, and Outcomes After Acute
Traumatic Spinal Cord Injury
Julio C. Furlan, MD, LLB, MBA, MSc, PhD, FRCPC,
FAAN
1, Di Wang, MSc 2. 1KITE Research Institute, University
Health Network; University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada,
2Praxis Spinal Cord Institute, Vancouver, BC, Canada.
Introduction: While concomitant traumatic brain injury
(TBI) is relatively common in individuals with spinal cord
injury (SCI), its impact on the outcomes post-SCI remain
under-studied. Using data from a national register, this study
examined the in ﬂuence of concomitant TBI on injury epide-
miology, management and outcomes of individuals with
acute traumatic SCI.

Methods: A propensity-score matched cohort study was
performed to compare a SCI+TBI group with a SCI-only
group. Both groups were matched on a 1:1 ratio using the
propensity score matching by age, sex, severity and level of
SCI, and Charlson Comorbidity Index. TBI was de ﬁned as a
Glasgow coma score (GCS) below 15 at the initial admission.
Data were obtained from the Rick Hansen Spinal Cord
Injury Registry (Canada) from 2004 to 2020.
Results: There were 1018 individuals with TBI+SCI and
3687 individuals with SCI alone. The propensity score
matching analysis revealed that being white (OR=5.332,
p=0.0265) is signi ﬁcantly associated with being in TBI+SCI
group, while having other body injuries (OR=0.095,
p=0.0065) is signi ﬁcantly associated with being in SCI-only
group. Further, TBI+SCI group is signi ﬁcantly associated
with in-hospital mortality. The odds of participants dying in
hospital is 2.442 times higher for the TBI+SCI group than
the SCI-only group. Although TBI+SCI group has signi ﬁ-
cantly more prolonged length of stay (LOS) in an acute care
facility than SCI-only group, both groups had similar LOS in
a rehabilitation center. The risk of being discharge to a nurs-
ing home/long-term care in a hospital setting to home of
TBI+SCI group is 1.949 times higher than SCI-only group.
Concomitant TBI does not signi ﬁcantly in ﬂuence change in
motor subscore from initial admission to ﬁnal discharge. The
odds of individuals with pain is 1.52 times higher for the
TBI+SCI group than the SCI-only group. The presence of
spasticity is not signi ﬁcantly different between the two
groups.
Conclusions: The results of this study highlight signi ﬁcant
differences between the TBI+SCI group and the SCI-only
group with regard to the injury epidemiology, survival, dis-
charge disposition, and presence of pain. Nonetheless, both
groups had statistically similar access to treatment services,
degree of motor recovery, and presence of spasticity at the
time of discharge from the rehabilitation center. Those results
suggest that concomitant TBI should be considered a major
potential confounder in future SCI research studies.

Introduction: Trauma has not heretofore been reported to
cause palinageusia, or persistent taste after swallowing.
Methods: Case Study: A 66-year-old left handed (patho-
logical) nasute married male was struck on the left side of his
head by a falling pole without loss of consciousness. Since
then, he has suffered from impaired ability to discriminate
between different aromas. He has a reduced ability to taste to
70% of normal without improvement since onset. He is able
to taste everything but everything is less ﬂavourful. Since the

head trauma, he has had postprandial taste of 2 minute dura-
tion whenever he eats, which never occurred prior to the
head trauma.
Results: Abnormalities in Neurological examination: Cra-
nial Nerve (CN) examination: CN III, IV, VI: bilateral pto-
sis. CN XII: Orofacial Lingual dyskinesia. Motor
examination: Drift Testing: right inward drift. Gait examina-
tion: unstable tandem gait. Cerebellar examination: decreased
rapid alternating movements on the right upper extremity.
Radiology: Magnetic Resonance Imaging brain: normal.
Discussion: Head trauma may cause damage anywhere
throughout the gustatory pathway. If the most peripheral
components of CN VII, IX, X, or the taste receptors are
affected, there may be damage induced ephaptic transmis-
sion, whereby touch or movement may cause a spontaneous
discharge of the gustatory neurons, a form of pathological
synesthesia. Having just swallowed food, inhibition of dis-
charge of recently ﬁred neurons may be dysfunctional, caus-
ing a reverse gustatory adaptation effect, whereby neurons
continue to ﬁre even though the inciting stimulus is no lon-
ger present. Alternatively, the rostral structures, including the
nucleus solitarius, the primary gustatory cortex in the insula,
or secondary taste centers in the caudal lateral orbitofrontal
cortex (de Araujo, 2009) may have been damaged. In this
instance, discharge after stimulus may represent a hyperactiv-
ity of neurons or lack of thalamic inhibition of associated
neurons. Peradventure, this may represent impaired post
traumatic swallowing mechanism with involvement of CN
IX, X, XII or cortical connections to these cranial nerves,
which then allows food remnants to remain in the mouth
while the patient remains unaware of them, inducing the per-
ception of palinageusia. On the other hand this may repre-
sent not true taste but rather a pathological synesthesia from
retronasal olfaction (Gruss, 2015.) In this instance, the palin-
ageusia may be due to hyperactive dysfunctional olfactory
neurons which is then misperceived as taste. In those who
present with head trauma, query as to chemosensory dysfunc-

Patients After Traumatic Brain Injury

Sarafraz, PhD, Linda Robayo, PhD(c), Brian Manolovitz,
PhD(c), Carlos Francisco Blandino, RN, Brian Arwari, PhD,
Evie Sobczak, MS, Danielle Bass, BS MPH, Pardis Ghamasaee,
BA MPH, Daniel Samano, MD MPH, Mohan Kottapally,
MD, Amedeo Merenda, MD, Salim Dib, MD, Jonathan Jagid,

Kristine O ’Phelan, MD, Jan Claassen, MD, Mark F. Walker,
MD. University of Miami, Miami, FL, USA.
Objective: Eye tracking assessments are examiner dependent
and can misclassify patients as unresponsive despite preserved
awareness. This study investigated video eye-tracking (VET)
as a tool to assess responsiveness in comatose traumatic brain
injury (TBI) patients in comparison to the standard bedside
clinical examination.
Methods: We recruited 20 healthy subjects (average age
34, 40% men, 15% Black) and 10 unresponsive TBI patients
(average age 29, 80% men, 50% Black) admitted to a neuro-
logical intensive care unit at a level-1 trauma center
(2020-2021). We recorded eye movements in response to
motion of the examiner ’s ﬁnger and face, a mirror, and an
optokinetic stimulus using eye-tracking glasses. We surveyed

ICU clinicians to judge whether patients are tracking based
on their clinical assessment. Heat maps and temporal graphs
of VET data were classi ﬁed by raters blinded to the clinical
assessments. Patients were classi ﬁed as “covert tracking ”
(tracking based on VET only), “overt tracking ” (VET and
clinical exam), and “no tracking. ” Three machine learning
models were used to test the classi ﬁcation of different states
based on VET data. The Coma Recovery Scale-Revised
(CRS-R) was performed on the day of the experiment. We
evaluated thalamocortical connectivity and structural integrity
using electroencephalogram (EEG), magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI), and auditory and somatosensory evoked
potentials. The ability to obey commands and the Glasgow
outcome scale extended were obtained at 6-month follow-up.
Results: The use of eye-tracker glasses was feasible in all
patients and healthy subjects. A third of patients had “covert
tracking” (CRS-R of 6, 8, 6), ﬁfth had “overt tracking ”
(CRS-R 22, 11), and half had no tracking (CRS-R 8, 6, 5, 7,
7). Histogram-based gradient boosting, random forest, and
gradient boosting had accuracies of 79%, 80%, and 78%,
subsequently, classifying the different states. Higher levels of
thalamocortical connectivity were present in “covert tracking ”
(p=0.02). All patients with “covert tracking ” recovered con-
sciousness at follow-up, and 80% in those without tracking
were unresponsive to commands at follow-up.
Conclusion: Eye tracking assessments can misclassify
patients as unresponsive, when VET shows that they have
“covert tracking, ” a state that is associated with a greater like-
lihood of recovering consciousness. This study shows that
evaluating eye movements of comatose patients with VET is
feasible and is a promising prognostication tool.

Increased Cerebral Oxygen Extraction
Zachary A. Vesoulis, MD MSCI . Washington University,
St. Louis, MO, USA.
Background: Vasomotion is the spontaneous, low-frequency,
rhythmic contractions of arteries which play a role in facilitat-
ing tissue oxygen delivery. Computational analysis can iden-
tify the strength of these oscillations in systemic or cerebral
blood ﬂow. Although the preterm brain is at signi ﬁcant risk
for injury from repeated hypoxia/ischemia, little is known
about the relationship between vasomotion and cerebral oxy-
gen extraction.
Objective: To identify the association between cerebral
hypoxia/ischemia (de ﬁned as increasing cerebral oxygen
extraction/decreasing cerebral saturation) and loss of cerebral
or systemic vasomotion in preterm infants.
Materials and Methods: Preterm infants born <32 weeks
with umbilical arterial lines were enrolled. Infants underwent
continuous cerebral NIRS monitoring for the ﬁrst 72h with
simultaneous capture of mean arterial blood pressure
(MABP) and pulse oximetry (SpO2). Simple error correction

K-M120. Life-Threatening Mass Effect After Large
Middle Cerebral Artery Stroke with and without
Hemorrhagic Conversion

1, David Greer, MD 2. 12Boston University
School of Medicine, Boston, MA, USA.
Intro: Life-threatening mass effect is the most feared early
complication after large ischemic stroke, occurring in up to
30-50% of patients with middle cerebral artery (MCA) occlu-
sion. Historically, investigators have not differentiated
between mass effect secondary to concomitant hemorrhagic
conversion (HC) versus mass effect due to swelling alone. In
this study, we aim to describe characteristics of patients with
large MCA stroke and compare characteristics between HC
subtypes (parenchymal, petechial, none).
Methods: We performed a two-center retrospective study
of patients with evidence of 1/2 MCA territory infarct who
presented within seven days of injury. We compared charac-
teristics in patients who had parenchymal HC, petechial HC
only, and no HC. Our primary outcome was death at thirty
days. Our secondary outcome was midline shift (MLS) at the
septum pellucidum 5mm or surgical decompression. We con-
ducted unadjusted logistic regression analyses to examine
associations between variables and HC status. We will then
construct multivariable logistic regression models for our out-
comes adjusting for hypothesized confounders including tis-
sue plasminogen activator, age, congestive heart failure,
admission blood pressure, glucose, time to mechanical
thrombectomy, and National Institute of Health Stroke Score
(NIHSS). We will also explore associations between HC
types in patients who had more than 0 mm of MLS, and
those who did not undergo withdrawal of life-sustaining ther-
apies within the ﬁrst 24 hours of admission.

Results: Of 924 patients who met our ﬁnal inclusion
criteria, mean age was 67.8 +/-15.5 and 446 were female
(48.3%). A total of 757 (81.9%) presented within 24 hours of
injury. One-hundred and sixty-three (17.6%) had parenchymal
HC, and 338 (36.6%) had petechial HC only. Two-hundred
and ninety-eight patients (32.3%) died within 30 days. Three-
hundred and ﬁfteen had MLS 5mm or surgical decompression.
In our unadjusted analyses there were signi ﬁcant differences in
age (69.1 v. 65, v. 69.4 years), hba1c (6.2 v. 6.3 v. 6%), maxi-
mum midline shift (8.5 v. 6.8 v. 5.6 mm), surgery (19.6%
v. 16.6% v. 5.7%) and death (34.8% v. 25.7% v. 36.2%)
between parenchymal, petechial, and non-HC patients.
Conclusions: Patients with large MCA stroke and various
degrees of HC differ in both baseline characteristics and out-
comes. Understanding risk factors and sequelae of mass effect
with and without HC has important implications for clinical
care treatment decisions and prognostication.
K-M121. Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule
(PECAM/cd31) Blockade Modulates Neutrophil
Recruitment Patterns and Reduces Infarct Size in
Experimental Ischemic Stroke

The in ﬁltration of polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) in
ischemia-reperfusion injury (I/RI) has been implicated as a
critical component of in ﬂammatory damage following ische-
mic stroke. However, successful blockade of PMN trans-
endothelial migration (TEM) in preclinical studies has not
translated to meaningful clinical outcomes. To investigate
this further, leukocyte in ﬁltration patterns were quanti ﬁed,
and these patterns were modulated by blocking platelet endo-
thelial cell adhesion molecule-1 (PECAM), a key regulator of
TEM. LysM-eGFP mice and microscopy were used to visual-

reperfusion. Visual examination showed heterogeneous leuko-
cyte distribution across the infarct at both 24 and 72 h post-
I/RI. A semi-automated process was designed to precisely
map PMN position across brain sections. Treatment with
PECAM function-blocking antibodies did not signi ﬁcantly
affect total leukocyte recruitment but did alter their distribu-
tion, with more observed at the cortex at both early and later
time points (24 h: 89% PECAM blocked vs 72% control;
72 h: 69% PECAM blocked vs. 51% control). This corre-
lated with a decrease in infarct volume. These ﬁndings sug-
gest that TEM, in the setting of I/RI in the cerebrovascular,
occurs primarily at the cortical surface. The reduction of
stroke size with PECAM blockade suggests that in ﬁltrating
PMNs may exacerbate I/RI and indicate the potential thera-
peutic bene ﬁt of regulating the timing and pattern of leuko-

Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is one of the leading causes of
mortality and disability in the United States. Few therapies
reduce long-term cognitive sequelae of TBI and there are only
limited options for rehabilitation. TBI is a mechanical injury
that initiates biochemical and cellular changes including activa-
tion of the innate and adaptive immune systems. Neu-
roinﬂammation plays an important role in TBI both in
contributing to central nervous system (CNS) damage and in
participating in recovery and has been proposed as an impor-
tant, potentially modi ﬁable, driver of secondary injury in ani-
mal and human studies. However, there is still no effective
immune therapy to modulate the neuro recovery pathways
post-injury. The mucosal immune system is a unique
tolerogenic organ that provides a physiological approach for the
induction of regulatory T cells. We found that nasal anti-CD3
monoclonal antibody induces an anti-in ﬂammatory immune
response that downregulates microglial neuroinﬂammation. In a
mouse model of multiple sclerosis, we found that nasally anti-
CD3 localizes to cervical lymph nodes where it induces IL-
10-secreting T cells that migrat e to the brain and suppresses
microglial inﬂammation. Here we report that nasal anti-CD3
antibody ameliorates in ﬂammatory milieu in the CNS and
improves outcomes after controlled cortical impact (CCI)
injury. We administered nasal anti-CD3 daily for 1-month after
CCI. We performed histopathology and behavioral analyses to
assess the effects of nasal ant i-CD3 on spatial learning,
hippocampal-dependent working memory, anxiety, and motor
function at 1-month post-CCI. We also performed high-
throughput RNA sequencing to characterize microglia in acute
(7 days) and chronic (1-month) TBI. Treatment results in
decreased ipsilateral brain edema and lesion volume and
improved anxiety, motor, and memory function at 1-month
post-injury. It also increased IL-10-secreting regulatory T cells
(CD4+FoxP3+) and IL-10 expression, decreased microglial acti-
vation, and reduced recruitment of peripheral monocytes in the
ipsilateral cortex at 7 days post-CCI. To assess the anti-
inﬂammatory role of IL-10 cytokine and CD4+FoxP3+ Tregs,
we neutralized IL-10 in vivo using C57BL/6 mice (with and
without nasal anti-CD3) and in a separate experiment, we
adoptively transferred splenic CD4+ T cells and CD4+ cells
depleted of FoxP3+ intraperitoneally from anti-CD3 and
isotype-treated TBI mice into non-treated TBI mice. We stud-
ied the effects of the neuralization and adoptive transfer on
behavior and microglial transcriptome at 1-month post-CCI
and found that the nasal anti-CD3 effect is IL-10-dependent

LB-M104. Anti-Seizure Prophylaxis in Pediatric
Traumatic Brain Injury
Nidhi Ravishankar, MD , Cemal Karakas, MD, Bethanie
N. Morgan, MD. Norton Childrens Hospital, Department of
Pediatric Neurology, Louisville, KY, USA.
Background: Post-traumatic seizures (PTS) are a serious and
debilitating consequence of pediatric traumatic brain injury
(TBI). However, there is still limited evidence regarding the

optimal management to reduce these seizures. Here, we per-
formed a literature review studying the safety and ef ﬁcacy of
drugs in reducing seizures following pediatric TBI.
Methods: All articles were screened that resulted from a
search of PubMed, using the keywords; “pediatric traumatic
brain injury and seizure prophylaxis ”, “anti-epileptic medica-
tions in pediatric TBI patients ” and “anti-seizure medications
in pediatric TBI ”, looking for reports of pediatric traumatic
brain injury (TBI), early and late PTS.
Results: Seven studies were identi ﬁed that studied the use
of phenytoin, fosphenytoin, phenobarbital and levetiracetam
in early and late PTS in the pediatric population.
Fosphenytoin and phenytoin were used interchangeably in
the studies identi ﬁed. The three studies evaluating phenytoin
showed the effectiveness of phenytoin vs. placebo to lower
early PTS, but no clear evidence of ef ﬁcacy in late PTS was
noted. While phenobarbital has not been as extensively inves-
tigated, given its side-effect pro ﬁ
le and pharmacodynamic
properties, there is no clear advantage to using it over phenyt-
oin based on the results of one study. Levetiracetam prophy-
laxis was effective in early PTS, with one study showing the
tolerability and effectiveness of levetiracetam in both early
and late PTS in the pediatric population. However, three out
of four studies reviewing levetiracetam showed no statistical
signiﬁcance.
Conclusion: There is insuf ﬁcient evidence regarding the
efﬁcacy of anti-seizure medications in reducing seizures fol-
lowing pediatric TBI. Based on current literature, phenyt-
oin and fosphenytoin have been noted as effectively
reducing early post-traumatic seizures after pediatric trau-
matic brain injury. Phenobarbital has also been effective
with signi ﬁcantly less usage in clinical practice, while there
is still insuf ﬁcient evidence to recommend levetiracetam. In
addition, prospective, randomized, controlled studies are
needed to examine the differences in effects of ASM use
with age, drug level monitoring to assess adherence to med-
ication, cost-bene ﬁt analysis of drugs and long term
adverse, as well as neuroprotective effects of different anti-
seizure medications.

abnormal myelin sheath. We present a case of HDLS in a
31-year old male with a proven diagnosis via genetic testing.

sion, anxiety, and tremors presented with progressively

maternal grandmother and mother were diagnosed with early-

Down’s syndrome. His mental exam was signi ﬁcant for
impaired delayed recall and concentration. His cranial nerve
exam was normal except for motor impersistence in his eyes.
He had a bilateral postural tremor in his hands with normal
strength in all four limbs. He was spastic and hyperre ﬂexic.
There was appendicular ataxia with both ﬁnger-nose and heel-
shin testing. His gait was spastic, and he could not tandem
walk more than three steps. He had a normal CBC, CMP,
B12 and folate levels, ESR, CRP, TSH, thyroid antibodies,
and HIV test. His CSF showed no white blood cells, a glucose
value of 67, a protein value of 52, no oligoclonal bands, a neg-
ative HSV titer, and a CSF ACE level of 0.9. His MRI brain
showed con ﬂuent periventricular predominant white matter
T2 ﬂair abnormalities while his cervical spine MRI was nor-
mal. Genetic testing revealed a CSF1R pathological variant,
which is associated with autosomal dominant HDLS and auto-
somal recessive neurodegenerative and dysosteosclerosis.
Discussion: Hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with
spheroids (HDLS) is a rare adult-onset autosomal dominant
disease associated with demyelination and axonal spheroids.
The colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1R) gene is usually the
mutated gene implicated in the disease, which encodes a pro-
tein that in ﬂuences the proliferation, regulation, survival, and
differentiation of macrophages and monocytes. HDLS tends
to have both cognitive and motor symptoms and takes a
rapid, progressive course.

diseases includes medical management of existing symptoms and
treatment of seizures, if present. There are a variety of experi-
mental treatment options, including bone marrow and umbilical
cord stem cell transplantation, gene therapy, and enzyme replace-

S230. A Curious Case of Nitrous Oxide-Induced Dorsal
Column Degeneration
Ajay Menon, MD
1, Cleo Zarina Reyes, MD 2. 1Department of
Internal Medicine, Lehigh Valley Health Network, Allentown,
PA, USA,
2Department of Neurology, Lehigh Valley Health
Network, Allentown, PA, USA.
Background: Degeneration of dorsal columns of the spinal
cord is a neurological complication of vitamin B12 (cobala-
min) de ﬁciency. If the lateral columns are also affected, this
is considered Subacute Combined Degeneration (SACD).
Here, we describe a case of dorsal column pathology from
functional B12 de ﬁciency due to recreational nitrous oxide
(N2O) use.
Case Presentation: A 67-year-old man with history of
gout presented with ambulatory dysfunction. He fell three
times in the past week due to feeling unsteady on his feet.
He complains of two weeks of bilateral lower extremity
numbness and tingling. It started from his toes and traveled
up to a band just below his navel. He denied any weakness,
diarrhea, or infectious symptoms. Neurological exam was
notable for loss of vibration and proprioception in the big
toes and medial malleoli bilaterally, but intact in the knees
and ﬁngers. No motor weakness or sensory de ﬁcit to temper-
ature and pinprick was appreciated. Deep tendon re ﬂexes

were normal. His right toe was down-going and left toe was
up-going on Babinski testing. Computed tomography of the
head was only remarkable for right thalamic lacunar infarct.
Magnetic resonance imaging of cervical and thoracic spine
with and without contrast revealed increased T2 signal inten-
sity in the dorsal aspect of the cord at the C2-C6 and
T6-T10 levels. Relevant laboratory ﬁndings were notable for
normal levels of hemoglobin (13 g/dL), B12 (430 pg/mL),
copper (81.2 ug/dL), and vitamin E. Rapid plasma reagin
was nonreactive and Lyme antibodies ELISA screen was neg-
ative. He had moderate elevation of methylmalonic acid
(MMA) 6.66 umol/L. Further questioning reveals that he
uses N2O recreationally for the past two years and the last
use was 2 months ago. He was started on high-dose B12
injections.
Discussion: Dorsal column degeneration has multiple eti-
ologies including B12 de ﬁciency, copper de ﬁciency/excessive
zinc ingestion, and infections like syphilis. B12 de ﬁciency
can be caused by poor intake or malabsorptive GI com-
orbidities. N2O use can also cause functional B12 de ﬁciency
by binding with and inactivating cobalamin, reducing its
effectiveness as a cofactor in the conversion of MMA to suc-
cinyl CoA. The subsequent accumulation of MMA leads to
demyelination. These patients, however, may have normal
serum B12 concentrations and it is crucial to look for ele-
vated levels of homocysteine and MMA. This case highlights
the signi ﬁcance of thorough history taking in these
population.

synaptic proteins. Some of the changes in synaptic proteins

supporting their use as ﬂuid biomarkers to clinically de ﬁne
those at risk for AD, to diagnose AD, and to follow disease
progression. Elderly adults with Down syndrome
(DS) demonstrate many clinical and pathological manifesta-
tions of AD (referred as AD-DS). However, few studies have
addressed synapse dysfunction in those with AD-DS or have
deﬁned whether such changes are accompanied by changes in
synaptic proteins. Nor have synaptic proteins been fully

S232. Alternative TDP43 Isoforms Underlying
Neurodegeneration in ALS and FTD
Megan Dykstra, BS, Elizabeth Tank, PhD, Sami Barmada,
MD PhD . University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA.
TDP-43 (TAR DNA Binding protein 43) is a ubiquitously
expressed nuclear RNA and DNA binding protein that func-
tions in RNA splicing, transcription, and transport. Cytosolic
TDP-43 aggregates together with nuclear TDP-43 clearance
are hallmark pathologies in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
(ALS) and the most common type of frontotemporal lobar
degeneration (FTLD). In both cell culture and animal
models, cytosolic TDP-43 deposits and nuclear TDP-43
clearance can independently drive neuron loss, but the origins
of TDP-43 mislocalization in ALS and FTLD with TDP-43
pathology (FTLD-TDP) remain obscure. We recently uncov-
ered shortened splice isoforms of TDP-43 (sTDP) that are
enriched in motor neurons, upregulated by neuronal hyperac-
tivity and form insoluble cytosolic inclusions in affected neu-
rons. By developing antibodies that selectively recognize
sTDP isoforms, we also observed in vivo sTDP deposits
within ALS motor neurons that colocalize with full-length
TDP-43. These ﬁndings provide a key link between two
characteristic features of ALS — TDP-43 pathology and neu-
ronal hyperexcitability. Even so, the regulation and function
of sTDP isoforms in healthy cells, as well as their contribu-
tion to neurodegeneration in ALS and FTLD-TDP, remain
unclear. Here we show that sTDP isoforms represent unsta-
ble splicing intermediates generated when TDP-43 binds to
its own transcript to stimulate autoregulation. Inhibition of
nonsense mediated RNA decay or calpains leads to sTDP
accumulation, suggesting that the abundance of these
isoforms is tightly regulated at both the RNA and protein
levels. Upregulation of sTDP results in stable cytoplasmic
hydrogels that sequester full-length TDP-43 and elicit
neurotoxicty in an RNA-dependent manner. Collectively,
these observations outline critical pathways responsible for
regulating TDP-43 production and abundance, highlight a
mechanism for TDP-43 pathology, and hint at novel
approaches for restoring TDP-43 function in ALS and
FTLD-TDP.

Dysfunction: New Insights into Alzheimer ’s Disease
Pathogenesis
Utpal Das, PhD
1, Katarzyna M. Zoltowska, PhD 2, Xinxin
Zuo, PhD1, Sam Lismont, MS 2, Lucia Chávez-Gutiérrez,
PhD2, William C. Mobley, MD, PhD 1. 1University of
California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA, 2VIB-KU Leuven
Center for Brain & Disease Research, Leuven, Belgium.
An imbalance in the levels of enzymatic products generated
by intramembrane proteolysis of the substrates by Gamma-
secretase ( γ-secretase) induces pathological consequences. Rel-
evant to Alzheimer ’s disease, a dysregulation of the γ-secre-
tase-mediated processing of the amyloid precursor protein
(APP) promotes the generation of aggregation-prone
amyloid-β (Aβ) peptides, including A β1-42. One conse-
quence is accumulation of A β42 in plaques in brain. But
increases in longer A β peptides exert several effects on neuro-
nal structure and function, including de ﬁcits in synaptic plas-
ticity with decreased LTP and increased LTD, tau
phosphorylation, oxidative stress, and disrupted protein traf-
ﬁcking. As of yet, how A β42 induces these effects is poorly
understood. Given a role for increased levels of the C99
product of APP (i.e., the APP 99 amino acid C-terminal frag-
ment; C99) in mediating cellular dysfunction, we investi-
gated the hypothesis that A β1-42 exerts product feedback
inhibition on γ-secretases that results in increased levels of
C99. We found that human A β1-42 inhibited γ-secretase in
cell-free conditions and that inhibition was strongly depen-
dent on an intact A β N-terminus. Remarkably, neither
murine A β1-42 nor human p3 (A β17-42) peptides inhibited
the enzyme. In cellular systems, recombinant human
Aβ1-42, as well as biologically derived A β, increased accumu-
lation of APP-CTFs. Importantly, accumulation of APP-
CTFs resulted in hyperactivation of RAB5, the small GTPase
that regulates fusion and traf ﬁcking of early endosomes. Col-
lectively, our ﬁndings identify a previously unknown function
of A β and point to the possibility that A β1-42 contributes to
AD pathology through inhibition of γ-secretase activity and
dysregulation of downstream endosomal structure and func-
tion. Our hypothesis points to the possibility that A β42 may
compete with substrates in addition to APP for processing by
γ-secretase, thus disrupting these substrate-product
relationships.

obesity and diabetes, among US adults aged 18 years or older
has risen by more than 35% in the last 20 years. Individuals
with the MetS have an increased risk of developing
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) compared to age- and gender-
matched controls. An increase in free fatty acids (FFAs), espe-
cially saturated FFAs (sFFAs) such as palmitate, is a main
characteristic of the MetS and clinical studies demonstrate
that higher levels of sFFAs in plasma is inversely correlated
with cognitive function and is a signi ﬁcant risk factor for
developing AD. Exosomes are a subset of extracellular vesicles
that allow intercellular communication and can spread patho-
logical proteins involved in AD, Parkinson ’s disease, and
prion diseases. Exosomal proteins accumulate in plaques in
AD brains, and inhibition of exosome secretion reduces
plaque load in 5XFAD mice. Similarly, extracellular vesicle
cargo composition is altered and vesicle production is higher
in plasma from humans with MetS, which can elicit in ﬂam-
mation through inter-organ communication of target tissues.
These ﬁndings indicate exosomes serve as the point of con-
vergence between MetS and AD. In this study, we used a cell
culture model of MetS to examine the possibility that
exosomes mediate pathology between oligodendrocytes and
cortical neurons. Human cortical neurons and human oligo-

the MetS. Cortical neurons developed insulin resistance (IR),
a key feature of MetS, after treatment with palmitate. Treat-
ment of naïve recipient cortical neurons with exosomes iso-
lated from the supernatant of palmitate-treated neuron

godendrocytes also developed IR with palmitate treatment.

exosomes from palmitate-treated oligodendrocytes culture
supernatant did not increase tau phosphorylation but rather
recipient naïve neurons developed IR. Our results suggest
that axoglial crosstalk between neurons and oligodendrocytes
via exosomes plays a role in two major pathological character-
istics of AD, tau phosphorylation and IR, under MetS condi-
tions. These ﬁndings provide insights into potential
mechanisms and new therapeutic targets linking the MetS
with AD.

gressive dementia, parkinsonism, and dystonia in adolescence
and early adulthood. Although causative mutations have been
mapped to the WDR45 gene (encoding the autophagy effec-
tor WIPI4), the mechanisms underlying how and why
WDR45 mutations result in selective toxicity in neurons are
unknown. In the present study, we use a human induced
pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based model of BPAN in which
we genomically edited cells with CRISPR/Cas9 to fuse
HaloTag to WIPI4 with or without simultaneous knock-in
of a BPAN-related nonsense mutation (Q18X), thereby
enabling direct and non-invasive visualization of wild-type
and mutant WIPI4 in live cells. In iPSC-derived neurons
(iNeurons), we found (1) deleterious effects of the Q18X
mutation on WIPI4 expression levels, localization, and traf-
ﬁcking, (2) impaired autophagic ﬂux, and (3) abnormal accu-
mulation of essential metals. We are also using this iNeuron
model of BPAN to test pharmacologic and genetic manipula-
tions for rescuing neuronal death. Together, our studies clar-
ify the neuron-speci ﬁc biology of WIPI4, unravel key
insights regarding the pathogenesis of BPAN, and elucidate
novel mechanistic details of neuronal autophagy targetable
for rescuing proteostatic dysfunction in neurodegenerative
disease.

sensory polyneuropathy (DSP). We evaluated NFL levels in
CSF and plasma in DSP in people with HIV (PWH) from

the same standardized clinical evaluation of DSP signs and symp-

6.71 years, 15.9% female, 16.9% black, 658.4% non-

52 (12, 190), 100 % on ART, 100% with plasma viral load
suppressed; and 51 PWoH, age 58.4+/-6.68 years, 41.2%
female, 18.0% black, 52.0% non-Hispanic white. Log10
CSF NFL was higher in those with more than 1 sign of DSP
(6.77+/-0.669) compared to those with 1 sign (6.54+/-
0.577) and those with 0 signs (6.49+/-0.662, p=0.0035).

and Thalamic Nuclei Volumes in a Cohort with HIV
Cynthia C. McMahan, BS
1, Devon K. Dietrich, BS 1, Tianxia

R. Smith, MD 1, Govind Nair, PhD 1. 1National Institute of

Background: Retinal axons project directly to the lateral
geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus. Accelerated vol-
ume loss in subcortical gray structures, including the thala-
mus, have been associated with HIV infection. Given the
procedural ease and availability of optical coherence tomogra-
phy (OCT) compared to MRI, we investigated the potential
for retinal thickness to act as a marker for thalamic volumes
in people with HIV.
Methods: 56 participants with HIV (virally suppressed
and on antiretroviral therapy for at least one year) and
28 HIV-negative controls (fro m similar sociodemographic
communities) had 3T MRI that included a T
1-weighted
MPRAGE scan. Images were segmented and volumes of
the whole thalamus and eleven thalamic nuclei and func-
tional hubs were determined using freesurfer (ver 7.2).
Spectral-domain OCT was used to measure the retinal
nerve ﬁber layer (RNFL) and ganglion-cell/inner plexiform
layer (GC-IPL), and the minimum value between eyes was
selected for each participant. Partial correlation analysis was
used to examine the association between retinal variables
and MRI volumes, while controlling for the effects of age,
sex, and estimated intracranial volume (Pearson ’sr
reported). Linear regression was used to assess the effect of
HIV status on retinal thickness, using these same variables
as covariates.
Results: After adjustment, GC-IPL (Least Squares Mean
(LSM) HIV-: 81.6, HIV+: 76.6, p=0.01) and RNFL (LSM
HIV-: 90.0, HIV+: 87.5, p=0.26) were reduced in people
with HIV. In the group with HIV, RNFL correlated with
volume of whole thalamus (r=0.286, p=0.038), and several
thalamic nuclei: LGN (r=0.272, p=0.049), mediodorsal-para-
tenial-reuniens (r=0.290, p=0.04), sensory hub (r=0.293,
p=0.03), and intralaminar (r=0.321, p=0.02). GCIPL corre-
lated with the anteroventral nucleus (r=0.275, p=0.046). No
correlations between retinal thickness and thalamic volumes
were seen in the HIV-negative control group. LGN also cor-
related negatively with age in the HIV group (r= -0.358,
p=0.007), but not in the control group (r=0.274, p=0.24).
Conclusions: Correlations of thalamic volumes and retinal
layer thicknesses indicate that OCT measurements may be
useful as surrogate markers for neurodegeneration of the thal-
amus. While we observed this effect in people with HIV, this
association should be considered in other disease states that
cause retinal thinning. The interactions between HIV disease
factors, age, sex, and thalamic volumes will be further
explored in future analyses.

Objective: Measures of tau phosphorylated at threonine
181 (p-tau181), neuro ﬁlament light chain (NfL), and glial
ﬁbrillary acidic protein (GFAP) from plasma are promising
biomarkers of Alzheimer ’s disease (AD) pathology and neu-
rodegeneration. The objectives of this study were to determine
if plasma biomarkers associate with concomitant AD pathology
in pathology-conﬁrmed neurodegenerative disease cases.

cally de ﬁned by the degree and distribution of the primary
neuropathology such as beta-amyloid, tau, alpha-synuclein,
and TDP43. However, neurodegenerative pathologies do not
exist in isolation and concomitant pathologies are common.
Plasma biomarkers of AD and neurodegeneration are in
development; their association with concomitant AD pathol-
ogy in non-AD neurodegenerative diseases is unknown.
Methods: 60 AD, 55 Lewy body disease (LBD), 9 progres-
sive supranuclear palsy (PSP), 12 corticobasal degeneration
(CBD), 22 frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP43
inclusions (FTD-TDP), and 1 multiple system atrophy
(MSA) pathology con ﬁrmed cases in the UPenn Center for
Neurodegenerative Disease Research CNDR cohort had
plasma collected within 3 years of death. A second cohort of
adults with clinical diagnoses of PD who were cognitively
normal (PD-NC, N=88), PD with mild cognitive impair-
ment (PD-MCI, N=42), and PD with dementia (PDD,
N=26) had plasma collected at study entry. P-tau181, NfL,
and GFAP were measured in plasma using the Quanterix
Simoa HD-X platform. Multivariate regression was used to
determine the association of biomarker with Alzheimer Dis-
ease Neuropathological Change (ADNC) and to determine
biomarker association with PD cognitive state.
Results: AD and LBD groups had the highest p-tau181
and GFAP levels, and FTD had the highest NfL levels.
Amount of ADNC was directly associated with p-tau181 and
GFAP levels, but inversely associated with NfL level. In LBD
cases, amount of ADNC was directly associated with GFAP,
but not p-tau181 or NfL. In clinical cases, PDD cases had
higher levels of NfL and GFAP, but not p-tau181 compared
to PD-MCI and PD-NC.
Conclusions: Plasma measures of p-tau181 and GFAP
associate with AD co-pathology across neurodegenerative dis-
eases and NfL and GFAP are elevated in PDD cases. Future
studies will examine the association of blood biomarker level
with longitudinal change in cognitive function and motor
decline in PD cases.

Although signi ﬁcant advances have been made in our under-
standing of protein metabolism and protein homeostasis, we
fundamentally do not understand how or why α-synuclein,
tau, and TDP43 accumulate in age-associated neurodegenera-
tive diseases like Parkinson ’s disease, frontotemporal demen-
tia, and ALS, respectively. While it is known that neuronal
lysosomes can degrade these proteins; the mechanisms within
lysosomes by which these proteins are degraded are not
known. The major class of lysosomal proteases are the cathep-
sins, and these proteases recognize very speci ﬁc linear amino
acid sequences. Thus, mutations in α-synuclein, tau, and
TDP43 have the potential to impact protein homeostasis,
prolonging protein half-life by impairing lysosomal degrada-
tion. While prior studies have identi ﬁed several factors con-
tributing to protein clearance by the autophagy-lysosomal
pathway, the role of cathepsins as modulators of lysosomal
activity and their speci ﬁcity towards α-synuclein, tau, and
TDP43 degradation has not been thoroughly investigated. In
addition, most cathepsin cleavage sites within α-synuclein,
tau, and TDP43 are not known. Therefore, we embarked
upon cathepsin speci ﬁcity pro ﬁling studies for the determina-
tion of precise cleavage sites within these three proteins. As a
prelude, using in vitro protease cleavage assays, we identi ﬁed a
subset of cathepsins that were capable of cleaving full-length
α-synuclein, tau, and TDP43. Next, using mass spectrometry,
we mapped the precise cleavage sites for these cathepsins on
these proteins. We found that cathepsin cleavage sites were
relatively evenly distributed within α-synuclein, enriched
within the microtubule-binding repeat region of tau, and clus-
tered within the unstructured, C-terminal domain of TDP43.
Fascinatingly, many cathepsin cleavage sites coincided with
disease-associated mutations in each of these proteins. Neuro-
degenerative disease-causing mutations are mainly thought to
increase self-association and aggregation of these proteins.
However, based on the map that we generated, we hypothe-
sized that α-synuclein, tau, and TDP43 mutations may slow
lysosomal degradation by affecting cathepsin cleavage speci ﬁc-
ity. We tested our hypothesis with in vitro enzyme activity
assays and protein half-life experiments in differentiated neu-
ronal SH-SY5Y cells. In doing so, we con ﬁrmed our hypothe-
sis and demonstrated that many disease mutations alter
cathepsin speci ﬁcity in vitro and extend the half-life of α-syn-
uclein, TDP-43 and tau in SH-SY5Y cells. Overall, our work
contributes the ﬁrst comprehensive maps of cathepsin cleavage
sites in α-synuclein, tau, and TDP43. In addition, our ﬁnd-
ings suggest that disease mutations in α-synuclein, tau, and
TDP43 can predispose to neurodegeneration with aging by
slowing the clearance of these proteins over decades.

Cerebral Adrenoleukodystrophy (CALD) is a devastating neu-
rodegenerative disorder that occurs most often in childhood.
Hematopoietic Stem-Cell Transplantation is most effective
when initiated prior to the onset of neurological symptoms.
Early identi ﬁcation of CALD is a signi ﬁcant challenge; there
is no established genotype-phenotype relationship. The earli-
est pathologic changes in CALD are decreased overall lipid
content, increased myelin very long chain lipid fractions, and
decreased myelin water content in histologically normal appe-
aring white matter (Theda, Journal of Neurological Sciences,
1992). Conventional medical imaging and other laboratory
tests are largely insensitive to these early changes. However,
diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) is an advanced in vivo nonin-
vasive MRI technique used to assess local neuronal architec-
ture. We hypothesize that early pathogenesis of the CALD
phenotype manifests as microstructural changes to white mat-
ter quanti ﬁable on DTI and would differ between progressive
and non-progressive disease. Thirty-three DTI datasets
(24 examples of disease progression; 9 non-progressors) were
preprocessed using motion correction, eddy correction, den-
oising, bias correction, and registered to a standard pediatric
brain template. Subsequently, a region of interest analysis of
fractional anisotropy (FA) was performed along the corpus cal-
losum (CC) proximal to the lesion, at the midbody of the
CC, and distal end of the CC. Subjects served as internal con-
trols and normalization of the data was performed by assessing
the relative change (i.e. slope) in FA proximal to distal from
the lesion. A Mann-Whitney U test for the difference between
the FA slope of the disease progressor group vs non-progressor
group was signi ﬁcant (p=0.019). An ad hoc analysis of differ-
ence in FA slope performed in normal appearing white matter
only (by removing the region of interest proximal to the
lesion) was also signi ﬁcant (p=0.011). These data suggest that
DTI may serve as an early biomarker of disease pathogenesis
affecting the local white matter microstructure, speci ﬁcally
normal appearing white matter, prior to when other conven-
tional tests reveal the phenotype. Future studies will examine
this prospectively with the aim to identify those in need of
hematopoietic stem-cell transplant earlier in the disease course
when the treatment is most successful.

Background: Over the last two decades, there has been a
rapid expansion of neuroimaging techniques to measure
underlying brain proteins like tau. One of the most widely
used ligands to measure In Vivo tau in Alzheimer ’s disease
(AD) is [ 18F] ﬂourtaucipir (FTP). Limited information exists
on the relationship between antemortem FTP uptake and the
postmortem burden of tau. The purpose of this study is to
determine how well antemortem ligand update matches the
burden of postmortem tau.
Material and Methods: We compared regional ante-
mortem FTP uptake with postmortem determined tau bur-
den using a phospho-tau marker (AT8) in four cases. These
four cases were on the AD spectrum and were selected to rep-
resent mild, moderate, and high FTP uptake. Quantitative
FTP uptake was determined using standardized uptake value
ratios (SUVR) from ﬁve established regions of interest
(ROIs) and was compared with categorical and quantitative
measures of immunohistochemically labeled tau using digital
pathology.
Results: Overall, categorical and quantitative neuropatho-
logical methods showed a good parallel with antemortem
FTP uptake. However, in some ROIs, we found disparities
between FTP SUVRs and tau burden, particularly in cases
with no or low tau PET content in the hippocampal regions.
In this region, different intra and extracellular distribution
patterns of histopathological tau were found.
Conclusion: In general, our ﬁndings support the notion
that FTP uptake is representative of the underlying tau bur-
den in AD cases. There are, however, discrepancies between
ﬂourtaucipir binding and the amount of tau measured in his-
topathological tissues. These ﬁndings have consequences for
regional reports of FTP uptake in AD.

Altered nucleocytoplasmic transport is emerging as a promi-

including Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), Alzheimer ’s
disease (AD), Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD) and
Huntington’s disease (HD). The nuclear pore complex
(NPC) and interactions between its individual nucleoporin
components and nuclear transport receptors regulate

and gene expression. Speci ﬁc nucleoporin abnormalities have
been identi ﬁed in sporadic and familial forms of neurodegen-
