disrupted nucleocytoplasmic transport. Recently using multi-
modal imaging of induced pluripotent stem cell derived
neurons (iPSNs) derived from a large number of patients
with familial or sporadic ALS, we have demonstrated that
nuclear accumulation of the ESCRT-III protein CHMP7 is
sufﬁcient to initiate NPC injury thereby linking CHMP7
and the ESCRT-III nuclear surveillance pathway to an early
event in ALS pathogenesis. Importantly, these studies dem-
onstrated that the characteristic loss of nuclear TDP-43 func-

downstream of this CHMP7 mediated NPC injury cascade.

determine whether CHMP2B mutations also disrupt the
NPC and downstream TDP-43 function. Here, using iso-

digms, we demonstrate the emergence of a signi ﬁcant defect
in the nuclear membrane and nuclear pore complex as well as
aberrant TDP-43 function as evaluated by qRT-PCR for
TDP-43 targets. Additional studies are now underway to
comprehensively characterize this pathogenic cascade in the
context of CHMP2B mutations and determine is antisense
oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting CHMP7 can repair this
injury as we have previously demonstrated for familial and
sporadic ALS.

Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) neuropathology is largely driven by
two pathological proteins, tau, and -amyloid, both of which
induce aspects of neuronal hyperexcitability and are thought
to play a role in the high comorbidity between AD and epi-
lepsy. Central to the progression of AD is the spread of tau
along neuronal networks likely via neuronal activity. Our pre-

hyperexcitability promotes the propagation of pathological
tau. We utilized the Five times familial AD (5XFAD) model
and an established pentylenetetrazol (PTZ) kindling method
to induce seizures in these and WT littermates. To model
pathological tau spread seen in AD, a cohort of animals also
underwent intracerebral injection of human AD-derived tau
(AD-tau) into the hippocampus and overlying cortex prior to
seizure induction. Western blots were performed for the Cl-
transporters, K

examined by western blot for phospho-tau AT8 [Ser202;

(hippocampus) and distal (frontal cortex) to injection site to
determine the effects of seizures on tau propagation. PTZ-
kindling enhanced the dysregulation of Cl- transporters,
NKCC1 and KCC2 (p<0.05, n =12-19) and GluA2/GluA1
ratios (p<0.05, n=12-19) in 5XFAD mice, while 5XFAD mice
showed decreased GABA
ARα1 (p<0.05, n=12-19). 5XFAD
mice showed elevated AT8 in the hippocampus compared to

vated AT8 levels in the frontal cortex across genotypes

propagation in both WT and 5XFAD mice. Thus, drugs

cell sequencing on the cortex of an animal model of TSC,

neurons. We found that layer 5 pyramidal neurons showed
substantial down-regulation of synapse-associated genes.

Diffuse Optical Tomography Imaging and Audiovisual
Movie Stimuli: Optimizing New Tools for Human
Studies of Typical and Atypical Brain Development
Kalyan Tripathy, BA
1, Morgan Fogarty, BS 1, Alexa Svoboda,
BA1, Mariel Schroeder, MA 1, Sean Rafferty, BA 1, Zachary

Background: Studies of functional brain development have
been constrained by mainstream neuroimaging methods.
MRI scanners present logistical challenges for imaging young
children, while alternative modalities like functional near-
infrared spectroscopy have traditionally lacked image quality
due to sparse sampling. Furthermore, conventional tasks for
brain mapping in adults elicit low task engagement, high
head motion, and considerable participant attrition in chil-
dren. As a result, typical and atypical developmental trajecto-
ries of processes such as language acquisition remain
unmapped during critical periods over the ﬁrst years of life.
Objective: To develop and evaluate high-density diffuse opti-
cal tomography (HD-DOT) imaging, an animated movie
stimulus library, and associated data analysis pipelines as tools
for mapping brain function in awake young children.
Methods and Results: We used an HD-DOT system that
we built with design features geared towards enhancing both
child comfort and image quality. An array with 11mm grid
spacing of 128 laser sources and 125 detectors using a 2-pass
source encoding pattern yielded up to 2601 usable measure-
ments per wavelength with <50mm source-detector separa-
tion across posterior, lateral, and dorsal surfaces of the head,
spanning 7 orders of magnitude of optical power. A library of
children’s movie clips was characterized as a stimulus set for
brain mapping ﬁrst in a cohort of highly sampled adults. We
found that with HD-DOT we could map reproducible corti-
cal responses to movies and contained features such as speech
and faces using a variety of animated clips. Variation in the

reproducibility, construct validity, and orthogonality of fea-
ture regressor maps could be partially explained by properties
of both movie stimuli (such as feature modulation and
orthogonality) and imaging data (such as inter-run synchroni-
zation). A multivariate approach to feature regression miti-
gated confounding of regressor maps by feature covariance.
Finally, the new imaging system, selected movies, and opti-
mized speech regressor analysis pipeline were used to map
receptive language function during movie viewing with HD-
DOT in a group of awake children aged 23-80 months.
Conclusions: HD-DOT imaging during movie viewing
can be used to map reproducible cortical responses to movie
features such as naturalistic speech in awake young children.
These methods and ﬁndings lay valuable groundwork for
future studies of functional brain development and plasticity
in both typically developing children and children with vari-
ous neurological disorders.

Background: Beta-propeller protein-associated neu-
rodegeneration (BPAN) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder
characterized by iron accumulation in the brain with spec-
trum of neurodevelopmental and movement phenotypes. In
anticipation of future clinical trials and to inform clinical
care, there is an unmet need to capture the phenotypic diver-
sity of this rare disorder and better de ﬁne disease subtypes.
Methods: A total of 27 individuals with BPAN were
included in our natural history study, from which traditional
outcome measures were obtained in 18 subjects. Demo-
graphic and diagnostic information, along with acquisition of
basic developmental skills and overall neurologic severity were
extracted from the medical records. Functional outcome mea-
sures were administered at the time of the evaluation or
applied retrospectively at the last clinical encounter for
patients who were not able to travel for in person. Based on
age and functional level, the following assessments were
administered: Leiter-3, Gross Motor Function Measure
(GMFM)-66-Item Sets, Vineland-3, and Peabody-2.
Results: Overall, cognitive function was more impaired
compared to gross motor function. Onset of symptoms of
BPAN within the ﬁrst 6 months of life was associated with
decreased gain of ambulation and gain of spoken language
(ambulation: log-rank mantel-cox test p=0.0015; gain of ﬁrst
word: p=0.0015). There was no difference in age at seizure
onset by age at initial symptom onset (p=0.8823). During
prospective outcome measure collection, attention, and
behavior limited performance. Overall, gross motor and adap-
tive behavior assessments were better able to capture the
dynamic range of function across the BPAN population than
the ﬁne motor and non-verbal cognitive ones. Floor effects

K-S113. Abnormal Ensemble Activity Underlies
Pathologic Changes in Social Behavior in Shank3 Mice
Nicholas Alonzo Frost, MD,PhD
1, Kevin Donahue, B.S. 2,
Vikaas Sohal, MD,PhD 2. 1University of Utah, Salt Lake City,
UT, USA, 2University of California, San Francisco, San
Francisco, CA, USA.
Abnormal social interactions are a hallmark feature of autism
spectrum disorders and are recapitulated in preclinical models
of these heterogeneous disorders. Underlying this abnormal
behavior are changes in microcircuit structure and function,
however it is unknown how changes in excitation or inhibi-
tion might alter how information is encoded during behavior.
We sought to understand at a multineuron or ensemble level
how information pertinent to different behaviors such as
social interaction are encoded in the medial prefrontal cortex
(mPFC). We then investigated how this encoding might be
altered in a mouse model of autism lacking the postsynaptic
scaffolding molecule Shank3. We show that underlying social
interaction are dynamic changes in the activity of single neu-
rons and ensembles which are speci ﬁcally active during social
interaction, and distinct from those activated during anxiety-
related behaviors. Mice lacking Shank3 have hyperdynamic
network responses characterized by abnormally increased
neurons which are positively modulated and fewer neurons
which are negatively modulated compared to wildtype mice.
Finally, we show that these hyperdynamic network responses
result in loss of encoding by multineuron patterns during
behavior. We propose that this less ef ﬁcient and imprecise
computation likely results in de ﬁcits in information routing
across distributed circuits during behavior.

Language Network at 4-6 Years Predict Language
Outcome at 8-11 Years?

Introduction: Children born extremely preterm (EPT,
<28 weeks gestation) are at risk for developmental language
disorders, which can have life-long sequelae. Previously, we
reported increased language network functional connectivity
in EPT versus term-born children studied at 4-6 years of age.
Hyperconnectivity was positively correlated with change in
standardized language scores over time. The aim of the cur-
rent study is to follow these children to 8-11 years to assess
the degree to which early hyperconnectivity can predict later
language outcomes.
Methods: 107 children had neuroimaging at 4-6 years
(53 EPT, 54 term). Participants completed a stories-listening
task for both functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)

and magnetoencephalography (MEG). No group differences
in fMRI activation were observed, so we generated a joint
activation map. We then parcellated it into 200 random units
for language network de ﬁnition. Centroids of parcels with
>10% activation served as nodes for connectivity analyses in
MEG. Using a linearly constrained minimum variance
beamformer, we estimated activity at each node. Trial-wise
frequency representations (2-70Hz) were obtained through
Fourier analysis. Debiased weighted phase lag index was used
to quantify coupling between nodes. Connectivity spectra
were compared between groups using cluster-based permuta-
tion testing. Network Based Statistics (NBS) was used to
identify signi ﬁcant subnetworks underlying group differences.
For the 31 children who have followed up to date, we
assessed the relationship of subnetwork strength at 4-6 years
to Core Language scores from the Clinical Evaluation of Lan-
guage Fundamentals, 5
th Edition, at 8-11 years of age.
Results: At 4-6 years, 21 children had incomplete datasets
or incidental ﬁndings, leaving 86 children (39 EPT, 47 term)
for connectivity analyses. There were no signi ﬁcant group dif-
ferences in age, sex, race, ethnicity, or parental education and
income. EPT had signi ﬁcantly increased functional connec-
tivity at 22-31Hz (cluster-wise p<0.05 10,000 permutations)
at 4 to 6 years. NBS identi ﬁed a signi ﬁcant bitemporal net-
work underlying functional hyperconnectivity in the EPT
group. To date, 31 children (15 EPT, 16 term) have com-
pleted follow-up neurobehavioral assessments. For these chil-
dren, EPT have signi ﬁcantly lower language scores (92 versus
109, p>0.05). Network strength at 4-6 years did not signi ﬁ-
cantly predict language scores at 8-11 years for EPT
(rho=0.062, p>0.05).
Conclusions: In this preliminary report of the ﬁrst 31 of
86 children followed to 8 to 11 years, early hyperconnectivity
was not predictive of later language skills. However, data col-
lection is ongoing.

understanding why hypoxia causes lasting functional de ﬁcits

K-S116. Modulating miR-218 in Human Motor Neurons
Using Assembloids
Neal Amin, MD, PhD
1, Shravanti Kulkarni, BS 1, Sergiu
Pasca, MD 2. 1Stanford University, Palo Alto, CA, USA,
2Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA.
In motor neuron diseases, neuromuscular junctions are lost
and motor neurons degenerate resulting in progressive paraly-
sis and death. Post-transcriptional gene regulation by micro-
RNAs (miRNAs) is hypothesized to be disrupted in motor
neuron diseases due to inherited mutations in proteins
involved in miRNA processing, such as TDP43, FUS, and
SMN. Yet, the role of speci ﬁc miRNAs in human motor
neuron gene regulation and function is not well character-
ized. I previously discovered that a single miRNA, miR-218,
is uniquely enriched and abundantly expressed in mouse
motor neurons. Furthermore, mice lacking miR-218
exhibited de ﬁcits in neuromuscular synaptogenesis and die
due to muscle paralysis - phenotypes associated with motor
neuron disease. Subsequent studies have implicated miR-218
dysregulation as a mediator of motor neuron disease in
humans. However, the relationship between miR-218 ’s

repression of target gene pathways and motor neuron pheno-
types has not been resolved, and the biological role of miR-
218 has not been previously investigated in humans, leaving
an important translational gap in our knowledge of human
motor neuron gene regulation and function. In response to
this challenge, we in the Pasca Lab have recently developed a
three-dimensional, human induced pluripotent stem (hiPS)
cell-derived model of human motor neuron development and
function, called cortico-motor assembloids, by fusing
cortical, spinal, and skeletal muscle spheroids. I am now
using this novel system to model the impact of miR-218
upon motor neuron development, target pathways, and
human speci ﬁc-features of post-transcriptional gene regu-
lation. I have generated CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-
out hiPS cell lines that eliminate miR-218 expression
and am using a motor neuron ﬂuorescent reporter system
to investigate motor axon projections into muscle. I have
also developed miR-218 overexpression vectors to inves-
tigate the potentially bene ﬁcial effects of miR-218
replacement. I will identify the key biological pathways
affected by miR-218 using single cell and bulk trans-
criptomics. These experiments will provide insights into
the neurobiological role of human miR-218, a motor
neuron-selective gene regulator with direct implications
for our understanding of motor control and for RNA-
mediated regulatory pathwa ys that may underlie motor
neuron disease pathology.

Objective: In rodent models of hypoxia-ischemia (HI), males
show larger anatomic injuries, distinct motor de ﬁcits, and
worse cognition after HI relative to females. Microglia, the
brain’s resident macrophages, have sex-dependent develop-
mental trajectories and gene expression patterns. Lesion and
transplantation studies show microglia play different roles in
male and female brains after HI or stroke. We examined the
macrophage response 3 days after postnatal day 10 (P10) HI
in the hippocampus, a hypoxia-sensitive brain region critical
for learning.
Methods: We used a modi ﬁed Vannucci model with P10
right carotid artery ligation followed by hypoxia at FiO2 8%
for 45 minutes. At P13, mice were euthanized and lesion
size, if present, was measured. Brains were ﬁxed then sec-
tioned for immunohistochemistry with Iba1 antibody.
Images were analyzed in ImageJ for % area of Iba1+ pixels.
Results: Of 95 mice treated with HI, 12 (27%) male HI
mice and 7 (18%) female HI mice had a grossly visible pale
lesion on the surface of the brain. Of these mice, the lesion
size was signi ﬁcantly larger in males (mean 12.3mm2) than
females (mean 5.5mm2); this is consistent with the literature.

A 7-month-old boy born to consanguineous parents presented
to our clinic with developmental delay, nystagmus, central
hypotonia, extremity hypertonia and dysmorphic features.
MRI revealed delayed myelination and diffusion restriction
(DWI+/ADC-) in the dorsal brainstem, cerebellar peduncles,
and projection ﬁbers. Whole exome sequencing as trio revealed
a homozygous variant of uncertain signi ﬁcance (c.4T>G, p.-

sive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 13 (OMIM 616881),
inherited from heterozygous parents. Hikeshi mediates heat
shock-induced nuclear accumulation of heat shock proteins,
including HSP70, to protect cells from stress (Kose, Cell,
2012). In order to clarify the signi ﬁcance of the variant, func-
tional studies were performed. Fibroblasts from proband and
heterozygous mother were cultured in DMEM+20% FBS.
Western blot analysis of cell lysates revealed absent Hikeshi
protein from proband ﬁbroblasts contrasted with normal
expression in cells from mother. The cells plated on Poly-D-
Lysine coated coverslips were subjected to heat stress in culture
media +10mM HEPES (pH7.4) at 43
/C14C for 1hr. Alterna-
tively, prior to plating on coverslips, patient cells were trans-
fected with a plasmid to provide independent translation of
Hikeshi and mNeonGreen proteins. Following heat shock, the
cells were ﬁxed with 2% PFA and cold methanol and then
immunostained with HSP70 antibody alone, or dual labeled
with mNeonGreen antibody. After detection with ﬂuorescent
secondary antibodies, images were captured using confocal
microscopy. After heat stress, whereas the mother ’s cells dis-

band’s cells revealed failure of nuclear localization. These data

Masquerading as Spinocerebellar Ataxia
Mary Vo, MD, PharmD

Lakhani, M.Sc. 3, Chengbing Wang, Ph.D. 3, Margaret E. Ross,

2Center for Neurogenetics, Weill Cornell Medicine, New York,

Background: Adult onset Nieman Pick C (NPC) is a rare
progressive ataxia caused by lysosomal accumulation of
unesteriﬁed cholesterol resulting in severe disability and
death. The diagnosis of NPC can be challenging as clinical
features overlap with other more common hereditary ataxias.
This study pursued the molecular genetic basis of adult-onset
cerebellar ataxia manifesting in two siblings. A prior diagnosis
of spinocerebellar ataxia type 2 (SCA2) based on an ataxia
gene panel was questioned when the younger sibling devel-
oped similar symptoms but had discordant genetic results.
Methods: Neurologic examination, whole exome sequence
(WES), targeted sequence to establish genome phasing, cyto-
chemical and biochemical studies of ﬁbroblast cultures were
employed.
Results: The pedigree and neurological examinations
suggested a recessive or possibly dominant cerebellar ataxia.
WES showed the siblings were both compound heterozygous
for two rare variants in the NPC1 gene—one pathogenic,
stop gain at p.Arg934Ter (NM_000271.4), and a missense
change, p.Pro471Leu (NM_000271.4), of uncertain signi ﬁ-
cance. Filipin staining of ﬁbroblast cultures showed lysosomal
cholesterol accumulation and biochemical assay demonstrated
impaired cholesterol esteri ﬁcation.
Conclusions: The study established the correct molecular
diagnosis of biallelic, adult onset Niemann-Pick type C
(NPC) disease in a patient initially diagnosed with SCA.
Additionally, the p.Pro471Leu variant was identi ﬁed as likely
pathogenic. Inaccurate molecular diagnosis will deprive NPC
patients of treatment options. Investigation using WES is jus-
tiﬁed when a detected expansion size is in the borderline
range for pathogenicity.

S256. FXTAS Associated CGG Repeats Generate Toxic
Aggregation-Prone Chimeric Proteins Through
Translational Frameshifting
Peter K. Todd, MD, PhD , Shannon Wright, PhD. University
of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA.
CGG repeat expansions in the FMR1 5’UTR cause the neu-
rodegenerative disease Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syn-
drome. These repeats form stable RNA secondary structures
that support aberrant translation in the absence of an AUG
start codon (RAN translation), producing aggregate-prone
peptides that accumulate within intranuclear neuronal inclu-
sions and contribute to neurotoxicity. To assess the relative
contribution of RAN translation from different reading
frames to repeat triggered neurodegeneration, we expressed
AUG-initiated products from constructs containing either
100 CGG repeats or non-repetitive sequences using alternate
codons. Intriguingly, the most abundant RAN translation
product, FMRpolyG, was markedly less toxic when generated
from a construct lacking the CGG repeat. While exploring
the mechanism of this differential toxicity, we observed that
CGG repeats support a +1 translational frameshift within the
CGG repeat from the arginine to glycine reading frame.
Frameshifts occur within the repeat and are largely dependent
on RNA sequence and structural features. Chimeric R/G
peptides form structures distinct from those formed by either
pure arginine or glycine peptides, and these chimeras induce
toxicity in cultured rodent neurons. Together, this work sug-
gests that CGG repeats support translational frameshifting
and that chimeric RAN translated peptides may contribute to
pathogenesis in FXTAS.

supports disrupted transport of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial

Somatic mutations arise inexorably in the genomes of non-
neoplastic cells during neurodevelopment, and continue to
accumulate even in post-mitotic cells such as neurons. These
mutations leave distinctive patterns of mutation, ‘mutational
signatures’, in the genome that directly relate to their etiol-
ogy, thus enabling interpretation of cellular history. The full
scope of human neurological disease caused by somatic muta-

developmental somatic mutations has not been established.

approach which both increased the accuracy and throughput
of mutation detection and in addition distinguished muta-
tions (complementary in both strands of DNA) from DNA
damage (variants present in only one strand of DNA). In
human neurons ranging from gestational age 14 weeks to
infancy, both types of genetic variation showed patterns of
mutation that change with developmental age.

Objective: MECP2 Duplication syndrome (MDS) is a rare
disease trait caused by copy-number gains including MECP2.
The most prevalent clinical features include infantile hypoto-
nia, severe neurodevelopmental delay, frequent respiratory
infections, refractory epilepsy and functional gastrointestinal
problems. Each individual present with a unique duplication
size and gene content, which has been proposed to contribute
to the clinical variability. So far, studies have not shown a
consistent genotype-phenotype correlation. Our previous
study in a cohort of 30 MDS individuals showed that at
least 26% of the duplications are complex genomic
rearrangements (CGR), the majority in the form of inverted
triplications ﬂanked by duplications (DUP-TRP/INV-DUP)
with individuals carrying triplications spanning MECP2
being more severely affected. Thus, we hypothesized that
CGRs are more common than anticipated in MDS and that
lack of understanding hinders proper genotype-phenotype
correlations.
Methods: We applied custom-designed, high-resolution,
array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) targeting
the X and Y chromosomes, short-read whole-genome-
sequencing (WGS), and optical genome mapping techniques
to investigate the genomic structure at the Xq28 region in
111 unrelated individuals with MDS. Additionally, as a pilot
study, we performed western blot on lymphoblast cells from
11 subjects to investigate how the genomic structure impact
MeCP2 protein levels.
Results: The duplication size ranged from 278 kb to 16.5
Mb. The CGRs were found in 43%, the majority of which
involved triplications (19%; 1/3 of them included MECP2)
and terminal duplications (21%; 57% of those carried a
translocation). Western blot analysis showed that there is no
correlation between the size of duplication and MeCP2 pro-
tein levels. However, a clear correlation was found between
the duplication structure and MeCP2 protein level,
i.e. simple duplications have 1.4-1.8 fold increase, CGRs
have 2.8 to 3.6 fold increase and triplications have 4.2 to 4.7
fold increase. Genotype-phenotype correlation analysis
showed that triplications including MECP2 have the most
severe phenotype and are mostly lethal in the ﬁrst few years
of life, further con ﬁrming our gene dosage hypothesis. Indi-
viduals with CGR have relatively lower developmental quo-
tients, suggestive of more severe neurodevelopmental
impairment, compared to simple duplications.
Conclusion: Genomic complexity is highly prevalent in
MDS and this complexity likely underlies the phenotypic vari-
ability and severity. More importantly, each individual ’s
unique MeCP2 level resulted from genomic structure con ﬁrms
that personalized medication dosing is needed to optimize the
treatments that target MeCP2 RNA and MeCP2 protein.

Transcription Throughout the Brain After Subcutaneous

Administration of a PATrOL ™-Enabled Genome-
Targeting Compound in the R6/2 Huntington ’s Disease
Transgenic
Robert M. Friedlander, MD, MA . University of Pittsburgh,
Pittsburgh, PA, USA.
Objective: Deﬁne allele-selectivity, dose-response and
cortico-striatal distribution of mutant huntingtin knock-
down in the brains of R6/2 transgenic mice following subcu-
taneous delivery of a PATrOL ™-enabled compound that
inhibits transcription, as a prelude to nomination of a devel-
opment candidate.
Background: HD is a progressive autosomal dominant
neurodegenerative disease caused by a CAG repeat expansion
in exon 1 of the huntingtin ( HTT) gene resulting in a toxic
protein. Multiple tissues are affected throughout the body.
No therapies exist that alter the natural history of HD. The
PATrOL™ platform compounds can cross the BBB and
invade the duplex genome in a sequence-speci ﬁc manner to
inhibit transcription. NT-0100D directly engages the CAG
expansion to sterically block RNA polymerase.
Design/Methods:Four-week-old female R6/2 mice and wil-
dtype B6-CBA were treated subcutaneously with NT-0100D
b.i.w. x 8 weeks at 5, 10 and 21mg/kg. The Rotarod test was
performed throughout the study. At 12 weeks of age, mutant
and wildtype brain HTT mRNA levels were determined by
qRT-PCR. HTT aggregates were quantiﬁed across brain regions
by IHC and con ﬁrmed by western blotting. Neuro ﬁlament
light chain (NfL) levels were measured in serum at sacri
ﬁce.
Results: Subcutaneous delivery of NT-0100D inhibited
transcription of mutant HTT >75% across the brain in a
dose-dependent manner (p<0.001; all doses). No change in
wild type HTT was observed. Assessment of aggregates by
IHC showed a dose dependent decrease with the 21 mg/kg
dose showing a signi ﬁcant reduction. Immunoblot analysis
from brain showed a similar signi ﬁcant reduction. No reduc-
tion in wild type HTT was observed in livers or brains of
treated animals . NfL levels were unchanged with treatment.
Disease onset was delayed at the highest dose. Dose-
dependent trends in functional improvement were noted.
Conclusions: NT-0100D can be subcutaneously delivered,
cross the BBB, selectively reduce mutant huntingtin through-
out the brain without inducing neurotoxicity and promises a
patient-friendly whole-body solution for patients with HD.

Background: Patients with neuroin ﬂammatory and neuro-

assist in establishing diagnoses that guide treatment.

designed for in-depth investigation of undiagnosed neuro-

Background: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) is cau-
sed by mutations in a gene encoding a peroxisomal trans-
porter ( ABCD1) and is characterized by tissue accumulation
of saturated very long chain fatty acids. Most males with
ALD develop in ﬂammatory cerebral demyelination (cALD)
but the underlying mechanism remains unknown. Mechanis-
tic studies have been limited by the absence of a cALD phe-
notype in the Abcd1-null mouse.
Objective: We hypothesized that the NLRP3
inﬂammasome, which can be triggered by excessive saturated
fatty acids, contributes to cALD lesion pathogenesis. We
sought to measure NLRP3 activity in human brain tissue
from boys with cALD in murine brain tissue generated from
a novel mouse model of cALD.
Methods: We used immunohistochemistry and ELISA assays
to evaluate NLRP3 and effector cytokines in post-mortem brain
tissue (n=3 cALD; n=3 control) and cerebrospinal ﬂuid (cALD,
n=20; control, n=9). We generated a cALD phenotype in mice
by using MOG
35-55 peptide to induce experimental autoim-
mune encephalitis in male mice fed a 0.2% cuprizone diet
(n=10 Abcd1-null; n=10 wild type). We used MRI and immu-
nohistochemistry to evaluate myelin loss, gliosis, immune cell
inﬁltration, and NLRP3 inﬂammasome in mice.
Results: Both human and murine cALD lesions shared
common features of myelin phagocytosis, myelin loss, abun-
dant microglial activation, perivascular in ﬂammation, T-cell
and B cell in ﬁltration, and gliosis. Brain MRI of the cALD
mice revealed demyelination with associated gadolinium
enhancement of the medial corpus callosum in a pattern sim-
ilar to human cALD lesions. Compared to wild-type controls,
Abcd1-null mice had more severe in ﬂammation, demyelin-
ation, and IL-18 activation. IL-18 immunoreactivity co-
localized with macrophages/ microglia in the perivascular
region of both human and mouse brain tissue. Finally, IL-18
was signi ﬁcantly higher in cerebrospinal ﬂuid from boys with
cALD compared to pediatric controls.
Conclusions: Our data provide evidence of NLRP3
inﬂammasome activity in the cerebrospinal ﬂuid and brain
macrophages/microglia of cALD patients. Our novel mouse
model of cALD re ﬂects similar ﬁndings and suggests loss of
Abcd1 function predisposes to more severe cerebral in ﬂamma-
tion and NLRP3 pathway activation. These ﬁndings invite

further investigation into the role of NLRP3 and cell death
pathways in cALD lesions as possible new therapeutic targets
to inhibit disease progression.

Objective: We describe a rare case of Posterior Reversible
Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES) in a patient on Axitinib
for renal cell cancer.
Background: PRES is a rare neurological syndrome char-
acterized by headaches, seizures, visual changes, altered con-
sciousness and other focal neurological ﬁndings. It is known
to be caused by multiple triggers including chemotherapy
agents leading to vasogenic cerebral edema. We report a rare
case associated with Axitinib which is a tyrosine kinase inhib-
itor increasingly used in renal cancer.
Design/Methods: Case Report
Results: A 66 year old gentleman with history of metastatic
renal cancer on Axitinib for three months presented to the
emergency department by ambulance with altered mental status.
Patient’s wife found the patient with dysarthria and confusion
and he was last known normal few hours before presentation.
Patient was noted to be hypertensive on arrival and initial labs
revealed elevated lactic acid. Patient had a CT brain without
contrast which showed small area of hypoattenuation in the left
occipital lobe. The patient was admitted to the hospital for fur-
ther management. CT angiogram head and neck showed extra-
cranial left vertebral artery occlusion and fenestration in the
basilar artery. MRI brain with and without contrast was further
performed which showed extensive vasogenic edema in bilateral
occipital, posterior temporal and inferior parietal lobes. There
was faint contrast enhancement in the bilateral occipital lobes.
The patient had an electroencephalogram which showed mild
generalized slowing consistent with nonspeciﬁc encephalopathy.
The patient was initially started on Levetiracetam for seizure
prophylaxis which was later discontinued. Axitinib was immedi-
ately discontinued and a tapering dose of Dexamethasone were
started after discussion with his oncologist. His symptoms
resolved spontaneously and he was later discharged home in one
day after admission. He had a follow-up PET body scan which
did not show any intracranial metastasis.
Conclusions: Axitinib is commonly used in renal cancer
and advanced thyroid cancer. In patients who develop clinical
and radiological features of PRES, the drug should be imme-
diately discontinued. Early recognition of PRES is crucial
given its reversibility with appropriate management.

Background: CNS cryptococcosis is classically seen in immu-
nocompromised patients and is often rapid in onset. Sarcoid-
osis can manifest variably and signify immune dysfunction.
We present a case of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis in a
patient with a history of dormant sarcoidosis.
Case presentation: A6 6y e a r - o l dw o m a nb e g a ne x p e r i e n c -

ing headaches, generalized weakness, and ambulatory dysfunc-
tion over a period of months. Her medical history was notable
for distant ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and pulmonary sar-
coidosis. Her sarcoidosis was diagnosed at least one decade
prior, considered inactive, and the patient was not taking medi-
cations. She was HIV-negative and not otherwise immunocom-
promised. CT head showed calvarial lesions, and MRI
demonstrated communicating hydrocephalus and vertebral, iliac
and calvarial osteolytic lesions. Malignancy was ruled out
through biopsy of iliac and vertebral lesions and negative CSF
cytology. The patient continued to deteriorate, with worsening
headaches and ambulation, mild confusion, and weight loss.
Two years after initial symptoms, she was hospitalized with dis-
orientation, paucity of speech, and an inability to stand. MRI
brain revealed worsened hydrocephalus with transependymal
ﬂow, areas of cortical edema, and leptomeningeal and sub-
ependymal enhancement. Due to concern for neurosarcoidosis,
lumbar puncture was initially deferred due to risk of herniation
and the patient was given high-dose IV steroids. However, she
continued to worsen and ultimately required a ven-
triculoperitoneal shunt. CSF from the shunt revealed a positive
Cryptococcal antigen (1:4) and she was started on anti-fungal
therapy. Subsequent lumbar puncture yielded CSF with a
Cryptococcal antigen (1:512), lymphocytic pleocytosis, and an
elevated protein level. Unfortunately, the patient continued to
worsen and eventually passed away from presumed CNS
cryptococcosis.
Discussion: This case describes chronic cryptococcal
meningoencephalitis in the background of “inactive” sarcoido-
sis and absence of other immunocompromise. The “immune
paradox” of sarcoidosis refers to excessive in ﬂammation found
at granulomatous lesions coupled with development of periph-
eral T lymphocyte anergy. Given that immunity against cryp-
tococcal infection is primarily T lymphocyte-mediated, this
immune paradox may account for our patient ’s development
of disseminated cryptococcosis (evidenced by her numerous
bone lesions) and ultimately fatal CNS cryptococcosis.
Conclusion: Awareness of the association between sarcoid-
osis, active or inactive, and CNS cryptococcosis is essential
for early diagnosis and potentially adequate treatment of the
infection. CNS cryptococcosis may manifest subacutely or
chronically, rather than fulminantly. This should not deter
the clinician from considering the diagnosis, as prompt treat-
ment is imperative for improved outcomes.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) results
from active JC virus infection in the brain of people with com-
promised cellular immunity, most strongly linked to impaired
CD4+ T cell function. While the underlying pathophysiology
is not completely understood, B cell-depleting therapies are
also associated with an increased risk of PML. Indeed, epide-
miological studies, based primarily on inpatient hospital claims
data and voluntary adverse event reporting, suggest PML is
5 times more likely among patients with non-Hodgkin lym-
phoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia when rituximab is
used. The increasing number of available B cell depleting
agents, together with their wide clinical use, obligate improved
understanding of this risk.To explore risk factors associated
with development of PML in the setting of B cell depleting
therapy, we retrospectively reviewed clinical, radiological and
laboratory data collected under the NIH PML natural history
protocol. Among 86 patients enrolled on study, 31% had pre-
vious exposure to B cell depleting agents, 85% of which were
represented by rituximab. Eighteen % of exposures were as
monotherapy, but the majority of patients had been exposed
to more than 1 immunosuppressive drug. Hematological
malignancy was the most common underlying condition
(78%), with the remaining patients having either autoimmune
disease or primary immunodeﬁciency. Ninety-six % of patients
had associated CD4 lymphopenia, with 74% having CD4
counts below 200. Of interest, considering all patients in our
cohort with PML related to hematological malignancy, 21%
of patients had never been exposed to B cell depleting agents,
highlighting the contribution of the underlying condition
itself. JCV antibody index is a validated biomarker for assessing
risk of development of PML in patients with multiple sclerosis
treated with natalizumab. The widely ranging results of JCV
index available in a subset of our cohort, suggests this bio-
marker is not reliable for risk strati ﬁcation in the setting of B
cell depleting therapies.Overall, PML is a rare complication of
B cell depleting therapy. Treatment and disease-related cofac-
tors contribute greatly to this adverse outcome. Since there is
no speciﬁc biomarker for risk strati ﬁcation of PML in cases of
B cell-depleting therapy, heightened awareness, identi ﬁcation
of cofactors and prompt investigation of new onset neurologi-
cal symptoms are indicated. This work supported by NINDS.

S267. Bilateral Parsonage Turner Syndrome in a Patient
with Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis
Ezekiel Gonzalez-Fernandez, MD, PhD , Oriana Sanchez,
MD, Mark Anderson, MD. University of Mississippi Medical
Center, Jackson, MS, USA.
Background: Idiopathic brachial plexopathy or Parsonage
Turner Syndrome (PTS) is an uncommon neurologic syn-
drome that typically presents with sudden onset shoulder
pain, usually unilateral, followed by weakness, numbness,
and dysesthesias. Viral illnesses and recent immunizations are
the most common risk factors for PTS. Autoimmune diseases
such as Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) have also been
highly associated with PTS.
Case Report: We report a 56-year-old woman with a his-

tory of SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren ’s disease and Hashi-
moto Thyroiditis admitted to the hospital for management of
isolated thrombocytopenia and acute renal failure that then
developed bilateral upper extremity pain, weakness, and numb-
ness for one week after a complicated hospital course. The
patient was also recently diagnosed with hemophagocytic
lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) for which she was started on
etoposide, cyclosporine and dexamethasone. The patient was
admitted to the ICU for over three weeks and intubated. After
extubation she noticed generalized weakness in all four extrem-
ities. A few days later the weakness in her legs improved but
she remained unable to move both arms. Symptoms were
suspected to be secondary to steroid treatment and neurology
was consulted. Neurologic exam was relevant for decreased
tone of bilateral upper extremities and 1/5 strength. There was
sensory impairment to temperature and pinprick involving
both of her arms. No dermatomal distribution or sensory level
loss was noted and vibratory sensation remained intact. Her
legs were antigravity, without sensory impairment. EMG
showed severe bilateral brachial plexopathy, without evidence
of diffuse peripheral polyneuropathy or myopathy. MRI of the
cervical spine was unremarkable and bilateral MRI of the bra-
chial plexus was not diagnostic, however, there was diffuse
atrophy and homogeneous mild enhancement in the shoulder
musculature bilaterally concerning for PTS. The patient was
started on methylprednisolone 1,000 mg for three days
followed by a long steroid taper.
Conclusions: It is important to keep PTS on the differen-
tial diagnosis in patients with exams exhibiting lower motor
neuron signs involving upper extremities only. Bilateral pre-
sentations are rare, but if there is any suspicion pertinent
paraclinical tests should be ordered. Prior case reports have
described neurological manifestations of HLH, including
polyradiculoneuropathy which raises suspicion for HLH as a
possible trigger for PTS.

Immunomodulatory Mechanism in Treatment of

Introduction: Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) is a cytoplasmic
tyrosine kinase with essential role in B cell activation, prolif-
eration, and survival. BTK also expresses in myeloid cells and
control their function. Recently oral administration of BTK
inhibitor (BTKi) in phase 2 clinical trial showed reduction of
inﬂammation and number of gadoliniums enhancing lesions
in the brain MRI of MS patients. However, the underlying
BTK mechanism of action to subside neuroin ﬂammation is
not well understood. T cells play an important role in patho-
genesis of neuroin ﬂammation in Multiple Sclerosis (MS).
However, BTK has not shown to be expressed in human T
cells, its inhibition signi ﬁcantly subsides in ﬂammation in

indirectly control T cell pathogenicity in neuroin ﬂammation.
Here for the ﬁrst time, we show that Evobritinib (speci ﬁc
BTKi) suppresses in ﬂammatory cytokines and function of
human T cells.
Methods: Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs)
were obtained from healthy donors(n=8) and cultured in
XVIVO-15 in 96 well plate with concentration of 2x10 ^6
cell/ml. Cells were stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28 (1ug/ml)
in the presence and absence of Evobritinib (0.1 ug/ml) for
5 days. IFN-g, IL-17, IL-2, TNF-a, GMCSF, IL-5 and IL-
13 were measured in cell supernatant by Luminex assays. In
last 4 hour of culture, PMA, Ionomycin and golgi plug added
to cells followed by staining for CD4, CD8, IFN-g, IL-17
and GMCSF. Cell were analyzed by multicolor
ﬂowcytometry. To evaluate proliferation of T cells, similar
experiment was done using palmar blue in last 4 hours of cul-
ture and ﬂuorescent measurement in treated and control
groups.
Results: There was no change in cell viability following
Evobritinib treatment but treatment decreased proliferation
of cells signi ﬁcantly in dose dependent manner. Treatment
with BTK inhibitor signi ﬁcantly decreased IFN-g producing
CD4(Th1) and CD8(Tc1) T cells compared to control.
Cytokine measurement showed signi ﬁcant decrease in T cell
inﬂammatory cytokines including IFN-g, TNF-a, IL-2 and
GMCSF in the supernatant of evobritinib treated cells. No
change was noted in IL-17, IL-5 and IL-13 implying no
effect on Th2 and Th17 cytokine production.

modify in ﬂammatory pro ﬁle and function of both CD4 and
CD8 T cells by suppression of Th1 and Tc1 cells in human
PBMCs. Current ﬁndings demonstrate a novel immunomod-

neuroinﬂammation.
S269. Case of Concomitant CNS Coccidioidomycosis and
Cytomegalovirus Infection
Paunel Agyei, MD , Rodrigo Hasbun, MD, MPH, Rajesh
Gupta, MD. University of Texas Health Science Center at
Houston, Houston, TX, USA.
Background: Coccidioidomycosis is an infection caused by
dimorphic fungal species, Coccidioides immitis and posadasii
which are usually found in the southwestern United States,
northern Mexico, and Central and South America. Central
nervous system (CNS) coccidioidomycosis is rare and usually
presents with a basilar meningitis. Additional complications
include hydrocephalus, cerebral vasculitis, and cerebral
infarcts. We present a case of a patient with a nearly missed
diagnosis of coccidioidomycosis due to concomitant cytomeg-
alovirus (CMV) infection and discordance of ventricular and
lumbar cerebral spinal ﬂuid (CSF) results.
Case Presentation: The patient was a 36-year-old man
who presented to the hospital after reporting a one-week his-
tory of headaches, decreased appetite, and chills. His initial
neurological exam did not reveal any focal de ﬁcits. Human
immunodeﬁciency virus was not detected. Magnetic reso-
nance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast showed
markedly thickened leptomeningeal enhancement in the basal
cisterns with enlargement of the ventricular system. The
patient had worsening of his mental status and a lumbar
drain was placed due to hydrocephalus. Due to continued
decline in cognition, the lumbar drain was replaced with an
external ventricular drain (EVD). Initial CSF results from the
lumbar drain revealed hypoglycorrhachia, neutrophilic
pleocytosis, and an elevated protein level. He was started on

empiric coverage for tuberculosis meningitis. The mycobacte-
rium tuberculosis polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in the
CSF resulted as negative and antibiotics were discontinued.
Subsequently, CSF CMV PCR resulted as positive, and he
was started on ganciclovir. His CSF fungal cultures, CSF
cryptococcal antigen and histoplasma urine antigen were neg-
ative. Several repeat CSF pro ﬁles from the EVD showed
improvement in pleocytosis, hypoglycorrhachia and protein
levels. He completed a 14-day course of ganciclovir and was
discharged with a diagnosis of CMV encephalitis. Following
discharge from the hospital, CSF coccidioides immunoglobin
G was found to be positive. He developed worsening head-
aches, neck pain, photophobia, and cognitive impairment
and was readmitted to the hospital. He was started on
amphotericin B for treatment of CNS coccidioidomycosis
and later transitioned to voriconazole. MRI brain obtained
2 weeks later showed improvement in previously seen basal
cistern enhancement.
Conclusion: Although rare, CNS coccidioidomycosis can
have a high mortality rate if left untreated. Therefore, it is
essential to consider this diagnosis and be aware of the most
appropriate diagnostic testing, associated complications and
to provide early treatment to patients.

core features de ﬁne the diagnosis: subacute neurological com-
plaints (most commonly ataxia, dysarthria, and diplopia),
numerous enhancing lesions bilaterally “peppering” 2 of the

vent relapse.

history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia and hyper-
tension presented with progressive right-sided weakness over
the past four months. One day prior to arrival, the patient
developed slurred speech and was unable to raise his right arm
or right leg due to weakness. CT angiogram of head and neck
showed chronic left vertebral artery occlusion with no acute

S271. CNS Tuberculoma Mimicking Malignancy in a
Patient from Africa
Shaweta Khosa, M.B.B.S.
1, Glenn E. Mathisen, M.D. 1,
Gurveer Singh Khosa, M.B.B.S. 2, Shri Kant Mishra, M.D. 1.
1Olive View-UCLA Medical Center, Sylmar, CA, USA, 2Indira
Gandhi Medical College and Hospital, Shimla, India.
Objective: To describe a diagnostically challenging case of
intracranial tuberculoma.
Background: CNS tuberculosis is a rare manifestation of
Mycobacterium tuberculosis and can present as tuberculous
meningitis, intracranial tuberculoma, and tuberculous abscess.
Design/Methods: We present a 38-year-old male with no
past medical history who presented with headache, nausea
and vomiting for 1 week. Patient moved to USA from
Uganda three years ago. He denied any prior history of TB
or sick contacts.
Results: On examination, no motor or neurological de ﬁ-
cits were noted. Ct scan of the head showed a large mass in
the left basal ganglia measuring 4.5 x 4.5 x 5.5 cm. MRI of
the brain showed mildly irregular, lobulated mass in left basal
ganglia, with predominantly solid enhancement and extensive
vasogenic edema. CT chest showed nonspeci ﬁc pulmonary
micronodule. MRI spectroscopy showed ﬁndings suggestive
of mass with increased cellularity such as lymphoma. Lumbar
puncture showed normal CSF studies except for elevated pro-
tein. Meningoencephalitis and infectious work up were
unremarkable. The patient underwent brain biopsy with
pathology consistent with lymphoid tissue. Patient was dis-
charged on dexamethasone taper and levetiracetam. Repeat
brain biopsy at the outside hospital showing ﬂorid
lymphohistiocytic in ﬂammation with granulomas with
multinucleated giant cells, necrosis, and gliosis. Patient was
readmitted at our facility for further evaluation and ongoing
confusion. Due to inconclusive specimens from the two pre-
vious biopsies patient underwent a third brain biopsy which
again showed lymphohistiocytic in ﬂammation with back-

ground gliosis. Although sputum AFB smear and cultures
were negative; given high concern for the possibility of TB,
he was started on empiric TB treatment. Finally, a diagnosis
of intracranial tuberculoma was con ﬁrmed after AFB cultures
from abscess resulted positive after 1 month. The patient was
discharged home on antitubercular treatment and is currently
doing well on follow-up.
Conclusion: CNS tuberculomas are not uncommon in TB-
endemic regions and are usually associated with concomitant
meningitis. Our patient lacked ﬁndings of meningitis and pres-
ented with a radiographic appearance that initially suggested a
CNS malignancy. AFB smears on tissue were negative; how-
ever, a de ﬁnitive diagnosis of CNS tuberculoma was made fol-
lowing a “third” biopsy when tissue was sent for AFB culture.
This case emphasizes the capacity of CNS tuberculosis to
mimic CNS malignancy. While such cases are uncommon in
the United States, tuberculosis should be considered in
unexplained CNS mass lesions and aggressive measures should
be taken to obtain tissue for AFB smear, culture and PCR.

Background: Neurologic abnormalities in people with HIV
(PWH) on suppressive antiretroviral therapy are subtle and
difﬁcult to measure using only clinical methods. Objective
measurements including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
brain volumes are increasingly important for identifying pat-
terns of brain abnormalities in this population.

Objectives: 1) Identify if PWH have atypical brain struc-
ture patterns, demonstrative of potential disease states. 2) Use
clustering to identify patterns in MRI brain degeneration
between PWH and controls.
Hypothesis: PWH have lower subcortical gray matter
(SGM) volume compared to controls. This region will assist
in identifying patterns of neurodegeneration among PWH.
Methods: PWH and HIV-negative controls enrolled
through the National Institutes of Health and Department of
Defense in a natural history study assessing neurologic out-
comes in PWH. All subjects underwent MRI, and brain vol-
umes were derived via FreeSurfer. To identify subjects with
atypical brain volumes, percentile values across brain regions
were calculated using a computational framework developed
by Potvin et al.
1 This framework normalized brain volumes
adjusted for age, sex, estimated intracranial volume, and MRI
scanner. Two-sample t-tests evaluated the effect of HIV on
the 19 brain structure variables, and Box-Cox transformation
was applied to non-normal variables. Since brain volume vari-
ables are correlated, principal component analysis (PCA) with
varimax rotation was performed for dimensional reduction to
identify clusters of MRI phenotypes. Then, a two-sample t-
test was performed to evaluate the difference between PWH
and controls for each retained principal component (PC).
Results: SGM volume percentile, the primary variable,
was signi ﬁcantly reduced in PWH compared to controls
(55
th vs. 46 th percentile; p=0.022). Exploratory analyses rev-
ealed similar relationships in the right thalamus (p=0.017),
left thalamus (p=0.031), right caudate (p=0.042), and left
caudate (p=0.033). The retained PCs accounted for 76.8%
of the total variance. For each rotated PC, the structure vari-
ables having strong correlation with the PC, the percent of
total variance accounted for, and the t-test p-value are: PC1)
sum of ventricles; bilateral lateral, third, and fourth ventricles
(18.7%, p=0.382); PC2) SGM, bilateral thalamus, brainstem
(14.2%, p=0.029); PC3) bilateral putamen and accumbens
(13.4%, p=0.650); PC4) bilateral hippocampus (11.1%,
p=0.228); PC5) bilateral caudate (11.0%, p=0.088); and
PC6) bilateral inferior lateral ventricles (8.5%, p=0.476).
Conclusions: Our results show unique degenerative MRI
phenotypes within PWH, primarily with SGM volume loss,
and allow for more speci ﬁc characterization of brain atrophy
patterns in PWH.

Microglia mediated neuroimmune responses are thought to
contribute to Alzheimer Disease (AD). Many microglial sub-
types have been described experimentally in vitro and in vivo.
In addition, disease models demonstrate numerous in ﬂamma-
tory stimuli that could potentially activate microglia during AD
pathogenesis. Despite the improved understanding of microglia
biology, it has been challenging to corroborate which of these
many processes occur in the context of human AD brain, in
part due to limitations in molecularly phenotyping microglia
with sufﬁcient resolution. To capture the heterogeneity of the
microglial response in age and AD, we developed a method to
enrich the numbers of myeloid nuclei that can be sequenced
from frozen autopsy brain samples yielding ~5,000 myeloid
nuclei per sample. For this study we performed single nuclei
RNAseq and clustering analysis on over 127,000 myeloid
nuclei isolated from 12 AD and 10 age-matched control frozen
dorsolateral prefrontal cortex autopsy tissue samples. In addi-
tion to previously described microglia phenotypes, we identiﬁed
novel subpopulations that have not yet been reported in human
brain tissue studies but would be predicted by disease model
and in vitro experiments. Three subpopulations exhibited gene
expression patterns suggesting predominant role in endo-
lysosomal activity, each with a distinct metabolic and in ﬂam-
matory signature. One endolysosomal subpopulation was more
abundant in AD subjects than controls and was uniquely
enriched for genes involved in nucleic acid detection,
inﬂammasome activation and interferon signaling. Further, this
inﬂammatory endolysosomal cluster was enriched for differen-
tial expression of known AD risk genes. Applying the
pySCENIC method to analyze gene regulatory networks rev-
ealed unique transcription factor driven expression modules
associated with speci ﬁc myeloid clusters highlighting upstream
transcriptional regulators of microglia phenotypes. IRF3 and
IRF7 regulated modules were speciﬁc to the AD enriched clus-
ter. Our study is the ﬁrst to demonstrate the expansion of a
novel microglia transcriptional subtype with expression of genes
involved in endolysosomal activity and interferon pathway
induction in human brain, supporting a relationship between
these two pathways in AD pathogenesis. These results highlight
the heterogenous nature of the microglia response to AD
pathology and inform efforts to target speci ﬁc subtypes of
microglia in the development of novel AD therapies.
S277. Encephalitis of Unknown Etiology: Elusive
Diagnosis in the Case of a Patient with Q Fever and
Multiple Animal Exposures
Shaweta Khosa, M.B.B.S.
1, Katherine Lyman, M.D. 2, Gurveer
Khosa, M.B.B.S. 3, Shri Kant Mishra, M.D. 1. 1Olive View-

Medical Center, Bakers ﬁeld, CA, USA, 3Indira Gandhi
Medical College and Hospital, Shimla, India.
Objective: To contribute to better understanding the phe-
nomenon of encephalitis of unknown etiology, by describing
such a case in a patient with history notable for multiple ani-
mal exposures and zoonotic infections.
Background: Encephalitis demands a multisystemic
workup encompassing possible infectious, neoplastic, par-
aneoplastic, and primary in ﬂammatory etiologies. Even with
comprehensive workup, the cause of encephalitis remains

unknown in up to 40-70% of cases.
Design/Methods: A patient hospitalized at Olive View-
UCLA Medical Center in Sylmar, California was selected for
case study based on unique features of his encephalitis presenta-
tion. The patient was followed throughout his hospitalization
as well as outpatient follow-up visits over a three-month period.
Results: A 55-year-old man with no signi ﬁcant past medical
history was found unresponsive, agitated, and gasping for air fol-
lowing one day of malaise and muscle aches. The patient had a
hobby of caring for feral cats, possums, skunks, and racoons,
and had sustained a recent cat bite. He was hospitalized for
altered mental status and respiratory failure requiring intubation.
Diagnostic work up was largely unremarkable including history,
blood test, CSF analysis, neurological imaging, and EEG. While
intubated, the patient displaye d altered sensorium, agitation,
photosensitivity, and signs of upper motor neuron weakness.
Hospital course was complicated by fever and rapidly progres-
sive renal failure requiring hemodialysis. The renal failure was
thought to be due to rhabdomyolysis (peak CK 6,666U/L).
Patient was successfully extubated on day 11 of hospitalization.
His mental status improved with no residual motor or neurolog-
ical de ﬁcits. During hospitalization, the patient underwent a
broad infectious, rheumatological, autoimmune, and neoplastic
workup, which was largely negative, except for a Q fever phase
2 serum IgG positive (1:64) with IgM negative. Q fever PCR
sent to CDC also resulted back positive. A repeat CSF was also
signiﬁcant for a white blood cell count of 10 (70% lympho-
cytes) with elevated glucose.
Conclusion: The patient ’s most notable diagnostic ﬁnding
was his positive Q fever IgG, which has been known to cause
heterogeneous neurological symptoms. This presentation may
constitute an example of severe neurological consequences
resulting from Q fever infection and works toward a fuller
understanding of the neurologic effects of Q fever. This case
also provides perspective on the potential role of zoonotic
infections in patients presenting with encephalitis following
domestic animal exposures.

SARS-CoV-2 infection is thought to have profound, sometimes
long-term, effects in the brain even in cases of mild infections.
Affected participants in clinical studies have reported cognitive
decline, fatigue, and in-vivo brain magnetic resonance
(MR) imaging have shown atrophy, especially in the grey mat-
ter (GM). There have been several reports of thrombosis and
inﬂammatory inﬁltrates in the brain in histopathological stud-
ies, which have not been widely reported in-vivo. Ex-vivo MR
microscopy (MRM) and corresponding histology offers a
unique opportunity to better understand more subtle MRI sig-
nal intensity changes associated with vascular leakage and
inﬂammation. Autopsy brain tissues from 16 patients who died
after SARS-CoV-2 infection were studied. Formalin-ﬁxed tissue
blocks were scanned on a 11.7T MRI at 100-micron isotropic
resolution or higher. Olfactory bulbs were imaged at 25-micron
isotropic resolution. Select regions were examined by immuno-
histochemistry (IHC) for vascular integrity ( ﬁbrinogen), and
thrombosis (CD61). MRM revealed vascular pathology pre-
dominantly in the brainstem. It showed multifocal areas of high
signal intensity in the walls of the microvessels which could be
regions of microthrombi within the lumen of the vasculature.
Additionally, some microvessels showed hypointense signals on
the abluminal side of the vessels indicating microhemorrhages.
Sections made through these regions were immunostained and
showed leakage of serum proteins in perivascular regions with
platelet aggregates in the lumen sometimes occluding the small
blood vessels and occasional red blood cells in the parenchyma.
Collagen IV staining showed thinned out basal lamina around
many compromised blood vessels. Platelet aggregates identi ﬁed
by CD61 staining were extensively found in the microvessels
regardless of ﬁbrinogen leakage in all brain regions. Platelet
aggregates completely occluded small blood vessels, adhered to
the endothelial cells, or were present in the luminal space.
There was perivascular in ﬂammation in these areas of linear
hyperintensities on MRM. Brainstem nuclei were localized by
MRM and immunostaining showed microglial cell activation
and neuronophagia in these regions. The presence of multiple
vascular pathologies in the same region in the same individual
indicates the complexity of the vascular pathology that can only
be revealed by high resolution microscopy. The extensive
brainstem pathology may explain some of the symptoms in
patients with Long-COVID.
S279. Fusobacterium Necrophorum as a Rare Case of
Fulminant Meningoencephalitis in Context of COVID-19
Co-Infection
Claire Delpirou Nouh, MD , Mohammed F. Hussein, MD,
Robert Hamilton, MD. The University of Oklahoma Health
Science Center, Oklahoma City, OK, USA.
Introduction: Documented bacterial co-infection is uncom-
mon in SARS-CoV-2 infection. We present a case of fulmi-
nant Fusobacterium necrophorum meningoencephalitis in the
context of concomitant COVID-19 infection.
Background: Fusobacterium necrophorum is an anaerobic
Gram-negative rod from the Bacteroidaceae family involved in
rhinopharyngeal and otitic infections. Meningitis from this
bacterium is rare, usually follows an upper respiratory tract
infection (URI), and has high morbidity and mortality rates.

Bacterial meningitis from nasopharyngeal organism co-
infection in COVID-19 has been reported but also remains
uncommon. We present a case of fulminant bacterial menin-
goencephalitis following both recent in ﬂuenza A and active
concomitant COVID-19 co-infections. URI from these viruses
is hypothesized to have led to contiguous bacterial spread.
Methods: Case report
Results: 17-year-old previously healthy boy with full vacci-
nation against COVID-19 including a booster and with
recent mild in ﬂuenza A URI two weeks preadmission with
complete clinical recovery was admitted for acute meningoen-
cephalitis manifested by fever, 4 days of headache, and rap-
idly progressive confusion. At time of admission he tested
negative for in ﬂuenza A and B, but nasal COVID-19 PCR
was positive with serum leukocytosis (42 K/mm
3). Stat com-
puted tomography (CT) of the head revealed extensive
opaciﬁcation of both sphenoid sinuses and ethmoid cells but
otherwise unremarkable brain. Cerebral spinal ﬂuid (CSF)
was turbid with neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis
(36 K/mm
3), hypoglycorrhachia (1 mg/dL), and elevated pro-
tein (> 2000 mg/dL). CSF showed Gram-negative rods and
culture grew Fusobacterium necrophorum . Blood cultures,
HIV serology, and urinalysis were negative. CT neck did not
show abscesses or suppurative lymphadenopathy. MRI brain
demonstrated multiple areas of parenchymal restricted diffu-
sion and leptomeningeal enhancement consistent with infec-
tious meningoencephalitis, as well as a developing empyema
along the right temporal lobe and right cerebellum. Trans-
thoracic echocardiogram was negative for infectious endocar-
ditis. Patient initially received empiric dexamethasone,
ceftriaxone, and vancomycin later adjusted by culture results
to meropenem, metronidazole, and penicillin
G. Neurological status worsened on hospital day two with
symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) and early
signs of herniation requiring intubation. He received aggres-
sive ICP management with hyperosmolar therapy and exter-
nal ventricular drain placement. Unfortunately, our patient
developed malignant refractory cerebral edema with subse-
quent mortality.
Conclusion: Fusobacterium necrophorum is a rare but often
fatal cause of bacterial meningitis, frequently complicating a
viral upper respiratory illness. COVID-19 infection may
increase the risk of contiguous spread. Prompt identi ﬁcation
and appropriate treatment is key to improving outcome.

of Bacterial Meningitis After Neurosurgery

Objective: Nosocomial bacterial meningitis is one of the
major complications after neurosurgery. We performed
nanopore 16S amplicon sequencing from cerebrospinal ﬂuid
(CSF) to evaluate bacterial meningitis in patients who under-
went neurosurgery.
Methods: Among the patients who visited the neurosur-
gery department of Seoul National University Hospital
between July 2017 and June 2020, those with clinically
suspected bacterial meningitis were included. 16S rDNA
PCR was performed from the CSF, and nanopore sequencing
was performed for up to 3 h. The reads were aligned to the
BLAST database. In each case, the culture and the 16S rRNA
gene amplicon analysis were simultaneously performed and
compared with each other, and we retrospectively reviewed
the medical records. Genuine infection was determined by
the identical results between conventional culture study and
the sequencing, or clinically determined in cases with incon-

sistent results between the two methods.
Results: Of the 285 samples obtained from 178 patients
who had 16S rDNA PCR, 41 samples (14.4%) were diag-
nosed with genuine infection. A total of 56.1% (23/41) of
the samples with genuine infection showed a false-negative
culture test. In particular, 16S amplicon sequencing was use-
ful in evaluating patients at the initial tests who had infection
with intraventricular hemorrhage (Culture false-negative
rate = 100%), subarachnoid hemorrhage (Culture false-
negative rate = 77.8%), and systemic cancer (Culture false-
negative rate = 100%), which are risk factors for central fever.
Moreover, 16S amplicon sequencing could suggest the possi-
bility of persistent bacterial meningitis in empirical
antibiotic use.
Conclusion: CSF nanopore 16S sequencing was more
effective than conventional CSF culture studies in postopera-
tive bacterial meningitis and may contribute to evidence-
based decisions for antibiotic maintenance and
discontinuation.

overt neurologic symptoms, over one-third of patients suffer
impairments in working memory and other cognitive
domains compared to age-matched controls. Despite these
devastating complications, little is known about the effects of
SCD within the brain at the cellular level. In this study, we
assessed changes in microglia, astrocytes, and neurons within
the hippocampus of 6-8-month-old male and female homo-
zygous SCD mice (HbSS) compared to heterozygous (HbAS)
and wild-type (HbAA) animals using the Townes model in
which human sickle or adult beta globin gene is inserted into
the murine beta globin gene (n=4-5 per group). We hypothe-
sized that increased microglia (Iba-1) and astrocytes (GFAP)
in the mouse hippocampus would colocalize with areas of

S284. Neurovascular Injury with Complement Activation
and Inﬂammation in COVID-19
Myoung-Hwa Lee, PhD . NIH/NINDS, Bethesda, MD, USA.
Objective: The objective of this study was to characterize the
neuropathological changes in patients with COVID-19 and
determine the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms.
Methods: Nine post-mortem cases (7 males and
2 females; age 24-73 years) were studied. Patients had died
during the ﬁrst wave of the pandemic (March to July
2020). Comorbidities included diabetes, hypertension, and
substance use disorder. Five patients died suddenly of infec-
tion, while the remaining patients died within days to weeks
after onset of symptoms. SARS-CoV-2 infection in patients
was con ﬁrmed on antemortem or postmortem testing.
Immunohistochemical analysis was performed on autopsied
brain tissues including the olfactory bulb, frontal and tem-
poral lobes, basal ganglia, hi ppocampus, thalamus, mid-
brain, pons, medulla oblongata, and cerebellum. Descriptive
analysis of the pathological changes and quantitative ana-
lyses of the in ﬁltrates and vascular changes were performed.
Gene expression pro ﬁles in region of interests (ROIs) of the
brainstem were further investigated using the NanoString
GeoMX™ DSP platform.
Results: Although SARS-CoV-2 could not be detected in
the brain by immunostaining, PCR analysis and RNA scope,
microvascular damage and thrombus formation were present
in the brains of all patients. Immunostaining for ﬁbrinogen
and IgM was found in the brain parenchyma and CD61+
platelet aggregates were found adherent to the endothelial
cells along vascular lumina. This was accompanied by exten-
sive endothelial cell activation identi ﬁed by PECAM-1 and
von Willebrand factor (vWF). Immune complexes with acti-
vation of the classical complement pathway were found on
the endothelial cells. Immunostaining for complement com-
ponents, 1q and 4d (C1q, C4d), IgG and IgM on vascular
endothelial cells shows minimal staining in the brains of non-

COVID-19 patients, but strong staining in COVID-19
brains. Perivascular in ﬁltrates composed mainly of macro-
phages and some CD8+ T cells were found extensively.
CD4+ T cells and CD20+ B cells were rare. Astrogliosis was
also prominent in the perivascular regions. Microglial nodules
were predominantly present in the hindbrain in association
with focal neuronal loss and neuronophagia. Spatial trans-
criptomics indicated that genes involved in vascular, meta-
bolic, and immune signatures were dysregulated in the
brainstem of COVID-19 patients. Correlation analysis rev-
ealed a positive relationship between microvascular injury
and inﬂammatory in ﬁltrates.
Interpretation: Antibody mediated cytotoxicity directed
against the endothelial cells is a key event leading to disrup-
tion of the blood-brain barrier, microthrombosis, perivascular
inﬂammation, and neuronal injury. This study suggests that
therapeutic approaches targeting the development of immune
complexes should be considered.

S287. Post-COVID-19 Transverse Myelitis with
Progressive Neurologic Decline: Why Do Some Patients
Fare Worse Than Others?

Objective: To report a case of post-COVID-19 transverse
myelitis with progressive neurologic decline despite
treatment.
Background: Transverse myelitis as a neurologic complica-
tion of COVID-19 infection has been increasingly reported
in literature. Most of these cases have shown good recovery
with IV steroids with/without IVIG or plasmapheresis. The
pathophysiology of myelitis remains uncertain, but both
direct viral infection and secondary immunologic response
have been postulated as possible theories. Case Summary:

COVID-19 pneumonia and recovered without treatment.
Two week later, she started having distal left upper extremity
spastic weakness that progressed over the next three months
to involve the bilateral lower extremities in addition to uri-
nary retention. Her exam revealed decreased power (paresis)
in her bilateral lower and distal left upper extremities with
hypertonia and hyperre ﬂexia. Her MRI thoracic spine ruled
out a compressive lesion and showed small syrinx at the level
of T6-T8. The images were signi ﬁcantly motion-degraded,
and it was dif ﬁcult to ascertain the presence or absence of an
intrinsic cord signal. CSF analysis revealed elevated WBCs
(50/cumm) with a lymphocytic predominance, mildly elevated
protein (61 mg/dl), oligoclonal bands (8) unique to CSF and
elevated IgG (7.6 mg/dl). The MRI Brain did not show any
acute ﬁndings. The infectious/autoimmune/paraneoplastic
panels, anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies, and anti-MOG antibodies
were negative. Despite treatment with two courses of IV pulse

extensive patchy T2 hyperintense signal along the length of

continued to show lymphocytic pleocytosis.

19 myelitis improve with immune-modulatory treatment,
our patient continued to worsen. A better understanding of
the underlying pathophysiologic mechanism of myelitis is
necessary to guide treatment in such cases.

Background: Early in the Covid pandemic, reports started to

emerge of patients with lingering symptoms following recov-
ery from acute infection, so called “Long Covid ” (Miners,
2020; Nath, 2020; Troyer, 2020). Despite the high preva-
lence of neurological symptoms like brain fog and memory
dysfunction (Davis, 2020), most research has relied on sur-
veys or clinical tools typically used to assess declarative mem-
ory (Alemanno, 2021; Méndez 2021; Taquet, 2021). To our
knowledge, no studies have examined Long Covid patients ’
ability to learn and consolidate a procedural motor skill.
Methods: We addressed this question in a group of
108 patients with Long Covid and 108 age- and sex-matched
controls. Participants performed a well-characterized motor
sequence typing task alternating 10-second practice with
10-second rest for 36 trials over 12 minutes (Bönstrup,
2020; Bönstrup, 2019; Buch, 2021). The following day, per-
formance was tested to evaluate overnight consolidation. The
behavioral endpoint measure was correct sequence typing
speed (Buch, 2021) . Data were ﬁtted to a 3-parameter
model (initial performance, maximum performance, learning
rate). Simple reaction times (RT) were measured twice: at the
beginning and the end of the experimental session.
Results: On average, patients had experienced 50 weeks of
symptoms at time of testing. Long Covid patients’ typing speed
was slower than healthy controls at the beginning of the session
(p=0.00075). While learning ra t e sw e r ec o m p a r a b l ea c r o s s
groups (p=0.142), at the end of training Long Covid patients
had not reached the same performance level as controls
(p=0.046). Overnight consolidation was not statistically different
between groups (p=0.58). Fourteen patients were hospitalized
during their acute infection; they did not perform differently to
patients who were not hospitalized. There were no sex differ-
ences when comparing healthy, long covid or combined groups.
Pre-task RT was slower in Long Covid patients than in healthy
controls (Covid 373/C6131ms, controls 317/C643ms) but did not
predict initial or ﬁnal typing speed, nor learning rate in either
group. Post-task RT was also faster in both groups, marginally
more so in patients (Covid 353/C6
117ms, controls 314/C651ms).
Conclusions: Long Covid patients exhibited slower starting
performance. While they learned the skill at about the same pace,
they failed to reach the same typing speed as healthy controls by
the end of the task. Reaction times, here used as a measure of
attention, did not exhibit a direct link with learning metrics.

Childhood cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy (CCALD) is a fatal
inﬂammatory demyelinating disorder. Patients with ALD
undergo intensive biannual contrast-enhanced MRI screening
to capture early-stage in ﬂammatory demyelination, followed
by rapid referral to hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation.
Long-term gadolinium-retention has been demonstrated in
children with repeated exposure to gadolinium-based contrast
agents (GBCAs). Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) is
an effective tool to detect new and enhancing lesions in multiple
sclerosis and can accurately predict blood-brain barrier integrity
(enhancement status) without the need for GBCAs (Deh, Jour-
nal of Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2018). We hypothesize that
QSM can discriminate between active inﬂammatory (enhancing)
and inactive non-in ﬂammatory (non-enhancing) lesions in
CCALD. We performed a region-o f-interest analysis on QSM
sequences in the splenium of 3 non-lesional ALD controls,
splenial lesion of 1 untreated patient with active CCALD
deﬁned by the presence of a characteristic T2-hyperintense lesion
with lesional enhancement on T1-post contrast MRI, and
2 patients with inactive CCALD de ﬁned by the absence of
lesional enhancement (1 untreated patient with self-arrested
CALD and 1 patient treated with stem-cell transplant). The 3T
brain scanning protocol consisted of standard T1W sequence for
anatomical structure, T2W and T2W FLAIR sequences for
lesion detection, post-Gadolinium T1W sequence for detecting
blood-brain barrier disruption, and multi-echo 3D GRE
sequence for QSM. QSM was reconstructed from complex
GRE images using a fully auto mated Morphology Enabled
Dipole Inversion algorithm zero-referenced to the ventricular
cerebrospinalﬂuid (MEDI+0)(Liu, Magnetic Resonance in Medi-
cine, 2018). T1W, T2W and T2W FLAIR images were bias
ﬁeld corrected, brain extracted and linear coregistered to the
QSM image using the FSL toolbox (Jenkinson, NeuroImage,
2012). The average QSM value obtained from the splenium
from the non-lesional ALD controls is -33.7ppb. The QSM
value obtained from the area of lesional enhancement within
the splenium of the patient with active in ﬂammatory CCALD
is -21.9ppb. The average QSM value obtained from the non-
enhancing splenial lesions in the patients with inactive non-
inﬂammatory disease is 11.0ppb. These early data suggest that
QSM values differ in non-lesional normal appearing white mat-
ter in ALD controls, enhancing disease, and non-enhancing
arrested lesions in CCALD, the reby discriminating active vs
inactive demyelination. QSM may serve as a surrogate bio-
marker to diagnose blood-brain barrier breakdown in CCALD.
This would reduce repeated exposures to GBCAs during
contrast-enhanced MRI surveillance and may serve as a bio-
marker for response to therapy.
S290. Ramsay Hunt Syndrome with Trigeminal
Neuropathy
Crystal Lu, BSN, MSN , Laura Wu, MD, PhD. UTMB,
Galveston, TX, USA.
Objective: Our objective is to present a case of Ramsay Hunt
syndrome (RHS) with trigeminal neuropathy.
Background: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster
oticus) is a neurological syndrome caused by reactivation of
varicella zoster virus. Cranial seven and eight are typically
affected, and patients present with ipsilateral severe facial
paralysis, tinnitus, and vesicles in the ear. On rare occasions,
RHS can also affect cranial nerve ﬁve, nine, and ten. Compli-
cations include hearing loss, blindness, and post-herpetic
neuralgia.

Case Presentation: A 64-year-old male presented to the
neurology clinic with a six-month history of progressive right
facial numbness and weakness, which was ﬁrst noted at his
right lower gum while ﬂossing. Subsequently, he noticed
hyperacusis, tinnitus, and right-sided facial weakness, hearing
loss, and ear pain and fullness sensation. Initial neurological
examination found decreased sensation in all three branches of
the right trigeminal nerve, decreased right side corneal re ﬂex,
atrophied right masseter and temporalis muscle, and weakened
peripheral aspect of the right face. Brain MRI with contrast
was unremarkable. Cerebral spinal ﬂuid analysis was negative
for infection. All lab work for possible causes of multiple cranial
neuropathies, including tuberculosis, Lyme, sarcoidosis, Sjogren
Disease, antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic anti-
bodies, and human immunodeﬁciency virus, returned negative.
Electromyography with blink re ﬂex study showed right-sided
facial neuropathy and trigeminal neuropathy with active dener-
v a t i o ni nt h et e m p o r a l i sm u s c l e .H i ss y m p t o m sc o n t i n u e dt o
progress, and he began to experience right-sided numbness and
taste disturbance of the tongue, vertigo, and worsening tinnitus.
A referral to otorhinolaryngology discovered right-sided white
lesions in the back of his throat. The patient was diagnosed
with RHS and prescribed valacyclovir. His facial weakness
improved, but he later experienced post-herpetic neuralgia
along the trigeminal nerve ’s maxillary branch as well as right
hemi-facial spasm. His disease course was also complicated by
neurotrophic keratitis of the right eye, which required corneal
transplantation.
Discussion: Although the trigeminal nerve can be
involved in RHS, it is rarely a presenting symptom. Our
case is unique because no reported literatures have dis-
cussed RHS patients with both masseter and temporal
muscle atrophy, indicating trigeminal nerve ’s motor branch
involvement, and facial sensation loss. Herpes zoster infec-
tion should be considered as a possible etiology in patients
with multiple cranial neuropathies. Diagnosis of trigeminal
herpes zoster and RHS can lead to timely intervention and
improved patient outcomes.

Background: Capnocytophaga canimorsus , a gram-negative
rod found in the oral ﬂora of dogs and cats, is an extremely
rare cause of bacterial meningitis with an incidence of 0.03
cases per million adults in the US. Here, we describe the case
of a young immunocompetent woman who developed severe
bilateral sensorineural hearing loss due to C. canimorsus
meningitis.
