Case Presentation: A 38-year-old female with hypothy-
roidism presented with 2 days history of worsening headache,
nausea, vomiting, and bilateral hearing loss. She was afebrile
and neurological exam was only notable for bilateral hearing
loss. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) studies revealed signi ﬁcantly
elevated WBCs (4,612/cmm) with 79% neutrophils, elevated
protein (348 mg/dL), and low glucose (<1 mg/dL), consistent
with bacterial meningitis. Cultures were drawn and vancomy-
cin and ceftriaxone were initiated. Blood and CSF cultures
returned growing C. canimorsus and she was continued on
ceftriaxone. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain
was notable for a lack of FLAIR suppression on multiple
bilateral sulci, suggesting meningitis. She denies being bitten
by her dogs and cat but says she was potentially scratched
and licked by her dogs. On day 4 of presentation, otolaryn-
gology and neurology were consulted for worsening hearing
loss. She was started on an empiric trial of methylpredniso-
lone 60 mg daily for 5 days. Magnetic resonance angiogram
of the head did not show any aneurysm and computed
tomography of the temporal bone did not exhibit signs of
ﬁbrosis. HIV antibody testing was negative. Audiogram dem-
onstrated precipitous sloping indicating severe bilateral hear-
ing loss. She completed a 14-day course of intravenous
antibiotics and a 15-day steroid taper with mild improvement
in hearing. Repeat audiogram in 3 months showed improve-
ment in higher frequencies and patient reports subjective
improvement of her hearing to about 55%.
Discussion: C. canimorsus meningitis was mostly observed
in immunocompromised patients, risk factors include sple-
nectomy, alcoholism, receipt of steroids. It is uncommon
among young immunocompetent individuals. Identi ﬁcation
of the pathogen is often delayed due to its slow growth on
culture media. This case demonstrates a rare but severe com-
plication of C. canimorsus meningitis. While early initiation
of steroids in patients with pneumococcal meningitis is
known to be associated with reduced risk of post-meningeal
hearing loss, its utility in patients with C. canimorsus menin-
gitis is unknown. This is the ﬁrst case of steroid use in
C. canimorsus meningitis with reported improvement in
hearing.
S292. Submandibular Gland Abscess Leading to Cytokine
Release Syndrome: A Case Report
Nina D’Amiano, BS, Jonathan Lai, BS, Christopher
Primiani, MD, Christopher Primiani, MD, Mona N. Bahouth,
MD, PhD. Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine,
Baltimore, MD, USA.
Background: Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS) is a systemic
inﬂammatory response characterized by fever, constitutional
symptoms, and multi-organ dysfunction. While most com-
monly caused by immunotherapy, in particular chimeric anti-
gen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, CRS can also be incited by
infections or drugs. If CRS affects the central nervous system
(CNS), patients may develop neurological de ﬁcits and neuro-
behavioral issues including aphasia, altered level of conscious-
ness, impaired cognitive skills, motor weakness, and seizures.
Objective: This case details the diagnosis of a patient with
CRS, which is a rare pathology and a diagnosis of exclusion.
Case Presentation: A 71-year-old woman with a history
of primary myelo ﬁbrosis and breast cancer presented with
acute onset of altered mental status. Initial vital signs were
notable for severe hypertension, tachycardia, and fever. On

neurological exam, the patient was nonverbal, with poor
attention to speaker, spontaneously moving all extremities. A
ﬂuid collection was noted at the angle of the jaw. A compre-
hensive analysis, including blood tests, CSF analysis, EEG,
and neuroimaging, was performed. Severe leukocytosis was
noted and brain MRI demonstrated scattered areas of diffu-
sion restriction and diffuse T2 white matter hyperintensities.
Over the course of her hospital stay, serial imaging demon-
strated the progression of T2 hyperintensities. A broad differ-
ential diagnosis was considered, but ultimately, CRS was the
most likely diagnosis. In this case, the inciting event was
likely an infectious etiology, suspected to be the submandibu-
lar gland abscess that was present at the time of admission.
Conclusion: The diagnosis of CRS is challenging since it
can affect multiple organ systems. Although more rare, this
ADEM-like syndrome can affect the CNS should be included
in the differential diagnosis for patients with multifocal neu-
rological de ﬁcits, leukocytosis, and imaging non-suggestive of
stroke. A higher index of suspicion for CRS should be con-
sidered for those with recent infection, exposure to drugs or
immunotherapy, or known immune dysregulation as in the
presentation in this case. Certain laboratory ﬁndings as well
as the course of the disease can be suggestive of CRS and
help to distinguish it from pathologies with similar presenta-
tions, such as PRES, vasculitis, or CNS lymphoma. While
CRS is traditionally associated with immunotherapy, and
more recently with COVID-19 infection, our case highlights
the importance of considering other potential etiologies.

disorder for which there are a lack of disease-modifying thera-

the brain. Additionally, neuroin ﬂammation in the form of

the context of AD pathogenesis are still unclear. Greater
understanding of these mechanisms could lead to the devel-
opment of novel disease modifying therapies. Astrocytes are
key players in the neuroin ﬂammation of many neurodegener-
ative diseases. Activated microglia release in ﬂammatory fac-
tors which convert homeostatic astrocytes into reactive
astrocytes. These reactive astrocytes, which are de ﬁned by
unique morphology and gene expression pro ﬁle, can kill neu-
rons and modulate A β deposition in AD models. The gut

S294. The Potential Role of Histopathological Screening
for Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy-Related In ﬂammation
in Cortical Intracerebral Hemorrhage Requiring Surgical
Evacuation
Fortino Velasco, IV, MD , Manuel Hazim, BS, MS, Tamra
Ranasinghe, MD. Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist, Winston
Salem, NC, USA.
Introduction: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related in ﬂam-
mation (CAA-RI) is a rare, but reversible condition secondary
to an in ﬂammatory response to β-amyloid deposits within
the cerebral vessels in patients with cerebral amyloid
angiopathy (CAA). CAA-RI is associated with cognitive and
behavioral changes, headaches, focal neurologic signs, sei-
zures, and the presence of one or more cortico-subcortical
hemorrhagic lesions. Probable diagnosis of CAA-RI can be
determined with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), though
deﬁnitive diagnosis requires brain biopsy. Initiation of treat-
ment with immunosuppression for CAA-RI has been associ-
ated with improved clinical outcomes and decreased
recurrence, making prompt diagnosis and treatment key.
Case Presentation: A 65-year-old female with a history of
hypertension, hyperlipidemia and type 2 diabetes presented
with global aphasia, left gaze deviation and right hemi-body
weakness. CT head without contrast demonstrated a left
temporo-parietal intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) measuring
3.23 cm x 6.44 cm with approximately 52 cc volume,
with overlying subdural hematoma and intraventricular
hemorrhage. No vascular abnormalities were seen on CT
angiography of the head and neck. MRI brain without con-
trast was performed which redemonstrated the left temporo-
parietal ICH, as well as multiple additional scattered cortical
microhemorrhages, which was suggestive of probable CAA.
In addition, the MRI FLAIR images demonstrated extensive

bilateral hyperintensities with asymmetric involvement of the
right temporal lobe concerning for the in ﬂammatory variant
of CAA. The patient ’s hospital course was complicated by
worsening of the patient ’s right sided weakness and repeat
CT head demonstrating developing hydrocephalus. The
patient subsequently underwent craniotomy for hematoma
evacuation and drain placement. The histopathology of the
evacuated tissue demonstrated β-amyloid peptide on immu-
nohistochemistry, increased T-cells and macrophages sur-
rounding and within the blood vessel walls compatible with
CAA-RI. The patient was initiated on oral prednisone and
followed up in outpatient stroke clinic.
Conclusion: A timely and de ﬁnitive diagnosis of this rare
CNS in ﬂammatory vasculopathy allows for initiation of
immunosuppression, a treatment unique to this variant of
CAA. Prompt treatment with immunosuppressive therapy
decreases the risk of morbidity and mortality associated with
CAA-RI. Hence, in all patients ≥ 55-years-old who undergo
surgical evacuation of a cortical ICH, we propose the utility
of a histopathological screen evaluating for CAA-RI.

K-S121. Acute Flaccid Myelitis: Role for Enterovirus-
Induced Nuclear Pore Complex Dysfunction in
Pathogenesis

1, Malavika Jayaram, M.S. 1,
Jeffrey Rothstein, M.D., Ph.D. 2. 1Kennedy Krieger Institute,
Baltimore, MD, USA, 2Johns Hopkins School of Medicine,

Acute ﬂaccid myelitis (AFM) is an emerging polio-like illness
that causes paralysis in children via toxicity to spinal motor
neurons. AFM is caused by enteroviruses, and Enterovirus
D68 (EV-D68) has been responsible for multiple worldwide
outbreaks of AFM in recent years. The enterovirus life cycle
involves the disruption of nucleocytoplasmic transport, all-
owing RNA binding proteins that typically reside in the
nucleus to participate in viral replication in the cytoplasm,
and disrupting the nuclear export of host mRNA. Similar
deﬁcits in nucleocytoplasmic transport have been implicated
in neurodegenerative disorders, most notably the motor neu-
ron disease Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). We there-
fore hypothesize that enterovirus-induced nucleocytoplasmic
transport dysfunction contributes to the selective motor neu-
ron toxicity that occurs in AFM. Here, we demonstrate that
EV-D68 proteases cleave multiple nucleoporins. This process
disrupts the permeability barrier of the nuclear pore complex
for proteins and diminishes the ef ﬁciency of RNA export.
EV-D68 proteases are suf ﬁcient to cause toxicity to human
iPS-derived motor neurons. These ﬁndings begin to elucidate
the role of the nuclear pore complex in AFM pathogenesis
and suggest possible targets for neuroprotective therapies.

M252. A Needs Assessment and Initiative to Improve
Neurology Resident Satisfaction with Morning Report
Brian Stamm, MD , Sarah M. Brooker, MD PhD, Deborah
Huang, MD, Danny Bega, MD, Neena R. Cherayil,
MD. Northwestern University, Chicago, IL, USA.
Background: Morning report (MR) is an important educa-
tional experience in many neurology residencies. MR typi-
cally involves a resident discussant talking through an
unfamiliar case and detailing neuroanatomic localization, dif-
ferential diagnosis, and therapeutic approach with guidance
and teaching from senior residents and faculty leaders.
Though MR is a common part of medical training, it has
been dif ﬁcult to study systematically given inter-institutional
variability in its structure, format, and frequency. In order to
better understand the educational needs of our neurology res-
idents, we conducted a survey regarding the MR experience
and then altered MR curricula with an aim to improve over-
all resident satisfaction with MR.
Methods: Cases presented at MR were recorded beginning
in July 2021, including working diagnoses and whether the
cases were encountered in the inpatient or ambulatory set-
ting. In December 2021, an eight-question mid-year survey
was sent to all PGY2, 3, and 4 neurology residents to assess
the following: ﬁelds of neurology that warrant more/less rep-
resentation in MR; conditions from ﬁelds of neurology that
residents feel most/least comfortable diagnosing and treating;
diversity of case mix; satisfaction with MR; and an open-
ended free-response on ways to improve MR.
Results: The most common subspecialty presented in morn-
ing report cases (n = 64) during the ﬁrst half of the academic
year (July-December 2021) was vascular neurology (31.3% of
cases) followed by epilepsy (15.6%). For this ﬁr s th a l fo ft h e
year, no cases presented were from the outpatient setting. The
survey response rate was 14/21 (67%) of eligible participants.
Residents felt the following ﬁelds were over-represented: vascu-
lar neurology, neurocritical care, and epilepsy. The top three
ﬁelds that residents wanted more represented were: neuromus-
cular, cognitive neurology, and movement disorders. Similarly,
residents felt least comfortable with neuromuscular and most
comfortable with vascular neurology. In the free-response sec-

tion, multiple residents requested more outpatient cases.
Conclusions: Surveyed residents at our institution felt
least con ﬁdent with and desired more representation from
predominantly outpatient ﬁelds within neurology. We thus
designed a schedule of prepared morning report cases to be
presented by senior residents, during the second half of the
academic year (January-June 2 022). The senior residents
are instructed to preferentially pick outpatient-based cases
from the previously underrepresented ﬁelds. We will
administer another survey in June 2022, to gauge satisfac-
tion with this new model and determine whether the pro-
gram was successful in improving resident satisfaction
with MR.

gene represent unique diagnostic challenges. We report a
unique patient with a heterozy gous pathogenic titin vari-
ant and a heterozygous titin variant of uncertain signi ﬁ-
cance (VUS).

gressive bilateral leg weakness. He was not a ﬂoppy baby.

than other kids in school playing sports. He noted leg weak-
ness while Playing football in middle school. He also had sore
hips. As a freshman in high school, he was not able to ﬁnish
all the workouts. Running a mile or so, he felt that his legs
would have a feeling as if they would lock up and he could
not run further. In college, he was not able to increase weights

also has trouble going downstairs, he must hold onto the rail-

15 years, scoliosis was noted on Xray for workup of hip sore-

ankle dorsiﬂexion weakness, high-arched palate, right thoracic

biceps femoris, deltoid, biceps brachii and ﬂexor carpi radialis

M254. Activation of Keratinocyte-Linked G-Protein
Coupled Receptors Remodels Dorsal Root Ganglion
Neurons Single-Cell Transcriptomic Pro ﬁle in Painful
Diabetic Neuropathy
Dale George, Ph.D.
1, Daniela Maria Menichella, MD, Ph.
D.2. 1Northwestern University, Chicago, IL, USA,
2Northwestern University, Wilmette, IL, USA.
Painful diabetic neuropathy (PDN) is one of the most com-
mon and intractable complications of diabetes. PDN is char-
acterized by small- ﬁber degeneration, which can progress to
complete loss of cutaneous innervation and is accompanied
by neuropathic pain. Uncovering the mechanisms underlying
degeneration of cutaneous nerves in PDN remains a major
challenge to ﬁnding effective and disease-modifying therapy.
Sensory nerve afferents normally extend into the epidermis in
close communication with keratinocytes, but degenerate in
diabetic skin. Keratinocytes are closely juxtaposed to cutane-
ous nerve terminals, enabling communication between
keratinocytes and cutaneous nerves. We investigated potential
mechanisms that mediate this communication in the High-
Fat-Diet mouse model of PDN. We genetically expressed
stimulatory DREADDs (hM3Dq) into K14 basal
keratinocytes (K14) in mice as a tool for mimicking the acti-
vation of Gq-linked G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) in
K14 expressing cells. We have shown that activation of these
DREADDs reduced innervation of the epidermis indicating
that activation of K-14 Gq-linked GPCRs can regulate nerve
ﬁber degeneration in the epidermis. We used bulk and
single-cell RNA (scRNA-seq) sequencing from skin and Dor-
sal Root Ganglion (DRG) taken from mice expressing
hM3Dq into K14 keratinocytes comparing control mice
receiving saline and mice receiving CNO to activate K14
keratinocytes expressing hM3Dq. Bulk RNA sequencing
of the epidermis revealed changes in a set of genes associ-
ated with neurite outgrowth, including class III
semaphorins, potentially impacting cutaneous nerve degen-
eration. Using RNAScope we found dramatic changes in
the expression of semaphorins and their receptors in dis-
tinct DRG neurons subtypes. Using single-cell RNA-seq
from lumbar DRG we pro ﬁled the transcriptome of
10,000 individual DRG cells and found that hM3Dq
mediated stimulation of keratinocytes induced changes in
DRG single-cell gene expression pro ﬁle resulting in the
identi ﬁcation of a novel DRG neuronal subtype among
the nonpeptidergic nociceptors (NP1.2). Our ﬁndings
indicate that activation of basal keratinocytes Gq-linked
GPCRs can result in profound changes in DRG neuronal
transcriptomic pro ﬁle leading to a phenotypical switch
(plasticity) of DRG neurons. Furthermore, our results sug-
gest possible therapeutic effects of activating or blocking
speci ﬁc keratinocyte Gq-linked GPCRs for promoting

axon regeneration in PDN.

Gad Antibody-Spectrum Disorder or Mitochondrial
Disease?
Ahmed Harazeen, MD , Kian Abdul-Baki, MD, Xiangping
Li, MD, Laura J. Wu, MD. University of Texas Medical
Branch, Galveston, TX, USA.
Objective: To present an intriguing case of progressive myoc-
lonus and ataxia with positive family history.
Background: Antibodies against glutamic acid decarbox-
ylase (GAD) are associated with various neurological syn-
dromes including stiff person syndrome (SPS), cerebellar
ataxia, limbic encephalitis and progressive encephalomyelitis
with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM). GAD antibody-
spectrum disorders are usually sporadic. MERRF (myo-
clonic epilepsy with ragged red ﬁbers) is caused by muta-
tions in mitochondrial DNA usually characterized by
myoclonus, epilepsy, ataxia and myopathy. A mitochondrial
disease may be suspected when there is a history of maternal
inheritance.
Case Presentation: A 49-year-old African American male
with history of progressive “tremors” and ataxia for about
3 years presented to the hospital with worsening generalized
weakness, dysarthria and dysphagia. He was admitted to the
intensive care unit and required intubation due to acute
respiratory failure from aspiration pneumonia. He has history
of seizures and had a breakthrough seizure during hospitaliza-
tion. The initial exam showed bifacial weakness and
decreased deep tendon re ﬂex on lower extremities. Five days
immunoglobulin therapy was initiated under the suspicion of
acute in ﬂammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy. On the
following neurological examination, the patient had signi ﬁ-
cant general myoclonus and dysmetria on all limbs. Myoclo-
nus were not stimulus sensitive and persisted during sleep.
The patient had no nystagmus, limb stiffness or encephalopa-
thy. Patient has family history with similar presentations in
his mother, sister, and nephew. His nephew has a con ﬁrmed
diagnosis of MERRF. Brain MRI, electroencephalography,
and cerebral-spinal ﬂuid (CSF) are essentially normal except
mild cerebellar atrophy and slightly elevated protein
(57 mg/dL). Electromyography showed sensory axonal poly-
neuropathy with no evidence of demyelinating neuropathy or
myopathy. Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase antibody (GAD)
titer was high (> 250 IU/mL, range 0.0-5.0). Voltage-gated
potassium channel antibody (VGKC) was also elevated
(86 pmol/L, range 0-37). Mitochondrial genetic test result is
still pending.
Discussion: Mitochondrial diseases present with a wide
range of clinical expressions. MERRF is characterized by
myoclonus, typically as the ﬁrst symptom, and is associated

M256. Antibody Response to HML-2 May Be Protective
in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
Marta Garcia-Montojo, PhD
1, Elena Rita Simula, MS 2,
Saeed Fathi, MS 1, Cynthia Mcmahan, MS 1, Anubrata Ghosal,
PhD3, James Berry, MD 3, Merit Cudkowicz, MD 3, Abdel
Elkahloun, PhD 1, Kory Johnson, PhD 1, Gina Norato, MS 1,
Leonardo Antonio Sechi, PhD 2, Avindra Nath, MD 1.
1NINDS, Bethesda, MD, USA, 2University of Sassari, Sassari,
Italy, 3Sean M. Healey & AMG Center for ALS and the
Neurology Clinical Research Institute, Massachusetts General
Hospital, Boston, MA, USA.
Introduction: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devas-
tating neurodegenerative disease with a median survival time
of 4 years. Factors that trigger the onset of the illness are
poorly understood. Human endogenous retroviruses
(HERVs) are genomic sequences of retroviral origin that con-
stitute around 8% of the human genome. HERVs are highly
expressed in stem cells but get mostly silenced after cell dif-
ferentiation. Reactivation of HERV-K (HML-2) has been
found in subsets of individuals with Amyotrophic Lateral
Sclerosis (ALS). This study examines the antibody response
against HML-2 in ALS and analyzes its possible clinical
relevance.
Methods: Antibodies to HML-2 envelope (env) were ana-
lyzed using a peptide array for epitope mapping and by a
peptide ELISA in 237 ALS individuals and 242 healthy con-
trols. Total IgG levels were measured by ELISA. Extracellular
levels of HML-2 were analyzed by digital PCR.
Results: Antibodies in the sera of ALS individuals recog-
nized more peptides derived from HML-2 env compared to
healthy controls (p<0.0001). ALS individuals had higher
levels of HML-2 (p=0.02) and antibodies against a select
HML-2 env peptide (p<0.0001). 51.05% of ALS individuals
and only 19.83% of controls had antibodies against the
HML-2 peptide (AUC = 0.711, p < 0.0001), while there
were no differences in total IgG levels. The levels of extracel-
lular HML-2 DNA in serum (p=0.03) and the number of
HML-2 env peptides recognized by ALS sera (p=0.03) corre-
lated with the disease duration. In ALS, lower levels of
HML-2 antibody were associated with widespread disease
and individuals with higher levels of antibodies had a higher
probability of survival.
Interpretation: There is a differential antibody response
against speci ﬁc epitopes of HML-2 env in ALS and controls,
probably due to epitope spreading due to persistent antigenic
exposure following reactivation of the viral genes. Humoral
response against HML-2 seems to be protective against dis-
ease progression. Evaluation of this response in longitudinal
studies is necessary to determine its value as ALS biomarker.
Moreover, antibodies against HML-2 could be a therapeutic
option for individuals with ALS.

Predominantly Low-Income, Black U.S. Patient
Population

3University of Rochester, Rochester, NY, USA, 4Johns Hopkins
University, Baltimore, MD, USA.
Introduction: Polyneuropathy is a disabling, painful condition
associated with falls and reduced quality of life. Black people
and people with low-income are underrepresented in existing
polyneuropathy studies. The Flint Neuropathy Study aims to
describe polyneuropathy prevalence and associated risk factors
in predominantly Black, low-income communities.
Methods: Patients >40 years of age presenting to the Hur-
ley Medical Center Outpatient Internal Medicine Residency
Clinic primarily serving Medicaid patients in Flint, Michigan
were enrolled. Demographics, clinical characteristics includ-
ing prior diagnoses, medication use, anthropomorphic mea-
surements, fasting lipids, fasting glucose, and Hemoglobin
A1C, were collected. Glucose intolerance followed the 2021
ADA diagnosis and classi ﬁcation of diabetes mellitus criteria,
whereas metabolic syndrome followed the harmonized criteria
from the IDF, NHLBI, AHA, WHF, IAS, and IASO socie-
ties. Polyneuropathy was de ﬁned using the Michigan Neu-
ropathy Screening Instrument Combined Index (MNSICI).
Descriptive statistics were assessed using means and frequen-
cies. Univariate associations between polyneuropathy and glu-
cose intolerance and metabolic syndrome were assessed using
chi-square tests.
Results: 139 participants (53% female, 58.9 years. 66%
Black, 50% Medicaid, 25% < high school education) have
enrolled to date. At enrollment, 74 (53%) reported a history
of diabetes or pre-diabetes. Criteria for metabolic syndrome
was met in 88 (63%). 4 were newly diagnosed with diabetes
and 35 were newly diagnosed with pre-diabetes during the
study. Mean MNSICI score was 2.69 (SD 1.87) with
67/139 (48%) meeting criteria for polyneuropathy. 49/67
(73%) of those with polyneuropathy endorsed neuropathic
pain. 41/67 (61%) had previously undiagnosed poly-
neuropathy, including 25/77 (32%) of participants with
known diabetes. Polyneuropathy was associated with a his-
tory of glucose intolerance (OR 4.45 [95%CI: 1.55-12.72]
p<0.01) as well as metabolic syndrome (OR: 2.63 [95%CI:
1.28-5.4] p<0.01).
Conclusions: Polyneuropathy is extremely common and
underrecognized in this predominantly Black, low-income
patient population. Characterizing reasons for polyneuropathy
underdiagnosis is essential to address gaps in risk factor and
neuropathic pain management and improve patient outcomes.

M260. Concurrent Acute Myositis and Guillain-Barre
Syndrome in COVID-19 Infection - A Rare Case Report
Ruben Blanco, MD 1, Jessie Pichardo, MD 1, Hassan Abdullah
Shakeel, MBBS, MD 2. 1Pontiﬁcia Universidad Católica
Madre y Maestra, Santiago, Dominican Republic, 2Allegheny
General Hospital, Pittsburgh, PA, USA.
Introduction: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is a heteroge-
neous disorder that often follows a viral infection. Plenty of
cases of GBS associated with COVID-19 infection has been
reported. Acute myositis has also been reported as one of the
complications of COVID-19 infection. But there is no such
report of having both acute myositis and GBS concurrently
in a patient with a COVID-19 infection. Here we report
cooccurrence of GBS and acute severe myositis presenting
with acute quadriparesis and muscular pain.
Case Presentation: A 65-year-old lady presented with
bilateral leg pain for one week. She also had a cough and pro-
gressive paresthesia of distal lower extremities evolving to the
upper limbs leading to quardiparesthesia and quadriparesis.
Her illness started with an upper respiratory tract infection
one week back. The neurological examination showed mildly
dysarthric speech, quardiparesthesia, quadriparesis, reduced
tone in all extremities, and absent deep tendon re ﬂexes.
Other cranial nerves were intact. Her COVID-19 PCR
turned out positive, and Creatine Kinase (CK) was markedly
raised (5467 U/L). Neurophysiological studies and CSF anal-
ysis were consistent with GBS. A muscle biopsy con ﬁrmed
the diagnosis of myositis. Subsequently, treatment was started
with IV ﬂuids to hydrate her because of underlying muscular
inﬂammation. She was treated with IV methylprednisolone
and IV immunoglobulin (IVIg), and her condition improved.
Discussion: This case is unique and different from the
other reported cases in the literature because the patient had
acute myositis and GBS in co-occurrence with COVID-19
infection. The clinical and electrophysiological ﬁndings were
consistent with acute in ﬂammatory demyelinating poly-
neuropathy (AIDP). Although raised CK levels are reported
in at least 25% of GBS patients (Hosokawa T, BMC Neurol,
2020), a gadolinium muscle MRI or a muscle biopsy is
required to prove muscle in ﬂammation. In contrast to the
previously reported cases of GBS-associated rhabdomyolysis
(Scott AJ, Postgrad Med J, 1991 and Saxena A, Indian J Crit
Care Med, 2014), the cause of elevated CK in our case was
acute myositis which was con ﬁrmed with muscle biopsy.
Conclusion: COVID-19 infection presenting as acute myo-
sitis with GBS is a rare co-occurrence. This case underscores
the importance of clinical vigilance and judgment to consider it
a differential diagnosis which may signi ﬁcantly alter the treat-
ment approach and help in prompt diagnosis and treatment.
M262. Effects of Efgartigimod Treatment on Humoral
and Cellular Immune Responses: Analysis of T-Cell-
Dependent Antibody Response in Cynomolgus Monkeys
Jenna Casey, PhD
1, Mario Cocco, PhD 2, Daniel Thwaites,
PhD2, Christopher Cooper, BSc 2, Gordon McPhie, MSc 2,
Ornella Binazon, PharmD 1, Mahan Moshir, MSc 1, Peter
Vanhoenacker, PhD 1, Dieter Defever, BSc 1, Christa Kneip,
PhD1, Sophie Steeland, PharmD, PhD1,G w e n d aP y n a e r t ,P h D1,
Peter Ulrichts, PhD1, Judith Baumeister, PhD1. 1argenx, Ghent,
Belgium, 2Labcorp Early Development Laboratories Ltd.,
Harrogate, United Kingdom.
Introduction: Efgartigimod is a human immunoglobulin G

1 (IgG1) antibody Fc-fragment that reduces IgG, including
pathogenic IgG autoantibody levels through neonatal Fc recep-
tor (FcRn) blockage. Owing to the novel mechanism of action
of efgartigimod, its impact on adaptive humoral and cellular
immune responses to antigen challenge warrants further inves-
tigation. Objective: To determine whether treatment with
efgartigimod in cynomolgus monkeys had an impact on
humoral and/or cellular immune responses to keyhole limpet
hemocyanin (KLH), a prototypical T-cell-dependent antigen.
Methods: Six male and 6 female cynomolgus monkeys were
divided 1:1 to receive either intravenous 100 mg/kg
efgartigimod or vehicle control once weekly for 11 weeks,
followed by a 9-week recovery period. Subcutaneous KLH chal-
lenges (10 mg each) occurred at weeks 4 and 8, with an addi-
tional challenge at week 5 of the recovery period. Outcomes
reported include timing and magnitude of anti-KLH IgM and
IgG responses, total IgG, and elicited levels of interferon-gamma
secretion of PBMCs in response to KLH recall challenge.
Results: Clear anti-KLH IgG and IgM induction was seen
after KLH immunization in both groups. Consistent with
the mode of action of efgartigimod, total IgG levels decreased
from day 8 through day 38 in efgartigimod-treated animals
(average 0.4-fold change with respect to average pre-
treatment levels), before returning to pre-dose levels. Broadly
similar anti-KLH IgG titers were generally noted in
efgartigimod-treated animals for the duration of the dosing
and recovery phases, compared with controls. The exception
was a decreased mean anti-KLH IgG antibody response on
days 71 and 77 of the dosing phase (approximately 4- and
8-fold in females; 2- and 9-fold in males, respectively) follow-
ing the second KLH immunization on day 56 in
efgartigimod-treated animals, compared with respective con-
trols. Similar anti-KLH IgM titers were noted in
efgartigimod-treated animals throughout the dosing or recov-
ery phase, compared with controls. A similar positive T-cell
response (interferon-gamma secretion) to the immunizing
agent KLH was also observed in both groups.
Summary/Conclusion: These data demonstrate that
efgartigimod treatment did not affect the antigen speciﬁc activa-
tion of the immune response or T-cell response in cynomolgus
monkeys. A clear antigen-speci ﬁc IgG response was mounted
under efgartigimod treatment, and an increased production of
antigen-speciﬁc IgG in response to stimuli was seen. In the
context of vaccination or infection, efgartigimod treatment is
not expected to impair generation of immune responses.
M263. Efﬁcacy of Rapamycin in a Xenograft Model of
Inclusion Body Myositis
Chiseko Ikenaga, MD, PhD , Andrew Wilson, MS, Nicole
Reed, MS, Thomas E. Lloyd, MD, PhD. Johns Hopkins
University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD, USA.
Objective: To determine the ef ﬁcacy of rapamycin in a xeno-
graft model of inclusion body myositis (IBM).

Methods: Muscle biopsy samples were obtained from a
67-year-old woman who was diagnosed with clinico-
pathologically de ﬁned IBM and a 50-year-old woman who
showed mild hip ﬂexor weakness but had normal muscle his-
tology for use as control. Xenografts were performed on
14 nod-Rag1[null]IL2r γ[null] (NRG) mice lacking the ability
to generate mature B cells, T cells, and innate lymphoid cells,
including natural killer cells (7 IBM and 7 control). After the
xenografts had fully matured (3 months), four mice in each
group were fed encapsulated rapamycin (14 mg/kg food) for
3 months, and xenografts were harvested for analysis. Three
mice with IBM and control xenografts were administered pla-
cebo (eudragit). Frozen sections of the xenografts were
analysed by histochemistry and immunohistochemistry in a
blinded manner.
Results: IBM xenografts exhibited MHC-I up-regulation
of the muscle ﬁbers and endomysial in ﬂammatory in ﬁltrates
of CD3+ T cell while control xenografts did not show these
features. All the rapamycin fed mice showed marked eleva-
tion of serum rapamycin levels after 3 months (42.1 /C64.6
ng/mL) whereas levels were undetectable in mice fed placebo
(< 2.0 ng/mL). Among the IBM xenografts, rapamycin
treated xenografts showed fewer CD8+ T cells compared with
the placebo group (441 /C6173 cells/mm
2 (rapamycin group),
1148 /C6261 cells/mm 2 (placebo group), p = 0.02) while
there was no signi ﬁcant difference in the number of CD4+ T
cells between rapamycin treated xenografts and the placebo
group (967 /C6284 cells/mm 2 (rapamycin group), 980 /C650
cells/mm2(placebo group), p = 0.94). There was no signi ﬁ-
cant difference between the two groups regarding myo ﬁber
density or the presence of p62-positive aggregates.
Conclusion: In this small pilot study in xenografts from a
single IBM patient and control, rapamycin reduced the num-
ber of endomysial CD8+ T cells without altering the number
of CD4+ T cells, suggesting one potential mechanism by
which rapamycin may show ef ﬁcacy in IBM by depletion of
cytotoxic T cells. Studies of xenografts from three additional
IBM patients and controls, including longer treatment with
rapamycin (5-6 months), are ongoing.

Background: Recent advances in tool development to identify
repeat expansions using whole-genome sequencing data has
allowed the unbiased interrogation of these repeats in the path-
ogenesis of neurological disorders. Frontotemporal dementia
(FTD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) are closely
related conditions along a clinical spectrum, of which the main
and shared cause of disease is the intronic repeat expansion of
the C9orf72 gene. Unsurprisingly, other repeat expansions
have also been implicated in other neurological diseases. This
supports the notion that expression of pathogenic repeat
expansions plays a mechanistic role in disease pathogenesis and
are prime candidates for antisense oligonucleotide therapy in
modulating the expression of aberrant expanded proteins.
Methods: Using whole-genome sequencing data, repeat
sizing on ten repeat expansion motifs were quanti ﬁed using
the ExpansionHunter-Targeted tool. The discovery cohort
consisted of 2,442 FTD/ALS patients, 2,599 Lewy body
dementia (LBD) patients, and 3,158 neurologically healthy
individuals. Results were replicated in an independent cohort
of 3,674 FTD/ALS patients and 210 neurologically healthy
participants. Identi ﬁed pathogenic repeat expansions were
validated at the bench by PCR and Sanger sequencing.
Results: Pathogenic expansions in the huntingtin ( HTT)
gene (>= 40 CAG-repeats) were identi ﬁed in three (0.12%),
and ﬁve (0.14%) FTD/ALS patients in the discovery and
replication cohorts, respectively. Pathogenic HTT expansions
were absent in the LBD or healthy cohorts. None of the
FTD/ALS pathogenic HTT expansions carriers had
choreoathetosis or a family history of Huntington ’s disease.
Clinicopathologic analysis on brains from two ALS/FTD
patients with HTT expansions revealed the presence of aggre-
gates positive for huntingtin, ubiquitin, and p62, as well as
the occasional cytoplasmic mislocalization of TDP43. Neo-
striatal atrophy, a pathological hallmark of Huntington ’s

Conclusions: Our ﬁndings implicate HTT repeat expansions

FTD/ALS genetic screening panels.
M266. Feasibility of At-Home Motor Assessments Using
Wireless Technology in Patients with Myelopathy: Pilot
Data from CYGNET, an Observational Study of Patients
with Adrenomyeloneuropathy
Asif Paker, MD
1, Caroline Bergner, PhD 2, Wolfgang Köhler,
PhD3, Florian Eichler, PhD 4, Lauren Glenn, MD 1, Steven
Zelenkofske, MD 1, Marc Engelen, PhD 5. 1SwanBio
Therapeutics, Cambridge Mass, MA, USA, 2University
Hospital, Leipzig, Germany, 3University of Leipzig Medical
Center, Liepzig, Germany, 4Massachussetts General Hospital,
Boston, MA, USA, 5Amsterdam University Medical Centers,
University of Amsterdam, Amsterdam, Netherlands.
Objective: To demonstrate feasibility of home-based gait and
mobility assessments using data from a prospective natural his-
tory study of patients with adrenomyeloneuropathy (AMN).
Background: AMN is a rare, inherited, neurodegenerative
disorder of the spinal cord affecting adults with mutations in
the ABCD1 gene. AMN is characterized by a dying-back
axonopathy leading to lifelong disability. Symptoms include
progressive spasticity and leg weakness, impaired vibration
and position sensation, and bladder disturbances. Quanti ﬁca-
tion of disease progression in AMN is challenging owing to
substantial phenotypic and visit-to-visit variability. One solu-
tion to address this variability is to measure traditional func-
tional motor tasks more frequently using technology such as
wireless motion sensors during clinic and remote visits. Here,
we assess the feasibility and test-retest reliability of the
motion sensors in the clinic and at-home setting and relate it
to the standard measurements performed in clinic setting.
Methods: CYGNET (NCT05008874) is an ongoing pro-
spective, multicenter, observational study that will enroll up
to 80 male patients with AMN and follow them for ≥ 2 years
with annual clinic visits and quarterly remote visits. Gait and
balance assessments include postural body sway parameters,
2-minute walk test, Timed-Up-and-Go, and ﬁve times sit to
stand. In clinic, standard methods are used to calculate time
and distance. Wireless motion sensors enable quanti ﬁcation
of the temporal-spatial components of gait assessments such
as stride velocity, stride length, and trunk range of motion
both in the clinic and at home.
Results: Over 15 patients between 18-69 years of age with
Expanded Disability Status Score 1-6.5 have been enrolled
and entered into this analysis. Comparisons of in-clinic and
home data collected at baseline and month 3 utilizing wire-
less technology will be presented.
Conclusions: Use of wireless motion sensors can provide

an objective assessment of gait, stability, balance and func-
tional abilities of an individual both in their natural and the
clinical environment. This ﬁnding will help inform the
design of future clinical trials evaluating potential therapeu-
tics, including gene therapy for AMN.
Funding: This study was sponsored by SwanBio
Therapeutics.
M267. Generalized Weakness: Viral Infection or
Myasthenic Crisis. A Case Report of MAB Intervention to
Prevent Myasthenic Crisis
Violet M. Awori, MD , Mary A. Willis, MD. University of
Mississippi Medical Center, Jackson, MS, USA.
Background: Covid 19 has been shown to cause neurological
manifestations due to direct infection by the virus or by the
body’s innate and adaptive immune response to infection.
1,4
Patients with underlying neurological conditions can also be
impacted by Covid 19 due to the use of immunosuppressant
therapy. It can be challenging to determine in the emergency
setting if symptoms are due to a viral infection versus the
underlying neurologic condition. Sometimes therapies are
withheld due to this uncertainty. Studies done during the
ongoing Covid 19 pandemic, have shown an increased risk of
hospitalization and death in Covid 19 patients with myasthe-
nia gravis (MG) compared to those without.
2,3 Not much is
known about the safety and ef ﬁcacy of monoclonal antibody
treatments for Covid 19 in myasthenic patients.
Discussion: A 32-year-old woman with acetylcholine
receptor positive MG presented to the Emergency Depart-
ment (ED) with a 2 day history of fever, chills and bilateral
upper and lower extremity weakness. She reported a fall and
gait impairment for one day. Her last IVIG administration
was in 2017. She was on azathioprine, prednisone and
pyridostigmine, and was fully vaccinated for Covid 19 per
CDC recommendations. Her blood pressure was 142/80,
pulse rate 108, temperature 100.1 F and respiratory rate
18/minute. Signi ﬁcant neurological ﬁndings included power
3/5 in bilateral elbow and knee extensors, with the rest of the
muscle groups at power 5/5. Covid PCR test was positive.
Basic Laboratory investigations and a Chest X ray were
unremarkable, and pulmonary mechanics, revealed a NIF of
-50. The patient received a monoclonal antibody cocktail for
Covid 19 infusion in the ED. She reported improvement and
was discharged home after 48 hours. She was seen in clinic a
month later and reported no residual symptoms.
Conclusion: Monoclonal antibody treatment administered
soon after the onset of symptoms is safe and may prevent
myasthenic crisis. Treatment for Covid 19 and variants
should not be withheld uniformly in patients with neuromus-
cular junction disorders.

M268. Genetic Modi ﬁers Determine the Symptom Onset
Age Among ALS/FTD Patients Carrying the C9orf72
Repeat Expansion
Sara Saez-Atienzar, PhD 1, Ileana Lorenzini, PhD 2, Ruth
Chia, PhD 1, Christopher E. Shaw, PhD 3, Rita Sattler, PhD 4,
Isabella Fogh, PhD 3, Bryan J. Traynor, Phd, MD 1. 1National
Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA, 2Department of
Neurobiology, Barrow Neurological Institute, Phoenix, AZ,
USA, 3United Kingdom Dementia Research Institute, Maurice
Wohl Clinical Neuroscience Institute, King ’s College London,
London, United Kingdom, 4Barrow Neurological Institute,
Phoenix, AZ, USA.
Intronic repeat expansions in the C9orf72 gene are the most
common genetic cause of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). One of the most vari-
able features of the C9orf72-related neurodegeneration is the
wide range of age at onset observed among carriers, ranging
from the fourth to the tenth decade of life. Using an exten-
sive genetic analysis based on genetic risk scores in 19,614
ALS cases and 57,710 controls, we identi ﬁed that the risk of
sporadic ALS disease accelerated the age at symptom onset by
three years among C9orf72 c arriers. The results were vali-
dated and replicated in two independent cohorts of
817 C9orf72 carriers and 699 C9orf72 carriers, respectively.
We also discovered that variants within the cytoskeletal path-
way are the primary mediators of this effect. Finally, we inte-
grated the genetic data with C9orf72-disease transcriptomics
from the motor cortex, drug perturbations, and cell-based
high throughput screening experiments to identify drugs to
delay the age of onset among the C9orf72 patients. This
approach nominated drugs that can be prioritized for preclin-
ical development. In conclusion, these ﬁndings represent a
signiﬁcant step forward in understanding the C9orf72-related
pathology and lays the grounds for future preclinical develop-
ments in ALS and FTD.
M269. GQ1b-Positive Miller-Fisher Syndrome Associated
with Ipilimumab and Nivolumab Salvage Therapy for
Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma
Karishma Popli, BS, MBE , Bipasha Mukherjee-Clavin, MD,
PhD, Kemar E. Green, DO. Johns Hopkins University School of
Medicine, Baltimore, MD, USA.
Background: Miller Fisher syndrome (MFS) is a rare
peripheral axonal and demyelinating neuropathy character-
ized by a triad of ataxia, are ﬂexia, and ophthalmoplegia.
Immunotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) is
potentially thought to contribute to immune-mediated
adverse events that trigger MFS. We present a novel case of
anti-GQ1b positive MFS with after immune checkpoint
inhibitor salvage chemotherapy for metastatic renal cell carci-
noma (RCC).
Case Report: A 76-year-old male with hypertension,
hyperlipidemia, prostate cancer, and metastatic RCC
previously on ipilimumab and nivolumab salvage chemother-
apy presented for intermittent diplopia, ptosis, and bilateral
upper extremity weakness. Exam revealed bilateral pseudo-
internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) with mild fatigability,
and left greater than right ptosis with subthreshold improve-
ment after ice-pack test. There was also bilateral deltoid and
quadriceps weakness with mild tenderness to palpation, are-
ﬂexia, truncal ataxia, and a wide-based ataxic gait with dif ﬁ-

culty rising from a seated position. Labs were notable for
elevated creatine kinase (CK), erythrocyte sedimentation rate
(ESR), stable normocytic anemia, and new AST-predominant
hepatocellular transaminitis. Pyridostigmine and prednisone
were initiated and his lower extremity weakness rapidly
improved; however, left eye ptosis continued. Electromyogra-
phy did not show evidence of any demyelinating neuropathy,
neuromuscular junction disorder, or myopathic process; anti-
GQ1b antibody titer was positive. Five sessions of plasma
exchange were then completed while continuing
pyridostigmine; prednisone was tapered. Three months later,
his ocular and bulbar symptoms were completely resolved.
Discussion: The painful proximal weakness, elevated CK
and transaminases were concerning for ICI-associated myosi-
tis. The ptosis and ophthalmoplegia with fatiguability were
concerning for ocular myasthenia gravis secondary to immu-
notherapy versus an immune-mediated orbital myositis.
While myositis and myasthenia gravis are well established
adverse events associated with ICI therapy, the broader differ-
ential also included Lambert Eaton myasthenic syndrome
and the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain Barre Syndrome
given the classic triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and are-
ﬂexia. The positive anti-GQ1b titer con ﬁrmed MFS and
myositis as immune-mediated adverse events. These neuro-
logic adverse effects are thought to arise from the interaction
of the immune checkpoint inhibitors against inhibitory T-
cells leading to uninhibited T-cell activation that attacks
tumor cells as well as healthy tissue, triggering autoimmune
conditions.
Conclusion: This case highlights the importance of con-
sidering immunotherapy-related adverse events, speci ﬁcally
MFS, in patients who present with acute-onset, progressively
worsening neurologic conditions with ophthalmoplegia. It
also suggests that serology testing for common neurologic
adverse events might be useful.

Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a univer-
sally fatal neurodegenerative disease with no cure. While the
pathogenesis of ALS remains unknown, recent studies suggest
that multiple distinct pathogenic mechanisms may converge
on a single ALS phenotype. Human endogenous retroviruses
(HERVs) are repetitive genetic elements found in all individ-
uals and are actively expressed in adults in disease states,
including ALS. HERVs entered our genome millions of years
ago as exogenous retroviruses and integrated into the
germline. Activation of the envelope (env) protein of the
HML-2 subtype of HERV-K, has been directly linked to
motor neuron disease in both ALS patients and mouse
models.
Methods: We leveraged a dataset of 1,517 ALS patient
and 539 control (54% no known neurological disease, 46%
other neurological disease) bulk RNA-sequencing samples
made available through the New York Genome Center
(NYGC) ALS Consortium to determine if there were sub-
groups of ALS patients with elevated expression of HML-2
features.
Results: We discovered that HERV-K feature expression
was highly variable in the ALS patient brain and spinal cord.
To identify patients with high levels of HERV-K transcripts
we utilized both supervised and unsupervised computational
approaches. The unsupervised approach combined HERV
features with non-repetitive element genes as well as patient
and control samples. We found that high HML-2 expression
was signi ﬁcantly associated with an over 3x increased odds of
having ALS as well as increased odds of limb onset ALS with-
out dementia. The supervised analysis utilized a threshold-
based approach to quantify the overall expression of
HERV-K features of interest. Using machine learning with a
75% training and 25% testing data split, we discovered that
a lysine methyl transferase (KMT2A) and an ataxin
(ATXN7) were the most important non-repetitive element
protein coding genes in terms of predicting overall HERV-K

M272. Identi ﬁcation of Predicted Key Interaction
Domains of TDP-43 Reveals Involvement in Downstream
Cellular Events

Department of Neurology, Feinberg School of Medicine,
Northwestern University, Chicago, IL, USA.
Background: TDP-43 is a DNA/RNA binding protein that
is implicated in key cellular events, and it has numerous
domains with distinct functions. TDP-43 pathology is one of
the most broadly observed proteinopathies in amyotrophic
lateral sclerosis (ALS) and is de ﬁned by protein aggregations
including phosphorylated TDP-43. It is important to identify
the correlation between protein-protein interactome activity
with its key functions, and how these protein interactions
contribute to disease pathology.
Methods: To identify the location of the interaction sites
of these proteins High Ambiguity Driven protein −protein
Docking (HADDOCK) software was utilized. This program
takes input of the two protein structures and analyzes different
potential conformations for proteins interaction. The output is
the lowest possible energy interaction dimer. This newly formed
dimer complex is then analyzed to determine the locations of

interaction between TDP-43 and binding partners. After repeti-
tive analysis with TDP-43 and all of its known binding part-
ners, the amino acid residues that interact in each protein
pairings are assessed. The interactome data is utilized to visualize
which of the binding partners interact within the established
domains of TDP-43. The resulting proteins predicted to be
interacting within each domain underwent computational analy-
sis via Ingenuity Pathways Analysis (IPA) to highlight the associ-
ated canonical pathways, upstream and downstream regulators
and signiﬁcantly affected cellular pathways.
Results: The recurrent interaction residues of TDP-43
with binding partners represent the key areas within the
amino acid sequence that will have the greatest impact on
functionality if inactivated by mutations or otherwise. Addi-
tionally, the predicted binding partners within each of the
established domains help predict druggable domains as well
as the functionality and downstream effects of each of the
domains within TDP-43.
Discussion: Our analysis represents a novel computational
approach to protein-protein interaction analysis, which provides
data on the downstream cellular events associated with the
binding partners of TDP-43 and its key functionally active
domains. The speciﬁcd o m a i n“mapping” also provides a poten-
tial avenue for the identi ﬁcation of key spots for drug develop-
ment. In addition, these studies will help understand why
mutations in different regions lead to speci ﬁcp a t h o l o g i e s ,a n d
how more personalized treatment strategies can be developed.

Background: Accumulation of misfolded superoxide
dismutase-1 (SOD1) is a pathological hallmark of
SOD1-related amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and is
observed in sporadic ALS, where its role in pathogenesis is
controversial. Therapeutic approaches that lower disease-
associated transcripts are in development for SOD1-ALS and
other neurodegenerative conditions. Prior studies indicate
that SOD1 has a long half-life (~25 days) in the human cere-
brospinal ﬂuid (CSF) with similar kinetics in the nervous sys-
tem tissue and CSF. Understanding in vivo protein kinetics,
including half-life, may clarify how SOD1 in ﬂuences neu-
rodegeneration and inform optimal dosing for therapeutic
lowering of SOD1 and other long-lived proteins.
Methods: We employed a stable isotope labeling tech-
nique paired with mass spectrometry to determine SOD1
protein kinetics and concentration in CSF of SOD1 muta-
tion carriers and sporadic ALS participants.
Results: In participants with SOD1-A4V mutations,
known to cause rapidly progressive ALS, mutant SOD1 pro-
tein exhibited a faster half-life and displayed lower concentra-
tion compared to corresponding wild-type SOD1 protein. In
contrast, SOD1-D90A and SOD1-A89V mutations, associ-
ated with milder ALS phenotypes, showed prolonged or
unchanged turnover relative to wild-type SOD1, respectively.
Thus, SOD1 mutations variably impact protein kinetics and
stability. In addition, we applied this approach to sporadic
ALS participants and found that SOD1 turnover and concen-
tration is no different compared to controls indicating that
altered kinetics of soluble CSF SOD1 is not associated with
sporadic ALS.
Conclusion: These results highlight the ability of stable
isotope labeling approaches to discern the in ﬂuence of disease
mutations on protein kinetics and support implementation of
this method to optimize clinical trial design of drug dosing
for gene therapies for neurological disorders.
M274. In Vivo Quantitative MRI to Assess Nerve
Pathology in an HNPP Mouse Model
Yongsheng Chen, PhD , Yimin Shen, PhD, Daniel Moiseev,
BS, Zafar Wazir, BS, Bo Hu, PhD, Jun Li, MD, PhD. Wayne
State University School of Medicine, Detroit, MI, USA.
Introduction: HNPP is caused by a heterozygous deletion of
the human PMP22 gene. The pathological hallmark of
HNPP nerve is paranodal myelin thickening, called
‘tomacula’, which is readily detectable in Pmp22 heterozy-
gous knockout ( Pmp22+/-) mouse (a model of HNPP)
around 10-weeks old. The size and prevalence of tomacula
increase over the ﬁrst 6 months of mouse life, but tomacula
degenerate during aging. In addition, our lab has discovered
that myelin junction disruptions take place even during the
early development, leading to excessive myelin permeability
in HNPP nerves. Myelin junction disruptions and tomacula
at various stages would alter the myelin content and water
content in HNPP nerve. This study utilizes multiparametric
quantitative MRI (qMRI) methods to track pathology
changes in mouse sciatic nerves.
Methods: Pmp22+/- (n=9) and Pmp22+/+ (n=8) mice
were imaged with in vivo 7T qMRI at 3-, 6-, and 12-month
old (mo), to quantify the bilateral sciatic nerve in several bio-
physic properties, including T1, T2, proton density (PD),

magnetization transfer ratio (MTR), fractional anisotropy
(FA), mean diffusivity (MD), axial diffusivity (AD) and radial
diffusivity (RD). After the MRI at 12-mo, nerve conduction
studies were performed, followed by sciatic nerve dissection to
prepare semi-thin sections and teased nerve ﬁbers for mor-
phological and biochemical experiments, as described.
Results: There were signi ﬁcantly lower nerve PD
(p=0.002) and T1 ( p=0.006) values in Pmp22+/- mice com-
pared with those in Pmp22+/+ mice at 6-mo. In contrast, the
nerve T2, MTR, FA, MD, AD, and RD values were compa-
rable at 6-mo. There was no difference for all qMRI indices
between the two groups at 3-mo. Longitudinal data measured
from 3- to 6-mo showed signi ﬁcantly reduced nerve PD
values for Pmp22+/- ( p=0.012) mice. In contrast, the nerve
T2, MTR, and T1 values were unchanged for both groups
from 3- to 6-mo. The 12-mo data collection is ongoing.
Conclusions: This work demonstrated that multi-
parametric qMRI is able to assess in vivo mouse nerve pathol-
ogy longitudinally. The qMRI results in this study indicate a
lower total water content in Pmp22+/- nerves compared with
those in wild type nerves at 6-mo, which is in line with the
excessive myelin due to tomacula (thus, a relatively reduced
water content) in Pmp22+/- nerves. Ongoing research is to
correlate qMRI ﬁndings with morphological, electrophysio-
logical, and biochemical readouts from the same nerves to
ﬁnd molecular substrates responsible for the qMRI changes.

Background: AChR mutations causing slow-channel con-
genital myasthenic syndrome (CMS) are dominantly
inherited with prolonged channel opening kinetics. How-
ever, the pathogenic mechanism of recessively inherited
CMS mutations with slow-channel kinetics has not been
characterized. The 13 residue-long Cys-loop plays a key role
in coupling agonist binding to channel gating. Though only
one residue in Cys-loop is invariant in all Cys-loop recep-
tors, the loop length is unchanged among all subunits across
all species. However, its signi ﬁcance in receptor activation
has never been addressed.
Methods: Whole exome and Sanger sequencing, AChR
expression in HEK cells, α-bungarotoxin binding assay, single
channel patch-clamp recordings, maximum likelihood

Satralizumab, a Therapeutic Recycling Antibody
Targeting the IL-6 Receptor, in Patients with Generalized
Myasthenia Gravis

Background: Generalized myasthenia gravis (gMG), a rare,
chronic, autoimmune disease affecting the neuromuscular
junction, results in life-debilitating fatigable muscle weakness.
More effective, tolerable, and convenient therapies for a
broad patient population with gMG are needed. Interleukin
6 (IL-6) has been associated with disease activity and severity
in autoimmune diseases, suggesting IL-6 may be a viable
therapeutic target. Satralizumab, a humanized IL-6 receptor
monoclonal antibody, was engineered to provide durable sup-
pression of IL-6 signaling. Satralizumab has >3.5 years ’ efﬁ-
cacy and >7 years ’ safety data in patients with neuromyelitis
optica spectrum disorder in two phase 3 trials (SAkuraSky
[NCT02028884] and SAkuraStar [NCT02073279]).
Objective: LUMINESCE (NCT04963270) is a random-
ized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the
efﬁcacy, safety, pharmacokinetics (PK), and pharmacodynam-
ics (PD) of satralizumab in a broad patient population
with gMG.

Study design: LUMINESCE will enroll ~240 participants
(including ~20 adolescents aged ≥12 years) with seropositive
gMG (AChR-IgG+, MuSK-IgG+, or LRP4-IgG+), a Myasthe-
nia Gravis Foundation of America (MGFA) severity Class II-
IV, a Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living (MG-ADL)
score ≥5 (with a non-ocular contribution >50%), and who are
receiving stable background therapy. Participants will be ran-
domized 1:1 to receive either satralizumab or placebo in addi-
tion to background therapy. A 24-week double-blind period
will be followed by an open-label extension for ~2 years.
Endpoints: The primary endpoint is mean change in total
MG-ADL score at Week 24 (in the AChR-IgG+ population).
Key secondary endpoints include mean change in total MG-
ADL score at Week 24 (in the overall population), and evalu-
ating the ef ﬁcacy of satralizumab on function in daily life,
quality of life, clinical status, and disease severity in the
AChR-IgG+ and overall populations. Additional endpoints
include the safety, PK/PD, and the immunogenicity of
satralizumab. Serum and cellular mechanistic biomarkers will
be investigated to evaluate satralizumab activity and to
increase the understanding of disease biology in gMG.
Conclusion: LUMINESCE is the ﬁrst study to assess inhi-
bition of IL-6 signaling in gMG. LUMINESCE will assess
the ef ﬁcacy, safety, and PK/PD of satralizumab as an add-on
therapy in a broad patient population with gMG.
M278. Methadone Withdrawal Induced Dystonia
Pukhraj S. Nijhar, Student
1, Manmeet S. Sahni, student 1,
Alan R. Hirsch, MD 2. 1Aurues University School of Medicine,
Oranjestad, Aruba, 2Smell and Taste Treatment and Research
Foundation, Chicago, IL, USA.
Introduction: While heroin withdrawal has been noted to
induce dystonic movements (Ghosh, 2019), methadone
withdrawal has not heretofore been described to induce
dystonia.
Methods: Case Study: This 39 year old woman without a
past history of movement disorder, presented with a past his-
tory of opioid dependence with use of 140 mg per day of
methadone for 4 1/2 years. Two days prior to admission, she
used heroin, 1/2 gram intravenously. Upon admission, her
methadone was dropped from 140 mg per day to 100 mg
per day. Two days later she developed trismus and spasms of
the back and legs, acutely responding to 50 mg diphenhydra-
mine intramuscular, shortly thereafter the spasms recurred.
This required three additional injections at which point the
generalized spasms resolved. The trismus and muscle spasms
recurred multiple times a day over the next three days,
responding to intramuscular diphenhydramine. Because of
the persistent dystonic symptoms, the methadone was raised
to 140 mg a day at which point the dystonic movements
resolved and have not recurred.

Results: Mental status examination: Mood: anxious with
labile and fearful affect. Judgment: fair to poor. Mood:
depressed with a passive desire to die. Urine toxicology
screening: positive for heroin, opioids, methamphetamine
and cocaine.
Discussion: Dystonia, a form of hyperkinesia, is seen in
states of dopamine excess in the striatum (Jain, 2021). The
release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens is inhibited by
GABA A interneurons (Ghosh, 2019). Opioids act to inhibit
GABA A interneurons, thus disinhibiting the dopaminergic
neurons leading to dopamine excess and dystonia (Ghosh,
2019). Opioids, including methadone, act on the ventral teg-
mental area inhibiting GABA A interneurons, thus
disinhibiting dopamine neurons, causing dopamine release,
leading to dystonia. Opioid (including methadone) with-
drawal does the opposite, enhancing GABA A interneuron
ﬁring leading to a reduction of dopamine release and thus a
relative dopamine depletion state. A dopamine depleted state
is not known to cause dystonia, but rather parkinsonoid-like
features. This conundrum can be explained with the assump-
tion that dystonia is not from the striatum but rather from
the cerebellum (Le doux, 2022). Dystonia has been postu-
lated to be primarily due to abnormalities in the cerebellar-
basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuit (Gianni, 2022). In those
who present with acute dystonia, query as to methadone use
and withdrawal is warranted and in those who are on metha-
done whom develop dystonia, treatment with increasing
methadone dosage may be worthwhile.
M279. Mitochondrial Dysregulation Occurs Early in ALS
Motor Cortex with TDP-43 Pathology and Suggests
Maintaining NAD
+ Balance as a Therapeutic Strategy
Kate Pauss, B.S. , Mukesh Gautum, PhD, Hande Ozdinler,
PhD. Northwestern University, Chicago, IL, USA.
Mitochondria is one of the key cellular organelles that gener-
ate ATP, and metabolites required for various cellular func-
tions. In diseases, such as ALS (amyloid lateral sclerosis), we
and others ﬁnd early mitochondrial defects, such as dys-
regulation of NAD+ balance. Since TDP-43 pathology is
broadly observed in a wide spectrum of ALS patients, includ-
ing sALS, fALS, and ALS/FTLD, it is no surprise that mito-
chondrial problems are also associated with TDP-43
pathology. Our results with high performance liquid chroma-
tography and mass spectrometry, and metabolomic pro ﬁling
of healthy and diseased TDP-43 motor cortex further corrob-
orated low levels of NAD+, suggesting maintaining NAD+
balance as a potential therapeutic strategy. We recently dis-
covered that regardless of species, the upper motor neurons
(UMNs) of patients (a.k.a. Betz cells) and UMNs of well-
characterized mouse models (a.k.a. CSMN) display very early
and profound mitochondrial defects when they are af ﬂicted
by TDP-43 pathology, revealing that translation is at a cellu-
lar level. Therefore, we focus our attention to the cells,
namely to the diseased UMNs. We thus generated
UCHL1-eGFP mice, which genetically labels UMNs with
eGFP expression, so that they can be distinguished among
other cortical cells and neurons in culture. Since nicotin-
amide mononucleotide (NMN) has been shown to improve
NAD+ levels, we investigated whether NMN treatment
would restore the health of diseased UMNs using the
prpTDP-43A315T-UeGFP mice, which is the UMN
reporter line with TDP-43 pathology. We ﬁnd that short-
term NMN treatment improves the overall health of UMNs

diseased by TDP-43 pathology, as quantitatively measured
by extension of axon outgrowth and enhanced arborization,
in vitro. Most interestingly, NMN treatment also restores
mitochondrial stability, especially at the site of inner mem-
brane, which is the key component for its function. In sum-
mary, we identify early mitochondrial defects in ALS motor
cortex with TDP-43 pathology, identify a druggable target,
and show preliminary results revealing the importance of
maintaining NAD+ balance for improved UMN health.

mutations causing congenital myasthenic syndrome (CMS)

M282. NU-9 Improves Health of HSOD1G93A Mouse
Upper Motor Neurons In Vitro, Especially in
Combination with Riluzole or Edaravone

Baris Genc, PhD, Mukesh Guatam, PhD, Benjamin Helmold,
Undergraduate, Hande Ozdinler, PhD. Northwestern
University, Chicago, IL, USA.
Even though amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a disease
of the upper and lower motor neurons, to date none of the
compounds in clinical trials have been tested for improving
the health of diseased upper motor neurons (UMNs). There
is an urgent need to develop preclinical assays that include
UMN health as a readout. Since ALS is a complex disease,
combinatorial treatment strategies will be required to address
the mechanisms perturbed in patients. Here, we describe a
novel in vitro platform that takes advantage of an UMN
reporter line in which UMNs are genetically labeled with
ﬂuorescence and have misfolded SOD1 toxicity. In a previ-
ous study, both hSOD1
G93A and prpTDP-43 A315T ALS
mouse models treated by daily oral gavage with NU-9 from
postnatal day (P)60 to P120 showed signi ﬁcant improvement
in structural integrity of both mitochondria and endoplasmic
reticulum within diseased UMNs and reduced UMN degen-
eration. Here, we continue to investigate UMN health by
observing axon outgrowth and arborization, two established
neuronal health parameters, in response to NU-9. We report
that NU-9, an analog of the cyclohexane-1,3-dione family of
compounds, improves the health of UMNs with misfolded
SOD1 toxicity more effectively than riluzole or edaravone,
-the only two FDA-approved ALS drugs to date-. Riluzole
was identi ﬁed to mainly reduce astrogliosis and edaravone
was reported to be a free-radical scavenger. On the other
hand NU-9 improves mitochondrial health, reduces protein
aggregation and improves cytoarchitectural integrity. Since
these compounds have different mode of actions, we investi-
gated NU-9 in combination with riluzole or edaravone, and
found an additive effect on improved UMN health, as they
extended longer axons and displayed enhanced branching
and arborization. These results suggest the importance of
cell-based and mechanism-focused drug discovery so that
enhanced improvements can be achieved by combinatorial
approaches.

Introduction: IC14 (atibuclimab) is a monoclonal anti-
CD14 antibody that may target T-regulatory (T-reg) cell
function. A previous phase 1 trial of 10 participants with
amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) demonstrated initial safety
of IC14 for a single cycle of treatment. We provided long-
term treatment with IC14 to 17 individuals with ALS via an
expanded access protocol (EAP) and documented target
engagement, safety, and disease endpoints.
Methods: Participants received intravenous IC14 every
two weeks. Consistent with FDA guidelines, participants
were ineligible for clinical trials and the EAP was inclusive of
a broad population. Participants unable to travel to MGH
due to the COVID-19 pandemic or disease progression, were
transitioned to infusions in-home or local clinics. Blood sam-
ples for hematology, chemistry, and coagulation were col-
lected to monitor safety. The Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R) was adminis-
tered monthly to track disease progression. Respiratory func-
tion was measured through slow vital capacity tests - data for
this is limited due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Whole
blood and serum were collected to determine monocyte
CD14 receptor occupancy (RO), soluble CD14, and anti-
drug antibodies (ADA). Ex vivo T regulatory functional
assays were performed with ﬁve participants.
Results: Participants received IC14 for up to 103 weeks
(average: 30.1 weeks, range: 1-103 weeks). Treatment-
emergent adverse events were uncommon, mild, and self-lim-
ited. There were 18 serious adverse events (SAEs) which were
related to disease progression and unrelated (17) or likely
unrelated (1) to IC14. Three participants died due to disease
progression. Most participants achieved >80% monocyte
mCD14 RO on a 14-day dosing schedule, although one
individual required more frequent dosing (every 10 days) to
achieve >80% RO. ADA were detected in only one partici-
pant and were transient, low titer, and non-neutralizing. T-
regs were isolated from the available longitudinal samples and
assayed for suppression of CD4 T cell proliferation and cyto-
kine production versus baseline T-reg activity.
Conclusion: IC14 administration to ALS patients was safe
and well tolerated in this EAP, with no signi ﬁcant changes in
laboratory tests and no drug-related SAEs. Measuring RO

M285. TDP-43 Regulates Splicing of Human
Endogenous Retrovirus-K Envelope Gene: Role in
Neurodegenerative Diseases
Darshan Pandya, M.D. , Marta Garcia Montojo, Ph.D,
Avindra Nath, M.D.. National Institute of Neurological
Disorders and Stroke, Bethesda, MD, USA.
Background: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is a
ubiquitous nuclear protein involved in RNA splicing. Cyto-
solic aggregates are found in cortical neurons of amyotrophic
lateral sclerosis (ALS) patients as well as in frontotemporal
dementia, limbic predominant age-related TDP-43 encepha-
lopathy, and some patients with Alzheimer ’sd i s e a s e .H o w -
ever, its role in disease pathophysiology is poorly
understood. Human endogenous retroviruses (HERVs) com-
pose 8% of the human genome via millions of years of inte-
gration into germ cells. They are critical in embryogenesis
but are silenced in adults. HML-2 is a subtype of HERV-K,
and its envelope (Env) protein is neurotoxic and upregulated
in the CNS of ALS patients. HML-2 env mRNA can
undergo secondary splicing to produce np9 and rec from
HML-2 Type I and Type II proviruses, respectively. By
manipulating TDP-43 expression in vitro, we assessed the
relationship between TDP-43 and levels of HML-2 env and
its spliced products.
Methods: Since overexpression of TDP-43 produces cyto-
solic accumulation, wild-type (WT) TDP-43 was over-
expressed or knocked down via transfection in HEK293 cells.
M337V, a TDP-43 mutant found in a subset of ALS
patients, was similarly assessed. Levels of env, rec, and np9
transcripts were then evaluated using qRT-PCR.
Results: Overexpression of wild type TDP-43 resulted in
>6-fold increase in expression of rec transcript levels
(6.46/C63.31, p=0.006) and knockdown of TDP-43 resulted
in signi ﬁcant reductions in rec (0.65 /C60.28, p=0.025) and
np9 (0.58 /C60.23, p=0.004) relative to transfection with a
control empty vector. Env levels were unaffected by either
treatment (1.054 /C60.29, p=0.68). Rec:env and np9:env ratios
were also measured. Overexpression of TDP-43 increased the
rec:env ratio (6.17 /C63.22, p=0.007). Knockdown reduced the
rec:env ratio (0.7 /C60.37, p=0.076) and np9:env ratio
(0.6/C60.23, p=0.025). Transfection with the M337V TDP-
43 variant has thus far mirrored the effects WT TDP-43
transfection on rec and np9 transcripts levels.
Conclusions: TDP-43 cytosolic accumulation is widely
found in CNS tissue of ALS patients, and HERV-K
(HML-2) elements are implicated in the pathology of
ALS as well. Our in vitro experiments demonstrate direct
correlations between WT and ALS-speci ﬁcm u t a n tT D P -
43 expression and resultant rec and np9 transcript levels.
This phenomenon may delineate a role for TDP-43 in
HML-2 neurotoxicity, potentially through the secondary
splicing of HML-2 env. Rec and Np9 expression should
be evaluated in disease states as possible therapeutic
targets.
M286. The Effect of Surgical Weight Loss on Neuropathy
in the Severely Obese
Evan L. Reynolds, Ph.D., Maya Watanabe, B.S., Melissa
Elafros, M.D., Ph.D., Mousumi Banerjee, Ph.D., Eva
L. Feldman, M.D., Ph.D. , Brian C. Callaghan, M.D., M.S..
University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA.
Objective: The aim of this study was to determine the effect
of surgical weight loss on neuropathy outcomes in people
with severe obesity.

Methods: We completed a prospective cohort study of
participants with severe obesity who underwent bariatric sur-
gery. At baseline and at 2 years following bariatric surgery,
participants had outcome measurements and underwent met-
abolic phenotyping. The updated National Cholesterol Edu-
cation Program criteria were used to de ﬁne the metabolic
syndrome and its individual components. The co-primary
outcomes were changes in intraepidermal nerve ﬁber density
(IENFD, units= ﬁbers/mm) at the distal leg and proximal
thigh. Secondary outcomes included nerve conduction stud-
ies, Michigan Neuropathy Screening Instrument (MNSI)
questionnaire and examination, Neuro-QOL, and quantita-
tive sensory testing (QST).
Results: Among 138 baseline participants, 80 (mean (stan-
dard deviation) age: 45.6 (11.2) years, 72.5% female) com-
pleted 2 years of follow-up. Participants lost 31.9 (17.5)
kg. All metabolic syndrome components improved with the
exception of blood pressure. IENFD in the proximal thigh
(baseline: 15.0 (7.9), 2-year: 18.4 (7.5), p<0.01) improved
and IENFD in the distal leg (baseline: 8.5 (6.9), 2-year: 8.6
(6.0), p=0.92) did not signi ﬁcantly change. Signi ﬁcant
improvements were observed on the MNSI questionnaire,
Neuro-QOL, and QST vibration threshold.
Conclusions: Surgical weight loss was associated with
improvements in all metabolic parameters except blood pres-
sure, and IENFD of the proximal thigh improved after
2 years. Metabolic and neuropathy speci ﬁc outcome improve-
ments were more robust than a previous comparable study of
medical weight loss.

M288. Upper Motor Neurons are a Target for Gene
Therapy and UCHL1 is Necessary and Suf ﬁcient to
Improve Cellular Integrity of Diseased Upper Motor
Neurons
Angela Ahrens, Bachelor ’s, Barıs¸ Genç, PhD, Öge Gözütok,
PhD, Hande Özdinler, PhD. Northwestern University,
Chicago, IL, USA.
Upper motor neuron (UMN) degeneration is a hallmark of
ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), which is a rare motor
neuron disease with no effective cure. Since movement starts
in the brain, our goal is to develop effective treatment strate-
gies to improve the health of diseased UMNs. Here, we
reveal that UMNs are indeed valid cellular targets for gene
therapy. In addition, we identify UCHL1 (ubiquitin C-
terminal hydrolase-L1), as a novel gene that improves the
health and cellular integrity of UMNs that are diseased due
to two important, yet unrelated, causes of ALS, namely
mutant SOD1 toxicity and TDP-43 pathology. Directed
delivery of UCHL1, speci ﬁcally to the diseased UMNS,
improve their cellular stability, soma size and reduce the
extent of vacuolization observed in their apical dendrites. We
utilize AAV2-mediated gene delivery either by retrograde
transduction upon spinal cord injection, or via direct motor
cortex injection. These cellular improvements are observed in
the UMNs of both hSOD1
G93A and prpTDP-43 A315T mice,

which are well characterized mouse models for mutant
SOD1 toxicity and TDP-43 pathology, respectively. Our
ongoing studies aim to improve the extent of selective UMN
transduction upon direct motor cortex injection, and to
deliver UCHL1 to the ALS motor cortex in an effort to
investigate the impact of improving UMN health to the over-
all motor neuron circuitry.

Nervous System Involvement

Background: West Nile Virus (WNV) is a mosquito-borne
RNA virus that in recent years has become endemic to the
United States. Although many patients infected with WNV are
asymptomatic, some may develop symptoms ranging from mild
febrile illnesses to severe nervous system involvement, including
meningitis and acute ﬂaccid paralysis. Those with nervous sys-
tem involvement have increased morbidity and mortality; there-
fore, swift diagnosis and intervention is required.
Case Report: A 69-year-old African American man with
coronary artery disease, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus
presented with acute onset bilateral leg weakness, numbness
of hands and feet and frequent falls that started two days
prior. Initial neurological examination revealed symmetric
bilateral weakness of proximal and distal upper extremities
with 4/5 strength, bilateral hip ﬂexion weakness with 1/5
strength and bilateral knee ﬂexion and extension weakness
with 4/5 strength. Deep tendon re ﬂexes were absent in all
four extremities. There were no sensory de ﬁcits. Cerebral spi-
nal ﬂuid (CSF) was relevant for marked elevated protein
(241), mild elevation of glucose (72) and no pleocytosis or
xanthochromia. Creatine kinase was elevated (2324), likely
secondary to falls. MRI of the brain, cervical, thoracic, and
lumbar spine were unremarkable. Electromyogram and nerve
conduction study demonstrated prolonged left tibial F waves,
prolonged median motor latency, moderate slowing and
reduced recruitment, which was concerning for early non-
length dependent demyelinating neuropathy. The weakness
rapidly and asymmetrically progressed. By day 7, he had
decreased tone throughout, with worsening strength of bilat-
eral upper extremities, bilateral knees, bilateral hand grip, and
worsening dorsiﬂexion and plantar ﬂexion bilaterally. This was
concerning for incipient acute in ﬂammatory demyelinating
polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP). He was started on IVIG
therapy of 0.4 g/kg/day for ﬁve days. The patient ’s pulmo-
nary function remained at baseline and his strength contin-
ued to improve. He was discharged to acute rehab on day
17, with normal strength of bilateral upper extremities,
