K-M123. Brain Structure and Clinical Endpoints in
Myotonic Dystrophy Type 2
Araya Puwanant, MD, MS
1, Laura A. Flashman, PhD 1,
Carolina Burgos Aguilar, MS 1, Joseph Rigdon, PhD 1, Suzanne
Craft, PhD1, Peggy Nopoulos, MD 2. 1Wake Forest School of
Medicine, Winston Salem, NC, USA, 2University of Iowa,
Iowa City, IA, USA.
Background: Myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2) is a pleio-
tropic multi-systemic disease. Although muscle weakness is
the main symptom in DM2, almost 70% of the patients
report cognitive de ﬁcits as one of the most disabling symp-
toms, which markedly affects their quality of life. Previous
studies suggest that cerebral white matter (WM) is primarily
affected in DM2. However, brain imaging studies incorpo-
rate with cognitive and motor endpoints are extremely
limited.
Objective: To evaluate quantitative magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) measures of brain structure with a focus on
white matter integrity and their relationships with cognitive
and motor endpoints in DM2.
Methods: Structural 3T brain MRIs were acquired in
10 adults with DM2 and 10 age and gender-matched con-
trols. Brain morphometry and WM integrity were assessed
using T1 MP-RAGE and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI)
sequences, respectively. DTI scalars, including fractional
anisotropy (FA), radial diffusivity (RD), and axial diffusivity
(AD), were compared between the two groups. A comprehen-
sive battery of cognitive and motor measures was performed
and correlated with MRI measures using Spearman ’s
Correlation.
Results: Of 20 participants (60% female), mean age (62.2
vs. 62.6 years) and education (16.4 vs. 17.5 years) were simi-
lar between two groups. Compared to controls, the DM2
group showed a signi ﬁcant reduction in global measures of
cerebral gray matter volume in both cortex and deep struc-
tures (mean difference, -0.03; P-value<0.01), but not the
white matter volume. Widespread abnormalities in DTI mea-
sures (lower FA, higher RD) were among the most robust
ﬁndings in DM2 (mean differences of FA, 0.04; P-
value<0.01 and RD, 0.00004; P-value<0.01), indicating that
the pathology is within WM microstructures. Although not
signiﬁcant, the DM2 group scored lower than controls in all
cognitive domains, particularly executive function (mean dif-
ference, -12.5; P-value=0.07). All motor endpoints were sig-
niﬁcantly different between groups. We found a very strong
correlation between cerebral RD and grip strength ( rho=
-0.81, P-value=0.005), while FA was strongly correlated with
a test of executive function ( rho=0.71, P-value=0.02). RD
was also moderately correlated with a 10-meter gait speed
(rho=0.55, P-value=0.12).
Conclusion: Our pilot data demonstrate robust differences
in brain structure, explicitly cerebral gray matter volume and
WM integrity between the DM2 group vs. controls. The
strong correlations between DTI measures and clinical end-

points support the notion that WM integrity plays an impor-
tant role in executive function and mediating motor
performance already compromised from dystrophic muscle
pathology in DM2.

K-M125. Characterizing Dysphagia-Related
Complications for Persons Living with ALS

Background: Difﬁculty swallowing (dysphagia), caused by
weakness and/or spasticity of the muscles of mastication,
affects up to 85% of persons living with ALS and is one of
the most severe and debilitating symptoms of the disease.
Due to the degenerative nature of ALS, management
options for dysphagia are limited. At present, our under-
standing of the frequency of complications associated with
dysphagia in this population is limited. As a result, best
practices for dysphagia management are unclear and practice
patterns surrounding dysphagia management are highly
variable.

Objective: The goal of this work is to improve our under-
standing of the frequency of complications of dysphagia to
help inform decision-making surrounding dysphagia or
patients living with ALS.
Methods: Data was extracted from the Mass General Bri-
gham (MGB) Healthcare System Research Patient Data Reg-
istry (RPDR), which allows researchers to access medical
record information from patients that have been cared for
within the MGB Healthcare System. We identi ﬁed patients
with inclusion criteria including ICD10-CM diagnoses of
amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (G12.21) and an emergency
room visit or inpatient admission at Massachusetts General
Hospital or Brigham and Women ’s Hospital during the
period from January 1, 2019, through December 21, 2019.
Dysphagia or dysphagia-related complications associated with
emergency room visits or inpatient admissions were de ﬁned
as those hospitalizations with ICD-10 diagnosis codes for
dysphagia (R13.10-R13.13), aspiration pneumonia (J69.0),
gastrostomy complication (K94.1, Z43.1), dehydration
(E86.0), or malnutrition (E46). Descriptive statistics were
used to describe the total and cause-speci ﬁc number and pro-
portion of participants who experienced a dysphagia-related
complication.
Results: In total, 374 participants with ALS were seen
between 1/1/19 and 12/31/19. Among those, two hundred
and twenty-three (60%) had a hospitalization. Twenty per-
cent of all patients had dysphagia-related complications asso-
ciated with the hospitalization. Among those participants
with hospitalization, seventy- ﬁve (34%) participants had
dysphagia-related complications. Sixteen percent of hospitali-
zation were associated with gastrostomy complications, 13%
with dif ﬁculty eating/drinking, 13% with aspiration pneumo-
nia, and 11% with malnutrition and/or dehydration.
Conclusions: For patients living with ALS, dysphagia-
related complications are associated with 1/3 of ED and hos-
pital admissions and appear to be present in patients with
feeding tubes (gastrostomy complications) and without feed-
ing tubes (dehydration/malnutrition). Future work examining
differences in dysphagia-related complications between
patients with and without feeding tubes as well as patient
characteristics associated with dysphagia-related complications
is critical to help improve decision-making surrounding dys-
phagia management.

and multisystemic features. A potential biomarker of disease

with disease-speci ﬁc motor endpoints in patients with DM2.

thigh and calf compartments in both legs. MFF (%) was cal-

ber of comparisons; thus, the signi ﬁcant level was set at
α=0.05/4 or 0.0125.

(89% female), and the mean disease duration was
20/C612 years. The highest MFF at the thigh was the posterior
compartment (39.7 /C612.9%), and the calf was the lateral
compartment (35.1 /C68.7%). The mean MFF of the posterior
thigh compartment was signi ﬁcantly correlated with a
6-minute walk distance ( ρ=- 0.90, P-value=0.001), while the

M215. Case Report of an Older Glioblastoma Patient
Surviving More Than 12 Years After Treatment with
Cilengitide in Addition to Standard Therapy
Huda Alalami, MD , Jethro Hu, MD, Xuemo Fan, MD,
Serguei I. Bannykh, MD. Cedars Sinai Medical Center, Los
Angeles, CA, USA.
Objective: To report the very long-term survival without dis-
ease recurrence in an older patient with glioblastoma after
treatment with cilengitide in addition to standard therapy.
Background: Glioblastoma is the most common malig-
nant brain tumor. Median survival is ~15 months in the gen-
eral population, and worse in older patients. Less than 1% of
patients survive longer than 10 years. Integrins have been
implicated in tumorigenesis due to their role in cell adhesion
and migration and their ability to allow for intercellular com-
munication. Cilengitide, a selective αvβ3, and αvβ5 integrin
inhibitor, was studied in several trials for patients with
glioblastoma.
Results: A 77-year-old (age at diagnosis) woman was
found to have a left temporoparietal MGMT methylated

glioblastoma after presenting with right visual ﬁ
eld de ﬁcits in
2009. She underwent near gross total resection of the tumor.
The tumor had retained expression of PTEN and MAPK.
No mutations in IDH or ATRX were detected. Genetic test-
ing revealed mutations in TERT promoter, TP53, SYNE1,
NF1, PTEN, FBXW7, POLD1, ERG, and PRKDC. She
was enrolled in the CENTRIC trial, a phase III clinical trial
studying the addition of cilengitide to standard therapy for
patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma with methylated
MGMT promoter. In 2013, the initial results of the study
failed to meet the endpoint of prolonged overall survival and
progression-free survival, therefore the study was halted. The
patient chose to continue receiving cilengitide through com-
passionate use until 2016. Surveillance brain MRI has been
obtained every three months and shows no radiographic evi-
dence of recurrence so far.
Conclusion: Although it is known that methylated-
MGMT promoter is one of the few positive prognostic fac-
tors in GBM, overall survival remains poor in older patients.
This case highlights a rare clinical response to treatment in
an older female who has survived more than 12 years without
disease recurrence after receiving cilengitide in addition to
standard therapy. Her outcome may have been in ﬂuenced by
the expression of PTEN and the methylation of MGMT,
which are associated with improved outcomes. Although the
development of cilengitide was halted for lack of ef ﬁcacy, the
existence of individual responders such as this patient sug-
gests that further study of integrin inhibition for glioblastoma
patients may be worth pursuing.

Objective: Adult gliomas tumors are occasionally confused

fuse glioma, who had a CSF analysis including oligoclonal

by a trained neurologist.

tory of seizure or radiotherapy treatment (p>0.05).

Background: Recent literature has described the develop-
ment of communicating hydrocephalus after gamma knife
radiosurgery (GKRS) in patients with vestibular
schwannoma (VS). However, there is minimal detail regard-
ing the extent of recovery in these patients with CSF
shunting. This information would help clinicians weigh the
risks and bene ﬁts of shunt surgery. We describe two such
patients who received shunt placement and made a signi ﬁ-
cant recovery.
Case 1: 81-year-old female who had GKRS 20 months
ago for VS presented with a one-month history of progressing
gait instability, cognitive decline, and lethargy. Due to con-
cern for hydrocephalus, a diagnostic high-volume lumbar
puncture (LP) was performed. Opening pressure was
23 mmHg and CSF showed elevated protein of 316.2. Her
Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) initially was 12 and
did not change signi ﬁcantly (11 one hour post-LP, 12 ﬁve
hours post-LP), however her timed 9-meter walk improved
from 36 to 21 seconds after LP, so patient underwent ven-
triculoperitoneal (VP) shunt surgery. 52 days after VP shunt
placement, she was seen in the clinic. Her MoCA was
24, and she could walk 9 meters in 10 seconds.
Case 2: A 79-year-old female who had GKRS 6 months
ago for VS presented with a two-week history of progressing
gait instability, cognitive decline, lethargy, and urinary incon-
tinence. A diagnostic high-volume LP was performed. Open-
ing pressure was 25 mmHg and CSF showed elevated
protein of 66.2. Her MoCA initially was 10 and did not
change signi ﬁcantly (11 one hour post-LP, 11 ﬁve hours
post-LP), however her timed 6.5-meter walk improved from
75 to 47 seconds after LP, so patient underwent VP shunt
surgery. 49 days after VP shunt placement, she was seen in
the clinic. Her MoCA was 25, and she could walk 6.5 meters
in 13 seconds. She had no further episodes of incontinence.

period in patients with vestibular schwannoma following
GKRS. Unlike idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus,
where patients can have a limited recovery after shunt place-
ment, patients with this form of secondary hydrocephalus
appear to make a signi ﬁcant recovery in gait and cognition
following shunting.

M220. Integrin a4b1 Blockade Improves Locomotion in
Mice with CD19-CAR T Cell Neurotoxicity
Lila Faulhaber, BS , Olivia D ’Costa, BS candidate, Juliane
Gust, MD PhD. Seattle Children ’s Research Institute, Seattle,
WA, USA.
Background: Neurotoxicity remains a serious concern in

chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell treatment for
hematologic malignancies. It affects ~40% of patients and
can lead to seizures, coma, and in rare cases death from
cerebral edema. The mechanism of this toxicity remains
poorly understood. In a mouse model, we have shown that
>10% of brain capillaries become plugged by leukocytes by
day 6 after infusion of CD19-directed CAR T cells. This
is associated with impairments in exploration and motor
function. We hypothesized that neurotoxicity could be
ameliorated by blocking the adhesion molecule interaction
between circulating leukocytes and the brain endothelium,
thus restoring capillary blood ﬂow. Since the interaction of
integrinα4β1 with VCAM1 is key to T cell neuro-autoim-
munity, we tested whether blocking integrin α4 can
decrease brain capillary plugging and improve behavioral
neurotoxicity.
Approach: Integrin α4 antibodies (2mg/kg, clone PS/2)
were given intravenously to mice on days 1,3, and 5 after
CAR T cell infusion. We measured daily neurologic symp-
tom scores, open ﬁeld behavior, and expression of VCAM1
on brain endothelium. To determine the effect on brain cap-
illary perfusion, we injected DiI-coated 2 μm microbeads
i.v. on day 6 after CAR T treatment and sacri ﬁed the mice
8h later. The number of beads that were found lodged in
brain capillaries on histologic analysis was interpreted as a
proxy measure for non ﬂowing capillaries.
Results: Mice treated with anti-integrin α4 antibodies had
improved locomotion speed compared to mice treated with
isotype control antibodies (2.3cm/s vs 1.4cm/s). However,
the number of microbeads that accumulated in brain capil-
laries was higher in the mice treated with integrin α4 anti-
bodies (198% of isotype control).
Conclusions: Integrin α4 blockade improved behavioral
measures of neurotoxicity in CAR T cell treated mice, but
paradoxically increased brain capillary plugging. This surpris-
ing result could indicate that brain capillary plugging does
not directly cause behavioral changes, and that interactions
between immune cells, which also require integrins, play a
role in modulating neurotoxicity.

Cushing Disease (CD) and/or Nelson Syndrome (NS) by ana-
lyzing the outcomes of complete r emission and optimal overall
survival as well as comparing it with conventional neurosurgery.
Methods: Descriptive and clinical studies in English or Span-
ish belonging to diagnosed CD and/or NS patients, who have
hypercortisolemia secondary to ACTH-producing pituitary ade-
noma were included. Patients that have undergone conventional
RT or SRS as a primary intervention, were included as well as
studies comparing any of these radiation procedures to
conventional neurosurgery. The databases queried were
MEDLINE, SCOPUS, GOOGLE SCHOLAR, VHL, and

assessment of each included study was performed with the
NHLBI tools.

assessed for inclusion. Of those, thirty-three studies included
in this review were evaluated in various parameters, and data
such as demographic information, type of RT, dosage,
region, time until remission, and complications were
extracted. Most of the studies published from 1972 to 2019
were from the US (48.65%), 19 of them belong to patients
subjected to SRS and 14 to RT as initial treatment. A total

puted tomography (CT) scan of the chest which revealed bilat-
eral pulmonary nodules. The HIV test was negative.
Subsequently, the patient underwent a core needle biopsy
of the left axillary lymph node which revealed CD20,
CD10, c-MYC, and BCL6 positive lymphoid cells. The Ki-
67 proliferation index was greater than 90%. Fluorescence
in situ hybridization (FISH) s tudies showed the MYC::IGH
rearrangement while negative for the BCL2 and BCL6
rearrangement. A diagnosis of Burkitt lymphoma was made.
The patient was started on oral dexamethasone 4 mg every
6 hours with concern for spinal cord compression. And
received one round of radiation therapy. The patient was
considered a nonsurgical candidate. A goals of care discus-
sion was held, and the patient opted to forgo any antitumor
treatment and be discharged to hospice.
Here we report a unique case of sporadic Burkitt lymphoma
presenting with weakness of the lower extremities with primary
involvement of the right paraspinal tissue with epidural exten-

rare and is seen primarily in the endemic variant. Treatment
involves chemotherapy; common regimens include CODOX-M
with IVAC and dose-adjusted EPOCH.

Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common type of malig-
nant brain tumor among adults, with a median overall sur-
vival (OS) around 15 months. Several variables (tissue
genetics, extension of surgery, tumor volume, overall health
status) are currently used in clinical care as well as in treat-
ment trials for prognosis and strati ﬁcation. Even though
GBMs derive from cells in the white matter (astrocytes) that
is organized with a speci ﬁc spatial geometry (topology)
related to the organization and density of brain connections,
to-date no prognostic factor has considered the effect of
GBM loci and their impact on white matter ﬁbers. Here,
we computed a new connection density index from struc-
tural clinical brain MRI scans to quantify the average num-
ber of white matter connections affected by a GBM.In a
ﬁrst cohort of GBM patients (n=92) we found that the con-
nectivity density index signi ﬁcantly correlated with overall
survival (OS)(r=-0.46, p<0.001), and that this relationship
was stronger than other common prognostic factors. When
we added the density index to the prediction model of sur-
vival, the variance explained increased by 10%. This cor-
responded to log-rank p < 0.001 in a Kaplan-Meyer
analysis. Moreover, in contrast to other factors, the predic-
tion accuracy of the connection density index was indepen-
dent of the overall number of surviving patients in the
cohort. When we tested this connectivity density index in
an independent cohort (n=52), OS prediction showed an
overall accuracy of 84%. Our results suggest that GBM
prognosis strongly depends on the location of the tumor.

a useful presurgical predictor of OS and a necessary covari-
ate for disease-modi ﬁers clinical trials. This study provides a
fundamental shift in our understanding of the pathophysiol-
ogy of GBM: from a perspective in which GBMs are iso-
lated from the brain architecture to one in which they
interact with it. This new framework might pave the way
for new strategies of surgical and pharmacological interven-
tions in GBM.

Plexiform neuro ﬁbroma (PNF) is a hallmark tumor of the
peripheral nervous system that occurs in persons with neuro-
ﬁbromatosis type 1 (NF1). PNF are associated with a ~10%
lifetime incidence of transformation to malignant peripheral
nerve sheath tumor (MPNST), a devastating form of sarcoma
that is the leading cause of premature death in individuals
with NF1. Malignant transformation of PNF often occurs
through the development of atypical neuro ﬁbroma (ANF)
precursor lesions, which can be challenging to distinguish
from PNF and low-grade MPNST by conventional histo-
pathological criteria. Moreover, robust molecular diagnostic
markers that reliably discriminate PNF, ANF and MPNST
have yet to be established. To de ﬁne the transcriptional alter-

of these complex and heterogeneous neoplasms, we quanti-

regions from 35 peripheral nerve sheath tumor (PNST) sam-

continuum. Tissue regions conforming to consensus histo-
pathologic criteria were digitally annotated by an expert clini-
cal pathologist and subsequently microdissected for RNA

regulating tumor progression, microenvironment, and
immune response. We observed reduced CDKN2A transcript
expression amongst ANF and MPNST, concordant with
observations that neuro ﬁbroma progression is frequently asso-
ciated with copy number loss of the 9p21 cytoband encoding
the CDKN2A locus. Pathway analysis identi ﬁed three distinct
molecular subclusters predominated by PNF, ANF, and
MPNST respectively and characterized by unique signatures
of cytokine/chemokine signaling, antigen presentation,
immune response, metabolic stress, epigenetic regulation,
DNA damage repair, hypoxia, apoptosis/survival, prolifera-

further demonstrate transcriptional coherence of these signa-

models of NF1-associated PNST driven by conditional inac-

conventional histopathological criteria in NF1-associated
PNST diagnosis and ultimately to stratify neuro ﬁbromas at
high risk of undergoing malignant transformation to inform
risk adapted care.

Introduction: Alexia is a disorder of reading, and it can pre-
sent with or without writing involvement. Alexia with
agraphia is associated with left angular gyrus lesions, whereas
alexia without agraphia involves the splenium and left occipi-
tal lobe. It has been reported usually due to left posterior
cerebral artery infarct, although it can result from other
pathologies. Here, we present a case of alexia without
agraphia associated with a left occipital glioblastoma, and this
underlying cause has only been reported twice in the
literature.
Case Report: A 78-year-old white male with a past medical
history of hypertension and bilateral macular hole, presented
to the neuro-ophthalmology with acute onset of dif ﬁculty
reading and “brain fog. ” Although he could recognize the

that his mental status was normal other than the prior brain
fog. He denied any history of stroke.On examination, vision
was 20/20 in both eyes and there was no relative afferent
pupillary defect, and motility was full. Humphrey visual ﬁeld
revealed a right homonymous hemianopsia. OCT of the reti-
nal nerve ﬁber layer was normal, and OCT macula revealed
atrophy of the temporal aspect of the retina in the right eye.
Although the patient had 20/20 visual acuity, he could not
identify many words. However, he did not have any dif ﬁculty
writing complex words. MRI of the brain and orbits with and
without orbits several weeks later revealed a large dominant
enhancing centrally necrotic occipital lobe mass at the superior
margin of the left occipital lobe lesion, which was highly suspi-

Discussion: Pure alexia is a rare but classic disconnection
syndrome. Left visual cortex damage, such as posterior cere-
bral artery infarct or glioblastoma, contributes to the right
visual ﬁeld de ﬁcit, and splenial involvement further discon-
nects the left visual input from angular gyrus and Wernicke ’s
area. As a result, written word information cannot be
processed or comprehended. Because the connection between
angular gyrus and language and motor centers are still intact,
written ability is preserved, and so are other language func-
tioning such as ﬂuency, naming and repetition. This case
highlights an interesting cause of alexia without agraphia sec-
ondary to a glioblastoma.
M229. A Case of Visual Snow Syndrome Successfully
Treated with Lamotrigine
Ahmed Abbas, MD , Sarah Kendroud, DO. Southern Illinois
University School of Medicine, Spring ﬁeld, IL, USA.
Objective: To report a disabling case of Visual Snow Syn-
drome (VSS) that signi ﬁcantly improved with Lamotrigine
and provide an overview of treatment options.
Background: VSS presents with dynamic continuous
bilateral whole visual ﬁeld tiny dots for more than three
months with at least two of the following: palinopsia,
enhanced entoptic phenomena, photophobia, and nyctalopia.
It is thought to be due to dysfunctional central visual
processing and occipital cortex hyperexcitability.
Case Summary: We present a case of a 23-year-old male
with a history of depression and migraine without aura who
presented with a ﬁve-month history of visual disturbances,
including continuous tiny dots over the whole visual ﬁeld,
which he described as TV static, palinopsia, photophobia,
and tinnitus. The palinopsia was so severe and disabling that
he quit driving and working. His neurologic exam, ophthal-
mologic exam, which included perimetry, and MRI Brain
with/without contrast were normal. He was diagnosed with
VSS and treated with Lamotrigine, which was slowly tapered
to 200 mg/day with signi ﬁcant improvement of his visual
symptoms and functional status.
Discussion: This case is an example of a severe disabling
presentation of VSS and highlights the need for effective
treatment options. Data regarding pharmacologic treatment
is limited to case reports/series, a single retrospective study,
and systematic reviews. There have been no randomized clin-
ical trials performed to date. Lamotrigine is the most pre-

scribed medication, but only 19.2-22.2% of patients report
subjective improvement. Topiramate showed improvement
in two reported cases, but there is also one report of worsen-
ing symptoms. Propranolol, Verapamil, Sodium Valproate,
Naproxen, Baclofen and Sertraline were reported to be effec-
tive in at least once instance.
Conclusion: VSS is a potentially disabling disease with
limited pharmacologic treatment options. The best evidence
exists for Lamotrigine, which is only effective in about 20%
of the patients. Further research on both pharmacologic and
non-pharmacologic treatment options such as
neuromodulation is needed.

value=0.006) and the left cerebellar lobules VIIb/VIII
(size=65mL, cluster-level FWE-corrected p-value=0.02),
along with a cluster of increased FC within the precuneus/
posterior cingulate cortex (size=69 mL, cluster-level FWE-
corrected p-value=0.02). No signi ﬁcant FC changes emerged
for the DMN component.
Interpretation: The MBCT-vision Study, one of the ﬁrst
treatment trials in VSS, shows that MBCT-vision is a feasible
treatment for VSS, with signi ﬁcant improvements in self-
rated symptom severity and impact to life, more marked at
3-months compared to one-week post-intervention. fMRI
analysis showed functional reorganization of the VN, involv-
ing both visual and extra-visual areas.

Purpose: To evaluate the clinical presentation, treatment,
and outcomes in adult patients with histiocytic disorders
involving the eye, orbit, optic nerve, or cavernous sinus.
Design: Observational retrospective chart review.
Participants: Adult patients (age ≥18 years) seen at Mayo
Clinic from 1/1/1996 to 7/1/2021 with histiocytic disorders.
Inclusion criteria were: 1) diagnosis of a histiocytic disorder
by biopsy and appropriate clinical phenotype; 2) available
medical records; 3) eye, orbital, optic nerve or cavernous
sinus involvement.
Methods: Retrospective chart review.
Outcome Measures: Response to therapy was measured in
clinical and radiographic impact.

Results: Thirty-two patients were identiﬁed: 7 patients with

cavernous sinus involvement was present in 3/7 patients with
LCH, 1/8 RDD patients; all other groups had multisystem
disease. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed optic nerve
sheath involvement in 2/7 LCH patients, in 14/15 ECD
patients, and the 1 RDD/ECD patient. Diffuse (>75%) orbital
involvement was seen in 12/15 ECD patients and 1/7 LCH
patient. Extraocular muscles were involved in 4/7 LCH and
3/15 ECD. Lacrimal gland involvement was seen in 4/7 LCH,
1/15 ECD, and 2/8 RDD. Eye involvement was seen in 1/15
ECD patients, 6/8 RDD, and 1/1 mixed RDD/ECD. The
cavernous sinuses were involved in 1/7 LCH, 5/15 ECD, and

in whom it was tested (14/24, 58%) with a median logMAR

of treatment and response was variable across disease types.

M233. Posterior Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia of Lutz:
An Overlooked Phenomenon
Robert Fekete, MD . New York Medical College, Valhalla,
NY, USA.
Introduction: Posterior Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia
(INO) of Lutz, also called reverse INO, is a rare clinical phe-
nomenon involving abduction de ﬁcit, which is different from
the well known anterior INO with adduction de ﬁcit. Discus-
sion of this phenomenon is not typically included in neurol-
ogy residency teaching curricula.
Methods: Medline was queried for "posterior internuclear
ophthalmoplegia" resulting in 20 articles, with publication
dates from 1962 to 2018.
Result: Posterior INO is thought to occur from a pontine
lesion between the parapontine reticular formation (PPRF)
and sixth nerve nucleus. Published case reports list central ner-
vous system (CNS) Lupus, multiple sclerosis, pontine glioma,
pontine warning syndrome as possible causes. Myasthenia
gravis can also produce a mimicker likely due to pseudo
abducens palsy. Other differential diagnostic considerations
include chronic lymphocytic in ﬂammation with pontine peri-
vascular enhancement responsive to steroids (CLIPPERS) and
myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibody disease.
Conclusion: Posterior INO can be an important diagnos-
tic clue to CNS autoimmune, neoplastic, and vascular
pathology.

Background: Visual symptoms are common following con-
cussion. While vision encompasses > 50% of the brain ’s
pathways, widely-accessible performance measures that are
easily administered by sports parents and other lay personnel
are lacking. Rapid automatized naming (RAN) tasks have
been investigated for nearly a century in the setting of head
trauma and other disorders. The Mobile Universal Lexicon
Evaluation System (MULES) test of picture naming and the
Staggered Uneven Number (SUN) test of number naming,
demonstrate increased time scores in concussion and other
neurologic disorders; these tests have recently demonstrated
equivalent reliability indices with paper-pencil versions vs. an
app-based research platform, the Mobile Interactive Cogni-
tive Kit (MICK). The purpose of this investigation was to
examine the feasibility of MICK administration of the
MULES and SUN tests to a cohort of Division 1 college
football players at pre-season baseline and post-injury.
Herein, we present the baseline and feasibility data for the
MICK app in this population.
Methods: The MICK App is a digitized version of the SUN
and MULES, accessible on tablet devices and currently available
for research purposes. The app is semiautomated for use by par-
ticipants, supervised by non-medical personnel. Participants
(n=83) from the Michigan State University Football Team
underwent pre-season baseline testing under conditions typical
for sideline testing. Each participant completed two trials of each
test. Total completion times for each trial for MULES and
SUN using the MICK app were recorded; magnitudes of best
scores and between-trial learning effects were determined.
Results: Average MULES times were 55.2 /C612.8 seconds
(trial 1) and 42.0 /C611.0 seconds (trial 2); the average for best
of two trials was 41.8 /C610.9 seconds. Average SUN test times
were 59.4/C610.5 seconds (trial 1) and 56.1 /C69.9 seconds (trial
2); the average for best trial was 55.5 /C69.9 seconds. Consis-
tent with most timed performance measures, there were sig-
niﬁcant learning effects between the two baseline trials for
both MULES (p<0.0001, paired t-test, mean 13.3 sec) and
SUN (p<0.0001, mean 3.3 sec).
Discussion: The MICK App can be feasibly administered
in the setting of pre-season baseline testing in a Division I
football environment. These data provide a foundation for
post-injury sideline testing with comparison to baseline in
the setting of concussion, with potential use for return-to-
play decisions in a key athletic constituency. Consistent with

M235. Remote Expert Diagnosis by Video-Oculography
is More Accurate Than In-Person ED Diagnosis in Acute

Introduction: Diagnosis of vertigo/dizziness (hereafter, “ver-
tigo”) is challenging for many emergency department
(ED) clinicians. Video-oculography (VOG) is routinely used
in specialty clinics but not in EDs. VOG recordings might
facilitate correct ED diagnosis of vestibular disorders such as
benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) and vestibular
neuritis, but the accuracy of remote assessment of acute ver-
tigo using VOG is unknown. In the context of a multicenter
diagnostic strategy trial, we compared accuracy of ED diagno-
ses to remote, VOG-based expert diagnoses.
Methods: The AVERT trial (NCT02483429) was per-
formed at six tertiary-care EDs (2/6/2018-3/9/2020). We
prospectively recruited adult ED patients with acute vertigo
plus ataxia and/or evidence of nystagmus. Potentially eligible
patients underwent a structured history and examination,
including VOG (ICS Impulse, Schaumberg, IL, USA) and
standardized neurologic rating scales. VOG included exami-
nation for spontaneous, gaze, and positional nystagmus;
head-impulse tests of the horizontal vestibulo-ocular-re ﬂex;
and alternate cover testing for skew deviation. We compared
real-world ED team primary diagnoses to research diagnoses
by a single, experienced oto-neurologist using VOG record-
ings and a brief clinical summary from the ED charted
record, thereby simulating remote, VOG-based, expert
teleconsultation. The expert selected their diagnoses from a
list of 12 validated diagnoses. Diagnoses were then grouped
into prespeci ﬁed schemas of varying granularity (3/6/12 cate-
gories). Gold-standard diagnoses were made by a multi-
disciplinary panel using ED charts, structured history and
exams (including VOG), plus a one-week oto-neurology eval-
uation, repeat VOG and MRI, and one-month phone/record
review follow-up.
Results: We enrolled 130 patients (52.3% female; 76.9%

white, non-Hispanic) with a mean age of 59.2 /C615 years;
21 with unknown ﬁnal diagnoses were excluded. Diagnostic
accuracy for the oto-neurologist using VOG was much higher
than the ED primary diagnosis (3-category schema: 72.5% vs
22.9%, p<0.001; 6-category schema: 63.3% vs 18.3%,
p<0.001; 12-category schema: 61.5% vs 17.4%, p<0.001).
Even greater differences were identi ﬁed when comparing
diagnostic sensitivity for identifying BPPV (69.8% vs. 9.3%,
(p<0.001) and vestibular neuritis (83.3% vs. 20.8%,
p=0.003). Stroke sensitivity was not signi ﬁcantly different in
this small sample (n=14, 57.1% vs 42.9%; p=0.5).
Conclusion: Remote VOG evaluation by oto-neurologists
in ED vertigo presentations could substantially improve diag-
nostic accuracy, particularly for common inner ear disorders.
Limitations were that a single expert determined the VOG-
based diagnoses and this individual was a member of the ﬁnal
multi-disciplinary panel.
M236. Testosterone Overtreatment and Intracranial
Hypertension in a Young Man
Pankhuri Banerjee, MBBS , Zaur Komachkov, Bachelors of
Biology, Dmitri Kovalev, M.D., Elena Shanina, MD PhD.
UTMB Neurology, Galveston, TX, USA.
Introduction: Studies have shown that women with increased
levels of circulating androgens develop Intracranial Hyperten-
sion (IH) at an earlier age. Androgens have effects on cerebro-
spinal ﬂuid (CSF) dynamics, creating hyperviscosity,
erythrocytosis, and decreased absorption. The human choroid
plexus expresses androgen receptors and testosterone directly
modulates CSF secretion from the choroid plexus.
Case: A 35-year-old Caucasian healthy man presented with
blurred vision, visual obscurations and occasional headaches
affecting his driving. His evaluation revealed grade-2
papilledema, increased CSF opening pressure with mildly ele-
vated CSF protein, and normal cell count. The patient was tak-
ing intramuscular testosterone cypionate treatments through a
so-called “LT (Low Testosterone) Clinic for mild hyp-
ogonadism, to restore vitality and bodybuilding goals. His regi-
men exceeded regular replacement therapy dose and was in the
range of the female-to-male transgender reassignment treat-
ments. His total and free testosterone levels were more than
2-fold above the upper limit, accompanied by suppressed
hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis, and elevated hemoglobin
and hematocrit. MRI brain and orbit demonstrated ﬁndings of
IH including empty sella, protrusion of the optic nerve heads,
ﬂattening of the globes, and tortuous optic nerves with sheath
distention. CT-angiogram was negative for venous sinus
obstruction. Elevated CSF protein investigations for autoim-
mune and in ﬂammatory etiologies, including sarcoidosis and

demyelinating disorders, infectious panels, and neoplastic/
paraneoplastic workup were negative. Spinal imaging revealed
degenerative changes in the C1-C2 and L5-S1, potentially
explaining mild protein elevation. The patient started treatment
with acetazolamide in conjunction with cessation of testoster-
one supplementation under endocrinology recommendations.
This led to gradual improvement of papilledema, visual acuity,
and resolution of headaches. His repeated hormonal levels
gradually normalized.
Discussion: Testosterone-induced IH has been reported
during transgender transition treatment. A recent study docu-
mented excess of circulating androgens in patients with idio-
pathic IH and provided new insights into the mechanisms of
the disorder. The exogenous administration of testosterone is
widely advertised as a remedy to promote youth, vitality, and
wellness and is often used uncontrollably by “LT-clinics”
widespread across the country. This case adds to evidence of
deleterious androgen effects on CSF regulation and illustrates
the importance of dose monitoring and caution against over-
prescribing testosterone replacement therapy.
M237. Unilateral Dilated Nonreactive Pupil: A Rare Case
of Holmes-Adie Syndrome (HAS)
Ahmed Harazeen, MD , Xiangping Li, MD. University of
Texas Medical Branch, Galveston, TX, USA.
Objective: We present a patient with new onset unilateral
dilated nonreactive pupil, who is found to have Adie tonic
pupil and absence of deep tendon re ﬂexes in lower extremi-
ties, consistent with the diagnosis of Holmes-Adie syn-
drome (HAS).
Background: Unilateral dilated nonreactive pupil can be
an ophthalmologic emergency, which often lead to an urgent
evaluation of stroke or aneurysm. However, it could also
occur as a benign ﬁnding in Holmes-Adie Syndrome (HAS).
The cause for this disorder is unknown, although considered
to be benign, symptoms may result from autonomic
dysfunction.
Case Presentation: A 35-year-old Hispanic female with
no past medical history presented to the emergency room
with new onset headache, blurry vision, and anisocoria. Patient
noticed that her pupils became unequal for 3 weeks. Neuro-
logical exam showed anisocoria worse in light with dilated
ﬁxed pupil on left (7mm), are ﬂexia in lower extremities, and
decreased temperature and pin prick in a stocking distribution
(vibration and proprioception intact). CT angiogram head and
neck did not reveal any aneurysms or dissections. MRI brain
was unremarkable. After ruling out all other potential neuro-
logic causes, Adie tonic pupil is suspected clinically. Ophthal-
mology was consult. Testing with 0.125% pilocarpine revealed
constriction of left pupil, consistent with parasympathetic
denervation hypersensitivity. Her lab work including rheuma-
tological and neuropathy workup were unremarkable.
Conclusion: This case study highlights the importance of
recognition of the Holmes-Aides Syndrome, which can lead
to either unilateral or bilateral dilated pupil with near light
dissociation. HAS is characterized by degeneration of the cili-
ary ganglion or postganglionic parasympathetic neuron. Cur-
rently, the etiology of HAS is unclear, and the therapeutic
options are restricted to symptomatic management. We
believe that reporting this case would add more information
to the existing fund of knowledge.
Neurorecovery and Neuroplasticity
S297. A Placebo-Controlled Phase I Study of NVG-291 in
Healthy Subjects, Targeting CNS Receptor Protein

Tyrosine Phosphatase Sigma (PTP σ)
Daniel D. Mikol, MD, PhD , Marc DePaul, PhD, Betty
Lawrence, BSc, Nana Collett, MS, MBA, Judy Toews, MSc,
Matvey Lukashev, PhD. NervGen, Vancouver, BC, Canada.
Background: Substantial data from animal models of spinal
cord injury (SCI), multiple sclerosis (MS) and Alzheimer ’s
disease (AD) have suggested that increased deposition of
chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs) in response to
CNS damage plays a signi ﬁcant role in inhibition of CNS
repair (Muir, Exp Neurol, 2019). The inhibitory effects of
CSPGs are mediated in part by PTP σ, a CSPG-binding
receptor type protein tyrosine phosphatase (Shen, Science,
2009). NVG-291 is a cell-penetrant peptide mimetic derived
from the regulatory wedge domain of human PTP σ and
administered as a once-daily subcutaneous (SC) injection. A
rodent analogue of NVG-291 has been reported to improve
functional outcomes, axonal regeneration, remyelination and
neuroplasticity in animal models of CNS damage (Lang,
Nature Comm, 2018; Luo, Nature Comm, 2018).
Objectives: There are no approved pharmacologic treat-
ments to restore function following CNS damage, whether
due to trauma or disease. This randomized, triple-blind,
placebo-controlled trial assesses the safety, tolerability, and
pharmacokinetics (PK) of single (SAD) and multiple ascend-
ing doses (MAD) of NVG-291 in healthy adult subjects.
Materials and Methods: 37 subjects were randomly
assigned into 6 SAD cohorts of SC dosing of NVG-291
(dose range 0.032 mg/kg - 0.864 mg/kg) or placebo. 3 MAD
cohorts of ~18 subjects are planned to receive NVG-291 or
placebo SC once-daily for 14 days, with NVG-291 doses
exceeding human equivalent levels that showed ef ﬁcacy in
animal models of nervous system damage. In a separate
cohort, cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) is being collected to mea-
sure NVG-291 concentration.
Results and Discussion: Across SAD cohorts, the most
common adverse event (AE) has been injection site-related
(ISR), more frequent in the NVG-291 group; all ISR-AEs
have been mild and transient. Other than ISR-AEs, there
were no AEs that were clearly increased in NVG-291 vs. pla-
cebo-treated subjects. Across the ﬁrst two MAD cohorts to
date, blinded analysis of safety shows that AEs are mild except
for a singular transient grade 2 elevation of lipase that nor-
malized during treatment. There were no serious AEs or
effects on vital signs, electrocardiograms, or laboratory assess-
ments. The PK pro ﬁle of NVG-291 shows good dose-propor-
tionality, with C
max < 1 hour. NVG-291 has been safe and
well tolerated to date to support the advancement to clinical
trials in SCI, MS, and AD, planned to initiate in 2022.

S298. Myoelectric Interface for Neurorehabilitation
(MINT) Conditioning Improves Arm Function in
Severely Impaired Chronic Stroke Survivors
Abed Khorasani, PhD, Vivek Paul, MBBS, Na Teng Hung,
BS, Joel Hulsizer, BS, Prashanth Prakash, MS, Marc
W. Slutzky, MD, PhD . Northwestern University, Chicago,
IL, USA.
Arm impairment after stroke is due not only to weakness and
sensory loss, but also to abnormal co-activation between mus-
cles. Previously, we designed a myoelectric computer interface
(MyoCI) to reduce this abnormal co-activation (a new mech-
anism of action) with in-lab training in chronic stroke survi-
vors (Mugler et al, Neurorehabilitation Neural Repair 2019).
The MyoCI mapped EMG from abnormally co-activating
muscles to orthogonal components of cursor movements, and
training required decoupling these muscles to acquire targets
in those mapping directions. Here, we report interim results
of a randomized controlled trial of MyoCI using a novel,
wearable version —the Myoelectric Interface for Neuro-
rehabilitation (MINT). MINT is gami ﬁed and designed for
home use to enable high-intensity training and broad adop-
tion. We tested 3 different variants of the “MINT condition-
ing” paradigm. We included participants with chronic
hemiparesis from a stroke causing severe arm impairment
(Fugl-Meyer Assessment of upper extremity of 7-30). Partici-
pants were randomized to one of 4 groups, based on how
they trained: 2 muscles at a time (2D), 2D plus reaching in
the muscle pulling direction (Reach), 3 muscles at a time
(3D), or one muscle at a time (sham control group). Partici-
pants were asked to train 90 min/d, 5 d/wk at home, and
1 d/wk in the lab, for 6 weeks. We identi ﬁed abnormally co-
activating muscles using correlation between 12 EMGs
recorded during reaching to the front and side. A blinded
occupational therapist measured arm function using the
timed portion of the Wolf Motor Function Test at baseline,
end of training and 4-week follow-up. To date, 37 partici-
pants have completed the 6-week training. They averaged
85/C618 min and about 300 daily repetitions of daily training.
At 6 weeks, WMFT showed a nonsigni ﬁcant trend of greater
improvement from baseline over all experimental groups than
in sham controls (mean -3.8 vs. -1.9 s, p=0.23, t-test), with
an even stronger trend in the 3D group (-7.8 s, p=0.09).
Improvement was signi ﬁcant, and even greater, at 4-week
follow-up (-12.9 s in 3D group, p=0.02; -9.5 s overall groups
vs. -1.9 s for sham, p=0.01). These gains were all greater than
the minimum clinically important difference (1.5 s). Active
reaching range of motion also improved in experimental
groups more than sham. These results suggest that reducing
co-activation with MINT improves arm function and is not
just overcoming learned non-use.
S299. NeurocuresNY: A Novel Clinical Trial Platform to
Find Treatments for Chronic Neurologic Disability
Cristina Falo, PhD
1, Amy Bialek, MSPT 1, Susan Wortman-
Jutt, MSPT 1, Jeremy Hill, PhD 2, Russell L. Hardesty, PhD 2,
Timothy T. Fake, MSPT 2, Jonathan R. Wolpaw, MD 2,
Bradford C. Berk, MD, PhD 3, Rajiv R. Ratan, MD, PhD 1,
Tomoko Kitago, MD 1. 1Burke Neurological Institute, White
Plains, NY, USA, 2National Center for Adaptive
Neurotechnologies, Stratton VA Medical Center, Albany, NY,
USA,
3Aab Cardiovascular Research Institute and University of
Rochester Neurorestoration Institute, University of Rochester
School of Medicine and Dentistry, Rochester, NY, USA.

Background: Chronic neurological disability due to stroke is
an area of great unmet need, with more than 7 million stroke
survivors in the United States. NeuroCuresNY (NCNY), a
multi-center clinical trial platform, was formed to address this
need by ﬁnding treatments that signi ﬁcantly reduce impair-
ment for patients who are living with the long-term effects of
stroke. NCNY leverages the resources and expertise of acade-
mia, government, and industry to establish a platform trial to
efﬁciently evaluate the safety and ef ﬁcacy of multiple experi-
mental treatments for chronic stroke and other neurological
disorder Pre-clinical and clinical studies suggest that the ner-
vous system is more receptive to training for a short period of
time after injury (i.e. the sensitive period). In chronic stroke,
improvements with training alone are generally limited; how-
ever, therapeutics such as drugs or devices that are designed
to protect or repair a circuit, reopen circuit plasticity,
enhance axonal conduction, or alter the immune system may
reopen the sensitive period to make training more effective.
Combinatorial treatments coupling intensive training with
plasticity-promoting interventions are therefore a promising
approach to enhancing neurological recovery in the chronic
stage. NCNY will use robotic training devices because they
deliver standardized, quanti ﬁable, intensive upper-extremity
training for stroke survivors focused on impairment reduc-
tion, as well as objective measurement of motor outcomes.
We hypothesize that combinatorial interventions will lead to
greater reductions in upper extremity motor impairment than
training alone for chronic stroke survivors.
Participants: Eligible participants will be chronic stroke
survivors with residual upper limb weakness.
Study Design: All participants will undergo six weeks of
robot-assisted upper limb therapy (RT), three times per week,
for a total of eighteen sessions. Participants will be randomized
to an intervention, which will consist of RT combined with
one of the investigational products (IP), or RT combined with
placebo/sham. There may be multiple IPs that are tested
within the platform at a given time. Outcome assessments will
be conducted before training, mid-training, end of training,
and at 6 and 12 weeks post-training. The primary outcome
measure will be the change in upper limb motor impairment
(Fugl-Meyer) while secondary outcomes will be change in
Action Research Arm Test and Stroke Impact Scale. Explor-

of novel combinatorial treatments to reduce chronic neuro-
logical disability.

Introduction: Upper extremity motor impairment is com-
mon and persistent after stroke. Methods based on guided,
repetitive, task practice such as Constraint-induced Therapy
and robotic rehabilitation have been shown to be effective in
reducing impairment in populations of chronic stroke
patients, but individual responses are highly variable. If base-
line measures could be used to predict response to an inter-
vention, then it would be possible to establish realistic
rehabilitation goals and effectively allocate resources. The pre-
dictive model could also provide insight into biological and
psychological substrates for response to therapy. Our aims
were to address these goals of prediction and understanding
of mechanism in patients with chronic hemiparesis after
stroke.
Methods: The intervention used a combination of robot-
assisted therapy (75% session time) and functional arm use
in real-world tasks related to the recently practiced move-
ments in the robot (25% session time.) Participants had
36 intervention sessions over 12 weeks. Baseline measures
include the Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer Assessment, Wolf
Motor Function Test, Action Research Arm Test, Stroke
Impact Scale, questionnaires on pain and expectancy, MRI,
transcranial magnetic stimulation multiple muscle mapping,
kinematics, wearable-based accelerometry, and genomic test-
ing. The goal of the prediction methods was to predict a clin-
ically meaningful ( ≥ 5 point) increase in Fugl-Meyer using
logistic regression.
Results: The average increase in Fugl-Meyer was 4.6
/C61.0 SE; median 2.5, N=42. Approximately one-third of
participants had a clinically meaningful response to the
intervention. The selected logistic regression model had a
receiver operating curve with AUC=0.99 (Std Error = 0.01,
95% Wald con ﬁdence limits: 0.967 - 1) that showed little
evidence of over ﬁtting. Six variables that predicted response
represented impairment, functional, and genomic mea-
sures, including time after stroke, whether dominant side
was affected, proprioceptive function, time to complete
Wolf Motor Function tasks, grip strength, and Klotho
genotype. TMS and MRI measures did not survive the var-
iable selection process. Most outcomes derived from wear-
able data did not change signi ﬁcantly over the course of the
intervention.
Conclusion: A simple weighted sum of six baseline factors
can accurately predict clinically meaningful impairment
reduction after outpatient intensive practice intervention in
chronic stroke. While goals for people affected by stroke
include better ability to participate in desired activities,
reduction of impairment may be a critical ﬁrst step to those
goals. Further validation and generalization of this model will
increase its utility in clinical decision-making.

and potential ef ﬁcacy of intense rehabilitation therapy pro-
vided early post-stroke via telehealth methods, which enables
seamless transitions of care from inpatient rehabilitation facil-

after stroke suggests great potential to promote plasticity
with intensive rehabilitatio n therapy, but most patients
do not get this due to limited access, changing rehabilita-
tion therapy care settings, provision of low therapy doses,
and poor compliance. We have previously found (Cramer
et al, JAMA Neurol, 2019) that in patients averaging
4 months post-stroke, intensi ve rehabilitation therapy can
be delivered in the home usin g telehealth methods, pro-
ducing substantial functional gains. Here we examined
delivery of this telerehabili tation program to patients
early post-stroke, initiat ed during IRF admission.
Methods: Patients with hemiparetic stroke admitted to an
IRF (California Rehabilitation Institute or MossRehab)
received daily telerehabilitation targeting arm motor function
in addition to standard of care. Treatment consisted of 36 ses-
sions of 70-min duration, half of which were supervised by a
licensed OT or PT via videoconference, over a 6-week
period. Telerehabilitation sessions consist of functional
games, exercise videos, education, and daily monitoring of
several behaviors.

median 18 days from stroke to consent, age 61.5 /C611.5, and
arm Fugl-Meyer score 35 /C68 (out of 66). Four patients

dures, and home too small). Two adverse events were consid-

non-serious: a patient with hemianopsia felt nausea when using

Fugl-Meyer scores increased by 20 /C611 points. Digital motor
assessments, acquired daily using the telerehabilitation system,
were concordant with these gains. Patients enrolled in Phila-
delphia could be treated remotely by therapists in Los Angeles.

and potential efﬁcacy of providing intense rehabilitation therapy
via telehealth methods during the critical period in the weeks
following a new stroke. This approach enables daily exam of

M290. Acute Effect of Suvorexant on CSF Amyloid-Beta,
Tau, and Phospho-Tau Dynamics
Brendan P. Lucey, MD , Haiyan Liu, MD, Nicolas
Barthelemy, PhD, Kwasi Mawuenyega, PhD, Samir Chahin,
BS, David Freund, BA, Cristina Toedebusch, BA, Vitaliy Ovod,
MA, James Bollinger, PhD, Randall Bateman,
MD. Washington University School of Medicine, St Louis,
MO, USA.
Background: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is characterized by
deposition of amyloid- β (Aβ) as insoluble plaque
(i.e., amyloid-positive), tau hyperphosphorylation (p-tau) and
aggregation, neuronal degeneration and synaptic loss, and
eventual cognitive dysfunction, dementia, and death. Forma-
tion of A β and tau pathology is dependent on concentration
and phosphorylation, respectively. Soluble forms of A β and
tau, proteins critical to AD pathogenesis, change in cerebro-
spinal ﬂuid (CSF) with sleep-wake activity: 1) CSF A β and
tau increase during wakefulness and decrease during sleep in
both mice and humans; 2) overnight sleep deprivation
increases CSF A β and tau levels by ≥30% via increased pro-
duction/release; 3) p-tau, an early step in tau-mediated neu-
rodegeneration, is also affected by sleep deprivation
depending on the speci ﬁc site of phosphorylation. Orexins
are wake-promoting neuropeptides and blockade of the
orexin system with a dual orexin receptor antagonist
(DORA) increases sleep. Using a DORA to increase sleep in
mice decreased both soluble A β and amyloid deposition. The
effect of DORAs on tau or p-tau is unknown. Based on these
ﬁndings, we tested the effect of a DORA, suvorexant, on
CSF Aβ, tau, and p-tau in humans.
Method: In-dwelling lumbar catheters were placed at
~20:00 in 38 cognitively normal adults aged 45-65 years old.
CSF was sampled every 2 hours for 36 hours. Participants
were randomized to receive placebo (N=13), suvorexant
10 mg (N=13), or suvorexant 20 mg (N=12) at 21:00 on
Night 1 (hour 1) and 21:00 on Night 2 (hour 25). CSF A β,
tau, and p-tau were measured by mass spectrometry.
Result: We found that suvorexant 20 mg acutely decreased
the p-tau-181/tau-181 ratio (a measure of the tau phosphory-
lation occupancy at threonine-181) by ~10-15% compared
to placebo and decreased the CSF A β concentration by
~18% compared to placebo. There was no difference between
the suvorexant 10 mg and placebo groups.
Conclusion: This study shows that suvorexant, a ﬁrst-in-
class DORA to be approved by the Food and Drug Adminis-
tration (FDA), acutely decreases A β and tau phosphorylation
in human CSF within hours. Future research is needed to
determine how DORAs such as suvorexant affect AD bio-
markers over longer periods of time (e.g., weeks to months).

Breathing Disorders (SRBDs) in Individuals with Spinal
Cord Injury (SCI): Preliminary Results of a Mixed-
Method Study
Julio C. Furlan, MD, LLB, MBA, MSc, PhD, FRCPC,
FAAN

Milligan, BSc, MD, CCFP 3, Peter Athanasopoulos, BA 4, Mark
I. Boulos, BSc, MSc, MD, FRCPC 5. 1KITE Research Institute,
University Health Network; University of Toronto, Toronto,
ON, Canada,

Kitchener, ON, Canada, 4SCI Ontario, Toronto, ON, Canada,
5Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre; University of Toronto,
Toronto, ON, Canada.
Introduction: SRBDs are common but under-recognized
among individuals with SCI. We report preliminary results of
a mixed-method study focused on: (i) the feasibility of a
home sleep apnea test (HSAT); (ii) the validity of four ques-
tionnaires used to screen for SRBD; and (iii) the potential
association between SRBD and clinical features in the SCI
population.
Methods: This research study included consecutive adults
with subacute/chronic SCI ( ≥1 month post-injury) who
were at high risk for SRBDs. The study protocol included a
cross-sectional study and a qualitative analysis. The former
aims to: (a) evaluate the feasibility of a HSAT; (b) test the
validity of four screening questionnaires (i.e., Berlin, STOP,
Medical Outcomes Study Sleep Scale [MOS-SS], and
STOP-Bang questionnaires); and (c) examine the associa-
tion between moderate-to-severe SRBD and 3 clinical fea-
tures (i.e., neck circumference, body mass index [BMI] and
oropharynx opening as assessed using the Modi ﬁed Mal-
lampati classi ﬁcation [MMC]). At the end, participants were
invited to 1-hour semi-structured interview to share their
experiences when undergoing the HSAT (qualitative
research).
Results: To date, we recruited 25 individuals (11 females,
14 males; age range: 20-86 years, mean: 56.8) with motor
complete (n=7) or incomplete SCI at the cervical (n=17),
thoracic (n=6) or lumbar levels. Time from SCI onset varied
from 2 to 318 months (mean time: 94.8). Of these 25 partici-
pants, 18 successfully completed the HSAT, which revealed
an overall mean apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) of 16.8 events/
hour (range: 0.5-83.7). Our preliminary results revealed a sig-
niﬁcant correlation between the AHI and MOS-SS
(p=0.047). There was also a trend towards a correlation
between the AHI and the STOP-Bang (p=0.093). However,
there was no signi ﬁcant correlation between the AHI and the
scores from the Berlin (p=0.305) or STOP (p=0.565) ques-
tionnaires. AHI was not signi ﬁcantly associated with individ-
uals’ neck circumference (p=0.907), BMI (p=0.407), or
MMC (p=0.157). All 18 participants who successfully com-
pleted the HSAT endorsed the feasibility of the HSAT via
qualitative research.
Conclusions: Our preliminary results suggest that a HSAT
is a feasible screening method for the diagnosis of SRBDs
among individuals with SCI. The MOS-SS questionnaire is
the most valid screening questionnaire for this population.

M292. Catamenial Nocturnal Panic Attacks
Thujeevan Paramanandasivam, MD
1, Alan R. Hirsch,
MD, FACP2. 1Aureus University School of Medicine, Fair
Lawn, NJ, USA, 2Smell and Taste Treatment and Research
Foundation, Chicago, IL, USA.
Introduction: Obligate catamenial nocturnal panic attacks
have not hitherto been described.
Case Study: This 46 year old, right handed woman with
Generalised Anxiety Disorder described that her anxiety recurs
daily, 4/10 in severity, with 10 being the worst. Since teenage
years, she has suffered from panic attacks, with fear, diaphore-
sis, dizziness, racing thoughts and feelings as if she might do
something crazy. These would occur only when sleeping, last
10 minutes, 1-3 days prior to her menses. She had no daytime
panic attacks and no panic attacks that were not pre-men-
strual. These panic attacks awaken her throughout the night.
Results: Mental status examination: Able to remember
7 digits forwards and 5 digits backwards. Able to remember
4/4 objects in 3 minutes without reinforcement. Interpretation
of similarities: normal. Calculation: normal. Proverb testing:
normal. Clock Drawing Test: 4/4 (normal). Go-No-Go Test:
6/6 (normal). Patient Health Questionnaire-9: 6/30 (normal).
Discussion: Nocturnal panic attacks tend to occur during
the transition between stage 2 and stage 3 sleep (Smith,
2022; Craske, 2005). During the pre-menstrual period, there
is an increase in stage 2 sleep and stage 3 sleep variability
(Parry, 1988) and an increase in estrogen ﬂuctuation, and
increased parahippocampal gyrus blood ﬂow (Tushaus,
2017). Increase in estrogen ﬂuctuation may facilitate a “cen-
tral limbic hyperconnectivity ”, and thus an increase in anxi-
ety and panic attacks (Herzog, 1999). Estradiol similarly has
been shown to increase excitability in hippocampal and para-
hippocampal regions (Herzog, 2008). During stages 2 and
3 of sleep, there is an increase in parahippocampal blood
ﬂow, which suggests that there could be further activation in
parahippocampus when sleep stages 2 and 3 are prolonged
premenstrually (Braun, 1997). Gamma-aminobutyric acid
(GABA) ﬂuctuates with circadian rhythm (Baker, 2007). On
a cellular level, catamenial nocturnal panic attacks may be
related to decreased GABA receptor discharge (Memon,
2018). In the late luteal, pre-follicular phase in the menstrual
cycle, progesterone is metabolised to allopregnanolone which
acts as an allosteric modulator of GABA-A neurotransmission
(Herzog, 2015). Withdrawal of allopregnanolone pre-
menstrually causes a change in GABA-A receptor sub-unit
composition, reducing in ﬂuence of GABA (Driver, 2008),
and increase excitability in the peri-aqueductal grey, hippo-
campi, parahippocampi regions and amygdala (Lovick,
2006). Reduction in GABA activity in the parahippocampal
region has been associated with an increase in panic attacks
(Goddard, 2022; Lydiard, 2003). In those with panic disor-
der, query as to catamenial exacerbation of nocturnal panic
attacks is warranted.
M293. CPAP Therapy for Sleep-Related Breathing
Disorders (SRBDs) Improves Sleep Quality, Daytime
Alertness, Fatigue, and Mental Health in People with
Chronic Spinal Cord Injury (SCI)
Julio C. Furlan, MD, LLB, MBA, MSc, PhD, FRCPC,
FAAN
1, Sander L. Hitzig, DEC, BA, MA, PhD 2, Mark

I. Boulos, BSc, MSc, MD, FRCPC 3. 1KITE Research Institute,
University Health Network; University of Toronto, Toronto,
ON, Canada, 2St. John’s Rehab Research Program, Sunnybrook
Research Institute, Toronto, ON, Canada, 3Sunnybrook Health
Sciences Centre; University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada.
Introduction: SRBDs are common but under-recognized
post-SCI. We report preliminary data from our ongoing
study examining the potential cognitive and psychological
beneﬁts of CPAP therapy in people with chronic SCI and
moderate-to-severe SRBD.
Methods: This single-arm clinical trial (NCT04007380)
aims to evaluate the effects of 4 months of CPAP therapy on
cognition, mood, fatigue, anxiety, and stress in people with
SCI who were recently diagnosed with moderate-to-severe
SRBD. Outcome measures included the Epworth Sleepiness
Scale (ESS), Medical Outcomes Study Sleep Scale (MOS-
SS), Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS), Depression, Anxiety &
Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21), and Montreal Cognitive Assess-
ment (MoCA). The participants were also invited for a
1-hour semi-structured interview to share their experience
before and after the trial of CPAP therapy (qualitative analy-
sis). Adherence was de ﬁned as the use of CPAP for >4 hours/
night on >4 nights of the week.
Results: To date, we screened 24 individuals (7 females,
17 males; age range: 37-71 years; mean age: 58.2) with com-
plete motor (n=13) or incomplete SCI at the cervical (n=15)
or thoracic level. Time from SCI onset varied from 6 to
793 months (mean: 222.8). Of the 24 screened participants,
the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) varied from 2.6 to 83.7
events per hour (mean AHI of 24.4) and 20 individuals with
moderate-to-severe SRBD initiated a trial of CPAP therapy.
So far, 9 individuals have completed the trial, whereas two
individuals withdrew from the study. The overall mean
adherence rate to CPAP was 81.8%; mean nighttime CPAP
usage was 4 hours 56 min. Daytime sleepiness and sleep
quality signi ﬁcantly improved with CPAP therapy (pre-
ESS=10.1 vs. post-ESS=4.8, p=0.011; pre-MOS-SS=17.8
vs. post-MOS-SS=67.8, p=0.001). The FSS signi ﬁcantly
decreased with CPAP therapy (pre-FSS=45.1 vs. post-
FSS=28.4, p=0.005). Mental health indicators improved with
CPAP therapy (pre-DASS-21=19.2 vs. post-DASS-21=8.9,
p=0.022). There was a numeric increase in MoCA scores,
but this did not reach signi ﬁcance (pre-MoCA=25 vs. post-
MoCA=26; p=0.486). All 9 participants con ﬁrmed that
CPAP therapy had a major impact on their mental health
and cognition.
Conclusions: Our preliminary results suggest that 4-month
CPAP therapy signiﬁcantly improves sleep quality, and reduces
daytime sleepiness, fatigue, stress, anxiety and mood in people
with chronic SCI. These ﬁndings are supported by the results
of the qualitative analysis. There was a high (81.8%) adherence
to CPAP therapy (Funded by Craig H. Neilsen Foundation).

Narcolepsy is a rare, life-long sleep disorder with peak onset
typically in adolescence or early adulthood. To characterize
demographic characteristics and medical and psychiatric
comorbidities of patients with narcolepsy, an electronic
health record (EHR)-based search was conducted to identify
patients with narcolepsy who presented at Mayo Clinic
between 2000 and 2020. A diagnosis of narcolepsy was
deﬁned as having ≥1 narcolepsy-speci ﬁc ICD-9/10 code
(‘347.00’, ‘G47.419’, ‘347’, ‘347.01’, ‘G47.411’, ‘347.10’,
‘G47.429’, ‘347.0’, ‘G47.421’, ‘347.11’) and multiple dis-
ease supportive statements identi ﬁed in clinical notes using
a natural language processing algorithm based on bidirec-
tional encoder representations from transformers. A matched
control cohort to account for differences in demographics,
care utilization, and severity of illness was created after pro-
pensity matching for birth year, age at ﬁrst encounter at the
institution, sex, race, ethnicity, number of diagnosis codes,
and mortality. Common comorbidities were compared
between cohorts. The most common comorbidities were
ranked by the odds ratio (OR) of their occurrences, and
adjusted P-values based on Bonferroni correction were cal-
culated. Of 6,389,186 patients in the EHR database, 2057
patients with narcolepsy were identi ﬁed. In the narcolepsy
cohort (n=2057) and matched cohort (n=2057), median
(range) age at ﬁrst presentation to Mayo Clinic was
32 (17-48) years and 35 (12-52) years, respectively; 59.6%
and 58.9% were female; 92.6% and 94.6% were white; and
89.2% and 84.5% were non-Hispanic. The top com-
orbidities speci ﬁc to the narcolepsy cohort compared with
the matched controls were psychiatric and sleep-related dis-
eases such as restless leg syndrome (OR [95% CI]: 3.94
[3.09-5.02]; P<0.001), obstructive sleep apnea (3.27
[2.83-3.79]; P<0.001), chronic pain syndrome (2.20
[1.76-2.76]; P<0.001), depression (2.11 [1.86-2.40];
P<0.001), dysthymia (1.86 [1.54-2.25]; P<0.001), insomnia
(1.84 [1.57-2.17]; P<0.001), and anxiety (1.67 [1.46-1.89];
P<0.001). Other common comorbidities in the narcolepsy
cohort included migraine (1.96 [1.66-2.31]; P<0.001), irri-
table bowel syndrome (1.95 [1.56-2.45]; P<0.001), myalgia
(1.69 [1.45-1.97]; P
<0.001), asthma (1.52 [1.29-1.78];
P<0.001), and hypothyroidism (1.33 [1.14-1.55]; P<0.05).
This propensity-matched cohort study found that psychiat-
ric, sleep-related, and chronic pain comorbidities are com-
mon in people with narcolepsy. Understanding common
comorbidities in narcolepsy may help clinicians tailor thera-
peutics for optimal ef ﬁcacy and avoid aggravating underlying
conditions as well as bridging a better understanding of the
medical and mood-related challenges people with
narcolepsy face.

P≤0.001) with directional improvements observed for the
NT2 subgroup. Results of these subgroup analyses are gen-
erally consistent with previously reported REST-ON end-
points and support ef ﬁcacy of ON-SXB for DNS, as well as
daytime sleepiness, with a single bedtime dose in adults
with either NT1 or NT2.

M296. Ef ﬁcacy of Once-Nightly Sodium Oxybate (ON-
SXB; FT218) for Excessive Daytime Sleepiness and
Cataplexy: Post-Hoc Number Needed to Treat and Effect
Size Analyses from REST-ON
Michael J. Thorpy, MD
1, Thomas Roth, PhD 2, Clete
A. Kushida, MD, PhD 3, David Seiden, MD 4, Jordan Dubow,

FT218 is an investigational, extended-release, once-nightly
formulation of sodium oxybate (ON-SXB) for adults with
narcolepsy. ON-SXB treatment resulted in signi ﬁcant
improvement vs placebo (6 g, 7.5 g, and 9 g, all P<0.001)
for the coprimary endpoints of mean sleep latency on the
Maintenance of Wakefulness test (MWT), Clinical Global
Impression of Improvement rating, and number of weekly
cataplexy episodes, and the secondary endpoint Epworth
sleepiness scale (ESS) score, in the phase 3 REST-ON trial
(NCT02720744). Post-hoc analyses of numbers needed to
treat (NNT) and effect sizes were performed to further con-
textualize ON-SXB ef ﬁcacy. Participants in REST-ON (aged
≥16 years with narcolepsy type 1 [NT1] or type 2) were ran-
domized 1:1 to receive ON-SXB (1 week, 4.5 g; 2 weeks,
6 g; 5 weeks, 7.5 g; 5 weeks, 9 g) or placebo. Participants
were considered responders if the following criteria were met:
≥5-min increase from baseline in mean sleep latency on
MWT, score ≤10 on ESS, and ≥50% reduction from baseline
in mean number of cataplexy episodes. Effect sizes were cal-
culated using Cohen ’s d; NNTs were the inverse of the abso-
lute risk reduction. The modi ﬁed intent-to-treat population
included 190 participants (ON-SXB, n=97 [NT1, n=73];
placebo, n=93 [NT1, n=72]). For MWT response, all ON-
SXB doses (6 g at week 3, 7.5 g at week 8, and 9 g at week
13) had NNTs of 3; effect sizes were 0.7, 0.9, and 0.7,
respectively. A dose-response effect was seen for ESS with
NNTs of 6 (6 g), 4 (7.5 g), and 3 (9 g); effect sizes were
-0.5, -0.6, and -0.7, respectively (decreases signifying
response). The NNT for cataplexy response was 6 for ON-
SXB 6 g and 3 for 7.5 and 9 g; effect sizes were -0.7 (6 g)
and -0.8 (7.5 and 9 g). NNT results for MWT, number of
cataplexy episodes, and ESS suggest that only a small number
of patients (3-6) need to be treated with ON-SXB for
1 patient to have a meaningful positive result, with the 9-g
dose requiring the fewest number of patients (n=3).

Newly Treated with High Sodium Oxybate

Michael N. Cook, PhD 5, Julia Pitino, BS 6, Helen Latimer,
MPH6, Elizabeth C. Dabrowski, MS 6, William B. White,
MD7. 1Jazz Pharmaceuticals, Palo Alto, CA, USA, 2Mayo
Clinic, Rochester, MN, USA, 3Jazz Pharmaceuticals; Stanford
University Center for Sleep Sciences and Medicine, Palo Alto,
CA, USA, 4Wake Forest University School of Medicine,
Winston-Salem, NC, USA, 5Jazz Pharmaceuticals,
Philadelphia, PA, USA, 6Aetion, New York, NY, USA,
7University of Connecticut Health Center, Farmington,
CT, USA.
Introduction:Narcolepsy is a neurological disorder that is associ-

ated with multiple comorbidities, including hypertension, and
that requires long-term treat ment. Sodium oxybate is a rec-
ommended standard treatment in narcolepsy. At 6-9 g/night,
sodium oxybate contributes 1100-1640 mg of sodium to a
patient’s daily sodium intake. The sodium-hypertension relation-
ship is well established. This exploratory study compared
intermediate-term risk of developing hypertension among normo-
tensive narcolepsy patients initiating sodium oxybate (SXB) com-
pared with those not initiating sodium oxybate (control cohort).
Methods: IBM
® MarketScan® claims from January 2014
to February 2020 were analyzed. Eligible adults had continu-
ous insurance coverage and ≥1 narcolepsy claim or prescrip-
tion for sodium oxybate. Patients were excluded for prior use
of sodium oxybate, history of hypertension, or use of antihy-
pertensive medication within 13 months prior to cohort
entry. SXB and control cohorts were 1:2 propensity-score
matched to balance clinical and demographic characteristics.
Endpoints of hypertension diagnosis and a composite of
hypertension diagnosis or a new prescription for an antihy-
pertensive were assessed. Patients were followed for 180 days
or until ﬁrst occurrence of the outcome or discontinuation of
sodium oxybate in the SXB cohort. Risk per 100 patients
was reported and differences were evaluated using a logistic
regression model to estimate adjusted odds ratios (ORs) and
corresponding 95% con ﬁdence intervals (CIs).
Results: Of 118 million total patients included in the
IBM MarketScan database, 954 and 1906 were included in
the SXB and matched control cohorts, respectively. Most
(67%) were female and mean (standard deviation) age was
35 (12) years. Risk of incident hypertension diagnosis was
numerically higher in SXB (0.94) than control (0.52) cohorts
(OR=1.81 [95% CI, 0.73-4.46]). Risk of the composite end-
point of either diagnosis of hypertension or initiation of anti-
hypertensive therapy was higher in SXB (6.60) than control
(4.20) cohorts (OR=1.61 [95% CI, 1.15-2.27]).
Conclusions: This exploratory study demonstrated
increased hypertension risk in patients with narcolepsy
treated with sodium oxybate, consistent with known conse-
quences of excess sodium consumption. Support: Jazz
Pharmaceuticals

Introduction: Kleine-Levin syndrome (KLS) is mainly illus-
trated by intermittent episodes of hypersomnolence. Other
common features of this rare disease include compulsive
hyperphagia, unrestrained sexual drive, cognitive dysfunction,
and other abnormal behaviors. To understand the disease
and identify the pathological and neurological bases, we can
use functional neuroimaging studies such as fMRI-BOLD,
PET, or SPECT, that demonstrates brain metabolism during
different stages of the disease related to glucose and oxygen
consumption.
Methods: We conducted a systematic review, currently
under peer review, to investigate the neuroimaging features of
KLS patients and their clinical associations. This systematic
review was conducted by following the Meta-Analysis of
Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) and PRI-
SMA protocol reporting guidelines. We include only studies
written in the English language during the last 20 years and
conducted on human beings. We excluded systematic
reviews, metanalysis, and case reports.
Results: We found that there are speci ﬁc brain areas varia-
tions in the functional imaging studies selected, during symp-
tomatic, asymptomatic, and between episodes in patients
with KLS. These variations vary according to the study
(SPECT, PET SCAN, or fMRI-BOLD) used to identify
these modi ﬁcations, some of them are con ﬂicting and do not
always correlate with each other.
Hypersomnolence, the main feature of this syndrome dur-
ing the symptomatic periods, is related to diminished activity
of the thalami. Other clinical characteristics of KLS related to
abnormal behavioral changes like hypersexuality, and deper-
sonalization were also correlated with functional imaging
changes. During the asymptomatic periods, we found that
deﬁcits in the working memory (e.g., digit span, reading
span) characteristic of this stage were correlated with hyperac-
tivity of the thalamus and hypothalamus. Additionally, a
unique ﬁnding for all the functional imaging studies is that a
longer course of the disease leans to show improvement in
the results, which suggests that KLS patients tend to outgrow
the disease.
Conclusion: These ﬁndings should be taken with caution
by physicians when evaluating and associating neurological
imaging ﬁndings with the disease.
M299. Patient and Provider Preferences for Oxybate
Treatment for Narcolepsy: A Discrete Choice Experiment
Anne Marie Morse, DO
1, Lois Krahn, MD 2, Clete
A. Kushida, MD, PhD 3, Michael J. Thorpy, MD 4, Julie
Flygare, JD 5, David Seiden, MD 6, Amod Athavale, PhD 7,
Jennifer Gudeman, PharmD 6. 1Geisinger Medical Center, Janet
Weis Children ’s Hospital, Danville, PA, USA, 2Mayo Clinic,
Phoenix, AZ, USA, 3Stanford University Medical Center,
Stanford, CA, USA, 4Monteﬁore Medical Center, New York,
NY, USA, 5Project Sleep, Los Angeles, CA, USA, 6Avadel
Pharmaceuticals, Chester ﬁeld, MO, USA, 7Trinity Life Sciences,
Waltham, MA, USA.
Currently available immediate-release sodium oxybate (SXB)
and mixed-salt oxybates are dosed twice nightly (second dose
2.5-4 hours after ﬁrst). Extended-release, once-nightly SXB
(ON-SXB; FT218) is under FDA review. To characterize
drivers of oxybate treatment attribute preferences, discrete

choice experiments (DCEs) were conducted for both patients
and healthcare providers (HCPs). Thirty-minute web-based
surveys were ﬁelded to 1) adults with self-reported physician-
diagnosed narcolepsy with/without prior/current use of
oxybate, and 2) board-certi ﬁed/board-eligible HCPs treating
≥5 narcolepsy patients in the last month. Choice sets of
2 hypothetical treatment pro ﬁles were generated combining
attributes of twice-nightly SXB, twice-nightly mixed-salt
oxybates, and ON-SXB based upon their respective published
data. While viewing 12 choice sets, each participant indicated
(1) their preferred product overall, (2) the product that
would improve quality of life (QoL), and (3) the product that
would result in less patient stress/anxiety. Results were ana-
lyzed using a mixed logit model. For patients (n=120) and
HCPs (n=100), the most important attribute driving overall
product choice was dosing frequency (relative attribute
importance [RAI]: 26.0 and 46.1, respectively), with once-
nightly preferred over twice-nightly dosing (relative prefer-
ence weight [RPW]: /C625.6, /C643.6). Dosing frequency was
also the most important attribute for both patients and HCPs
for QoL (RAI: 28.7, 41.7, respectively) and reducing patient
anxiety/stress (RAI: 26.7, 44.0), with once-nightly preferred
over twice-nightly dosing (QoL RPW: /C625.7, /C638.5; patient
anxiety/stress RPW: /C623.9, /C641.6). Other drivers of overall
product choice for patients were clinical ef ﬁcacy and sodium
content (RAI: 23.5, 20.8) and for HCPs were adverse reac-
tions and sodium content (RAI: 19.7, 18.6). Attributes that
were less important for overall product choice for patients
were administration and other preparation (RAI: 2.7, 3.2)
and for HCPs were arti ﬁcial sweetener, dose measurement,
and administration (RAI: 0, 1.7, 3.4). Drivers of QoL prefer-
ence for patients were clinical ef ﬁcacy and sodium content
(RAI: 28.3, 20.9) and for HCPs were adverse reactions and
clinical efﬁcacy (RAI: 21.5, 18.6). Drivers of reducing patient
anxiety/stress for patients were clinical ef ﬁcacy and sodium
content (RAI: 17.4, 17.3) and for HCPs were adverse reac-
tions and sodium content (RAI: 18.2, 14.2). Dosing fre-
quency was identi ﬁed as the most important attribute driving
preference for overall product choice, QoL, and reducing
patient anxiety/stress for both patients and HCPs with once-
nightly preferred over twice-nightly dosing. If FDA approved,
ON-SXB may ful ﬁll an unmet need for a once-at-bedtime
oxybate treatment.

(SRBDs) on the Degree of Spasticity and Neuropathic
