Introduction: SRBDs, spasticity and neuropathic pain are
common post-SCI. This ongoing study examines the associa-
tion of moderate-to-severe SRBD with the degrees of spastic-
ity and/or neuropathic pain post-SCI.
Methods: This cross-sectional study included adults with
subacute/chronic SCI. SRBD was diagnosed using a home-
based/hospital-unattended screening test that quanti ﬁes
apnea-hypopnea index (AHI). The participants were grouped
into no/mild versus moderate/severe SRBD (AHI>15 events/
hour). Spasticity was assessed using the modi ﬁed Ashworth
scale (MAS). Participants taking baclofen had 1 point (mini-
mal clinically important difference [MCID]) added to their
MAS to estimate the actual MAS without treatment
(“MASC”). Pain level was assessed using the visual analog
scale (VAS). Participants on a ﬁrst-line pharmacological treat-
ment for neuropathic pain had 2.5 points (MCID)
added (“VASC”).
Results: To date, we have recruited 34 individuals
(12 females, 22 males; age range: 20-84 years; mean: 56.4)
with motor complete (n=16) or incomplete SCI at the cervi-
cal (n=28) or thoracic levels. Time from SCI onset varied
from 1.5 to 624 months (mean: 60.7). Mean AHI was 15.5
events/hour (range: 0.8-48.5). The no/mild-SRBD group
(n=21) did not signi ﬁcantly differ from the moderate/severe-
SRBD group (n=13) regarding their mean VAS (4.1 vs 3.5,
p=0.2345) or mean VASC (6.3 vs 5.2, p=0.1995). These
results were con ﬁrmed in regression analyses adjusted for age,
AHI, time post-SCI, and daily dosages of gabapentinoids, tri-
cyclic antidepressants and morphine (VAS: p=0.9917; VASC:
p=0.9218). Notably, there was an inverse correlation between
AHI and daily dosage of gabapentinoids (p=0.0211); how-
ever, there was no signi ﬁcant association between AHI and
tricyclic antidepressants (p=0.3217) or morphine (p=0.4497).
The no/mild-SRBD group did not signi ﬁcantly differ from
the moderate/severe-SRBD group regarding their mean MAS
(3.6 vs 5.9, p=0.1104); there was trend towards a higher
MASC in the moderate/severe-SRBD group (4.1 vs 6.6,
p=0.0727). These results were con ﬁrmed in the regression
analyses adjusted for age, AHI, time post-SCI, and daily dos-
age of baclofen (MAS: p=0.1348; MASC: p=0.0526, AHI:
p=0.0687, baclofen: p=0.0448).
Conclusions: These preliminary results suggest that individ-
uals with moderate-to-severe SRBDs may experience more
severe spasticity post-SCI, whereas neuropathic pain was not
associated with SRBD. Furthermore, participants with
moderate-to-severe SRBDs required lower daily dosages of
gabapentinoids than participants with no/mild SRBDs, which
suggests that gabapentinoids may improve sleep and/or indi-
viduals with moderate-to-severe SRBDs may have a greater tol-
erance to pain (Funded by ONF and Province of Ontario).
M301. To Sleep Perchance to Dream /C1/C1/C1But a Rose by
Any Other Name Would Not Smell as Sweet: Zolpidem
Induced Hyposmia
Shreya Dutt, Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of
Surgery
1, Alan R. Hirsch, Doctor of Medicine 2. 1Kamineni
Academy of Medical Sciences and Research Centre, Hyderabad,
India,
2Smell and Taste Treatment and Research Foundation,
LTD., Chicago, IL, USA.
Introduction: Zolpidem induced hyposmia has not hereto-
fore been discussed.
Case Description: A 42-year-old right-handed male with
chronic sinus infections, one year prior to presentation,

underwent cardiac ablation. One week later he noticed a sud-
den complete loss of taste and smell, with gradual improve-
ment over the next ﬁve years to the point where smell and
taste plateaued at 30% and 80% of normal, respectively. Due
to sleep onset insomnia, he was prescribed zolpidem 5 mg
nightly as needed. Within a few days his sense of smell and
taste diminished from baseline to 0% and 70% of normal
respectively. When the zolpidem was stopped, his ability to
smell and taste returned to their baseline levels. Abnormalities
in Neurologic Examination: Motor examination: left prona-
tor drift with a left abductor digiti minimi sign. Cerebellar
examination: low amplitude high-frequency tremor on exten-
sion in both upper extremities. Chemosensory testing: Olfac-
tory testing: Anosmia on: Phenylethyl Alcohol Threshold
Test Left (L)> -2.0, Right (R)> -2.0; Brief Smell Identi ﬁca-
tion Test: 3; University of Pennsylvania Smell Identi ﬁcation
Test: L=11, R=8. Retronasal Olfactory testing: Retronasal
Smell Index: 1 (anosmia); MRI of brain with and without
infusion: normal.
Discussion: Zolpidem, a GABA-A agonist with greatest
afﬁnity for omega 1 receptor subtype, functions as a sopo-
riﬁc agent, through its action in the Reticular Activating
System. It also acts on similar receptors in the olfactory
bulb, thus inhibiting the transmission of olfaction
(Benavides, 1993; Schiffman, 2018). The co-occurrence of
onset of hyposmia upon starting zolpidem and recovery
upon its discontinuation, strongly suggests zolpidem is the
primary pathogenic agent. It is possible that its mechanism
of action might work, not through the drug ’s effect in olfac-
tory bulb, but rather its secondary effects on cognition.
Zolpidem has been reported to impair cognitive ability
(Dennis, 1988). Secondary impact of this may have been
reduction of sensory processing of all stimuli including
olfaction (Elazzab, 2017). Detection of olfactory stimuli is
essential for detection of leak of natural gas, which is
impregnated with the olfactory additive ethyl mercaptan,
the threshold of which increases during sleep (Lopes, 2016).
Addition of zolpidem may reduc e the detection ability that
much further, leading to greater risk of gas explosion. In
those who are taking zolpidem and experiencing hyposmia
or anosmia, elimination of zolpidem may be worthwhile in
treating these conditions.

segments.text:
Case Report: 48-year-old man with metastatic atypical lung
carcinoid presented with progressive bilateral lower extremity
stiffness, and painful spasms.
segments.evidence: 48-year-old man with metastatic atypical lung carcinoid presented with progressive bilateral lower extremity stiffness, and painful spasms. Examination showed bilateral lower extremity weakness, increased tone and hyperreflexia in the upper and lower extremities. MRI of the brain showed extensive white matter T2 hyperintensity without abnormal diffusion restriction or contrast enhancement. MRI of the Cervical, Thoracic and Lumbar spine showed T2 hyperintensity in the dorsal column of the spinal cord. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed 72 nucleated cells and protein 109 mg/dl. Paraneoplastic panel was positive for anti-Amphiphysin antibodies 1:30,720 dilution in serum and 1:256 dilutions in CSF. He was diagnosed with paraneoplastic SPS and received 5 sessions of plasma exchange (PLEX) with significant improvement of symptoms.
